Demo and Pitch Craft

People, Leadership & Organisation — Communication & Stakeholder Management

At 4:52 p.m. on 14 September 2026, Meera Iyer stood in the glass-walled boardroom of Aavaran Commerce Cloud, a Bengaluru startup that sells demand-forecasting and reorder-automation software to grocery wholesalers, and watched the agenda scroll to item four: “Reorder Prediction — Live Demo (7 min) — Meera Iyer.” Three people sat around the table who mattered to what happened next. The lead investor from Aavaran’s Series A round had wired ₹6 crore into the company two years earlier and now held the swing vote on this board. A newer board observer, representing the growth-stage fund weighing whether to lead an ₹18-crore Series B, was seeing the product live for the first time. And Rakesh Bhalla, Aavaran’s own CEO, knew the runway math by heart — ₹14 crore in the bank, eleven months left, and a term sheet that would not move until this board approved a ₹4-crore budget extension to scale reorder prediction from 40 pilot distributors to 400.

Meera had built the feature. She had also built two decks about it, thrown both away, and spent six evenings rehearsing with a stopwatch on her desk. She knew the trap well: Aavaran’s engineers could walk anyone through eleven screens of the reorder dashboard, and every one of those screens was true, useful, and beside the point in a seven-minute slot where three people who had not built the product needed to leave the room believing one specific thing — that the feature already worked, on real distributors, with real money, and that ₹4 crore more would make it work at ten times the scale. Whether Meera got that across, or instead delivered an impressive tour that left the room unmoved, would not depend on the software at all. It would depend on how she structured the next seven minutes.

The idea

What Meera was practising has a precise name in product circles: demo-and-pitch craft, the discipline of building a short, high-stakes presentation in which a live product — not slides describing the product — supplies the evidence for a specific decision an audience is about to make. It is easy to confuse with public speaking or slide design, but its subject is narrower and more mechanical: given a fixed number of minutes and an audience that has not seen the work, which pieces of the product, shown in which order, build the strongest possible case for the one decision on the table?

The discipline was not invented by one person so much as codified by people who watched founders get it wrong at scale. Guy Kawasaki, the venture capitalist and former Apple marketing executive, published his “10/20/30 rule” for pitch decks in 2005 — ten slides, twenty minutes, thirty-point font — because he had sat through hundreds of pitches that mistook thoroughness for persuasion. That same year, Paul Graham built Y Combinator’s Demo Day around an even harder constraint: two minutes per founder, no exceptions, because a room of investors would forgive an unpolished product far sooner than it would forgive a founder who could not say, in two minutes, why it mattered. Both were responding to the same failure: builders who, handed a microphone, defaulted to a tour of their own work instead of an argument aimed at someone else’s decision.

If Meera had to leave her board with one sentence, it was this: a demo is not a tour of the product — it is an argument, and the product is the evidence, so every screen has to be doing a specific job for the one decision the room is about to make.

How it actually works

Stripped to its mechanics, building a seven-minute demo is a five-step process, and it is the third and fourth steps that most first-time presenters skip.

First, pin the single decision the audience must make the moment the seven minutes end. For Meera’s board, that was not “is the reorder feature good software” — it was “approve ₹4 crore to scale it to 400 distributors, yes or no.” Every later choice about what to show, and what to leave out, traces back to that one sentence.

Second, build a narrative arc rather than a feature list: a setup that names who is in pain and by how much, a tension beat that shows the specific moment the old way fails, a live-proof beat where the product itself resolves that failure in front of the audience, an evidence beat that shows the same result holding across many cases and not just the one on screen, and a resolution that states the ask plainly.

Third, every beat gets a time budget in seconds, not minutes, because a “two-minute” segment that quietly runs three eats into the ask at the end — the only part a board actually remembers voting on.

Fourth, and almost always left implicit, is rehearsing the failure path: deciding in advance exactly what to say and which backup screen to click to if the live product freezes, the network drops, or a number on screen looks wrong. Presenters who skip this either panic visibly or keep clicking through a broken demo hoping it recovers — both cost more credibility than the bug itself would have.

Fifth, the evidence at the resolution must be translated into the audience’s own decision criteria. A board wants payback period and unit economics; a customer wants hours saved; an engineering steering committee wants failure modes. The same pilot data gets reframed three different ways for three different rooms.

A worked example

Meera’s 40 pilot distributors moved, on average, ₹10 lakh of stock a month each. Before Aavaran’s reorder prediction, they ran out of fast-moving stock — the stockout rate — 18% of the time, which meant lost sales of 0.18 × ₹10,00,000 = ₹1,80,000 per distributor per month. After three months on the feature, the stockout rate fell to 6%: 0.06 × ₹10,00,000 = ₹60,000 lost. That is a saving of ₹1,20,000 per distributor per month, or ₹48,00,000 across all 40 — ₹1.44 crore of recovered sales value over the 90-day pilot.

Aavaran keeps 2% of recovered sales value as a success fee layered on top of its subscription. Two per cent of ₹48,00,000 is ₹96,000 a month from these 40 distributors, or ₹2,400 per distributor per month — ₹28,800 a year each. Scaled in a straight line to the 400 distributors the ₹4-crore ask would fund, that is ₹9,60,000 a month, an annualised run-rate of roughly ₹1.15 crore — the number Meera intended to put on screen at minute six.

BeatTimeWhat the board sees
Setup0:00–0:40One named distributor, monthly throughput and pain stated in rupees
Tension0:40–1:30The exact stockout moment: a fast-mover out of stock on a Tuesday morning
Live proof1:30–4:00Reorder prediction run live, on that distributor’s real data
Evidence4:00–5:3018% → 6% stockout rate, across all 40 pilot distributors
Resolution5:30–6:40₹4 crore, 400 distributors, ₹1.15 crore annualised run-rate
Buffer6:40–7:00Held in reserve for a stumble or an early question

Run the same arithmetic with one input changed and the pitch changes shape. The 400 distributors Aavaran wants to fund are not all ₹10-lakh-a-month accounts — many are smaller-format kirana distributors moving closer to ₹6 lakh a month. At that volume, stockout losses fall from ₹1,08,000 to ₹36,000, a saving of ₹72,000 per distributor per month, ₹28,80,000 across 40. The fee income halves to ₹57,600 a month from the pilot cohort, and the run-rate at 400 distributors drops from ₹1.15 crore to roughly ₹69 lakh a year — a materially smaller number for the same ₹4-crore ask. A sharp board member will ask which mix of the 400 Meera is actually counting on, and the honest answer changes what the money buys.

The nuances a learner must become aware of

A tour is not an argument

A feature tour visits every screen once, in build order; an argument visits only the screens that move the decision, in the order the decision needs them. The tell is simple: if you could delete half the screens and the audience would still reach the same conclusion, you were never making an argument.

Evidence is not anecdote

One glowing distributor quote is an anecdote. Forty distributors, a before-and-after measurement, and a defined pilot period is evidence. Boards and skeptical customers can tell the difference instantly, and conflating the two is the fastest way to lose credibility mid-pitch.

The time budget is a design constraint, not a formality

Treating seven minutes as “roughly seven minutes” instead of 420 seconds allocated to the second is how presenters arrive at the ask having already spent their credibility on the setup. The budget should be built before a single slide is drafted, not fitted to content afterward.

The live-demo risk paradox

Live proof is the most persuasive beat and the most fragile one. The right call depends on the audience and the stakes: a board that has seen the product before can tolerate real risk for real credibility; a large, compliance-heavy customer evaluating vendors for the first time is often better served by a rehearsed screen recording with a visible timestamp, because a frozen screen in front of a first-time buyer reads as a product risk, not a bad day.

Pitch craft is not sales polish

A beautifully produced deck can be substantively empty, and a rough one can carry a devastating argument. Polish changes how an argument is received; it cannot manufacture an argument that was not there. Confusing the two leads teams to spend rehearsal time on transitions instead of on the numbers.

What it cannot tell you

Demo craft is a communication skill layered on top of real evidence — it cannot repair weak product-market fit, and a well-built arc around a mediocre pilot only makes the mediocrity more legible, not less. The discipline earns trust for the evidence you actually have; it does not manufacture evidence you lack.

Evidence must fit the audience’s own criteria

Investors, customers and engineers are persuaded by different facts drawn from the same pilot: payback period for the board, hours saved for the buyer, failure modes for the engineers. Reusing one evidence slide across three audiences is a common shortcut that under-serves all three.

The interruption test

A well-built pitch survives being stopped at any random minute with the key point already made once. If the only place the core claim appears is the final slide, one interruption — a question, a fire drill, a dropped call — can cost the entire argument.

How it changes across contexts

The same mechanics produce visibly different demos depending on what is being sold and to whom, and on how young the company is.

ContextWhat the demo centres onEarly-stage vs. scale
ConsumerOne hero user flow built around an emotional delight moment, shown to a broad, often non-expert audienceEarly: the founder demos personally, live, on their own phone. Scale: pre-recorded, legally reviewed, A/B-tested for the exact wording.
B2BThe economic buyer’s specific decision criteria — time saved, cost avoided, risk reduced — usually on that buyer’s own dataEarly: the product itself is the pitch, live and unpolished. Scale: security review, a staged environment, and a rehearsed fallback are mandatory before any live click.
MarketplaceProof of liquidity on both sides — a real match or conversion happening between real supply and real demand, not just one side’s screenEarly: the chicken-and-egg proof is often manually staged with real but small numbers. Scale: the demo leans on aggregate liquidity metrics rather than a single live match.

Common mistakes

Four failure patterns recur often enough to be worth naming, each with a symptom an observer would notice from outside the room, the misunderstanding underneath it, and a cheap way to catch it before it happens live.

MistakeSymptomUnderlying misunderstandingCheap diagnostic
Feature-dump demoAudience checks phones; questions arrive about screens shown minutes agoMistaking completeness for persuasionCould you delete half the screens and still make the point?
No time budgetThe ask gets rushed or dropped in the last thirty secondsPreparing content, not rehearsing a performance against a clockTime each beat with a stopwatch three times before the real room
No failure path rehearsedDead air, or frantic re-clicking, when something breaks on screenAssuming “live” means “safe”Ask out loud: what do I say if wifi dies at minute three?
Jargon over outcomeAudience asks “so what does this mean for us?” after the live-proof beatTalking about the product instead of the decision it servesCould a non-technical listener restate the point in one sentence?

What good looks like

Meera ran her demo in 6 minutes 51 seconds. She opened on one distributor by name and the exact rupee cost of a Tuesday-morning stockout, showed the reorder engine catch the same pattern live on that distributor’s real data, then cut — without apology — to the 40-distributor evidence table before anyone could ask whether the live case was cherry-picked. She named the ₹4-crore ask and the ₹1.15-crore projected run-rate in the same sentence, and sat down with nine seconds of buffer unused. No slide had more than one number on it that mattered. When the network stuttered for two seconds during the live run, she kept talking through it, because she had already decided, the night before, exactly what she would say if it happened.

Closing

The board approved the ₹4 crore that afternoon, with one condition Meera had already anticipated: a follow-up memo, within two weeks, breaking the 400-distributor rollout by throughput segment, because the observer from the growth-stage fund had done the same arithmetic Meera had shown in her second pass and wanted the honest mix before the Series B term sheet was drafted. Meera’s reasoning, recapped for her own team afterward, was unglamorous: she had not tried to prove the product was impressive, only that it already worked and that the money would make it work at scale, and she had built every minute of the seven around that one sentence rather than around what her engineers were proudest of. What she wants to learn next is what happens after the seven minutes end — how to hold that same argument together live, under a skeptical follow-up question that was not on her rehearsed script.

Sit with these:

1. In the last pitch or demo you gave, could you name the one sentence every screen was in service of — and would your audience have named the same sentence?

2. If your live product had frozen at your most important moment, what exactly would you have said next, and had you decided that before you walked in?
exp40v2-comm.presenting:
Demo and Pitch Craft

People, Leadership & Organisation — Communication & Stakeholder Management · near-expert treatment

1. Two rooms, seven minutes each

On 22 October 2026, in a wood-panelled meeting room on the eleventh floor of an infrastructure contractor's Mumbai headquarters, Nandita Rao waited for the second of three vendors to finish. She ran product at Imaarat Build Systems, a Pune company that sells a rugged site-monitoring rig — four weatherproof edge cameras, a solar-backed gateway, and a progress-tracking application that compares what the cameras see against the construction schedule. The evaluation committee allowed each vendor seven minutes of demonstration and fifteen of questions. The contract covered 46 active sites at ₹9.4 lakh per site per year: ₹4.32 crore of recurring revenue, roughly 38% of Imaarat's book.

Nandita's problem was not a weak product. It was that her central claim — that the rig detects schedule slippage eleven days earlier than a site engineer's weekly report — took eleven days to demonstrate. She could not compress calendar time into seven minutes; she could only choose what stood in for it.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, on 2 December, Sohail Merchant faced the inverse constraint. He was product lead at Palki Mobility, a Hyderabad company whose product predicts intercity bus breakdowns from on-vehicle telematics and reschedules the fleet around them. Palki had run on 120 buses of a 1,240-bus private operator for seven months, and Sohail had seven minutes at the operator's annual operations review to justify expanding to the full fleet at ₹3.2 crore a year. His product could be shown live, in seconds — and that was the danger. The twelve-hour breakdown forecast was correct 71% of the time, so roughly three in ten buses flagged on stage would be a false alarm, and the operator's chief mechanical engineer, thirty-one years in depots, would be watching for exactly that.

One presenter could not show the thing that mattered; the other could show it too easily, and risked showing it being wrong. Both had seven minutes. These are not two problems but one, and the discipline for handling it is more formal, and more contested, than its reputation as a soft skill suggests.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A demo, precisely defined, is a constructed encounter between an audience and a working system, staged to supply evidence for a decision that audience is about to make. Three clauses carry it. Constructed: someone chose the path, the data and the order, which makes a demo an argument rather than an observation. Working system: an artefact that cannot be operated is a mockup, and the epistemic claim collapses. A decision about to be made: a demonstration with no pending decision is a status update in costume.

The craft was codified against a specific pathology. Through the 1990s, enterprise software selling had settled on the feature-by-feature walkthrough, in which completeness was the persuasive strategy: show everything, and the buyer will find what they need. Guy Kawasaki's 10/20/30 rule (2005) and Y Combinator's two-minute Demo Day slot were both reactions against it, resting on an attention argument — in a room of non-builders, the marginal screen has negative value because it displaces the screen that mattered. A different reaction formed at the same time: Jeff Bezos banned slides from Amazon's senior meetings in 2004 in favour of six-page memos read in silence, on the explicit ground that a performance measures the performer.

Those reactions have hardened into schools that do not agree, and a practitioner who cannot state the disagreement precisely will keep taking advice from whichever one spoke last.

The four positions a practitioner will actually encounter, and where each refuses to go.
SchoolWould signWould not sign
Compression (Kawasaki, Demo Day)Attention binds; anything that does not move the decision is subtracted.That a sophisticated audience will follow a long argument. They hold nobody does.
Narrative (Duarte, Raskin, strategic-narrative selling)Persuasion is a story form: name a change in the world, the stakes of ignoring it, the promised land.That the product speaks for itself; unframed, it is uninterpretable.
Written-analysis (Amazon six-pager, memo cultures)Capital decisions belong to a document read in silence, then argued; theatre is noise.That seven live minutes suits an irreversible spend. They attend, and discount it.
Hands-on / product-led (trials, sandboxes, PLG)The best demonstration is the buyer's own first session.That narration substitutes for use; every presented demo overstates ease-of-use.

A fifth position, from consultative selling, is narrower and sharper: never demonstrate before you have diagnosed. On this view a demo is a confirmation instrument, not a discovery one, and a vendor who demos in the first meeting has conceded that they do not know the buyer's problem. It cuts across the other four, and Nandita had internalised it most deeply: she spent four weeks before the bake-off getting three of the contractor's project managers to tell her, on record, what a schedule slip costs them.

3. Mechanics, worked

Expert practice has a spine that is rarely written down. It begins not with content but with a decision statement, then treats the minutes as a budget allocated against that statement under uncertainty.

Step one: write the decision, not the topic. Nandita's was not “show site monitoring” but “select Imaarat as monitoring vendor for the 2027 site programme, over two alternatives, at ₹9.4 lakh per site.” Sohail's was “extend from 120 buses to 1,240 at ₹3.2 crore.” The second form has a counterfactual embedded in it, and the demo must beat the counterfactual, not merely be good.

Step two: identify the load-bearing claim. In every pitch there is one proposition which, if believed, would settle the decision, and which the room does not currently believe. For Imaarat: this detects slippage earlier than your own engineers do. For Palki: a 71%-accurate forecast is operationally useful anyway. Everything else exists to make that claim credible or clear obstacles in front of it.

Step three: allocate seconds. Seven minutes is 420 seconds. An opening that establishes who is in pain and by how much cannot honestly be done under 40; a live sequence including a real system response cannot be done under 90 without cutting the response; the ask, restated with its number, needs 30. That leaves roughly 260 discretionary seconds, and the discipline is refusing to spend them on anything that is not the load-bearing claim.

Step four: price the live sequence. This step has a genuine formal treatment that almost nobody performs explicitly. Let G be the credibility gained when live proof succeeds; Gr the credibility from a recorded equivalent, lower but riskless; L the credibility lost when the live attempt visibly fails; p the probability of visible failure. Going live pays when (1−p)G − pL > Gr, which rearranges to:

p* = (G − Gr) / (G + L) — go live when the estimated failure probability is below p*.

Put Imaarat's numbers in. The committee has already seen two recorded walkthroughs, so a recording is worth little: G = 1.0, Gr = 0.5. A rig that fails to connect signals poor field reliability, the exact attribute being purchased: L = 2.0. Then p* = 0.5 / 3.0 = 0.167. Nandita's team had cold-booted the rig on mobile data 31 times in a fortnight with 4 failures — an estimated p of 0.13, below threshold but not comfortably. The formalism does not make the decision; it tells you which number to go and measure. Nandita spent two days reducing p instead of arguing about it, moving to a dual-SIM router and rehearsing on the venue's network, which took observed failures to 1 in 28.

Palki's numbers run the other way and expose the model's limit. Sohail's p of a wrong forecast on stage is 0.29 by construction, far above any plausible threshold — if a wrong forecast counts as failure. His insight was that it need not. A probabilistic product can redefine the demonstrated event: instead of showing “watch it be right,” show “watch it be right seven times in ten, and watch what the depot does with the other three.” Then p becomes the probability that the workflow mishandles a false alarm, which Palki had measured at 0.04. Redefining what is being demonstrated is the move that changes the arithmetic, and the most under-taught idea in the craft.

Step five: rehearse interruption, not delivery. A pitch optimised for uninterrupted delivery is fragile precisely in the rooms that matter, because senior rooms interrupt. Imaarat had minutes from four previous bake-offs at the same contractor; in three of the four, the first vendor question arrived before minute five. If the ask appears only at 6:30, the probability the room hears it as intended is close to a coin toss. Experts state the ask once in the first minute — as a frame, not a conclusion — and again at the end.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be written as testable claims. (a) There is a decision with a date. If nobody must choose by a known time, a written artefact travels better. True for both protagonists. (b) The audience's belief is the binding constraint, not the evidence. Where the evidence is thin, better presentation only makes a weak case legible. Palki's evidence was strong (seven months, 120 buses); Imaarat's thinner (nine sites, four months). (c) The product can be operated in the room, or a defensible proxy exists. Imaarat fails the first half and passes the second only because time-lapse replay of a real site is a proxy the committee accepts. (d) The audience can act. A demo to people without authority is a rehearsal, and should be labelled one.

Where is the idea actively misleading? First, when the decision is large and irreversible: the written-analysis school is right that a seven-minute performance is a poor instrument for a ₹4-crore commitment, which is why mature buyers gate the demo behind a document. Second, where value accrues over months: a demo that compresses it can only lie about the timescale, and the buyer will discover the compression. Third, in adversarial procurement, where polish is a proxy for the vendor's sales budget rather than product quality — the Indian public-sector tender process, with its technical-evaluation scoring sheets, is explicitly designed to discount it.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies really do

Multi-product portfolios. Each business unit wants ninety seconds, and the resulting demo shows six things badly and argues for nothing. Mature companies say they run integrated platform demos. What they do is nominate one product as protagonist, demote the rest to a transition sentence, and fight about which one every quarter.

Two-sided marketplaces. Liquidity cannot be shown from one screen, so the honest demo needs two devices and a real counterparty. A colleague in the next room playing the supply side is not cheating if disclosed and is cheating if not. Buyers watch whether the other side responds at human latency or at the speed of a script.

Regulated products. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, a health or lending demo cannot casually put a real person's record on a projector. Synthetic data is lawful but reads as fake: numbers too round, names too neat. Mature firms maintain a consented demo tenant — real customers who have specifically agreed to have anonymised records shown — and a review step that sits with legal, not sales. Firms without one improvise, and improvisation under DPDP is where incidents come from.

Hardware plus software. The golden-unit problem: the demo device is hand-selected, hand-calibrated and not the unit that ships. Every hardware company does this; what separates practice from malpractice is whether the presenter knows and states the gap. Imaarat's rig was a production unit pulled at random from a site in Talegaon precisely so Nandita could say so — a sentence worth more than the demonstration itself.

AI-native products. Nondeterminism defeats rehearsal: the same prompt answers differently in the room than it did the night before, so the golden prompt — the one input that always works — becomes an institution and then a liability, because buyers now test for it by supplying their own input. Mature AI vendors have conceded the point and moved to a two-part structure: a live run on the buyer's input, accepted as risky, then an aggregate evaluation across a held-out set, which is where the actual claim lives.

Organisational seams. The demo environment is the classic unowned asset: product builds it, sales uses it daily, nobody funds it, and it rots until a deal is lost. Worse is demo debt: a sales engineer shows an unreleased screen because it lands well, the buyer writes it into the contract schedule, and product inherits a commitment it never made. Companies that handle this keep a written list of what may and may not be shown, reviewed monthly, and treat a violation as a process defect rather than an individual failing.

6. Eight distinctions between competence and expertise

The ask is a frame, not a conclusion. Competent presenters build to the ask; experts state it at second 25 and again at the end, so the audience can answer “what are they asking for?” from minute one. The obvious reading — that revealing the ask early squanders suspense — is wrong because decision rooms are not audiences: a listener who knows what is being asked evaluates every later fact against it, which is exactly what you want if your facts are good.

Selection is legitimate; concealment is not. Every demo is cherry-picked, because someone chose the path. Experts pick their best case and then name the denominator unprompted: “this is our strongest site; here are all nine.” The tell is the volunteered base rate. The naive reading is that admitting selection weakens the case; in practice it converts the audience's inevitable suspicion into a settled question and buys the right to be believed about everything else.

Roughness and latency are content, not defects. Novices cut every load spinner; experts leave a real four-second wait in, because a system that never hesitates looks recorded, and a buyer who has bought software before knows what real latency looks like. Where the system thinks for twelve seconds, those seconds become either the weakest or the strongest part of the demo. The tell is that experts slow down rather than speed up, narrating what the system is doing and what it is not doing. The naive instinct is to fill the silence with product facts; the expert fills it with the reasoning the buyer will need thirty seconds later.

The room's real decision is often not the agenda's. Experts find out, days ahead, what happens if the meeting decides nothing, because the true competitor is usually delay rather than a rival vendor. The tell is a presenter who asks the sponsor, “what does deferring this a quarter cost you?” The obvious reading is that this is sales work, not product work. It is neither: it is the input that decides whether the pitch argues against a competitor or against inertia.

Falsifiable evidence is the only kind that persuades sceptics. An expert shows the case where the product did not work, early, with the number attached; the tell is a screen in the first half that reads like a concession. The naive reading is that this hands opponents ammunition. In fact a claim with no stated failure condition is unfalsifiable, and experienced buyers treat unfalsifiable claims as marketing, discounting the whole presentation rather than the one claim.

Specificity beats fluency. Two equally articulate presenters: one says “our customers see significant reductions,” the other says “the Chakan site, 14 August, eleven days of float recovered on the podium slab.” The second is believed. The tell is proper nouns and dates. The obvious reading is that specifics are anecdotes and aggregates are evidence; the resolution is that specifics establish the speaker has been near the work, which is the precondition for the aggregate being believed at all.

Everything shown becomes a promise. Experts refuse to show something that would land well but is not committed, even at the cost of a weaker demo. The tell is a presenter who says “that screen exists but is not in the 2027 scope, so I am not going to show it.” The naive reading is that this leaves value on the table. It does, for one meeting, and removes a category of contract dispute and roadmap distortion that costs far more over the following year.

The recovery line is drafted, not improvised. Experts decide in advance the exact sentence they will say if the system fails and the exact key they will press; the tell is that when something breaks, the tone does not change. The obvious reading is that this is stagecraft. It is closer to incident response, and its value is that a failure handled flatly with an immediate fallback reads as operational maturity — sometimes more persuasive than the demo working.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

Where the differences are real. Where they are not, the table says so.
TypeWhat changesEarly stage → scale
ConsumerOne emotional moment on a phone; the audience is usually an investor, not a user.Founder demos live on a personal handset → pre-recorded, legally reviewed, wording A/B tested.
B2B / enterpriseRuns on the buyer's own data or a convincing likeness; procurement scores it against written criteria.Product is the pitch → security review, staged tenant, mandatory fallback, named demo owner.
Platform / marketplaceTwo screens, two sides, real latency; a single side's screen proves nothing.Staged but real matches → aggregate liquidity metrics, since one live match proves too little.
HardwareThe device is in the room and can be handled; unit provenance is itself a credibility question.Disclosed prototype → random production pull, with certification (BIS, ARAI) as backing evidence.
AI-nativeLive behaviour is one sample from a distribution; the honest claim lives in the eval set.Live run on any input → buyer's input plus held-out eval results.
Deep-tech / long-cycleNo real difference from enterprise, except that a proxy for calendar time is mandatory.Same trajectory as enterprise.

The stage effect is stronger than the type effect and runs one way: as companies scale, the demo migrates from the person who built the product to someone who did not, and the craft shifts from argument construction to argument transmission. That migration is where quality is lost, because the second presenter inherits the screens without the reasoning that selected them.

8. Three worked examples

Bunkar Textile Cloud, Surat. Bunkar sells production scheduling to power-loom units. Through 2025 it ran a 25-minute walkthrough and closed 22% of 68 qualified demos. In January 2026 it rebuilt the format: 7 minutes, one load-bearing claim (loom idle time falls from 19% to 11%), the buyer's own order book loaded beforehand, the ask stated twice. Across the next 61 demos it closed 41%. Attributing all of that to format would be careless — the product also shipped a Gujarati interface in March — but the intermediate metric moved cleanly: the share of demos in which a decision-maker asked about price during the meeting went from 31% to 66%.

Ullas Diagnostics, Chennai — the failure. Ullas built a radiology triage model and demonstrated it to a four-hospital group in February 2026, running live on twelve chest films. It performed beautifully: eleven of twelve correct, the miss acknowledged. The group signed a paid pilot. Over 214 scans in the pilot, sensitivity came in at 79% against the 94% Ullas had quoted. The demo had not been dishonest about any single film; it was dishonest about the sampling, because the twelve films came from the curated set the model had been tuned against, and nobody had asked whether the demo set and the development set overlapped. The cost was not the ₹18-lakh pilot; it was that the group's radiology head became a negative reference in a market of perhaps forty buyers.

The recovery is the instructive part. Ullas did not re-pitch. It asked the group for 400 unseen films, ran blind, published 81% sensitivity internally, and rebuilt the demo so that the live run happens on films the customer supplies that morning and the headline number is always the held-out one. Win rate on the next nine opportunities was 4 of 9 — lower than the 6 of 9 the old, overstated demo had produced — but pilot-to-contract conversion went from 1 in 6 to 3 in 4. The company traded top-of-funnel for a funnel that did not leak.

Phulwari Fresh, Jaipur. A consumer fruit-subscription app pitching a seed round. The founder's original eight-minute pitch spent five minutes on supply-chain architecture. Restructured to lead with 40 seconds of a real customer's Sunday-morning reorder and then week-12 retention of 44% against a category norm nearer 20%, second-meeting conversion went from 3 of 17 investor meetings to 9 of 19. The architecture moved to an appendix that three investors read and the rest did not need.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Each failure mode has a symptom visible before the meeting, and a much larger cost after it.
Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching late
Tour instead of argumentThe deck is ordered the way the product was builtWhich screens could I delete without changing the conclusion?The decision defers a quarter
Demo-set contaminationNobody can say where the demo data came fromIs any of this data in our tuning set?A live reference turns negative — the Ullas outcome
Ask stated once, at the endRehearsals run 6:50 with no bufferIf I am stopped at minute four, has the ask been made?The room adjourns without a decision on the table
Unrehearsed failure pathThe presenter cannot name the fallback keyWhat exactly do I say and press if this freezes?A reliability doubt that outlives the meeting
Demo debtSales shows screens product has not releasedIs everything on this path in a committed release?Contractual commitments to unbuilt features
Evidence framed in vendor unitsThe metric on screen is one only the vendor usesWould the buyer's CFO recognise this number?A polite meeting, no internal champion

The pattern across all six is that the warning signs are cheap to detect and almost always detectable the week before. What makes them persist is that each is invisible to the person closest to the work: the builder cannot see that their ordering is build-order, and the model owner does not spontaneously wonder whether the demo films were in the tuning set. Every warning sign in that table is found by someone other than the presenter, which is the operational argument for a rehearsal with a hostile reader.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Live versus recorded. The live camp holds that risk is the point: a system operated in real time under an audience's gaze carries information that no recording can, and buyers know it. Their evidence is the asymmetry in buyer behaviour — buyers ask to see things live precisely when they suspect a recording is hiding something. The recorded camp holds that the variance is unpriced: a demo is a sample of size one from the product's reliability distribution, and betting a ₹4-crore decision on one draw is poor risk management when a recording conveys 80% of the information at zero variance. For the live camp to be wrong, buyers would have to discount live and recorded equally. For the recorded camp to be wrong, recorded demos would have to be discounted enough to swamp the variance saving. Nobody has run that experiment cleanly, and both camps cite win-rate data from populations that differ in uncontrolled ways.

Demo versus memo for capital decisions. The memo school's strongest form is not anti-visual; it is that a performance measures presentation skill, which correlates poorly with product quality and strongly with seniority and first-language effects, so organisations deciding from demos systematically misallocate. Its evidence is the observed variance when the same proposal is presented by different people. The demo school's strongest form is that a working system is the only evidence that cannot be written into existence — a memo can describe a product that does not run, and frequently does. The unresolved question is whether the bias from performance exceeds the bias from permitting claims never executed.

Whether to show failure in a competitive bake-off. The honesty camp holds that disclosed limitations raise the credibility of everything else, and that in any product with a real base rate the limitation surfaces in pilot anyway. The tournament camp holds something uncomfortable and possibly true: in a scored bake-off against vendors who do not disclose, the disclosing vendor loses, because evaluation sheets have a column for weaknesses and only one vendor has filled it in. Both can point to deals. The disagreement may be irreducible, because the right answer depends on the buyer's sophistication, which the vendor cannot observe in advance — and that, rather than any principle, is what Sohail and Nandita were each deciding.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this builds a good seven minutes. Someone who has internalised it differs in four ways. They spend far more time before the meeting than in it, most of it finding out what the room already believes. They are visibly willing to lose a meeting rather than overstate, and their most frequent sentence is a subtraction: “I am not going to show that.” They treat the demo as one instrument in a sequence with a document before it and a written follow-up after, not as the event itself. And they are unbothered when things break, because the failure path was settled days earlier. The signature is calm plus specificity: proper nouns, dates, denominators, and no rise in pitch when the network drops.

12. What each of them decided

Nandita went live with the production rig, powered from its own battery so that a venue power failure could not stop it, and opened by putting the unit on the committee table and saying where it had been pulled from. She spent 100 seconds on a time-lapse replay of the Talegaon site — the only honest way to buy eleven days of calendar time — and said plainly that it was a recording of real history, not a live detection. Her evidence beat covered all nine pilot sites, including the two where the system found nothing the engineers had not. She stated the ₹9.4-lakh-per-site figure at second 25 and at 6:40.

Sohail restructured around the miss. He ran the forecast live on the operator's fleet, let it flag eleven buses, then pulled up the previous week's flags and walked through the three that had been wrong, showing what the depot did: a nine-minute inspection, no bus withdrawn, no schedule impact. His load-bearing claim was never that the model was accurate; it was that a 29% false-alarm rate is affordable at ₹340 per inspection against an average breakdown cost of ₹1.9 lakh. He was arguing against the chief mechanical engineer's thirty-one years, and decided the only way to win was to concede the part of it that was true.

1. Sohail chose to demonstrate his product being wrong. Under what buyer conditions is that the winning move, and under what conditions does it simply lose a scored bake-off to a vendor who disclosed nothing?

2. Nandita could not show her central claim in seven minutes and substituted a replay. Where is the line between an honest proxy for time and a misrepresentation of what the product does live?

3. If performance measures the performer, what would your organisation change so that investment decisions stop rewarding presentation skill — and what would it lose?

13. Going deeper

Telling the customer story
The upstream skill: a demo is a story with the product as evidence; without the story the screens have nothing to serve.
Stakeholder mapping and management
Tells you whose decision the seven minutes is actually for, and who in the room can kill it without being the decision-maker.
Communicating with leadership
Extends the craft to the unrehearsed follow-up, where most credibility is won or lost.
Writing as a PM superpower
The memo school's tooling. A demo that is not preceded by a document is usually being asked to carry more than it can.
Decision records and DACI/RACI
Makes the seven minutes durable: without a recorded decision and owner, approval decays into a remembered impression.
Running effective meetings
Governs the container — agenda position, interruption norms, buffer — which decides whether the pitch is heard as built.
Status updates and stakeholder rhythms
The alternative to high-stakes single events: when the room already knows the evidence, the seven minutes becomes a vote.

Seven Minutes at the Hadapsar Depot

Kshamata Battery Intelligence and the Rathvahan Mobility Services selection, March 2026.

1. The night before

Pune, Sunday, 8 March 2026, 10.50 p.m. Sharanya Iyengar had the hotel room desk lamp angled onto a printout she had already marked in three colours, and on the laptop screen beside it, two versions of the same seven-minute demo script. In eleven hours she would stand in a converted training room at the Hadapsar bus depot, in front of six people from Rathvahan Mobility Services and two observers who had not been on any attendee list until Friday, and show them what Kshamata Battery Intelligence could do. The room would give her seven minutes of live demonstration and fifteen minutes of questions. Two other vendors had the same slot, before and after her.

The contract was worth ₹4.2 crore over three years, and it was not, by itself, the thing keeping her awake. What kept her awake was a four-page memo that had arrived at 6.20 p.m. Melbourne time from Dr Padma Venkataraman, Kshamata's principal reliability scientist, with the subject line Please do not show the 2.1% number on Monday. The number in question appeared on slide four of the deck the sales team had been using since October, on the company's website, and in the pilot business case that Rathvahan's own finance group had built and circulated internally three weeks earlier. Sharanya had read the memo four times. She agreed with most of it. She could not work out what to do with it by eight the next morning, when the run of show locked.

Her co-founder and chief executive, Devendra Kulkarni, had called twice from Bengaluru. Both times he had said a version of the same sentence: Sharanya, we are not going to win this by being the most careful people in the room. He had not said the other thing, which they both knew, which was that the Series B conversations he had opened in January all assumed a named Indian fleet logo by the end of the quarter.

2. How Kshamata got here

Kshamata Battery Intelligence was founded in Bengaluru in 2021 by Devendra Kulkarni and Arunima Bose, both of whom had spent the previous decade in powertrain validation, Devendra at a two-wheeler maker and Arunima in a battery-management-system group in Coimbatore. The company sold a software layer, not hardware: it ingested raw cell-level telemetry from an electric vehicle's battery-management system, reconstructed the degradation history of every module, and produced three things the fleet operator could act on — a state-of-health estimate per pack, a fault-precursor alert, and a residual-value figure that a leasing company or a bank could actually put in a spreadsheet.

The decision that constrained everything Sharanya could do in March 2026 had been taken in the summer of 2023. To win its first real customer, Kshamata had agreed to build its degradation model directly against that customer's fleet: 340 buses running nickel-manganese-cobalt packs, on gross-cost contracts in Surat and Indore, with four years of accumulated drive-cycle data. It was a superb dataset and a terrible commitment. The model that came out of it was tuned, deeply and in ways that were only partly documented, to that chemistry and that duty cycle. When the Indian bus market moved almost entirely to lithium-iron-phosphate packs across 2024 and 2025 — cheaper cells, flatter voltage curves, and a state-of-charge signature that is notoriously hard to read — Kshamata's advantage became, quietly, a liability. Arunima's team had begun a chemistry-agnostic rewrite in November 2025. It was, as of that Sunday night, about ten weeks from a production build, and ten weeks after 9 March is the third week of May.

3. The industry

India's electric bus market in 2026 was a policy market before it was a commercial one. The FAME II tenders aggregated by CESL had shown operators that an electric bus could be run on a gross-cost contract at a per-kilometre rate below diesel; PM e-Bus Sewa and, later, PM E-DRIVE extended that logic to hundreds of smaller cities. The buses themselves came from Tata Motors, Olectra, JBM, Switch Mobility and a handful of newer assemblers. The operators — companies like Rathvahan Mobility Services — took on something the municipal transport undertakings did not want: the asset, the depot, the charging infrastructure, the drivers, and, crucially, the residual risk on a battery pack that represented close to forty per cent of the vehicle's capital cost.

That residual risk was where software like Kshamata's found its market. A gross-cost contract pays per kilometre operated. A pack that degrades faster than the warranty curve allows either reduces range, forcing a mid-day charge that eats the schedule, or triggers a warranty claim against the pack supplier — and warranty claims are won or lost on telemetry evidence. Operators had learned by 2025 that arguing about degradation without instrumented, time-stamped, independently computed evidence was a losing posture. Standards work at ARAI and BIS on pack testing gave a vocabulary but not a settlement mechanism.

Two further forces bore on the decision. First, driver-behaviour telemetry — harsh braking, idling, depot dwell — is personal data about an identifiable employee, and after the DPDP Act rules came into force, every operator's legal team had started asking vendors questions they had not asked in 2023. Kshamata's answer was good but long. Second, the Gulf: Imtiaz Qureshi, Kshamata's sales director in Dubai, had spent eight months building a channel agreement with Rafeeq Bus Trading LLC, a fleet distributor serving operators in the UAE and Oman. Rafeeq's people had been direct. They would sign by 31 March if Kshamata could name a marquee Indian fleet as a live reference. Without it, the conversation moved to the next financial year.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence, as Sharanya reconstructed it in her notebook that Sunday, ran like this. In October 2025, Kshamata was invited to a discovery call and demonstrated its Surat analysis, which was excellent, because Surat was the fleet the model had been built on. In November, Rathvahan issued a limited RFP to four vendors. In December, Kshamata and one other vendor were invited to run a paid pilot: ₹18 lakh, sixty-one buses out of the new Pune LFP fleet, ninety days, depot telemetry piped nightly. In January, Kshamata's pilot dashboard went live and Rathvahan's finance group, working from the accuracy figure in Kshamata's material, built the business case reproduced as Exhibit 3. In February, Rathvahan shortlisted three vendors for a final demonstration.

Two things had since turned out to be wrong, and Sharanya was not sure the second one was even settled. The first: the pilot was never a validation exercise. Everyone had treated it as one. Nobody at Rathvahan had asked for the pilot's own accuracy back-test, because they assumed the published accuracy applied; nobody at Kshamata had volunteered it, because until late February nobody had run it. Dr Venkataraman ran it in the last week of February, over Holi, when the Coimbatore office was half empty, and produced Exhibit 2.

The second: the demonstration environment. What the pilot dashboard showed at the Hadapsar depot was not, strictly, live. Telemetry arrived in a nightly batch at 02:30, and the two tiles Joaquim Ferreira had designed as the visual centre of the demo — the residual-value gauge and the fault-precursor ticker — were rendered from the previous night's batch with a timestamp in nine-point grey. Nobody had hidden this. Nobody had said it out loud either. On Friday, Rathvahan's head of engineering, Meghna Rathi, had sent a one-line addition to the demo brief: please show us a pack alert being raised, not a screenshot of one.

5. The people

Sharanya Iyengar — Head of Product, Kshamata, Bengaluru; in Pune for the demo. Position: the seven minutes should show the LFP pilot, because that is the fleet Rathvahan is buying. Incentive: she owns the product roadmap and has argued internally since November that chemistry-agnostic modelling is existential. Not saying: she proposed the pilot scope herself, and chose sixty-one buses over the ninety Arunima wanted, to fit the ₹18 lakh the customer would fund.
Devendra Kulkarni — Co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru. Position: lead with the proven Surat result, answer LFP questions honestly if asked, and win the logo. Incentive: Series B conversations opened in January on the premise of a marquee Indian fleet; fourteen months of runway. Not saying: one prospective investor has already asked, in writing, for a customer reference call in April.
Arunima Bose — Co-founder and Head of Engineering, Coimbatore. Position: do not demonstrate anything live from the depot; the nightly batch is a real architectural limit and a live alert cannot be conjured on demand. Incentive: her rewrite is ten weeks out and a public failure would pull her team onto firefighting. Not saying: she can force a synthetic alert through the pipeline in about three hours, has done it before for an internal review, and has told nobody on the commercial side.
Dr Padma Venkataraman — Principal Reliability Scientist, Melbourne. Position: the ±2.1% figure must not be shown to this customer for this fleet; it is true and irrelevant. Incentive: her name is on the validation memo and on a conference paper due in June. Not saying: her own LFP back-test rests on sixty-one buses and five months, which she would not accept from anyone else, and she has taken a first-round call with a battery analytics group in Singapore.
Joaquim Ferreira — Principal Product Designer, Lisbon. Position: the residual-value gauge is the only screen anyone remembers; it should open the demo. Incentive: he has spent four months on it and it is the centrepiece of the product's redesign. Not saying: he knows the gauge is driven by the least validated of the three models, and has twice asked in writing for an uncertainty band on it, which was deprioritised.
Ritika Salunkhe — Customer Success Lead, Jakarta. Position: put a customer's voice in the seven minutes; the Indore depot manager has agreed to join on video for ninety seconds. Incentive: renewals are her number and reference customers are her leverage. Not saying: the Indore depot runs the old NMC fleet, and she has not told the depot manager which fleet the Rathvahan demo concerns.
Meghna Rathi — Head of Engineering, Rathvahan Mobility Services, Pune (the customer). Position: she wants to see an alert raised live, and she asks about estimator error before she asks about price. Incentive: she carries the warranty recovery target — ₹6 crore of claims against the pack supplier this financial year. Not saying: she was a battery engineer for nine years and privately doubts that any vendor can hold ±2% on LFP; she may be testing which vendor says so first.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the figure on slide four, and it is not false. It is the accuracy Kshamata achieves on the chemistry and duty cycle it was built for.

7. Voices

Dr Padma Venkataraman, memo, 8 March, 6.20 p.m. AEDT"I am not saying our model is bad. I am saying 2.1% is a measurement of a different fleet, and if we put it on a screen in front of an engineer who runs LFP buses, she will either not notice, which is worse for us later, or she will notice, and then nothing else we say on Monday will be believed."
Devendra Kulkarni, Slack, 8 March, 9.12 p.m. IST"Padma is right about the science and wrong about the room. Every vendor in that corridor tomorrow is quoting a number from their best fleet. If we are the only ones who arrive with a confession, we do not get credit for honesty, we get a lower score on slide four."
Arunima Bose, Slack, 8 March, 9.31 p.m. IST"There is no streaming path at Hadapsar. If Meghna wants to see an alert raised at 11.04 a.m., the only honest answer is that the pipeline runs at 2.30 in the morning. Anything else we show her is theatre with our own data."

8. The options as Sharanya sees them

Option A — Lead with Surat. Open on the four-year NMC degradation curve, the fleet where the model is strongest, show the warranty claim that Surat recovered in FY25, keep the ±2.1% on slide four, and answer LFP questions honestly if and only if they are asked. It is the most polished seven minutes available and the one the team has rehearsed. It also answers a question Rathvahan did not ask, about a fleet Rathvahan is not buying.

Option B — Demo the pilot as it is, error bars and all. Show the sixty-one Pune buses live, put Exhibit 2 on the screen, name the 6.8% and the 40–70% band problem, and pitch the ten-week rewrite as joint work with Rathvahan's engineering team. Meghna Rathi may respect it. She may also record a technical veto, which Annexure C permits her to do on her own.

Option C — Lead with the residual gauge. Joaquim's screen, which is the most memorable thing Kshamata has and is driven by the least validated model, framed around the refinancing line in Exhibit 3. It speaks to finance, who hold twenty-five points, and to the treasury event nobody has committed to.

Option D — Give the seven minutes away. Spend ninety seconds on Kshamata, hand four minutes to the Indore depot manager, and close on a question to the committee. Ritika's instinct. It concedes the demonstration points almost entirely.

Sharanya had written the four options on hotel stationery and then, underneath them, a fifth line she had not shown anyone: what if the demo is not the thing being scored? Meghna Rathi carries a ₹6 crore warranty recovery target. Exhibit 3's largest line is warranty claims. Kshamata's warranty claim pack is a prototype with a manual step; the rival bid from Kinaara Telematics Systems arrives with a mature one. It was possible that the entire argument about accuracy figures was an argument about the wrong screen, and that the seven minutes should be spent building a claim file in front of the committee — a thing Kshamata could do on Monday only by hand, and badly.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The run of show locks at 8.00 a.m. on Monday; slides go to Rathvahan's coordinator by then and cannot be swapped. Kshamata's bid price of ₹4.20 crore was submitted in January and cannot be revised in the room. The pilot data-sharing agreement permits Kshamata to display Rathvahan's telemetry to Rathvahan personnel only, and the Friday attendee list added a municipal transport undertaking officer and a CESL observer, neither of whom is Rathvahan personnel; Kshamata's counsel in Hyderabad had replied, at 8.40 p.m., that the position was "arguable either way" and that driver-identifiable fields should in any case be masked under the DPDP Act rules. Arunima's chemistry-agnostic build lands in the third week of May at the earliest. Runway is fourteen months. Rafeeq Bus Trading needs a named Indian reference by 31 March. And Dr Venkataraman's memo is now a document that exists, dated, in Kshamata's own systems.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 1 and 2 measure the same quantity and disagree by a factor of three. Which of them is the honest number to put in front of this customer, and what exactly makes it honest — the measurement, or the match between the measurement and the fleet being bought?
  2. Exhibit 3 was written by the customer and is the most flattering document in the process. What should Sharanya do about the fact that its central assumption came from her own sales deck?
  3. Exhibit 4 gives the demonstration thirty of a hundred points. What does the footnote about the 2024 selection, and Annexure C's technical veto, do to that weighting in practice?
  4. Arunima can inject an alert into the pipeline in three hours, and Meghna has asked to see an alert raised live. Where is the line between a prepared demonstration and a staged one, and who at Kshamata gets to draw it?
  5. Each of the four options answers a different question. Whose question should the seven minutes answer — the committee's, the head of engineering's, the finance group's, or the one Kshamata wishes it had been asked?
  6. It is Monday morning. Sharanya has to send a run of show at 8.00 a.m. and stand up at 11.00. What does she do, what does she say in the fifteen minutes of questions afterwards, and what does she tell her own board on Tuesday about how the decision was made?

11. 11.40 p.m.

Sharanya closed the second demo script without saving it. Outside, the last of the Holi-week hoardings were still up along the road to Hadapsar, and somewhere across the city a depot gateway would wake at 2.30 a.m. and push one more night of telemetry from sixty-one buses into a model that had been built, three years earlier, for a fleet in another state running a chemistry the market had already left behind. She had seven minutes, four options she did not believe in equally, a memo from Melbourne she could neither use nor unread, and a co-founder who would call again at seven.

Seven Minutes on the T-Hub Stage

Hyderabad, Wednesday, 11 February 2026, 9.40 p.m. Aparna Rao sat in the empty auditorium of T-Hub's Raidurg campus with her laptop open on her knees, watching the technical crew coil cable off the demo stage where, in fourteen hours, Avishkar Analytics Cloud would get seven minutes in front of forty investors, including a partner from Peak XV Partners and an associate from Elevation Capital, to make the case for a ₹35 crore Series A. Twice that evening, in a dry run on the venue's guest wifi, her product's live forecasting screen had frozen mid-query. She had until 7 a.m. — when the run-of-show froze for good — to decide how Avishkar would use its seven minutes.

1. Company background

Aparna and her co-founder Karan Mehta started Avishkar Analytics Cloud in Bengaluru in 2022, after eight years each at Flipkart's supply chain team and Ola's logistics engineering group. Their product, an AI forecasting layer distributors call Saral, sits on top of a wholesaler's order book and predicts what a kirana store or small retailer will need to reorder before the retailer itself asks — reading signals from ONDC network traffic, UPI settlement timing and festival calendars. It was not a new idea; large enterprises had used tools like Zoho Analytics or Tableau for demand sensing for years. Avishkar's bet was that the same discipline, priced and packaged for a ₹2-crore-turnover distributor rather than a listed retailer, was still missing from the Indian market.

By February 2026 the company had forty employees, annual recurring revenue of ₹3.2 crore, and eleven paying distributor clients across four states, plus one anchor account outside India: Andaz Wholesale Trading LLC, a Dubai-based FMCG distributor that had adopted Saral in 2025 after a regional expansion made manual reordering unworkable. The Series A round, if it closed, would fund a sales team and a second data-science hire; without it, the board had told Aparna plainly, Avishkar had eleven months of runway.

2. The situation

T-Hub had cut every company's demo-day slot from twelve minutes to seven that week, after two later-stage startups were added to the agenda. Aparna's team, spread from Pune to New Jersey, had spent the four days since learning this arguing, mostly over a Slack thread that ran through everyone's working hours somewhere in the world, about what to cut. The immediate crisis was technical: the rehearsal failures both occurred when Saral's live dashboard tried to pull fresh order data from Andaz's Dubai account over the auditorium's shared wifi, which the venue's own staff admitted was oversubscribed during conference week. Karan believed the fix was structural, not lucky timing — he did not trust conference wifi with a live pull under investor eyes, full stop. Daniel Osei, Avishkar's data scientist, thought the fix was almost the opposite: strip the live network dependency but keep a live number, computed locally. Meera Krishnan, running customer success from Singapore, had a different worry entirely — that a technical scramble was crowding out the human evidence Avishkar actually had, a client on camera saying the product mattered. And Robert Fine, the sales head, was watching the schedule of other pitches leak out and did not like what he saw.

3. The people

Karan Mehta — Co-founder & Head of Engineering, Pune. Wants the live query dropped entirely; argues one visible freeze in front of Peak XV Partners costs more than any authenticity gained, and that Avishkar has already proved the engineering in production.
Daniel Osei — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants to keep a real, on-the-spot forecast, but computed against a cached snapshot of Andaz's data carried on a local laptop, so the proof is genuine without depending on the room's network.
Meera Krishnan — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Holds a two-minute recorded interview with Andaz's operations head in Dubai, praising Saral's reorder accuracy, and believes that voice will land harder with investors than any dashboard.
Robert Fine — Head of Sales, New Jersey. Has watched twelve other T-Hub demo days and believes investors reward a tight growth narrative with a traction slide over any software shown live; worried a stumble here ends the round before follow-up meetings even start.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows why the round mattered as much as it did: growth was real, but thin enough that one bad seven minutes among forty investors was not a cost Aparna could easily absorb.

Exhibit 1 — Avishkar Analytics Cloud, traction at a glance
MetricFY24FY25Q3 FY26 (current)
Annual recurring revenue₹0.6 crore₹1.9 crore₹3.2 crore
Paying distributor accounts3811
Net revenue retention91%104%112%
Employees142940

Source: Avishkar internal MIS, board pack February 2026. NRR above 100% from FY25 reflects the Andaz Wholesale Trading LLC expansion.

Exhibit 2 is the rehearsal log that forced the decision — the two failures Aparna, Karan and the T-Hub production crew watched happen on Tuesday evening.

Exhibit 2 — Rehearsal log, T-Hub demo stage, Tuesday 10 February
TimeAttemptWhat happened
7.12 p.m.Dry run 1Live query to Andaz account timed out after 9 seconds on venue wifi; dashboard froze on loading spinner for 40 seconds before Karan force-refreshed.
7.31 p.m.Dry run 2Query completed in 6 seconds after switching to a personal mobile hotspot, but hotspot signal in the auditorium measured only two of five bars.
8.05 p.m.Venue IT checkT-Hub staff confirmed guest wifi is shared across all fourteen demo-day companies and cannot be prioritised for one pitch.

Exhibit 3 lays the three options Aparna was weighing against the clock itself, since the seven minutes, once split, could not be re-split on stage.

5. The options

Option A — Run the full live demo as planned. Aparna logs into Saral on stage and pulls a real forecast against Andaz's live account, exactly as rehearsed before the wifi trouble began. The upside is the clearest possible answer to the question investors actually ask a software company: does it work, right now, in front of me? The cost is that the two rehearsal failures were not random; the venue's own IT staff said the network cannot be reserved, so the same freeze could recur in front of the room that mattered most.

Option B — Hybrid: a recorded core with one live, network-independent query. Daniel's proposal: play a thirty-second recorded walkthrough of Saral's interface to set context, then run one live query against a snapshot of Andaz's order data cached on Karan's laptop the night before, so nothing depends on the auditorium's wifi. The forecast investors see is genuinely computed, not staged, but the plumbing risk is removed. The cost is preparation time overnight, a snapshot that is a day old rather than truly live, and a format Aparna would have to rehearse cold before 7 a.m.

Option C — A narrative pitch with Meera's client clip and no live software. Robert's preference: lead with the traction numbers in Exhibit 1, play Meera's recorded interview with Andaz's operations head, and close with the ask. Zero technical risk, and a format several successful T-Hub alumni had used. The cost is that Avishkar would be the only forecasting-software company on the agenda not to show its software, in a room that had just watched two other startups demo live; investors could reasonably wonder what it was hiding.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 actually tell you about the risk in Option A — is it a one-off wifi problem, or a structural one that will recur at 11.15 a.m. tomorrow?
  2. Whose evidence is stronger for this audience: a live number in front of them, or Meera's recorded testimonial from the client in Dubai? Does the answer change if the investor has already seen ten demos that morning?
  3. Option B still depends on a cached snapshot rather than a truly live pull. Is that a meaningful compromise of "real evidence," or a reasonable engineering choice that no investor would object to if it were explained?
  4. Given the ₹35 crore round and eleven months of runway riding on this slot, how should Aparna weigh a small chance of visible failure against a smaller amount of authenticity lost?

A note for the learner

This topic asks a narrow, practical question: can you show a live product and real evidence in seven minutes? The temptation in a high-stakes pitch is to treat "live" and "safe" as opposites and pick one — either the full risk of Option A or the full retreat of Option C. Both misread what investors are actually testing for. They are not grading Avishkar on whether the wifi in a shared auditorium holds up; they are grading whether the founder understands her own product and her own evidence well enough to show it under pressure without flinching.

The defensible path here is Option B. It keeps the two things the topic asks for — a live product and real evidence — while removing the one variable Aparna does not control and cannot fix by 7 a.m., the venue's shared wifi. A cached snapshot from the previous evening, openly computed live on stage rather than played back, is still a real forecast; it is not the same claim as a slide of past results, and a sophisticated investor will read the difference. Karan's instinct to avoid the network is sound engineering judgment, not risk-aversion for its own sake; Daniel's insistence on keeping a genuinely live computation, even against cached data, protects the storytelling core that a demo is the product in the founder's hands, not a story about the product. Meera's testimonial clip still belongs in the seven minutes, as sixty seconds of corroboration after the live query, not as a replacement for it. Robert's read of the room is worth taking seriously as a reason to rehearse the narrative framing hard, not as a reason to withhold the product itself, since a company built on live forecasting cannot afford to be the one team on the agenda that will not show its own dashboard.
