Difficult Conversations: The Arithmetic of Notice, Contribution and Trust

1. Two rooms, one week apart

At 06:40 on Wednesday, 9 September 2026, Vikram Raghunathan, director of product at Svaha Payments Network in Bengaluru, was woken by Wei Lin Tan, his site-reliability lead in Singapore. A reconciliation service shipped the previous Friday was mis-classifying 2.3 per cent of card and UPI transactions as duplicates and holding the matching settlements: over three days, ₹58 crore owed to 340 of Svaha's 1,900 merchants. The largest holding, ₹9.4 crore, belonged to Saudamini Quick Commerce, a Gurugram grocery-delivery firm on a ₹1.8 crore contract due for renewal in February.

By Thursday evening the defect was patched and every rupee released. Sixty-one merchants had filed tickets; 279 had not noticed. Vikram's Friday decision was not technical: whether to write to all 340 or answer only the 61, and how much causal detail to put in writing in an industry where the Reserve Bank of India's supervisory expectations make every written account a potential exhibit. His CEO wanted silence. Vikram's read was that 30 September, month-end close across 279 finance teams, would settle it for him badly.

Eleven days earlier in Pune, Ananya Bhattacharya, vice-president of product at Sthiti Cardiac Devices, had received a different kind of bad news. Sthiti sold Sumeru Hospitals Group a three-year, ₹6.2 crore deployment of its cardiac monitoring patch and clinician dashboard on one promised capability: automated arrhythmia burden analytics, live by 1 December 2026 for a new cardiac programme at four hospitals. On 14 August her validation lead flagged that sensitivity fell from 0.94 to 0.71 in patients with implanted pacemakers — nine per cent of the population, and the group least able to absorb a missed episode. The fix was not code but a re-validation study, a fresh submission to the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, and a date in early 2027.

Ananya had known four weeks and told nobody outside her function; Dr. Kavitha Menon, Sumeru's chief of cardiology, had already announced the programme internally. The two cases differ in almost every surface respect. What they share is the object of study: the point at which accurate information becomes painful, and the manner of delivery, not the content, decides whether it is believed again.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

A difficult conversation, precisely defined, is an exchange with three properties: the information is materially adverse to the receiver; the sender controls its timing, framing and channel; and the parties expect to transact again. Remove the third and it is an announcement; remove the second, an accident.

Its history runs through four traditions. The first is the Harvard Negotiation Project — Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes (1981), then Stone, Patton and Heen's Difficult Conversations (1999) — which claimed that every hard exchange is three conversations at once: what happened, what each party feels, and what the episode says about who they are. The second is Chris Argyris on defensive routines: people hold untested inferences as facts and design communication to avoid embarrassment, producing it later and larger. The third is the disclosure literature in finance, which found that managers hoard bad news and release it late, and that markets punish the delay more than the news. The fourth is crisis communication and legal counsel, organised around sequence, channel control and avoiding admissions that outrun the evidence.

SchoolWill signWill not sign
Relational (Stone, Patton, Heen)“Name impact and contribution before any remedy; the identity threat is the real content.”“Disclose at the first signal whether or not you can explain it.”
Disclosure economics (Argyris; hoarding evidence)“Delay is the dominant failure; publish at credible knowledge, incomplete.”“Stage the message to protect the counterpart's standing.”
Crisis communication (Benoit; regulated practice)“One account, one channel, one owner; sequence audiences deliberately.”“Volunteer a cause in writing before the investigation closes.”
Directness (Radical Candor)“Say it in the first sentence; choreography is condescension.”“Spend the first third of the meeting on feelings.”

The disagreement is real and unresolved. A practitioner who has read only the first school will disclose an unconfirmed root cause to a regulated customer and create a second incident; one who knows only the third will hold a factual account for eleven days and lose the relationship it was meant to protect. Command means knowing which proposition you rely on, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.

3. Mechanics: the knowledge gap and the notice window

Expert practice organises itself around two clocks running in opposite directions. The knowledge gap runs from the moment you could have told the counterpart to the moment you did; it is a liability, and it compounds. The notice window runs from their learning to the consequence; it is an asset, and the only thing you can still give.

Figure 1. Left band: time the sender has spent. Right band: time the receiver can still use. Delay converts the second into the first.

The discipline is to price both. Start with the receiver's direct loss, usually smaller than anyone expects. Saudamini's ₹9.4 crore was held three days; bridging it at 14 per cent per annum costs ₹9.4 crore × 0.14 × 3/365, about ₹1.08 lakh. Across all 340, ₹58 crore held a mean of 2.4 days gives aggregate harm of roughly ₹5.3 lakh — the entire measurable injury, against a renewal worth ₹1.8 crore from Saudamini alone. The incident is an order of magnitude smaller than whether the counterpart believes your next sentence.

The second calculation is the one experts run: expected twelve-month cost by posture, with the probability of independent discovery as the free variable.

PostureDirect cost (₹ lakh)Churn hazard on affected ARRExpected 12-month cost at p = 0.70
A. Answer the 61 tickets only614% of ₹11.9 cr if discovered123
B. Proactive note to all 340, no public post-mortem365% of ₹14.6 cr109
C. Proactive note, published post-mortem, supervisory filing444% of ₹14.6 cr, plus review risk on ₹2.1 cr pipeline124

Affected ARR ₹14.6 crore, of which ₹11.9 crore sits with the 279 who have not noticed; direct cost is credits at 0.5 per cent of held value plus support at ₹3,100 an hour; p is the chance those 279 discover the hold within 60 days.

Figure 2. Silence is cheaper only while discovery is unlikely. The crossing sits high, so the decision reduces to one number almost nobody measures.

Two second-order effects follow. First, the break-even probability is high — 0.62 — so on one incident in isolation silence often prices out as rational. Second, that is an artefact of pricing one incident: Svaha will have eleven a year, and the churn hazard under A is not 14 per cent per incident but a rising function of how often a merchant has been surprised. Three steps stay implicit: decide the policy before the incident; write the account before the meeting and treat the meeting as the edit; and name the counterpart's downstream conversation, because the person in front of you is rarely the one they fear.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

The conditions can be stated as claims testable in the room. First, the counterpart has decisions left to make. Sumeru does: with eleven weeks, Dr. Menon can stage the programme, bridge with manual Holter review, or re-tender a module. Svaha's merchants do not; the money is released, and what remains is a decision about Svaha. Where no decision remains, the conversation is about credibility alone and the option-generation the literature recommends becomes theatre.

Second, the sender has a causal account that survives scrutiny. Ananya does; Vikram has a proximate cause and not a root cause, and publishing the former as the latter is how one difficult conversation becomes three.

Third, the relationship has a future worth more than the disclosure costs. Both pass easily. Where they would not — a customer already in termination — the honest move is a factual notice without relational investment.

It actively misleads in three situations. When the news is a decision rather than an outcome — a deliberate “no” on a roadmap request — contribution-mapping invites the counterpart to negotiate it, which is not why you called. When statutory duty is engaged the sequence is fixed by law: Ananya cannot tell Sumeru before her own regulatory affairs function. And when the counterpart is not in good faith, the vocabulary of impact and identity becomes a lever they will pull.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Multi-product companies create a failure that has nothing to do with skill. Svaha's payments and lending arms share a customer list but not an account team; the merchant told about the hold hears nothing from lending, whose credit decisions used the same balances. Two-sided platforms compound this: the same fact must be told twice, in two frames, without the accounts contradicting each other when a user screenshots both.

Regulated hardware is Ananya's world, and its feature is a third participant not in the room. A causal narrative given to Sumeru is discoverable; a date commitment can constitute a claim about a device. Mature device firms use a split rarely written down: a clinical conversation, candid about mechanism and uncertainty, and a contractual one, narrow and precise, held by two people on the same call.

AI-native products break a premise the field rests on. A difficult conversation assumes a stable account of what happened; when the failing component is a model, the honest answer to “why did it do that?” may be unavailable and “will it recur?” is probabilistic. At Sanchit Underwriting AI, a Hyderabad firm whose model prices small-business loans, the product head opens adverse conversations with the measured error rate and the monitoring that would catch a recurrence rather than with a cause — a substitution regulated buyers accept and engineering-led buyers do not.

Figure 3. The conversation took eleven minutes; reaching it took sixty-one hours, forty-six of them internal queueing.

Figure 3 shows the seam that matters most and is discussed least. The craft literature is about the eleven minutes; bad news actually moves at the speed of the most anxious approver. Mature companies fix this by pre-authorising the conversation — a standing template, an agreed threshold, an owner who needs no CEO slot. Most say they have it; the audit is to measure detection-to-notification on the last three incidents.

6. Eight nuances that separate expert from competent

The counterpart's real fear is the conversation they must have next. The tell is sequence: they ask “can you put that in writing?” before “when will it be fixed?” The obvious reading is that they are building a file to blame you with. The accurate one is that they need a defensible account for their own board — which hands you the highest-leverage move there is.

Notice is a feature with measurable value, not a courtesy. The tell is an expert's first question after the news: “what decisions of yours does this date feed?” Competent practitioners apologise for lateness; experts price it. Eleven weeks lets Sumeru stage four hospitals sequentially, worth more than any credit Sthiti could offer.

A causal account is not a legal admission. The tell is grammar: the sentence contains a mechanism — “a duplicate-detection threshold matched legitimate retries” — and no adjective about fault. That reads as evasion; it is the opposite. It is more specific than “we made a mistake,” and it survives being forwarded.

Silence after delivery belongs to the receiver. The tell is that experts tolerate eight or ten seconds without speaking. The obvious move is to fill it with reassurance, and it is wrong: that converts the counterpart's processing time into an unforced negotiation against yourself, and those concessions are the ones people regret.

The written recap is the artefact; the meeting is the ritual that makes it credible. The tell is that the expert wrote the recap before the meeting and edits it during. That looks like pre-scripting something that should be spontaneous. In practice a draft visibly changed by the meeting is the strongest evidence of listening anyone receives.

Compensation offered early buys a receipt, not forgiveness. The tell is credits arriving before impact has been named: the conversation moves from the relationship to procurement, where it becomes a precedent and a line item. Experts wait until the counterpart has finished; often it is not wanted.

Who stands next to you is a decision, not logistics. The tell is an expert who brings the engineering lead for causal questions and takes the apology alone: bringing the team to be apologised for exposes them, excluding them makes the account unverifiable.

The second conversation is worth more than the first. The tell is that the expert books it in the same breath as the bad news — a date thirty days out, with something specific to show. Recovery is demonstrated, not promised: trust re-forms when the first follow-through arrives unprompted.

7. How the practice varies — and where it does not

Begin with what does not change, because most cross-context advice here is padding. The three-layer structure is invariant, as is the rule that impact precedes remedy. What varies is who counts as the counterpart, how many there are, and how much time sits between disclosure and consequence.

ContextWhat actually differs
ConsumerNo named counterpart and no conversation; the medium is a release note, and trust reforms across many shipments rather than one exchange. The craft is word choice, and whether anything is said at all.
B2B / enterpriseThe counterpart has their own board. Notice value is high, channel signals priority, and there are two conversations: yours, and the one they must have afterwards.
Platform and marketplaceTwo audiences with opposed interests get the same fact; the binding constraint is consistency between the accounts, not the quality of either one.
Hardware and physical goodsDates are less compressible and remedies physical, so notice is the only variable left; safety duties fix the audience order.
AI productsCausal accounts may be unavailable; experts substitute error rates, monitoring and bounded commitments, and say plainly that it is a substitution.

Stage changes less than founders expect and more than large-company executives admit. Early on the founder or PM has the conversation personally: trust is deep, but no account layer absorbs a misstep, and one badly handled slip can cost a logo worth five per cent of revenue. At scale the messenger is an account manager, and the PM's craft shifts to arming that person with an accurate account, a defensible plan and an honest distribution around the date. The failure there is not clumsiness but a summary the account manager cannot defend under two follow-up questions.

8. Three worked examples

Svaha, September 2026. Vikram chose posture B with one modification: a single factual note to all 340 naming the mechanism, that merchant's held amount and the release timestamp, with no published post-mortem and the supervisory filing handled separately by risk. Direct cost came in at ₹33 lakh against a ₹36 lakh estimate. Of the 279 who had not noticed, 44 replied, three escalated and none churned; Saudamini renewed at ₹1.9 crore. Vikram's own view was that the 46 hours of internal queueing, not the incident, was the real finding.

Sthiti, September 2026. Ananya built the date from the critical path, not from hope. Re-validation needed 118 more pacemaker-subgroup episodes; four sites recruiting 2.2 each per week gave 8.8 a week, or 13.4 weeks, rounded to 14. Analysis and report took three weeks, the CDSCO change notification six at the median. Twenty-three weeks from 14 September is late February; with a two-week buffer, 9 March 2027. She presented a distribution — 16 February at the tenth percentile, 9 March at the median, 27 April at the ninetieth — named recruitment rate as the variable that moved it, and offered weekly numbers as evidence Sumeru could watch. Sumeru staged across two hospitals instead of four and deferred ₹1.4 crore. They did not re-tender.

Sangam Freight Exchange, March 2026 — the one that failed. Devdatt Joshi, head of product at this Chennai marketplace matching shippers with fleet operators, had to withdraw a promised fuel-card integration that twelve operators, together 38 per cent of supply-side volume, had been told was coming. He delivered it competently: honest, eight weeks early, with a clear reason. He delivered it in a webinar. Three of the twelve had heard the substance a day earlier from a competitor. Four stopped accepting Sangam loads within a month, liquidity in two corridors fell 19 per cent, and gross merchandise value there fell ₹2.6 crore over the quarter.

The content was right; the channel was the message. A webinar told twelve people who between them were the business that the news was routine enough to broadcast. Recovery took eleven weeks and three things: personal visits by Devdatt and the CEO, a published quarterly ledger listing every promise and its status, and a six-month fee waiver worth ₹41 lakh, offered after the visits. Nine returned to previous volumes by August; two never returned calls. The instructive detail is that the waiver almost certainly did not do the work. The ledger did, converting an apology into a standing, checkable commitment.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The first is drip disclosure: the truth released in instalments sized to what the sender can bear. The warning is that each update is smaller than the last and the counterpart starts asking “is there anything else?” The diagnostic: is there a fact I hold that I would be embarrassed to have them learn elsewhere? Caught late, the cost is categorical — every future update is discounted, including the accurate ones.

The second is the laundered account, where the internal and external versions diverge in substance, not tone. The sign is a PM who cannot say the internal sentence in the external room; the diagnostic is to read both aloud. Caught late, it surfaces when an engineer and an account manager sit in the same customer meeting, and costs the relationship in an afternoon.

The third is remedy-first: leading with the plan, because the plan is the part the sender feels competent about. The sign is a counterpart who gets a reasonable recovery schedule and escalates anyway within a week. The diagnostic is whether impact was named before any fix was offered. Caught late, the escalation lands with someone senior who must be told the whole story again, by someone else.

The fourth is apology inflation. The sign is unmistakable and widely misread: the counterpart starts reassuring the sender. The emotional labour has moved to the injured party, and they will not tell you next time they are unhappy, because it is work. The diagnostic is a count: more than two apologies in fifteen minutes says something about the sender, not the news.

The fifth is audience error: telling the person in the room and forgetting the regulator, the board, the other side of the marketplace. The diagnostic is the forwarding test — would this survive being sent on unedited to each of them? Caught late, the damage is sequence, not content: someone important learns it second-hand.

The sixth is the point estimate: a new date offered as a single number, produced by the method that produced the first. The sign is that nobody can say what would move it. The diagnostic: can you state a tenth and a ninetieth percentile, and the variable driving the spread? Caught late this is the worst of the six, because a second miss confirms a pattern where the first was only an event.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is speed versus confirmation. The disclosure-economics position, steelmanned, is that bad-news hoarding is among the more robust findings in the field: adverse information is delayed, the delay is discovered, and the penalty for delay exceeds the penalty for the news. On that evidence Vikram should have written to all 340 on Wednesday, partially. The crisis-communication position, equally steelmanned, holds that a partial account which later proves wrong creates a second incident with a worse property — it shows that the sender's statements require revision — and that an unconfirmed causal claim in writing is a durable liability. For the first to be wrong, the revision penalty would have to exceed the delay penalty; for the second, counterparties would have to treat “here is what we know at 09:00, it may change” as a different speech act from a settled account. This turns on the counterparty's sophistication, and nobody has measured where the line falls.

The second is identity work versus directness. Stone, Patton and Heen rest on the observation that unaddressed identity threat resurfaces as displaced anger weeks later. The directness school rests on the observation that senior counterparts experience the choreography as condescension, and that the ritual itself signals the news is worse than it is. Both are right about different counterparts, and no test can be run in advance.

The third is compensation timing, where the service-recovery paradox — that a well-handled failure can leave satisfaction higher than no failure — has had a rough replication history. Believers lead with generous remedies; sceptics treat it as a rationalisation for breaking things. The fourth is who delivers: the accountable product manager, or the relationship owner. Underneath all four sits measurement: there is no accepted instrument for trust in a commercial relationship, which is why this remains an argument conducted in anecdotes.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this performs the structure: they name impact, map contribution, separate intent from effect, and can be watched doing it. Someone who has internalised it is mostly invisible, because the work has moved upstream. They decided the disclosure policy already, so the incident does not choose. They know their knowledge gap in hours. They write the account before the meeting and let the meeting change it. They say the hard sentence in one clause and stop. They treat the follow-up date as the deliverable. And they notice when they are about to use the apparatus to avoid a conversation that could simply be had — at senior level, the commonest way this competence fails.

12. Closing: what each of them did

Vikram sent the note to all 340 on Friday at 16:20, naming the mechanism and each merchant's own held amount, and asked his CEO for a standing disclosure threshold so the next one needed no sign-off slot. His reasoning was not the expected-cost table, which had favoured silence at the probability his team first guessed; it was that Svaha would face eleven of these a year and could not run a different policy each time.

Ananya told Dr. Menon on 15 September in person, with her regulatory lead present for mechanism questions and her commercial lead for the contract. She gave the distribution rather than a date, named her own thirty-one-day knowledge gap unprompted, and offered weekly recruitment numbers. She offered no discount, and Sumeru did not ask.

Three questions. First: Vikram's table favoured silence at his team's own estimate of p. On what grounds may a leader override an explicit quantitative analysis, and how would you tell that from ignoring inconvenient arithmetic? Second: Ananya's thirty-one-day delay was, by section 9's standards, a failure — yet those weeks produced the data that made her date credible. When is a knowledge gap an investment rather than a liability, and who decides? Third: Sangam's recovery worked through a published ledger rather than any conversation. How much of this topic is conversational craft at all?

13. Going deeper

Stakeholder mapping and management is the prerequisite this topic consumes under stress: every judgement above about audience order and forwarding risk assumes you know who holds what interest. Conflict and disagreement takes over where this ends, when the sides dispute the facts and not merely their consequences. Leading through a crisis asks whether the discipline survives with no eleven weeks and no Friday afternoon to prepare. Delivering bad news about the product narrows the lens to the thing you built rather than the date you promised. Communicating with leadership governs the internal half of every case here, usually the harder half. Telling the customer story and demo and pitch craft apply the same discipline when the news is good. Writing as a PM superpower matters most, because the recap, not the meeting, persists. Decision records and DACI/RACI prevent many of these conversations by making commitments and owners explicit before they break. And running effective meetings decides whether the eleven minutes are usable.

The Ramadan Call: A Difficult Conversation at Ekagra Product Cloud

Bengaluru, Monday, 12 January 2026

At 9:40 on a Monday morning, Ananya Rao, Vice President of Product at Ekagra Product Cloud, closed her laptop after a call with her engineering lead and sat still for a moment. In four days she had to decide what to tell Farah Al-Sayed, Vice President of Operations at Oorja Retail Group in Dubai, about a feature Ekagra had promised for the start of Ramadan — and that Ananya now knew, with data to prove it, was not going to work the way anyone had told Farah it would. The question was not whether to say something, but what to say, to whom, in what order, and how to say it so that Oorja's leadership still trusted Ekagra afterward.

1. Ekagra Product Cloud

Ekagra Product Cloud, founded in Bengaluru in 2018, sells a product analytics and customer-data platform that lets consumer brands track user behaviour, segment audiences and catch anomalies in transaction data in real time. Its natural comparison set in India was CleverTap, MoEngage and WebEngage, with Amplitude and Segment as the global names enterprise buyers asked about; Ekagra's pitch was that it understood Indian and Gulf retail patterns — UPI settlement quirks, multilingual catalogues, festival-driven demand spikes — better than any of them. By early 2026 the company had raised through a Series C, employed close to 900 people, and had crossed roughly ₹140 crore in annual recurring revenue. Engineering and data platform teams sat in Bengaluru and Pune; design in Berlin; data science in Toronto; customer success for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East ran out of Singapore; enterprise sales for the Gulf and the Americas was led from New Jersey. Ekagra had never had a large Gulf account until it signed Oorja Retail Group, a supermarket and e-commerce group headquartered in Dubai with operations across the UAE and Saudi Arabia and a fast-growing joint venture entering India. The Oorja deal, closed in 2024, was Ekagra's proof that it could serve an enterprise retailer outside India, and its renewal was being watched closely by the board.

2. The situation

Oorja had bought Ekagra's core analytics platform and, in late 2025, agreed to pilot Anomaly Alerts: a module flagging unusual transaction patterns — price errors, loyalty-point abuse, fraudulent returns — to Oorja's operations team in real time. Farah had built her Ramadan campaign around it. Ramadan 2026 begins around 18 February, and for a Gulf grocery retailer it is the busiest commercial season of the year, comparable to Diwali for Indian retail. Her team had already briefed store operations and referenced the feature in a readiness deck to Oorja's board.

On 8 January, Sofia Reyes, the data scientist in Toronto responsible for validating the anomaly model, ran a full-scale load test using a mirror of Oorja's actual transaction mix: English and Arabic product listings, AED and INR-denominated flows from the India joint venture, and the transaction volumes Oorja expected during Ramadan. The false-positive rate on English, AED-only transactions was acceptable. On Arabic-language SKU descriptions and India-linked INR flows, it was not: the model was misreading transliterated, mixed-script product names as anomalies at a rate that would flood Oorja's operations desk with false alarms. Rohan Mehta, Ekagra's engineering lead in Bengaluru, confirmed the finding and estimated a proper fix — retraining the model on multilingual data and rebuilding the ingestion pipeline — would take six weeks, past the Ramadan launch date. A narrower fix, covering English and AED transactions only, could ship on the original date, 30 January, but would leave out the Arabic-language and India-linked transactions making up roughly 60% of Oorja's volume.

Mei-Ling Chua, the Singapore-based customer success lead, had already sensed something was off: Farah's team had begun asking for store-manager training material two weeks early. Devika Nair, who led enterprise sales for the Gulf and the Americas from New Jersey, had closed the original deal and was now forecasting a ₹6 crore expansion tied to a successful launch; she wanted the 30 January date protected at almost any cost.

3. The people

Rohan Mehta — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru.
Wants a realistic, disclosed timeline. Does not want his team pressured into shipping a model he distrusts, or blamed later for a launch decision made above him.
Devika Nair — Head of Enterprise Sales, Gulf & Americas, New Jersey.
Owns the relationship and the ₹6 crore expansion forecast. Wants the 30 January date kept intact and is wary of a conversation that could put the whole account at risk.
Farah Al-Sayed — VP Operations, Oorja Retail Group, Dubai.
Has committed her leadership to the Ramadan rollout and briefed her board on it. Wants a working system for her busiest season and, above that, wants to trust what Ekagra tells her.
Mei-Ling Chua — Customer Success Lead, APAC & MEA, Singapore.
Closest to Farah day to day. Wants Ananya to call Farah directly and early, before Oorja's own testing or store rollout surfaces the problem first.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Oorja account snapshot, as of January 2026
MetricValue
Current annual contract value₹18 crore
Share of Ekagra's total ARR (~₹140 crore)~13%
Proposed Anomaly Alerts expansion (annualised)₹6 crore
Contract renewal decision dueApril 2026
Largest single account outside IndiaYes

Source: Ekagra Product Cloud account management records, compiled by Devika Nair's team, January 2026.

Exhibit 2. Anomaly Alerts false-positive rate by transaction segment
Transaction segmentShare of Oorja volumeFalse-positive rate
English listings, AED transactions40%2.1%
Arabic-language SKU descriptions44%14.6%
India JV, INR-linked flows16%11.3%
Blended, full catalogue100%9.8%
Oorja's stated tolerance threshold—3.0%

Source: load test by Sofia Reyes, data science, Toronto, 8 January 2026, using a mirror of Oorja's expected Ramadan transaction mix.

Exhibit 1 shows why Devika was reluctant to disturb the timeline: Oorja was Ekagra's largest account outside India and the model for further Gulf expansion. Exhibit 2 shows why Rohan and Sofia would not ship quietly: a blended false-positive rate of 9.8% against a stated tolerance of 3% meant a meaningful share of alerts reaching Farah's desk would be noise, not signal — during the season her team could least afford to chase false alarms.

Exhibit 3. The full fix lands roughly nine days after Ramadan begins, so any version shipped for the season's start is necessarily partial.

5. The options

  1. Ship the partial version and disclose the gap now. Launch on 30 January covering English and AED transactions, tell Farah plainly on the 16th that Arabic-language and India-linked transactions are excluded until the fix lands around 27 February, and offer a service credit. Upside: keeps most of the original commitment and treats Farah as a partner in the trade-off. Cost: the excluded segment is 60% of Oorja's volume, so the feature arrives materially smaller than promised, right at the season's opening.
  2. Delay the full launch to late February and say so now. Tell Farah on the 16th that Ekagra will not ship anything until the model works across the full catalogue, rather than hand her a partial tool during her highest-stakes weeks. Upside: nothing unreliable reaches her operations desk; avoids the risk in Exhibit 2 entirely. Cost: Oorja loses the feature for Ramadan this year, and the ₹6 crore expansion Devika forecast is almost certainly delayed past April.
  3. Ship the partial version and let the gap surface on its own. Launch on 30 January as planned, brief Farah only on what works, and address the shortfall quietly once the six-week fix is ready. Upside: preserves the announced date and avoids an uncomfortable call this week. Cost: if Oorja's own team discovers the false-positive pattern during Ramadan — which Exhibit 2 suggests is likely — they discover it alongside evidence that Ekagra already knew and said nothing, which risks the entire account, not only the expansion.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 actually tell Ananya about the size of the gap between what Farah was promised and what Ekagra can deliver by 30 January?
  2. Whose trust is most at risk in this decision — Farah's, Devika's forecast, or Rohan's team's confidence in their own leadership — and how do those risks trade off against one another?
  3. Independent of which version of the product ships, what does each of the three options communicate to Farah about Ekagra's reliability as a partner?
  4. If Ananya calls Farah on Wednesday the 14th, what should the first two minutes of that call contain, and what should they deliberately leave out?

7. A note for the learner

This case sits at the point where stakeholder management stops being routine and becomes a test of trust under pressure. The skill this topic teaches is not how to avoid delivering bad news — the false-positive rate in Exhibit 2 was not going away by staying quiet about it — but how to deliver a no, a slip or a failure so the relationship stays intact on the other side. A well-reasoned answer treats the conversation with Farah as a design problem in its own right, not an afterthought to the engineering decision: it leads with the evidence Ekagra already has (Exhibit 2), names the trade-off honestly instead of minimising it, and gives Farah real choices rather than a fait accompli.

Option 3 fails this test regardless of what the model eventually does, because it converts a technical shortfall into a credibility problem the moment Oorja discovers it independently — and Exhibit 2 makes that discovery likely during Ramadan itself. Between Options 1 and 2, the more defensible path is not to pick one for Farah but to call her before the 16th, walk her through Exhibit 2 directly, and let her choose between a smaller feature on time and a complete feature six weeks late, backed by a concrete gesture — the service credit — that shows Ekagra is absorbing some of the cost of its own miss rather than passing it all to her. That combination, offered early and in person rather than by email, is what turns a difficult conversation into evidence that Ekagra is a partner worth renewing, which is exactly what Exhibit 1 shows is at stake in April.

Difficult Conversations: Delivering a No, a Slip, or a Failure Without Losing Trust

On the evening of September 14, 2026, Meera Iyer, a senior product manager at Ekasutra Success Cloud in Bengaluru, sat with the sprint board open on one screen and a calendar invite on the other. The invite was for a call the next afternoon with Rohan Sabharwal, vice president of operations at Elaan Fashion Retail, a fast-growing Mumbai direct-to-consumer label and one of Ekasutra's larger customers at roughly ₹42 lakh a year. Ekasutra had promised Elaan a returns-and-refund automation module, internally called ReturnGenie, live by October 1 — comfortably ahead of Elaan's Diwali flash sale on October 20, the single biggest revenue day on their calendar. Meera's honest read of the sprint data was that the realistic delivery date was closer to the first week of November: not a two-day slip a client shrugs off, but a miss landing after the one date it existed to serve.

What made the call harder was that Rohan had already told his own board ReturnGenie would absorb the Diwali return surge without hiring temporary support staff. Whatever Meera said would decide three things at once: whether Elaan renewed in March, whether Rohan ever again took an Ekasutra date at face value, and whether her own VP of engineering, who would hear about the miss within the week regardless, trusted her estimates going forward. She had, by her own count, about eighteen hours to decide not just what to say, but how.

The Idea

A difficult conversation, in the precise sense used here, is any exchange in which conveying accurate information will cause the other party real pain, and in which the manner of delivery — not just the content — determines whether the relationship and the information's future credibility survive intact. The framework comes from the Harvard Negotiation Project: Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton, and Sheila Heen published Difficult Conversations: How to Discuss What Matters Most in 1999, extending Roger Fisher's earlier negotiation research. Their starting observation was that most professionals handle bad news in one of two failing modes: avoiding or delaying it, or delivering it as a flat verdict and considering the job done. Both optimize for the deliverer's comfort and both, reliably, cost more trust than the bad news itself would have if handled directly. The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib is this: every difficult conversation is actually three conversations running underneath one — what happened, what we feel, and what it says about who we are — and the meeting fails whenever only the first one gets addressed.

How It Actually Works

The three-conversation structure is not a script; it is a preparation discipline that changes what a manager notices before they open their mouth. Applied to Meera's eighteen hours, it works in a specific order.

Figure 1. The three layers running underneath any single hard message; a plan that only answers layer one leaves the other two to surface later, usually as anger the deliverer did not see coming.

First, she separates the three tracks on paper, privately: the facts of the miss, the feelings both sides will bring, and the identity each person needs protected. Second, she shifts from delivering a verdict to opening a learning conversation — entering the call assuming she does not have Elaan's full picture, including whether October 20 is truly immovable or a phased rollout could cover the highest-volume return categories first. Third, and this is the step practitioners most often skip, she separates intent from impact in her own language: the team intended to hit October 1, and, without using intent to soften it, the impact on Elaan's Diwali plan is real regardless. Fourth, she maps contribution as a system rather than a single cause — a security patch that pulled two engineers for six of ten working days, an estimate with no buffer, and a mid-sprint request from Elaan itself — because a scapegoat story collapses the moment someone checks it. Fifth, she names emotion out loud rather than letting the room pretend to be neutral: "I expect this lands badly with your board, and it should." Only after these four moves does she turn to options and a jointly chosen date, never a unilaterally announced one. The step almost everyone leaves implicit: she closes with a written recap inside the hour, because the spoken conversation rebuilds trust in the moment, but only the written one prevents a second difficult conversation about what was actually agreed.

A Worked Example

Meera's estimate was not a guess; it came from the sprint board. ReturnGenie was scoped at 90 story points, and the five-engineer team's trailing velocity across its last four sprints had been a steady 30 points per sprint. At that rate, three sprints would finish by September 26, comfortably inside the October 1 promise. But the first feature sprint, ending September 12, delivered only 15 points, because two engineers spent six of ten working days on an unplanned security patch. Going forward, the team discounted its velocity by 20 percent for how optimistic the original number had proven, to 24 points per sprint.

ItemPointsNote
Feature scope90Fixed at kickoff, Elaan sign-off
Delivered, sprint 1 (Sep 1–12)15Planned 30; security patch cost two engineers six of ten days
Remaining scope7590 − 15
Revised velocity24 / sprint30 discounted 20% for estimation risk
Sprints needed3.1 → 475 ÷ 24, rounded up to a whole sprint
Finish date, no change~Nov 7Four more sprints from Sep 12

Four whole sprints from September 12 lands the finish near November 7 — about three weeks after the October 20 sale, and useless for it. Rohan's likely first question, "what if we just add people?", deserves a second pass. Borrowing two engineers lifts headcount by 40 percent, but new engineers do not arrive at full output: they run at roughly a quarter of a normal share in their first sprint while the existing team's own output dips from onboarding them, then reach sixty percent by sprint two and ninety by sprint three. Running that through the same 75-point balance finishes the feature roughly two-thirds through the fourth sprint, close to October 22. Adding people shrinks the miss from three weeks to about two days; it does not erase it, and it costs the lending team's own roadmap. That distinction — a lever that helps a great deal without being a rescue — is exactly the precise, defensible fact Meera can bring into the room instead of a vague "we're looking at options."

Figure 2. The same 75 remaining points, run through two staffing assumptions: the gap between promise and reality shrinks with help but does not close.

The Nuances

It is not the same as conflict

Both sides may agree completely on what happened and still find the conversation hard, because the pain is in the consequence, not in a dispute over the record. Treating every hard message as a negotiation to be won misreads what is actually at stake.

It is often confused with feedback frameworks

Tools such as Situation-Behaviour-Impact or Radical Candor address how to comment on someone else's behaviour so they can change it. A missed deadline is not feedback on Rohan's behaviour at all; conflating the two leads managers to accidentally lecture a client on how to feel about the news.

It is not sugar-coating

Softening the words and stating the impact clearly are not opposites; the framework asks for both in the same sentence, not clarity traded for comfort. A message so cushioned the client leaves unsure a deadline moved has failed as badly as a blunt one that humiliates.

It does not apply to everything unwelcome

A purely administrative update with no ongoing relationship at stake does not need this machinery. Over-applying it turns routine updates into staged events, itself a signal that something is more wrong than it is.

It cannot tell you what the right call is

The framework governs how a decision is communicated, never whether it was sound. Meera could deliver flawless news about a bad decision, or clumsy news about a good one; a reader should never let skill at the first substitute for rigour on the second.

It assumes an ongoing relationship

The calculus changes when there is no repeat interaction. Much of the discipline exists to protect future trust; where there is no future to protect, the same investment may not be the efficient choice.

It assumes rough good faith

The method can be turned into leverage by a counterpart who performs anger or hurt identity to extract concessions. A thoughtful practitioner watches for the difference between a genuine reaction and a negotiating tactic in the same vocabulary.

The question to ask first

Before invoking any of this: am I actually avoiding a conversation that could simply be had directly? Escalating a minor update into a full three-conversation ritual can create the very sense of crisis the framework is meant to defuse.

Consumer, B2B, and Marketplace

How this plays out depends heavily on who is on the other end of the message, and how large the company delivering it has become.

ContextWhat changes
ConsumerRarely a named counterpart; bad news travels through release notes or support macros, and trust rebuilds across many consistent releases, not one dialogue.
B2BA named person with their own stakeholders, exactly as Rohan does for Meera; a direct, synchronous conversation is the highest-leverage tool, and skipping it for email is itself a signal.
MarketplaceDecisions are two-sided; news that helps sellers can quietly harm buyers or vice versa, so identity and contribution have to be worked out for two audiences before anyone is told anything.
Early-stage companyA founder or PM often has this conversation personally; trust runs deep, but there is no account layer to absorb a misstep, so the personal stakes are higher.
Large companyAn account manager is usually the actual messenger; the PM's job shifts to arming that person with an accurate account and a defensible plan, coaching them through the three conversations.

Common Mistakes

The first mistake is leading with the plan before acknowledging the impact. The symptom is a client who receives a reasonable recovery timeline and still escalates within days; the error is treating the conversation as a scheduling problem before the other side has felt heard. The cheapest diagnostic: check afterward whether impact was named before any fix was offered.

The second is burying the news inside a long status email rather than saying it out loud. The symptom is a client who discovers a slipped date from a changelog rather than from the person accountable; the mistake is choosing the channel most comfortable for the sender over the one matching the size of the news. The test: would this be said the same way, live, right now.

The third is quietly blaming a team or a client's own mid-project request to protect one's own identity. The symptom is subtle at first, but trust erodes over months as the internal and external stories visibly diverge. The diagnostic is to compare, word for word, what was told to the client with what was told to one's own manager.

The fourth is offering a new date built to end the conversation quickly rather than from the rigour that should have produced the first estimate. The symptom is a second broken promise weeks later, smaller but more damaging because it confirms a pattern. The diagnostic is whether the new number came from the same optimistic method, or a genuinely re-examined one.

What Good Looks Like

In the version that goes well, Meera opens by naming what happened in one sentence and the impact on Elaan's Diwali sale in the next, before mentioning a fix. She says plainly that she expects Rohan to be angry given what he has told his own board, and that the anger is fair. She lays out the contribution map — the patch, the missing buffer, the mid-sprint request — without assigning it to one person. She offers the two-scenario table above rather than a single date, letting Rohan choose between a phased rollout by October 18 or a full module by roughly October 22, both grounded in arithmetic a skeptical board member could check. She sends the written recap before day's end. Nothing removes the disappointment; what it removes is the second injury, the sense that Ekasutra did not know its own numbers or would not say them plainly.

Closing

Meera chose the phased option, agreed with Rohan on the call and confirmed in writing an hour later, and separately told her VP of Engineering that sprint estimates needed a standing buffer, not a one-off fix. The reasoning she gave her manager mirrored what she told Rohan almost exactly, which was, in her account, the point. Elaan renewed in March. The next topics worth studying are conflict and disagreement, which governs what happens when the two sides do not agree on the facts and not only the feelings, and leading through a crisis, which asks the same discipline to hold up with no eighteen hours to prepare. Two questions worth sitting with: will you know, before you open your mouth, what your own identity is riding on, not just the other person's? And how would you tell a counterpart who is genuinely hurt from one using that language to negotiate?

Eleven Seconds at the Gate: Pattan Terminal Systems and the Vasl Go-Live

Chennai, the night of Sunday, 22 March 2026

1. The night before

It had rained all evening in Besant Nagar, unseasonably, and by eleven o'clock Nandita Iyer had stopped pretending she would sleep. She sat at the dining table with two laptops open: on one, the slide her team had prepared for the steering committee at three o'clock the next afternoon, titled Thoothukudi Go-Live: Status Green with Watch Items; on the other, the spreadsheet from the dry run of 12 March, showing a ninety-fifth-percentile gate transaction time of 11.2 seconds against a contractual ceiling of 4.0.

Nandita had been Chief Product Officer of Pattan Terminal Systems for twenty-two months, long enough to learn that the hardest part of the job was not deciding what to build but deciding what to say, and to whom, and in what order. Tomorrow at three she would be on a call with Faisal Rahman, Chief Operating Officer of Vasl Ports Group in Dubai, who had staked his own credibility on Pattan when Vasl chose it over two better-known vendors. Also on the call: Pattan's head of sales, dialling in from New Jersey at 5:30 a.m. his time; the customer-success lead in Singapore; and a partner from Palash Capital Partners, who had asked for the dial-in on Friday with no explanation.

The slide said green. The spreadsheet said something else. Between them sat four facts Nandita had assembled over nine days and shared with no one outside her own product organisation: that the throughput requirement everyone had designed against might never have been agreed with Vasl's operations team; that two of Pattan's own measurements contradicted each other; that a customer-success manager had told Vasl's terminal manager in writing three weeks ago that the project was tracking to plan; and that the cheapest fix available would quietly undo a strategic decision the company had made in 2021 and sold to investors ever since.

2. Pattan Terminal Systems

Pattan Terminal Systems was founded in Chennai in 2013 by Anil Bhattacharya, a former terminal operations manager, and two engineers he met while automating a bulk berth in Visakhapatnam. Its first product was a terminal operating system — the software deciding where a container goes in a yard, which crane lifts it and what paperwork travels with it — sold to mid-sized Indian operators who could not afford the global incumbents. By FY26 Pattan employed about 1,150 people and expected recurring revenue of roughly ₹310 crore. Engineering sat in Pune and Chennai; the customs product group in Bengaluru; design in Berlin, inherited with a 2022 acquisition; data science in Toronto; customer success for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East in Singapore; enterprise sales in New Jersey.

The decision that shaped everything Nandita could now do was taken in 2021. Pattan's Indian customers ran deeply customised, on-premises installations, partly because their customs integrations — the CBIC's ICEGATE gateway, e-Sanchit filing, out-of-charge and let-export-order messages — had been built up port by port over years, and partly because port authorities were uneasy about yard data leaving the country. To sell abroad, Pattan needed something cleaner. Rather than refactor, the board approved a fork: the on-premises build would be maintained for Indian customers, and a new multi-tenant cloud build, Pattan Ocean, written for export markets. Meera Ganguly of Palash Capital Partners, who joined the board with that round, had argued for the fork and had argued ever since that Ocean was the whole equity story. The fork worked. It also meant the richest customs integration Pattan owned lived in a codebase Ocean could not call, and that every feature existing in one build had to be written twice or bridged.

3. The industry

Indian port software in 2026 was a crowded and suddenly fashionable place. PM Gati Shakti and the National Logistics Policy had pushed digital documentation into procurement checklists; the Unified Logistics Interface Platform and the port community systems run under the Indian Ports Association had made interoperability a compliance question rather than a nice-to-have. Adani Ports and SEZ, DP World and JSW Infrastructure were all investing in terminal automation. Indian firms such as Kale Logistics Solutions and Portall Infosystems competed for the documentation layer, while the terminal operating system itself remained dominated by long-established global products from vendors such as Kaleris and CyberLogitec, whose Indian references were thinner than their brochures suggested. That thinness was Pattan's opening.

Two regulatory currents ran through the Thoothukudi project. The first was customs: automated gates at an Indian container terminal must exchange five message families with ICEGATE, and a gate-in that cannot confirm out-of-charge status falls back to a manual counter. The second was the Digital Personal Data Protection Act. Pattan's gate automation read truck plates by optical character recognition and matched driver identity records; under Ocean that processing happened in a Dubai cloud region. Counsel's cautious January note called this "defensible with consent and a processing agreement, though not free of risk", and recommended, without insisting, that Indian gate data be processed in India.

Vasl Ports Group, headquartered in Dubai, ran feeder and multipurpose terminals in the UAE and Oman and in 2025 won a concession for a container berth at V.O. Chidambaranar Port, Thoothukudi — its first Indian operation, and the reason the Pattan relationship had become something closer to a joint bet. Its customers were global carriers whose schedules did not move: a vessel berths, a thousand boxes come off, and within four hours the trucks arrive.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

In September 2024 Vasl signed a five-year, ₹96 crore agreement for Pattan Ocean across three terminals, the Indian one sequenced last. In October 2025 the two companies agreed that Thoothukudi would cut over on 20 April 2026, ahead of the pre-monsoon peak and the start of Vasl's own service-level regime.

On 14 November 2025 a requirements document was signed off. It specified a peak of 420 truck transactions per hour across six gate lanes and a ninety-fifth-percentile gate transaction time of 4.0 seconds. Nandita had since established that the 420 came from a sizing spreadsheet prepared by Pattan's own solution architect out of berth-capacity arithmetic, not from Vasl's traffic data; Vasl's operations team had supplied two weeks of September gate counts, an off-peak month, and never formally endorsed the number. Nobody had said anything wrong. Nobody had checked either.

On 9 January 2026 the Pune performance team ran the load test summarised in Exhibit 2 and reported a p95 of 3.8 seconds. The result circulated widely and is the basis of the green status on tomorrow's slide. Its covering note said, in the fourth paragraph, that the test used synthetic container records with plate recognition disabled and only two of five ICEGATE message families implemented.

On 27 February the Bengaluru group delivered a bridge: a connector letting Ocean reach the three missing customs flows by calling the on-premises build at a Pattan-managed node in Chennai. It worked. Each round trip cost five to seven seconds.

On 12 March an end-to-end dry run at Thoothukudi, with real plate recognition, real customs messages and 180 trucks, returned a p95 of 11.2 seconds. Exhibit 3 sets that beside Paschim Coastal Terminals, a Pattan customer on the Gujarat coast running the on-premises build at 2.9 seconds — a comparison circulated inside Pattan as evidence that "the product is fine, the bridge is the problem", true in a narrow sense and misleading in every other.

On 18 March Dr. Priya Venkataraman's group in Toronto produced the queue simulation in Exhibit 4. On 19 March, Wei Tan forwarded Nandita the email he had sent on 27 February to Vasl's terminal manager describing the project as on track. On 20 March, Palash Capital asked to join.

Owns the commitment and the conversation. Believes the honest thing is to put the 11.2-second number in front of Faisal Rahman tomorrow. Has not said that she signed the November requirements document herself without querying the 420 figure, and expects to be asked about it in front of the board.

Has not said that his own 2025 scoping omitted plate recognition from the latency budget, or that three of his six senior Ocean engineers have resigned since December.
Sharmila Krishnan — Director of Product, Gateway and Customs, Bengaluru.

Has not said that she raised the missing families in a comment on the requirements document on 11 November, that nobody replied, and that she kept the link.
Lena Brandt — Principal Designer, Berlin.

Has not said that she has never seen an Indian gate at peak, and that her confidence rests on one video call with a Vasl supervisor in Sohar.
Dr. Priya Venkataraman — Head of Data Science, Toronto.
Built the queue model and will defend it. Wants the decision made on the curve, not on anecdote. Has not foregrounded that it assumes Poisson arrivals, while the September Thoothukudi sample shows heavy bunching after a vessel sails — a pattern under which her curve understates the queue.

Holds a ₹140 crore pipeline with two Gulf operators and one East African port, all of which have asked for a Vasl reference call after go-live. Wants 20 April held. Has not said that at a dinner in Dubai in January he told Faisal that Pattan would "make it right commercially" if the date moved — a sentence with no contractual existence and considerable memory.

Chose Pattan against advice and has told his own board Thoothukudi opens on schedule. Wants a working terminal more than a date, but has not said which he will defend if forced, and has begun asking for weekly rather than fortnightly reports.

Championed the 2021 fork and treats Ocean adoption as the central metric of the pre-IPO story. Has not said why she asked for tomorrow's dial-in, nor whether she already knows the 12 March result.

8. The options as Nandita sees them

By Sunday evening Nandita had written her options on a single sheet. The first: hold 20 April and harden the bridge, telling Faisal tomorrow to expect roughly seven seconds at go-live, proposing the two assisted lanes Lena had sketched, and waiving the first quarter's support fee. The second: slip to 15 June, finish the native customs flows in Ocean, absorb two months of liquidated damages at ₹1.2 crore each and a ₹14 crore milestone pushed into the next quarter. The third is Sharmila's: deploy the on-premises build at Thoothukudi, live on 4 May, the safest and cheapest of the three, and a direct contradiction of five years of strategy and of what Meera Ganguly tells investors about Ocean.

Each option, written this way, is a statement about what to build. None is a statement about what to say, and Nandita was uneasily aware that the three-o'clock call would turn on the second rather than the first. She had no answer to what happens to any of them if Vasl's operations team says 420 per hour was never their number — that the real peak is nearer 300, in which case Exhibit 4 puts the bridge inside tolerance, or nearer 480 in bursts, in which case it does not. Nor to whether Wei's 27 February email should be raised tomorrow or left to be found. And all three options assume the conversation is with Faisal, when the harder ones might be with Gurpreet about a promise made at a dinner, with Rajat about a scoping omission never named aloud, and with her own board about a document she signed.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The steering committee convenes at 3:00 p.m. IST on Monday, 23 March; Vasl's board pack closes on Friday, 27 March. The contract provides liquidated damages of ₹1.2 crore per month of delay, capped at ₹9.6 crore, and no relief for performance below the 4.0-second SLA except service credits once the terminal is live — so a slow system that goes live on time is, contractually, cheaper than a fast system that goes live late. Pattan's FY26 forecast assumes the ₹14 crore acceptance milestone in the April–June quarter; Palash Capital is preparing a pre-IPO round on Ocean's adoption. January's hiring freeze means any engineer-months come out of two other customers' roadmaps. Counsel's DPDP note is unresolved and applies to the bridge and Ocean alike, but not to the on-premises build. Three senior Ocean engineers have already gone.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Reading Exhibits 2, 3 and 4 together, what does Pattan actually know about how the Thoothukudi gate will perform on 20 April, and what does it merely believe?
  2. Exhibit 3 has been used inside Pattan to argue that "the product is fine, the bridge is the problem." What is wrong with the inference, and who benefits from its repetition?
  3. Whose is the difficult conversation here — Nandita's with Faisal, or one of the internal ones deferred for four months? What does continuing to defer each of them cost?
  4. If Nandita discloses the 11.2-second result tomorrow, what should she disclose with it: the load-test caveats, the disputed 420 figure, Wei's email, Gurpreet's dinner? Which omissions are judgement and which are concealment?
  5. Faisal said on 10 March that he could live with eleven seconds but not with being told in April that Pattan knew in March. Take him at his word: what does that imply about which options are survivable, and what does it leave unsettled?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Nandita do before three o'clock, what does she say on the call, and what does she tell her own board on Tuesday about how a document she signed came to specify a number nobody had verified?

At twenty minutes to two the rain had stopped. Nandita had a draft email to Faisal open in one window, four paragraphs long, and a draft message to Gurpreet in another, two lines long and rewritten eleven times. On her phone was an unanswered message from Wei: Still up. Do you want me to set up a call with Faisal before the steering committee, or do we go in cold? She had read it three times and had not replied.

People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Writing as a PM Superpower

Two product leaders, six weeks apart, discover that the document is not the report of the decision. It is the decision.

1. Two decisions that will be settled on paper

On 12 October 2026, Kavya Deshpande, vice-president of product at Roshni Grid Analytics in Pune, opened a blank document she had been avoiding for nine days. Roshni sells feeder-level load and outage analytics to eleven state distribution utilities and four private distribution licensees, on annual contracts worth ₹46 crore in total. One of its modules — a transformer-failure prediction service sold as an add-on — was consuming nine of Roshni's fifty-one engineers and was live at three customers. Two of those three were Roshni's largest accounts, at ₹7.2 crore and ₹5.4 crore a year. Kavya believed the module should be sunset. She also believed that saying so badly would cost Roshni a renewal, and that the board meeting on 6 November would not give her forty minutes to be subtle.

Eleven hundred kilometres away, on 19 November, Farhan Qureshi was in the same position with none of the same facts. Farhan was group product manager at Riyaaz Learning Cloud, a Mumbai company whose Classes 9 to 12 study app had 4.8 lakh monthly active learners and 61,000 paying subscribers at ₹499 a month. His team had built a large-language-model tutor that answered a student's own worked step rather than serving a pre-written hint, and in a four-week test it had lifted thirty-day retention from 38% to 46%. It also cost money every time a student thought out loud. Riyaaz's pricing review was on 30 November, and the founders had asked one question: does the tutor stay free inside the ₹499 plan, or does it become a ₹799 tier?

Neither decision was blocked on analysis. Both were blocked on getting five to nine people, most of whom would read the material once and at speed, to hold the same facts in their heads in an order that made the trade-off visible rather than arguable. That is why writing is not a soft skill adjacent to product management but the medium in which most consequential product management is performed.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define it precisely. Writing as a product-management practice is the use of expository prose — complete sentences, in a governed order, with sourced quantities — as the primary instrument for forming, testing and transmitting a decision. The claim is not that writing communicates thinking well, but that prose is a detector. A sentence must assert a relation between its parts, so a gap in reasoning shows up as a sentence you cannot finish. A bullet list has no such property; two fragments can sit adjacent for years without anyone noticing that the second does not follow from the first.

The practice was invented against a specific enemy. In 2004 Amazon's senior team banned slide presentations for major decisions in favour of six-page narratives read silently at the start of the meeting, on the reasoning — later set out in the 2017 shareholder letter — that the narrative structure of a good memo forces better thought and a better sense of what matters more than what. The lineage runs further back. Barbara Minto's pyramid method, developed at McKinsey in the 1960s and 1970s, had already argued that a reader should receive the answer first and the support in a hierarchy beneath it.

Four schools now disagree, and the disagreement is about mechanism, not about whether writing is nice.

The narrative school holds that the prose itself does the cognitive work. It will sign: a six-page narrative read in silence produces better decisions than any presentation of the same material. It will not sign that every artefact should be prose.

The structure school, descended from Minto, holds that the work is done by the logical tree — answer, then mutually exclusive supporting claims, then evidence — and that flowing prose is merely a serialisation of it. It will sign: a reader must be able to reconstruct the argument's skeleton from the headings alone. It will not sign that narrative voice adds rigour; to this school, a beautifully written memo with a broken tree is worse than an ugly one with a sound tree, because it hides the break.

The velocity school holds that writing is a tax that scales with organisational distance and should be paid only when that distance is real. It will sign: before product-market fit, in a team of nine sitting together, a six-page memo destroys more value than it creates. It will not sign that writing is optional at scale.

The record school, descended from the architectural-decision-record and DACI tradition, holds that the durable value is retrieval. It will sign: an undocumented decision will be re-litigated, and re-litigation is the largest hidden cost in a scaling organisation. It will not sign that the drafting process is where the value lives; to this school a memo written after the decision is still worth most of its price.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Experts do not write a memo and then check it. They execute a sequence whose middle steps are usually left implicit when the practice is taught.

The decision sentence comes first, before any drafting. Kavya's, written on a sticky note before she wrote a paragraph, read: Roshni should stop selling the failure-prediction module to new customers from 1 December and support the three live deployments for eighteen months; we will know this was wrong if either large account puts renewal at risk in writing.

Every number is tagged by provenance.Expert memos mark three classes in the text: measured (it came from a system, named), derived (it came from measured numbers by an arithmetic the memo shows), and assumed (nobody knows; here is the value, the basis and the sensitivity). The reason is second-order. Once assumptions are visibly tagged, the meeting's attention migrates to them automatically, which is where attention should go.

Alternatives get symmetric depth. The working test used by experienced reviewers is crude and effective: count the words spent on the rejected option. If the recommendation gets eleven hundred words and the alternative gets sixty, the alternative was not modelled.

The FAQ is drafted before the memo is finished, and it reorders the memo. Writing out the six questions the room will actually ask reveals which of them the body cannot answer. Kavya's FAQ produced one she could not answer well — whether Roshni's largest account had bought the platform because of the prediction module — and that question moved into the body as a section of its own.

The document is read in silence, in the room, before anyone speaks. It converts the currency of the meeting from confidence to reasoning.

There is a modest quantitative treatment, and it is about time rather than words. Since January, Roshni had recorded the median days between a question being raised in a leadership forum and a decision being recorded against it: 23 days across 31 decisions before the memo protocol, 9 across 24 decisions after. The cost side is arithmetically honest: Kavya spent about 11 hours drafting and two reviewers spent 3 hours between them. Fourteen person-hours of writing bought fourteen fewer days of nine engineers pointed at a module the company had already half-decided to stop selling — at roughly ₹1.4 lakh per engineer-month, about ₹5.9 lakh of directed effort.

4. The conditions, stated so they can be tested

Writing pays when specific conditions hold. Each is falsifiable, and each applies differently to our two protagonists.

C1: the decision is expensive to reverse. Kavya's passes — a sunset announcement cannot be unsaid to a utility procurement committee. Farhan's passes only partly; a price tier can be withdrawn in a fortnight.

C2: the deciders are not all in the room, or not all at the same time. Roshni's board includes an investor director in Singapore who will read the pack on a flight. Riyaaz's two founders sit eight feet from Farhan, which weakens the case for length.

C3: the disagreement is about facts or logic, not values or authority. Kavya's disagreement with her head of sales was factual — was the module load-bearing in the account? Farhan's disagreement with his founders was partly about values: whether a learning company should paywall the feature that most improves learning. Prose sharpens the second kind but cannot settle it, and a memo that pretends otherwise reads as manipulation.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. When the underlying evidence is thin, prose manufactures false precision. When the real blocker is authority, a memo becomes a weapon — circulated to build a coalition, with the decider's name in the header and the decider's actual objection absent. And when speed dominates, as in a live outage, the ritual is wrong: incident command runs on terse structured status, and a team demanding narrative during a P1 is performing a culture rather than practising one.

5. Hard edges: portfolios, platforms, regulation, hardware, AI

The single-product memo is the easy case. In a multi-product company the memo is often right for one profit-and-loss line and wrong for the portfolio. Mature companies handle this with a header field naming whose economics the memo is computed against, and a reader of record from outside the unit.

Two-sided businesses break memos in a particular way: an argument that reads as airtight from the demand side collapses when the same numbers are restated from the supply side. Marketplace writers run the core table twice, once per side.

Regulated contexts change what may be written at all. Roshni's customers are licensees under state electricity regulatory commissions, and its memos may surface in a customer audit. Counsel at such firms teach a narrow rule: write conclusions and evidence, not speculation about exposure. What mature companies say is that everything is written down; what they do is maintain a quiet perimeter around what is written down.

Hardware adds irreversibility on a calendar. A bill-of-materials freeze or a tooling order converts a soft recommendation into a cash commitment with a twelve-to-sixteen-week shadow, so hardware memos carry a decision-expiry date: after this date the recommendation is void because the option has closed.

AI-native products break the numbers themselves. Farhan's retention lift of eight percentage points was measured against one model version at one prompt configuration; a vendor update three weeks later could move it without anyone at Riyaaz changing a line of code. Competent AI memos therefore date and version their evidence explicitly — measured against model version X, week of Y, at temperature Z — and state their quantities as ranges.

At organisational seams, the failure is semantic rather than structural. A memo written in Roshni's analytics group used "feeder" to mean a distribution feeder; the same word in the customer's operations team included the sub-transmission tier. Two readers agreed on a sentence and disagreed about the world. Mature teams keep a short glossary at the foot of recurring memos.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The memo changes the writer's mind, not just the reader's

The competent practitioner writes down a conclusion they arrived at elsewhere. The expert expects drafting to alter the conclusion, and is suspicious when it does not. The tell: an expert can usually name the draft in which the recommendation flipped. The obvious reading — that a writer who changes position was sloppy in the first place — is exactly backwards; the memo did its job.

Answer-first is not the same as confidence-first

Beginners taught to lead with the recommendation assert loudly and defer all evidence. An expert's first paragraph carries the recommendation, one load-bearing number and the condition that would overturn it — which reads as less confident and is far harder to dismiss. The tell: a falsifier in the first six lines.

Assumptions are marked, not smoothed

A consistent memo makes every figure look equally solid. The expert breaks that surface, writing that a figure is assumed, on what basis, and what the recommendation looks like at half and double the value. The tell: a memo that names its own weakest number before a reviewer does. The obvious reading is that this invites attack; in practice it directs attack to ground the writer has already worked.

Length is spent on the appendix, not on the argument

Experts hold the argument to two or three pages and push derivations, cohort tables and method notes into appendices that most readers will never open and one reader will read with total attention. The tell: a short body with a long, well-ordered tail. A uniformly long memo is usually one whose argument was never resolved.

The FAQ carries the real disagreement

In strong memos the FAQ contains at least one question the author cannot answer well and says so. The tell: reading the FAQ alone tells you where the organisation is split.

The memo is addressed to whoever holds the decision right

Experts name the decider, the consulted parties and the decision type in the header, because a document written for a person who cannot say yes will not produce a yes. The tell: a header naming one person rather than a distribution list. The objection that this is bureaucratic misses that ambiguity about who decides is the commonest cause of a memo that is admired and then ignored.

Prose levels status, and also filters by language

Silent reading strips out seniority and vocal confidence, which is the point. It also advantages fluent English writers in organisations where most people work in their third language. Expert teams separate the two reviews, and hold that an awkward sentence carrying a sound claim outranks a graceful one carrying a weak claim. The tell: reviewers who comment on logic before grammar.

A memo has a second life as a record

Written for a decision, a memo is read eighteen months later as evidence of why. Experts append a four-line decision record after the meeting — what was decided, by whom, on what date, and what would trigger a revisit — because the memo's recommendation is not the decision the room actually reached. The tell: old memos with outcomes attached.

7. How this varies by product type and company stage

Much of the mechanic does not vary, and saying so plainly is more useful than manufacturing distinctions. Answer-first ordering, provenance tagging, symmetric alternatives and a named decider are as correct for a semiconductor roadmap as for a subscription price change. What varies is which evidence is admissible and who the reader is.

Consumer memos rest on behaviour, so they open with an observed sequence — what a learner did in the app at 10.40 on a Tuesday night — because aggregate conversion numbers without a mechanism are unfalsifiable. Enterprise and B2B memos rest on procurement and integration reality: the question is not whether users like the change but whether it survives a security review and a three-month approval cycle. Platform and marketplace memos must state the trade from both sides in symmetric form.

Stage matters more than type. In a nine-person seed-stage company the founders hold the whole context and a memo mostly documents what three people already agreed; the velocity school is right there. The inflection arrives when the first decision must be made by people who were not in the original conversation — typically between sixty and two hundred employees, or at the first second office. Roshni crossed it when its Chennai delivery team grew past its Pune product team; Riyaaz has not crossed it yet, which is why Farhan's two-page brief is not a compromise but the correct instrument. At scale the binding constraint inverts again: the problem is no longer writing memos but reading them, and the scarce resource becomes senior attention.

8. Three worked examples

Roshni's sunset memo. The core table did most of the persuading.
