Expected cost of renewal risk₹1.08 croreDerived

Read straight, the module looked marginally profitable and strategically dangerous to touch. The sentence that changed the room was not in the table: fourteen of two hundred and eight alerts had produced a work order, so the module's customers were paying for a service they were not operating. At the assumed 15% renewal risk the sunset was roughly break-even in year one; at 35% it was a ₹1.4 crore mistake. Kavya wrote both, and proposed an eighteen-month support commitment that priced the risk down rather than arguing it away.

Riyaaz's pricing brief. Farhan's arithmetic was smaller and tighter. Average tutor use ran at 47 minutes per active learner per month, at a measured inference cost of ₹0.38 per minute of interaction, giving ₹17.86 per learner-month against a ₹499 subscription — 3.6% of revenue. The load-bearing claim was retention: eight points on a base of 38% extended median subscription life from 4.1 to 5.2 months, worth roughly ₹549 of lifetime revenue per paying learner against ₹93 of inference. Farhan's brief recommended keeping the tutor in the base plan and stated the falsifier: if usage rose above 90 minutes a month without a corresponding retention gain, the economics inverted within a quarter.

The memo that failed. In February 2026, a Roshni product manager had written an eleven-page memo recommending a ₹1.9 crore integration with a meter-data vendor, projecting 4.8x return over three years. It was well written, well received and approved in one meeting.Its central quantity — a 35% attach rate among existing customers — was an analogy borrowed from a different market, set in the same confident register as the measured figures beside it. The realised rate after eight months was 6%. The memo failed because its form flattened the difference between a measurement and a guess, and its polish bought it too easy a review. The recovery: Roshni began requiring that any assumption carrying more than a quarter of a memo's projected value be pre-registered as a thirty-day test with a named owner before funding released, and Kavya's October memo was the first to be written under that rule.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The buried ask. Early sign: the first fifteen minutes of discussion are spent establishing what is being proposed. Diagnostic question: can a stranger state the decision after reading only paragraph one? Caught late, it costs a meeting cycle — at board cadence, a quarter.

The backfilled memo. Early sign: the document appears after the choice is made, uniformly confident, with no discarded option. Diagnostic: which paragraph would be different if the evidence had come out the other way? Caught late, the organisation keeps the cost, loses the forcing function, and stops trusting the format.

False precision. Early sign: three-significant-figure outputs from one-significant-figure inputs. Diagnostic: measured, derived or assumed? Caught late: ₹1.9 crore and two quarters.

Consensus prose. Early sign: the memo survives five reviewers without a single sentence being contested, because each contested sentence was softened. Diagnostic: what claim in here could someone competent disagree with? A memo nobody can disagree with decides nothing.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does the prose do the work, or does the structure? The narrative position rests on an observed mechanism — writers report catching gaps mid-sentence that survived outlining —. The structure position rests on the fact that most memos fail on their logical tree rather than their sentences, and that Minto's method delivered rigour for decades without narrative voice. Neither rests on controlled evidence; there is no randomised comparison of narrative against structured briefs on matched decisions. The narrative position weakens if teams trained only in structured briefs produce equal decision quality and equally low re-litigation.

Is writing a tax on speed? The velocity position is stronger than its caricature: in a co-located team where every decider holds full context, the memo's coordination value is near zero while its cost is eleven hours of the person best placed to be building. The counter-position holds that the cost is paid anyway, later, as re-litigation. What would settle it is decision-latency data of the kind Roshni collected, gathered across many firms and stages.

Does an AI-drafted memo retain the forcing function? One camp holds that the value was always in the artefact — a clear, ordered, sourced document a room can interrogate — and that a model drafting it from the writer's notes removes drudgery. The other holds that the value was in the act, that the gap you cannot write past is only detected by the person writing, and that a fluent draft handed to a reviewer produces the February failure at industrial scale: polish uncoupled from understanding. The strongest available test is behavioural rather than textual — whether writers using models still change their recommendation during drafting at the historical rate. The field has not settled this.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in ways visible before they write anything. They ask who decides before asking what to include. They keep a running ledger of the assumptions their team is operating on and can say which three would be most expensive to be wrong about. They treat a reviewer who finds a broken claim as having done them a favour worth several lakh rupees. Most tellingly, their memos contain sentences that cost them something — an admission that the number they most need is the one they do not have.

12. What Kavya and Farhan decided

Kavya sent five pages, with eleven pages of appendix, on 30 October. The board read for eighteen minutes in silence. The investor director's first question was the one from Kavya's own FAQ, and Kavya's answer was that she could not establish it either way, which is why the recommendation carried an eighteen-month support commitment rather than a clean withdrawal. The board approved the sunset for new sales on 6 November, with a review triggered if either large account raised renewal in writing.

Farhan sent two pages on 24 November. The tutor stayed inside the ₹499 plan. The founders added a condition Farhan had not proposed: a monthly review of minutes-per-learner against the 90-minute falsifier, owned by Farhan, reported in four lines. He has written those four lines every month since — the smallest and most durable form the practice takes.

Discussion questions

1. Kavya priced renewal risk at an assumed 15% and tested 5% to 35%. Was an eighteen-month support commitment the right instrument for an untestable assumption, or did it buy peace at the cost of the clarity the memo was written to produce?
2. Riyaaz's founders sit eight feet from Farhan. Did the two-page brief succeed because it was well written, or because the decision was small enough that any competent artefact would have worked?
3. Roshni answered the February failure with a rule about pre-registering assumptions. Such rules are usually obeyed for two quarters. What would make this one survive, and what would you measure to know?

13. Going deeper

Writing clearly — the sentence-level craft beneath all of this.

Customer-facing communication — the same discipline where the reader has no obligation to finish.

Asynchronous communication — how written decisions let a team split across Pune, Chennai and Singapore move at the speed of the clearest thinker.

Stakeholder mapping and management — who the memo is addressed to, and who must be consulted first.

Communicating with leadership — the compression problem: the same argument at five pages, one page and ninety seconds, without losing the falsifier.

Telling the customer story — supplies the observed sequence a consumer memo needs.

Demo and pitch craft — the live counterpart, where showing beats describing.

Decision records and DACI/RACI — turns a memo into something retrievable eighteen months later.

Running effective meetings — the silent read and the invitee cap are meeting design, not writing, and the memo fails without them.
case40v1-comm.writing:
Communication & Stakeholder Management · Case 40

Ojas Diagnostics Network: The Record of What We Knew

Hyderabad, Sunday, 22 November 2026, 11:15 p.m. IST

1. The night before

The Jubilee Hills apartment was quiet except for a generator two floors down. Aparna Raghunathan, Director of Product for Ojas Bridge, had a document open titled Ojas Insight — Note to the Board, 23 November. It held a heading, her name, and nothing else. The board call was at 8:30 the next morning, and the note had to circulate by 6:00 a.m., so that Rukmini Bhat, the chief executive, could read it on the drive in from Banjara Hills.

Rukmini's instruction on Friday was compressed. "Two pages. Written so I can read it aloud without translating it. Tell the board what we are selling, what consent we have for it, and what we are going to do." This note was different in a way she had been circling all weekend: it would not describe a decision so much as become the company's account of what it had known, and when, about the data under its most valuable product. Farida Qureshi, who ran legal and privacy from Delhi, had put it in one line: "Whatever you write on Sunday is our contemporaneous record. Write it as though the Data Protection Board is reading it in 2029."

Five days earlier an engineer in Bengaluru, Sandeep Pai, had asked a channel of nine people a small question about a database key: did the Insight training view, joined on the unified identity, not pull in everything back to 2019? By Friday it had grown into three irreconcilable accounts of a decision taken in March 2021: a product requirements document, a set of board minutes, a Jira ticket. She had read all three, and still could not say, in a sentence she would sign, what Ojas had decided in 2021.

On her second screen was the Dhairya General Insurance term sheet: ₹28 crore over three years, ₹8.4 crore in year one, signed on 5 November. Dhairya's board met on 4 December.

2. Ojas Diagnostics Network, 2013–2026

Ojas was founded in Hyderabad in 2013 by Dr Srinivas Kalyanam, a pathologist from the public system, and Harish Adiga, an operations manager. Their thesis was unglamorous: diagnostics was fragmented, quality varied street by street, and a chain that invested in accreditation could win on trust rather than price. By FY26 Ojas ran six NABL-accredited laboratories and 148 collection centres across Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Maharashtra, and reported revenue of ₹742 crore at an EBITDA margin of 14.8 per cent (Exhibit 2).

Two things changed the company's shape. Ojas One, a consumer app launched in 2019, carried 38 per cent of retail volume by 2026. Ojas Bridge, launched in 2021, sold structured, coded laboratory results through APIs to hospitals, insurers and health apps. Bridge was small — ₹61 crore in FY26 — but carried a 71 per cent gross margin against 39 per cent for retail, and it was why Drishti Growth Partners had led a ₹310 crore Series C in January 2024 at a ₹2,900 crore valuation.

The decision that constrains Aparna today was taken in March 2021 and was, at the time, uncontroversial. Ojas One and the laboratory system held separate patient identities: the same person appeared twice, once as an app user and once as a specimen. Project Sangam unified them under one hashed key derived from the mobile number. The document that authorised it ran to four pages, and on page three, under Open items, sat the sentence Aparna had now read forty times: "Unify identity across O1 and LIS/Bridge; consent parity assumed, to confirm with legal." No record of that confirmation exists. Dr Kalyanam had signed the document; so had the head of engineering, who left in 2023.

3. The industry

Indian diagnostics in 2026 was a market under margin compression. The listed chains — Dr Lal PathLabs, Metropolis, Thyrocare — had spent three years defending price against venture-funded entrants such as Redcliffe Labs and Healthians, while Tata 1mg, PharmEasy and Apollo 24|7 bundled tests into subscription plans. A lipid profile Ojas had sold at ₹690 in 2021 fetched ₹399 in Hyderabad in 2026; volume growth of 14 per cent produced revenue growth of six.

The regulatory ground had moved too. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission had made ABHA identifiers routine in referrals. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its rules had introduced an enforceable duty of notice and purpose-limited consent, a consent-manager architecture, and penalties up to ₹250 crore. Health data was not a separate category in the Act, but every lawyer Ojas consulted treated it as the highest-risk class. Meanwhile IRDAI's push toward risk-based pricing had made insurers hungry for exactly what Ojas held: longitudinal, laboratory-grade biomarkers on a stable identity.

That hunger was the premise of Ojas Insight, which turned nine years of results into cohort-level risk scores an underwriter could price against without seeing any individual report. Nikhil Ahluwalia's pipeline, built from New Jersey, held two Indian insurers, a third-party administrator, and Dawaam Health Holdings, a Dubai clinic group serving Indian expatriates. Darpan Pathology Group, Ojas's closest rival, had announced a similar product in September and said nothing publicly about consent.

4. What happened, and what has turned out to be wrong

The sequence matters more than any single fact in it (Exhibit 1).

In August 2022 the growth team rewrote the Ojas One consent screen. The old version listed six purposes and required a scroll; the new one offered one check box beside "I agree to Ojas using my health information to improve services and offer relevant products." Booking conversion improved nine percentage points. Lena Brückner, the Berlin design lead who drafted both, wrote in the review thread that the shorter text "does less work than it appears to." The comment was resolved.

In January 2024 Drishti's investment memorandum called Bridge's data asset "a defensible, compounding position." Nobody disputed it in writing. That September Farida commented on the Insight product brief: "Purpose limitation — secondary use for underwriting is not covered by the 2022 notice. Flagging." The thread was resolved eleven days later with no reply. It was closed by the then product lead, Divya Pillai, who has since moved to customer success in Singapore, remembers the conversation differently, and does not remember closing it.

In November 2025 Insight began a pilot with Dhairya on 4.1 lakh patients, producing an AUC of 0.78 against Dhairya's claims outcomes, versus 0.66 for the questionnaire model it replaced. Ashwin Balachandran, Dhairya's chief underwriter, called it the best external signal his team had tested.

In March 2026 Karthik Menon's team migrated Bridge to a new warehouse, and a backfill job re-keyed historical records against the Sangam key. The migration existed as tickets; no design document was written, because the team agreed it was "a lift and shift." Whether that backfill copied pre-2022 records into the store Insight reads is Sandeep's question. Karthik's first answer was no; his second, on Thursday, was that he needed a week.

On 5 November the Dhairya term sheet was signed. On 12 November the statutory auditor's interim management letter carried one observation under IT general controls: data provenance for the analytics warehouse is not evidenced by documentation of source-level consent. Rukmini read it as routine. Farida read it as the beginning of something.

What has turned out to be wrong is not one fact but a chain. Ojas believed the 2021 unification had been cleared by legal; no record supports this. It believed the 2022 notice covered secondary analytics; Farida and Lena say otherwise. It believed the training set was post-2022 only; Karthik can no longer confirm that. And it believed — hardest of all for Aparna to write down — that it had a functioning decision record, because every choice since 2019 was written up somewhere. Exhibit 3 is what happens when "somewhere" means three places.

5. The people

Aparna Raghunathan — Director of Product, Ojas Bridge, Hyderabad. Position: the note must state the consent gap plainly. Incentive: Insight is her promotion case, already tabled. Not saying: she approved the March 2026 migration without asking whether a design document existed.
Rukmini Bhat — Chief Executive, Mumbai. Position: the board needs a decision, not an essay. Incentive: a Series D conversation opens in February. Not saying: in October she told the board the deal was "signed in principle," before any term sheet existed.
Dr Srinivas Kalyanam — Co-founder and Chief Medical Officer, Hyderabad. Position: no patient should be surprised by what Ojas does with their results. Incentive: his name is on the accreditation. Not saying: he signed the 2021 PRD and read two pages of it.
Farida Qureshi — Head of Legal and Privacy, Delhi. Position: fresh, purpose-specific consent before any pre-2023 record touches Insight. Incentive: she is the named person if a complaint is filed. Not saying: her 2024 flag was a comment, not a memo.
Karthik Menon — Vice President, Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: clean cohort separation is achievable in seven months with eleven engineers. Incentive: his twice-deferred platform roadmap would finally be funded. Not saying: he does not know what the March backfill copied, and has told two people different things.
Ira Sequeira — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: restricting Insight to post-2022 records destroys it; AUC falls from 0.78 to about 0.71, below Dhairya's floor. Incentive: her first model in production. Not saying: 0.71 is one uncross-validated notebook run on 40,000 rows.
Nikhil Ahluwalia — Senior Vice President, Global Health Accounts, New Jersey. Position: close Dhairya, then Dawaam; Darpan is already selling. Incentive: 40 per cent of his variable pay rides on Insight bookings. Not saying: he demonstrated Insight in Dubai in September on a screen showing real cohort counts.
Lena Brückner — Design Lead, Berlin. Position: the 2022 screen was written to convert, not to inform, and Ojas should say so. Incentive: credibility; she has an offer elsewhere. Not saying: she wrote the softer copy after being asked to "keep it simple," and never escalated.
Divya Pillai — Director, Customer Success, Singapore. Position: hospital clients must hear this from Ojas first. Incentive: Deodar Hospitals Network, her largest account, renews in March. Not saying: she closed Farida's 2024 thread.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. Timeline, 2019–2026
Reconstructed by Aparna from Jira and page histories, 21–22 November. The March date is the migration cut-over; the backfill job's own start date is not recorded.
Exhibit 2. Ojas Diagnostics Network, FY26 financial summary

Audited, except Bridge gross margin, a management allocation of shared laboratory and platform cost, restated once.
Exhibit 3. Three records of one decision (Project Sangam, March 2021)

PRD v1.3, page 3, Open items"Unify identity across O1 and LIS/Bridge; consent parity assumed, to confirm with legal."Approved; consent question left open.
Board minutes, 26 March 2021, item 7"Noted the technical consolidation of patient identifiers. Management confirmed no change to data use."Board told nothing changed; never tested.
Jira SANG-114, closing comment"Merged. Unlocks analytics on full history — see roadmap item B-7 (risk scoring)."Engineering understood the purpose to be the use now disputed.
All three extracts are verbatim. The PRD's history shows "to confirm with legal" was added three days before sign-off, by an account since deactivated. No legal review ticket exists for March or April 2021.
Exhibit 4. Consent ledger by cohort, as of 31 October 2026

Cohorts before March 2021 were reconstructed from app build timestamps, not stored consent receipts; Ojas began storing receipts in November 2021. About 6.8 lakh patients in the first row have no retrievable receipt at all; walk-in forms were never versioned.

The 34 per cent comes from a 2025 wellness opt-in offering a ₹500 voucher; the 11 per cent from Ojas's July 2026 consent-refresh SMS, which offered nothing. Neither asked the question Insight requires.
Exhibit 6. Internal analysis: memo length and decision speed, 2024–2026
From 113 decision documents, prepared for the July 2026 operating review. It does not control for stakes: of the 14 documents over 2,000 words, 9 concerned capital expenditure above ₹5 crore or an organisational change. Rukmini has cited it twice this month.

7. Voices

Karthik Menon, direct message to Aparna, Thursday 19 November, 10:48 p.m."I told the channel there's a filter. I can't find the line. I'm not saying it isn't there — I'm saying I can't find it, and the person who wrote that config is on notice period. Give me a week."
Farida Qureshi, email to Aparna, Rukmini and Dr Kalyanam, Friday 20 November, 9:05 a.m."I want to be precise, because I have been imprecise before and it cost us. Consent must be specific and for a stated purpose. Underwriting risk scores are not the purpose stated in any notice before October 2023 — 61 per cent of the patient base. I am not saying we cannot ship. I am saying we cannot ship on those records and call ourselves compliant in the same sentence."
Nikhil Ahluwalia, reply-all, Friday 20 November, 9:40 a.m. IST"Respectfully — Darpan announces general availability in three weeks, and Dhairya's board meets 4 December. If our note says 'seven months and ₹4.6 crore', the deal is gone and the pipeline with it. Farida, can external counsel give a written view that the 2022 notice is defensible?"
Dr Srinivas Kalyanam, WhatsApp to Aparna, Saturday 21 November, 7:58 a.m."Aparna, I have re-read the 2021 document. I signed it. I read two pages. This is not a lawyer's problem, it is mine. Write what happened. Do not make it sound better than it was."
Ira Sequeira, comment on the draft note, Saturday 21 November, 3:22 p.m. IST"Please don't put 0.71 in a board document as if it were measured. If the board reads it as fact and the true number is 0.75, we will have talked ourselves out of the product. If it's 0.68, we'll have understated the problem."
Rukmini Bhat, voice note to Aparna, Saturday 21 November, 9:40 p.m."Two pages, Aparna. Look at the chief of staff's chart — long note, three meetings, no decision. Recommendation at the top. The board doesn't need the archaeology."
Lena Brückner, comment on the same draft, Sunday 22 November, 6:11 p.m. IST"The archaeology is the decision. In 2022 I made a screen shorter and a company richer, and nobody wrote down what we gave up. We are about to do the same to a board note."

8. The options as Aparna currently sees them

Option A — Ship on the consented cohort only. Restrict Insight to the 29.1 lakh patients in Exhibit 4's third row, disclose that to Dhairya, and renegotiate the performance floor. Defensible, and the product survives. But it treats Ira's 0.71 as a measurement, and rests on Karthik proving a separation he currently cannot.
Option B — Remediate first. Pause Insight, commission the seven-month separation and a re-consent campaign, and tell Dhairya FY28. Costs ₹4.6 crore against a ₹110 crore EBITDA base, and almost certainly the contract and Nikhil with it. It also assumes re-consent works; Exhibit 5 offers two rates a factor of three apart, and nobody has asked this question of these patients.
Option C — Ship on the full cohort, with indemnity and an opinion. Obtain external counsel's view that the pre-2022 notice supports "service improvement," secure indemnity from Dhairya, and proceed. The only option that meets 4 December. It rests the defence on a reading of a check box that the person who wrote it rejects, and turns a product question into a litigation posture.

Aparna had written these out on Saturday and been uneasy since. All three assume the 2021 decision has a single meaning waiting to be found. Exhibit 3 suggests it may not: the PRD, the minutes and the ticket may record three different decisions, never reconciled because nobody had to write them in one document. All three also assume the note's job is to choose. Farida's framing — that the note is a record before it is a recommendation — implies a fourth possibility Aparna cannot yet phrase: a note whose first section states what Ojas can and cannot presently establish about its own data, the commercial choice following from that. Rukmini would call that an essay.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The note is due at 6:00 a.m.; the board call is at 8:30 a.m. IST, Drishti's partner dialling in from Singapore and the audit-committee chair from London, where it is 3:00 a.m. Dhairya's board meets on 4 December and Ashwin Balachandran says his budget line does not roll over. The term sheet carries a performance floor of AUC 0.74 and a thirty-day termination right if it is missed in the first quarter of service.

Ojas must find ₹4.6 crore of unbudgeted remediation in a year whose plan already assumes 40 basis points of margin compression. Karthik's eleven engineers are not a free pool: three are committed to an ABDM integration promised to Deodar Hospitals Network by March, and the NABL surveillance audit falls in January. The auditor's observation cannot be unmade; if the March backfill did what Sandeep suspects, whether it should have been reported becomes live. And a consent failure is not cured by a good subsequent memo — though a bad one, written tonight, could make it considerably worse.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 3 gives three records of one 2021 decision. Which, if any, is the decision? What would have had to be written differently in March 2021 for this question to have an answer today?
  2. Exhibit 6 is being used to argue for a two-page note. What does it actually establish, and what would you need before letting it shape Monday's document?
  3. Exhibits 4 and 5 are incomplete in ways their footnotes disclose. How should a two-page note represent numbers its author does not trust — and what is lost either way?
  4. Most of the stakeholders are withholding something material. Which omission most damages the note, and can any document design make it surface before Monday?
  5. Rukmini wants the recommendation first, Farida wants the record first, Dr Kalyanam wants the account unflattering. These are three different documents. Is there one that satisfies all three, or must Aparna choose whom to disappoint?
  6. What should Aparna do on Monday morning, and what should the first three sentences say? If the board asks the question she most fears — "when did we first know?" — what is the honest answer, and what does giving it cost?

At 11:52 p.m. Aparna typed a first line: "Ojas Insight is commercially significant and legally unsettled, and the second fact is not a detail of the first." She read it three times, decided it was the truest sentence she had written all weekend, and that Rukmini would ask her to cut it. Below it the page was empty. In Toronto, Ira was re-running the model on a larger sample nobody had asked for. In Bengaluru, Karthik had gone quiet after eleven.

She had six hours, two pages, nine years of other people's writing, and no way to know which of the three records in Exhibit 3 the board had already believed for five years.
exp20v2-comm.writing:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Writing as a PM Superpower

On a Tuesday in September, Rohan Iyer sat in a Bengaluru conference room with eleven slides and a decision he could not get anyone to make.

Rohan was a senior product manager at Manthan Freight Cloud, a Bengaluru-built platform matching truck owners with shippers across nine Indian states and, since March, three lanes into the UAE. Manthan charged a flat 4% take-rate on every load, moving about ₹38 crore of freight value a month. For six weeks Rohan's team had been building a dynamic pricing engine that would let the take-rate float between 3% and 6% depending on lane congestion, fuel prices and idle trucks nearby. Finance wanted it live everywhere by Diwali. The operations lead, a decade into managing driver relationships, wanted it killed. Rohan had put both views into a deck and asked leadership to decide.

The meeting went the way these meetings usually go. The CFO skipped to slide nine and asked about revenue. The ops lead objected before slide two finished loading. After forty minutes the CEO, Meenal Bhonsle, said what she had said in August: "Send me something I can actually read, and I'll decide by Friday." Rohan left the room having presented for forty minutes and decided nothing. What he needed was not a better deck. It was a memo — and why a page of prose can do what eleven slides cannot is the idea this page is about.

The idea

Writing as a PM superpower means using complete, ordered sentences — not bullet fragments, not slides — to force a decision into a shape rigorous enough to survive scrutiny, before anyone has to defend it out loud. A memo is not a record of a decision already made; it is the instrument that makes the decision possible, because prose does not let you skip the step where two ideas do not actually connect. A bullet point can sit next to another bullet point forever without anyone noticing the second does not follow from the first. A sentence cannot.

The idea has a specific history in technology companies. Amazon's S-team stopped using slide presentations for major decisions in 2004, on Jeff Bezos's instruction, replacing them with narrative memos of roughly six pages that the whole room read in silence at the start of the meeting — a practice sometimes called the "study hall." Bezos's stated reasoning, later written into Amazon's shareholder letters, was that "the narrative structure of a good memo forces better thought and better understanding of what's more important than what." The practice spread through the profession over the following decade, and it now sits alongside the PRD (product requirements document) as one of the two core writing artifacts of the discipline — the PRD describes what should be built, the memo argues for what should be decided.

The sentence Rohan could say in a meeting without sounding glib is this: if you cannot write the decision in plain sentences with the numbers attached, you do not understand it well enough to ask anyone else to decide it. That is not a claim about style; it is a claim about where thinking actually happens, and under time pressure it happens more rigorously on the page than out loud.

How it actually works

A decision memo is not "writing down what I would have said." It has a specific mechanical shape, and good ones follow steps newcomers routinely skip.

Step one: state the question and the recommendation in the first paragraph, not the last. A memo that builds suspense — background, then more background, then the ask on page five — is the single most common failure mode, because the reader spends the whole memo guessing what they are being asked to approve.

Step two: lay out the context with sourced numbers, not adjectives. "Take-rate compression is a growing concern" tells the reader nothing they can check. "Take-rate fell from 4.4% to 3.9% in four months as three rivals entered the Chennai-Coimbatore lane" tells them something verifiable against Manthan's own billing data.

Step three: name the alternatives seriously, including the one you are not recommending. People leave this implicit most often — mentioning the alternative in a half-sentence, dismissing it, and moving on, which signals to a sharp reader it was never actually considered.

Step four: restate the recommendation, with reasoning that connects back to steps two and three, and name what would change your mind. A memo that cannot say what evidence would overturn its own recommendation is advocacy dressed as analysis.

Step five: specify what happens next — who does what, by when. And the truly implicit step: the memo is read silently, in the room, before discussion starts. That scheduling choice changes who wins the argument — from whoever presents with the most confidence to whoever reasoned most carefully on the page.

A worked example

Here is the arithmetic Rohan actually put in his memo's second section, reconstructed line by line.

InputCurrentProposed
Monthly matched freight value (GMV)₹38.0 crore₹38.0 crore
Effective take-rate4.0%4.6% (blended)
Monthly platform revenue₹1.52 crore₹1.75 crore
Estimated driver churn (30 days)3.1%4.5% (modelled)
Revenue lost to reduced GMV from churn—₹9 lakh
Net monthly gain—₹14 lakh

The blended 4.6% came from modelling the three busiest lanes moving to a 5.5% band during congestion and the seven quietest lanes dropping to 3.2% to keep trucks moving. The churn estimate of 4.5% came from a survey of 240 drivers Manthan ran in July, in which 18% said a visible price change would make them compare Manthan against BlackBuck or Rivigo before their next load — translated into a 1.45x multiplier on the 3.1% baseline, a conservative reading since stated preference typically overstates real switching. The ₹14 lakh net gain, against a base of ₹1.52 crore, is a number a reader can trace to two sources: Manthan's billing system and a named survey.

The second pass is what made the memo persuasive rather than merely tidy. Rohan's team reran the model at double the churn estimate — 9% instead of 4.5%. At that rate, GMV lost to departing drivers erased the entire revenue gain, turning the ₹14 lakh benefit into a loss of roughly ₹6 lakh a month. Showing that reversal — not hiding it — is what let Meenal ask the sharpest question in the eventual meeting: "What's our actual confidence in that 4.5%, and how would we know within thirty days if it's wrong?"

The nuances

A memo is not documentation

A PRD documents what is being built so engineering, design and QA can execute against a shared understanding. A decision memo argues for a choice so leadership can decide. Writers new to the practice often submit a status update — thorough, accurate, decision-free — when what was needed was an argument with a recommendation attached. The tell: does the document ask for anything?

Numbers must be traceable, not merely present

A number with no source is a bullet point wearing a decimal point. "Churn will rise to about 4.5%" reads identically whether it came from a 240-driver survey or from someone's gut, unless the memo says which. The discipline is to attach a source to every figure doing real work in the argument.

A memo without a recommendation is a report

Reports are useful, but they are a different artifact. Calling a report a "decision memo" sets up the exact meeting Rohan had in August, where a room full of information produces no action because no one was actually asked to choose anything.

Silent reading changes who wins the room

The mechanic that makes narrative memos work is procedural, not literary: everyone reads the same document, at the same pace, before anyone speaks — removing the edge held by the most confident presenter and replacing it with whichever argument holds up on the page. Teams that skip the silent-reading step usually find the memo changes little.

Length is a constraint, not a target

The six-page convention exists because a real constraint forces a writer to cut the argument to what matters. A ninety-page memo is not more rigorous; it usually means the argument was never resolved on the page.

What it cannot do

A memo cannot manufacture data that does not exist, and it cannot resolve a genuine disagreement about values — whether Manthan should prioritise driver trust over near-term revenue is a judgment call clear writing sharpens but does not settle.

Where it changes by context

In a consumer company, memos tend to open with a scene — a specific user, a specific moment of friction — because the argument rests on behaviour before it rests on a number. In a B2B company, memos carry more procurement and integration detail, since the reader is often deciding whether the change survives a customer's legal review, not just whether users like it. In a marketplace business like Manthan's, a memo must argue both sides of the trade at once — what changes for the shipper and what changes for the driver — because ignoring one side's incentives gets caught in the first sentence a two-sided thinker reads.

The habit also changes with company size. In an early-stage startup, the founder often is the memo — decisions happen in one fast conversation around a single table. As a company scales past the point where every decision-maker was in the original conversation, the memo becomes the mechanism that lets someone in Dubai or Singapore participate in a Bengaluru decision without being in the room.

Common mistakes

Burying the ask. Symptom: the room argues past each other for the first fifteen minutes because half of them are unsure what they are being asked to approve. Underlying error: treating the memo as an FYI rather than a request. Diagnostic: read only the first paragraph aloud — if a stranger could not state the decision from it, move the ask up.

Slide-thinking dressed as prose. Symptom: the document is technically sentences, but each one restates a bullet point rather than connecting to the one before it. Underlying error: the writer drafted the deck first and converted it. Diagnostic: read it aloud; a narrated list sounds different from an argument.

The strawman alternative. Symptom: the memo dismisses one other option in a single sentence. Underlying error: the writer never seriously modelled it. Diagnostic: does the alternative get its own numbers, or only an adjective?

Numbers with no home. Symptom: a skeptical reader asks "where did that come from?" and the writer reconstructs the source from memory. Underlying error: figures pasted in during editing rather than sourced during drafting. Diagnostic: can the writer name the exact system or survey behind every number, in one breath?

What good looks like

Three weeks after the first meeting, Rohan sent a two-page memo, not a deck. Paragraph one asked Meenal to approve a phased launch on the three busiest lanes only, holding the flat rate elsewhere for a quarter. Section two laid out the table above. Section three named the alternative — launching everywhere at once, which finance had wanted — and explained why it was rejected: the doubled-churn scenario made a full rollout a real risk, while a three-lane pilot capped that risk at under ₹2 lakh a month. It closed by naming what would earn a full rollout: churn on the pilot lanes staying under 5% for eight consecutive weeks.

The follow-up meeting lasted forty-five minutes, ten of them silent reading. The CFO's first question was about the churn multiplier, not the revenue number. The ops lead, for the first time in six weeks, did not object on principle; she asked whether eight weeks was long enough — a real question, not a rejection. Meenal approved the pilot before the meeting ended.

Closing

Rohan's team launched dynamic pricing on the Delhi-Jaipur, Mumbai-Pune and Chennai-Bengaluru lanes in October, at the proposed band, with a weekly churn dashboard the ops lead herself asked to own. The memo became a template other PMs at Manthan started copying, less because anyone mandated it and more because it visibly worked: decisions that used to take three meetings started taking one. What Rohan took from the episode was narrower than "write more" — the numbers he was least sure of were exactly the ones the memo forced him to write down first, because a sentence cannot hide an unexamined assumption the way a bullet point can.

The natural next skill to study from here is asynchronous communication more broadly — how a well-written memo lets a team spread across Bengaluru, Dubai and Singapore move at the speed of the clearest writer in the room rather than the loudest one.

Two questions to sit with:

1. Think of the last recommendation you made out loud in a meeting. If you had to write it as a two-page memo tonight, which number in it would you struggle to source?
2. What is the difference, in your own team's habits, between a document that reports and a document that asks — and which one do you actually write most often?

Two ways to see the mechanic

Elan Workflow Systems: The One-Page Decision

Chennai, Wednesday, 14 October 2026, 7:40 p.m. IST

Ananya Krishnan, Senior Product Manager for the Workflow line at Elan Workflow Systems, stared at a blank document titled "Yakeen Expansion — Recommendation." A calendar reminder sat beside it: the leadership sync was at 9:00 a.m. the next morning, Thursday, and the founder-CEO, Vikram Rao, had been explicit that afternoon. "No deck this time," he had written on the leadership channel. "One page. What you recommend, and why. I'll read the appendix if I need to. I will not sit through forty slides again." Ananya had until midnight to send it, so Vikram could read it before the room filled. Whether Elan should build a bespoke customs module for its largest prospective Gulf account was hers to recommend — but this time the document's shape was as much the test as the recommendation inside it.

1. Company background

Elan Workflow Systems was founded in Chennai in 2015 by two IIT Madras classmates who had watched mid-sized manufacturers and logistics firms run approval chains — purchase orders, vendor onboarding, exception handling — through email threads and paper registers. Elan's product, a configurable workflow and task-routing platform, let operations teams build multi-step approvals, SLA trackers and audit trails without code. By 2026 it had 520 employees across Chennai, Bengaluru and Pune, served 1,850 customers in manufacturing, BFSI back-office and logistics, and carried ARR of ₹210 crore after a 2024 Series C. It competed with Chennai-neighbour Freshworks, Zoho's operations suite, and increasingly monday.com and Asana. Elan's edge was depth: its engine handled compliance-heavy approvals lighter rivals treated as an afterthought — also why GCC logistics conglomerates had started calling.

2. The situation

Six months earlier, Yakeen Freight Holdings — a Dubai-headquartered freight and logistics group operating across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Oman — had piloted Elan's workflow product on forty seats inside its customs-clearance desk. It went well enough that Yakeen's chief operating officer, Faisal Al-Mansoori, now wanted Elan rolled out to all nine hundred operations staff group-wide, a deal Elan's sales team valued at roughly ₹14.2 crore ARR once fully ramped. There was one condition. Yakeen's customs documentation followed GCC-specific rules Elan's generic engine could not model without new work: multi-jurisdiction sign-off chains, Arabic-script fields, and integration with the UAE's customs single-window system. Elan's engineering estimate for a dedicated module was six engineers for four months — time that would come directly out of "Approvals 2.0," the platform overhaul that 214 existing customers, representing about ₹38 crore of ARR, had been requesting on Elan's product board for over a year.

Ananya had been through something like this, and that history was why Vikram had banned the deck. In April 2025, a similar request from a Singapore client was argued out over fourteen slides and a forty-message Slack thread; the room approved it under pressure, the module shipped six weeks late, and Approvals 2.0 slipped two quarters, souring several large domestic accounts. Ananya's task now was narrower and harder: write one page that made the trade-off, the numbers and her recommendation impossible to misread, holding supporting detail in reserve rather than parading it in the room.

The team she had to reconcile was scattered by design: an engineering lead in Pune, a data scientist in Toronto, a customer-success head in Singapore, a sales VP in New Jersey, each holding a different piece of the trade-off and none of them in the room when Ananya wrote.

3. The people

Rohit Deshmukh — Engineering Lead, Pune. Wants Approvals 2.0 protected; will build the module only if it spares the permissions layer his team has already started.
Priya Subramaniam — Data Scientist, Toronto. Wants the decision grounded in numbers, not urgency; built the model behind Exhibit 1 and worries a live pitch lets "our biggest deal" override the data.
Mei Lin Tan — Head of Customer Success, Singapore. Wants Elan to avoid another bespoke, hard-to-support module; remembers eleven months of escalations from the Singapore launch.
Neha Kapoor — VP of Sales, New Jersey. Wants the deal closed before Yakeen's November board meeting, and wants the memo to say yes plainly, without hedges a founder might read as doubt.

4. Exhibits

Exhibit 1. The Yakeen expansion, by the numbers

Proposed rollout (900 seats)₹14.2 crore ARR (steady state)
Year-1 recognised revenue if approved₹9.6 crore
Custom module cost (6 engineers × 4 months)≈ ₹1.4 crore fully loaded
Approvals 2.0 customers waiting (product board)214 accounts
ARR of those 214 accounts, combined₹38 crore
Elan total ARR₹210 crore
Source: Sales pipeline, engineering estimate, product-board export, October 2026.
Note: Priya's model tags roughly 40 of the 214 accounts, worth ₹9 crore, as "high dissatisfaction risk" if Approvals 2.0 slips past Q1 2027 again.
Exhibit 2. How Elan has decided things before
DecisionFormat usedTime to decideOutcome
Singapore customs module (Apr 2025)14-slide deck, Slack thread11 days, 3 meetingsApproved under pressure; shipped 6 weeks late; Approvals 2.0 slipped 2 quarters
Enterprise pricing change (Jan 2026)Email thread, 60+ replies19 daysReversed twice; two deals lost mid-cycle
API rate-limit redesign (Nov 2025)One-page memo, circulated 24 hrs ahead1 meeting, 45 minApproved with two open questions resolved in room; shipped on schedule

Exhibit 3. Ananya's forty-eight hours
Ananya's actual writing window is roughly five hours; the rest belongs to reading, not writing.

The three exhibits frame the decision Ananya must write, not just make. Exhibit 1 shows why the deal tempts and why the trade-off is real, not rhetorical: ₹14.2 crore of new ARR against ₹38 crore of existing ARR whose champions are already waiting. Exhibit 2 is the argument Priya wanted on paper: at Elan, format has tracked decision quality almost exactly — the one clean memo decided in forty-five minutes and shipped on time; the deck and the email thread each dragged past a week and left a worse outcome. Exhibit 3 is the constraint Ananya writes inside: not tonight's ideal memo, but the version that exists by midnight.

5. The options

Option A — Full build, with an explicit mitigation. Approve Yakeen's rollout and the module, but name the cost: flag the 40 high-risk Approvals 2.0 accounts for outreach, and ring-fence two of the six engineers so a reduced slice still ships on schedule. Upside: ₹14.2 crore ARR and a marquee Gulf reference, without leaving the loudest customers empty-handed. Cost: still slows the other 174 accounts, and asks Rohit's team to run two workstreams at once — where the Singapore delays began.
Option B — Decline the custom scope; offer configuration plus services. Tell Yakeen Elan will not build a bespoke module, but will configure existing features, backed by paid services, to approximate the workflow. Upside: protects Approvals 2.0 fully; no second one-off to maintain forever. Cost: likely shrinks the deal — Faisal says the workaround misses UAE single-window requirements, and Neha estimates this halves the odds of closing this quarter.
Option C — Defer, and commission a two-week discovery sprint. Recommend neither yes nor no, but a bounded sprint, staffed by two engineers, to scope a customs module general enough for other GCC prospects, turning a bespoke build into a platform capability. Upside: converts one client's request into a reusable feature, de-risking the "built for one logo" problem Mei Lin fears. Cost: pushes the decision past Faisal's board meeting, and Neha warns Gulf buyers rarely wait once a competitor is in the room.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. What does Exhibit 2 suggest about the link between format and decision quality at Elan? Is the pattern causal, or merely correlated with urgency?
  2. Evaluate Options A, B and C on revenue captured this quarter versus damage to the 214 Approvals 2.0 customers. Which trade-off would you accept, and which would you refuse regardless of deal size?
  3. What would the first three sentences of Ananya's memo say, and why does leading with the recommendation change how Vikram reads the rest?
  4. Four stakeholders hold conflicting, legitimate claims. How should one page represent them without flattening into vague consensus, or reverting to the deck Vikram banned?

7. A note for the learner

This case is not really about whether Elan should sign Yakeen. It is about what happens to a decision when the person who understands it best must compress it into a page. A short, structured memo — recommendation first, then the facts that justify it, then the costs being accepted, then what remains unsure — does not just report a decision already made in Ananya's head. It forces the decision, because vague trade-offs cannot survive being written next to a number. Exhibit 2 is the evidence: Elan's one fast, good decision was written as a memo before the meeting, not argued live in the room.

A well-reasoned answer does three things a weak one skips: it puts the recommendation in the opening line, not the conclusion; it quantifies the opportunity cost in the same units as the opportunity — ₹14.2 crore of new ARR weighed against a named, dated cost to named customers, not a vague "roadmap impact"; and it names what it does not resolve, flagging rather than hiding the open question about Rohit's permissions layer, because a memo that pretends to certainty it lacks will be trusted less next time.

On the substance, the most defensible path is a version of Option A, written honestly. Yakeen is a meaningful, GCC-anchoring account that Rohit's estimate and Priya's data both suggest is achievable without abandoning Approvals 2.0's highest-risk accounts — provided the memo commits explicitly, not aspirationally, to ring-fencing two engineers and a real date. Option C is the more comfortable answer, but Exhibit 2 cuts against comfort: deferring a decision with enough information to be made now has produced worse outcomes at Elan than making it, in writing, under a deadline. The memo Ananya sends tonight should say yes, say why, say what it costs, and say what Rohit still needs to answer — in that order, on one page.

Zehen Analytics Cloud: Who Decides on Qeemat?

A decision-rights case on DACI, RACI, and the discipline of writing it down

1. A Friday deadline in HSR Layout

On the morning of Wednesday, 23 September 2026, Priya Raghunathan, Director of Product at Zehen Analytics Cloud, stood at the whiteboard in the Bengaluru office with no clean answer on it. By Friday evening she had to tell the company's largest client, a Dubai-based retail distributor, whether Zehen would build a custom fraud-detection model before Diwali — a promise her head of sales had already made without asking her, data science, or the CEO. Engineering in Bengaluru and Pune was already reshuffling sprints assuming the answer was yes. Nobody could tell her who had authority to say no.

The immediate question was whether to build the custom model. The harder question, the one this case is really about, was why six weeks of confusion had been needed to discover that nobody had written down who decides.

2. Zehen Analytics Cloud

Founded in 2019 by two former Flipkart data engineers, Zehen Analytics Cloud sells one product: a returns-and-fraud analytics layer that flags refund abuse, address-fraud rings, and "wardrobing" before a refund clears. Clients connect Zehen to storefronts and marketplaces — Flipkart, Meesho, Nykaa, Myntra, increasingly ONDC — and its scoring engine, trained on pooled transaction patterns, returns a risk score in real time. It competes against Increff, Unicommerce, and in-house data teams.

By September 2026 Zehen had 240 clients and roughly ₹38 crore in ARR. Its largest account was Qeemat Retail Trading LLC, a Dubai-registered distributor reselling Indian D2C footwear, beauty, and apparel through its own app and forty outlets across the UAE and Saudi Arabia. Qeemat's contract was worth ₹4.2 crore a year, 11 percent of ARR, cited by the board as proof the model travelled beyond India. Losing it would not sink Zehen, but it would sink the growth story CEO Aakash Bhalla had told investors since the Series B.

3. Six weeks of assumptions

In early August, Farah Haddad, Qeemat's category director in Dubai, told Rohan Advani, Zehen's Head of Sales, that returns fraud had spiked over Ramadan and Eid and that her UAE address patterns were poorly served by a model trained mostly on Indian pincodes. She wanted a scoring model tuned to her market before Diwali, and mentioned that Increff had been courting her account. Rohan, dialling in from New Jersey at 6 a.m. to catch her, promised it would be ready. He did not check with product, data science, or engineering first; in his experience, deals this size were his to close.

Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune began scoping the request the following week, assuming a commitment that size had already been approved above them. Julia Fontaine, lead data scientist in Toronto, flagged a structural problem: forking the model for one client's geography would break the shared architecture and need ongoing maintenance she estimated at 15 percent of her time. She wanted a decision on the trade-off, not a deadline to work around. Lena Hoffmann, lead product designer in Berlin, was two sprints from shipping a self-serve flow for a new SMB tier aimed at ONDC sellers — a board-approved bet the CEO also wanted live before the same window. Pulling those engineers onto Qeemat's build would push her launch past Diwali, missing the season the tier was built for.

When Priya escalated in mid-September, she found the real problem was not the two deadlines. Rohan believed Sales could commit engineering work on deals under roughly ₹5 crore without product sign-off, a rule from a Q1 playbook. Julia believed architecture changes needed the CEO's sign-off, a precedent from a 2025 pricing change. Priya had assumed Product approved roadmap trade-offs and Sales only drove the client conversation, though nowhere written. Aakash recalled telling a March all-hands that Sales and Product should "sort it out themselves" below ₹5 crore — never minuted. Four people, four inconsistent beliefs, none recorded anywhere.

Exhibit 1: What was at stake, in numbers

4. The people

Rohan Advani, Head of Sales, Edison, New Jersey, manages Zehen's largest accounts across North America and the Gulf. He wants Qeemat protected at almost any cost: he closed the deal personally in 2023, is measured on expansion revenue, and has already given his word.

Julia Fontaine, Lead Data Scientist, Toronto, owns the fraud model's architecture. She wants it kept unified, since a fork for one account sets a precedent every large client will ask for, and her small team cannot maintain forks without headcount she lacks.

Lena Hoffmann, Lead Product Designer, Berlin, wants the self-serve SMB tier shipped on schedule. She has spent two months on the onboarding flow and sees Diwali as the entire commercial argument for the tier; a slip means waiting a full year.

Farah Haddad, Category Director at Qeemat Retail Trading LLC, Dubai, wants a fraud model reflecting her market, delivered on the promised timeline. She has real alternatives in Increff and Unicommerce, and no visibility into Zehen's internal conflicts — to her, a promise from Zehen's Head of Sales is a promise from Zehen.

Exhibit 2: The six weeks that led here

Exhibit 3: What each person believed about decision rights

Exhibit 3. Four sincerely held, mutually inconsistent beliefs — the cost of never writing a decision record for this class of request.

5. The options before Priya

Option A: Approve the full custom model on Rohan's timeline
Upside: Honours the promise, protects the ₹4.2 crore contract and Zehen's Gulf reference story before the board meeting.
Cost: Self-serve slips six weeks past Diwali; the model forks permanently, costing Julia's team 15 percent of ongoing capacity; every large client learns a verbal promise from Sales moves the roadmap.
Option B: Decline the fork; offer the November feature early plus a manual-review bridge
Upside: Keeps the model unified, protects self-serve and its projected ₹1.1 crore Year-1 ARR, avoids a precedent.
Cost: Real risk Qeemat downgrades or does not renew; Rohan's credibility with a client he personally committed to takes lasting damage.
Option C: A scoped release for Qeemat, paired with a written decision record
Upside: Brings the planned threshold feature forward for Qeemat by three weeks with one engineer, avoiding a fork; self-serve slips only one to two weeks; Priya also drafts a DACI for client-specific requests above ₹2 crore ARR, closing the gap that caused this.
Cost: Farah gets a partial win, not everything promised; Priya must manage that call carefully, and the fix takes time from other work.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Trace the six weeks in Exhibit 2. At which point did the missing decision record first cause real cost, not just risk?
  2. Using Exhibit 3, construct the DACI that should have existed before Rohan's call with Farah on 6 August. Who should be Driver, Approver, Contributors, and Informed?
  3. Compare Options A, B, and C using Exhibit 1's numbers. Whose incentives does each protect, and whose does it sacrifice?
  4. If Priya chooses Option C, what should she write down, and who needs to see it, so the next ₹4-crore request does not reopen this argument?

7. A note for the learner

This case is not really about fraud models or Diwali deadlines. It is about what happens when informal decision norms — Zehen did have some — are never converted into a decision record anyone can point to. A DACI (Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed) need not be elaborate. It must name, before pressure arrives, who drives the analysis, who has final approval, whose input is required, and who merely needs to know the outcome. Written down, it would have stopped Rohan from promising a build he could not authorise alone, and told Julia and Lena within a day whether their concerns would be weighed before a commitment, not after.

A well-reasoned answer does three things: treats the decision and the process failure as separate problems needing separate fixes; weighs the options on Exhibit 1's numbers rather than whoever argues loudest, since Rohan's urgency and Julia's caution are both legitimate inputs, not verdicts; and produces a decision record — naming the Approver, the rationale, and everyone's role, filed where the company can find it later.

The most defensible path is Option C. It protects the festive-season bet the self-serve tier depends on, avoids a permanent fork that would tax Julia's team forever, and still gives Farah a concrete improvement on her promised timeline — softened, not broken. Priya should hold the Approver role for engineering scope, since roadmap trade-offs sit inside Product's mandate; Rohan remains Driver of the client relationship; Julia and Lena are Contributors; Aakash, given the revenue, is Informed before the call, not surprised after it. Writing that down once stops Zehen from relearning this lesson at ₹4.2 crore a time.
exp40v2-comm.decision.records:
Decision Records and DACI/RACI

Near-expert treatment — who is driver, approver, contributor, informed, and whether the written answer is the true one.

1. Two rooms, two weeks apart

On 3 February, in a low building off Pune's Baner Road, Ishaan Deshmukh, Director of Product at Aparajita Imaging Devices, watched a decision he thought had been made in November get made again. Aparajita builds a portable ultrasound cart — 1,450 units in district hospitals across Maharashtra, Odisha and Assam — and had spent eighteen months training a model that highlights suspected pneumothorax on chest scans. The question was not whether it worked but what Aparajita would claim it did. Claim A described a worklist ordering aid, riding on the cart's existing Class B registration under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017. Claim B called it a flagged suspected finding, moving the software to Class C and a CDSCO pathway estimated at thirty-four weeks against Claim A's fourteen.

In November the leadership team had picked Claim A. In February the Chief Medical Officer reopened it: in her reading of the room she had never approved anything — she had been asked her view, given it, and watched a decision be announced. The VP of Regulatory Affairs believed the reverse. Both were reading the same one-page document, which listed six names under a heading that said, unhelpfully, Stakeholders. Meanwhile the subscription attached to the feature — ₹9,000 per cart per month on 620 carts — earned nothing, and eleven weeks of ambiguity cost roughly ₹1.53 crore.

Eleven days later and nine hundred kilometres south, Nandita Sridharan, Group PM at Anantya Freight Exchange in Chennai, faced a structurally different problem. Anantya matches 2,300 shippers with 11,400 small fleet owners on full-truckload lanes and moved ₹62 crore of freight value last quarter at a 4.2% take rate. Nandita wanted the load-matching screen to sort by a blended reliability score rather than lowest price. A 340-lane pilot lifted fill rate from 71% to 78% and cut day-of cancellations from 9.4% to 5.1%, but median price per load rose ₹380 on a ₹14,200 base, and loads won by owner-operators with fewer than three trucks fell from 22% to 13%.

Nandita's obstacle was not that nobody would approve, but that two people could and neither could approve for the other side. The VP of Shipper Growth would sign in an afternoon; the VP of Supply, whose team had spent two years recruiting those fleet owners, would not. Aparajita's record named the wrong people; Anantya's could not name a right one — the same symptom, a decision that will not stay decided.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A decision record is a dated, durable artifact stating a decision, the options rejected, the reasoning, the named holder of each role, and the condition under which it may be revisited. DACI and RACI are templates for the role portion. DACI — Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed — was formalised inside Intuit in the early 2000s and spread through Atlassian; it suits a single decision with a moment of closure. RACI — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — descends from the responsibility matrices of 1950s programme management, where the problem was hundreds of recurring tasks needing persistent owners. Bain's RAPID (Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide), published in 2006, is the third form and the most analytically interesting.

The problem it solves is narrower than usually described. Not forgetfulness: in any organisation above roughly thirty people, authority over a decision is genuinely ambiguous — not hidden, ambiguous — and the ambiguity surfaces only when someone acts on a reading others do not share. Jensen and Meckling's 1992 argument about specific knowledge holds that decision rights drift toward whoever holds the knowledge a decision needs, while formal authority stays where the org chart put it. A record forces the two to be reconciled out loud, in advance. Everything else — archival memory, onboarding, audit evidence — is a by-product.

Four schools disagree about what follows, and about specific propositions rather than emphasis. What each would and would not sign makes it usable.

SchoolWould signWould not sign
DACI / speed (Intuit, Atlassian)Ambiguity about who approves is the largest source of decision latency; exactly one Approver.That anyone but the Approver holds a veto. Contributors advise; they do not block.
ADR / rationale (Nygard, 2011)The durable value is recorded context and consequences; records are superseded, never edited.That a role matrix adds information. Who signed matters less than why.
RACI / programme (responsibility matrices)Accountability must be singular and persistent across recurring work.That a per-decision artifact scales; hundreds of decisions need a standing matrix.
RAPID / decision rights (Bain, 2006)Some parties genuinely hold vetoes; denying it hides the veto rather than removing it.That naming a single Decider suffices when an unnamed Agree-holder exists.

The live fault line runs between the first school and the fourth. RAPID's extra role is Agree — a party whose sign-off is genuinely required, distinct from the Decider and from mere Input. DACI collapses Agree into Contributor. Where no real veto exists, that removes a stalling mechanism and is a gift. Where a real veto does exist — a regulatory function that can refuse a filing, a compliance officer under RBI or CDSCO obligation, a supply-side executive whose team will not implement what they were not asked about — the collapse does not abolish the veto. It relocates it from the meeting, where it is cheap and visible, to the aftermath, where it is expensive and looks like insubordination.

A decision record is a claim about where authority actually sits. A confident but false one is worse than none: it converts a negotiable disagreement into a betrayal.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the steps left implicit

Experts do five things templates do not ask for. The first is framing at the right grain. "Should we ship AI triage?" is unanswerable; "Do we file under Claim A or Claim B for the FY27 release?" has a closure condition an outsider can recognise from the title alone. The second is the veto census, the step most often skipped. Before naming anyone, the Driver asks of each function: if this person refuses, can the decision still be executed? If not, that person is an Agree-holder, whatever the template calls them. Ishaan's record had four Contributors, of whom exactly one — the CMO, whose signature the CDSCO submission required — was one.

The third is pre-committing the decision rule. Will the Approver decide on the recommendation as written, or choose a third option? Will dissent be recorded and overridden, or must it be resolved? Stating this in advance stops a losing Contributor relitigating: they agreed to the rule before knowing the outcome. The fourth is a revisit trigger written as an observable — not "revisit in Q3" but "revisit if field sensitivity falls below 0.88." The fifth is supersession discipline: a record is never edited to reflect a change of mind, because editing destroys the evidence that would show whether the reasoning was wrong or merely unlucky.

There is a usable quantitative treatment, and it concerns reopening. A decision stands only if every party who believes themselves entitled to approve accepts the outcome. Let k be the number of plausible approvers and p the probability that one of them, on a decision they dislike, declines to treat it as settled. Empirically p sits near 0.25 where no approver has been named in writing, and near 0.05 where one has been named accurately. The probability the decision stands is (1 − p)k.

Approvers (k)Stands, unnamed (p = 0.25)Stands, named accurately (p = 0.05)Reopens per 100 (unnamed)
175%95%25
256%90%44
342%86%58
524%77%76

The table's interest is its shape, not its modest precision. Going from three plausible approvers to one raises the stand rate from 42% to 75%. Naming the approver accurately at k = 3 raises it from 42% to 86% — a larger gain, and the cheaper move. Note what the arithmetic exposes: naming an approver inaccurately does not move p to 0.05. It leaves the real Agree-holder where they were while giving everyone else false confidence, which is why Aparajita lost eleven weeks rather than two — roughly 0.25 × 11 × ₹12.9 lakh ≈ ₹35 lakh in expectation, against a census costing one afternoon.

4. When the practice applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. One: the decision is costly to reverse. Aparajita passes emphatically — a CDSCO filing under the wrong class is not withdrawn cheaply — and Anantya moderately, since a default sort reverts in a day but lost fleet-owner trust does not. Two: more than one party plausibly holds authority. Both pass; its absence is why records on single-owner decisions are theatre. Three: the reasoning will be needed later by someone not in the room. Aparajita passes for regulatory reasons; Anantya because the next PM to touch matching would otherwise rediscover the price-reliability trade-off from scratch. Four: the decision has a closure moment. Aparajita passes cleanly; Anantya half passes, because a matching default is a standing policy tuned continuously — the signal that a persistent RACI owner may serve better than a one-off DACI.

The practice is actively misleading in three situations. First, where the decision is cheap and reversible and the record costs more than the ambiguity it removes. Second, where nobody has the knowledge to decide: a name in the Approver box then manufactures false confidence and turns a research problem into a governance one. Third, where the record is pre-positioned blame allocation. The tell is a team that writes records eagerly for decisions likely to go badly and casually for those likely to go well — records for a future adversary rather than a future colleague.

5. Hard edge cases and organisational seams

Two-sided markets break the single-approver rule structurally, which is Anantya's situation. A matching default is not one decision with two sets of consequences; it is a transfer between constituencies with separate executive owners, and no template produces a legitimate single approver below the level where both P&Ls converge. Mature marketplaces escalate to the common owner and pre-delegate: changes moving supply-side share past a stated threshold require the COO, smaller ones do not. Anantya's pilot moved that share nine points, so escalation was structurally correct rather than a failure of nerve.

Regulated hardware-plus-software adds a seam. Aparajita's cart has a hardware train with tooling lead times in months and a software train shipping fortnightly, and the regulatory claim binds both. The expert move is to write the record against the binding constraint — the claim — rather than either train, and have both reference it rather than hold copies. Skip this and you get two records, consistent when written, that silently diverge.

AI-native products stress the revisit trigger, because the model approved in November drifts as data shifts. Mature teams write the approval against a stated performance envelope and treat exit from it as an automatic reopen rather than an escalation someone must be brave enough to raise; Aparajita's redrafted record names 0.88 field sensitivity as the floor. What such companies say and do diverge: governance documents describe standing model review boards, while in most the real practice is that one senior engineer notices drift and escalates informally. The record does not make the board real; it makes the engineer's escalation legitimate.

Multi-product firms hit the seam at shared platforms. When one team's decision consumes another's capacity, the consuming team is an Agree-holder in substance and almost never named, because the template is scoped to the deciding team. If execution needs a team outside the author list, that team holds a veto, written down or not.

6. Nuances that separate the expert from the competent

The veto census outranks the template

A competent practitioner fills the boxes; an expert first establishes who can actually stop the work, then fills them so the answer is visible. The tell is a function under Informed that also appears in the execution plan as a dependency. The obvious reading — that it will simply be told — is wrong, because dependency is veto by another name.

One approver is a design goal, not a fact to assert

Novices read "exactly one Approver" as an instruction to write one name. Experts read it as an instruction to arrange for one name to be sufficient — escalating until one person holds both constituencies, or negotiating delegation beforehand. The tell is one name in the box and four people in the meeting who all speak as though they were deciding.

Driver is a job, and it is the expensive one

The Driver does not decide; the Driver manufactures the conditions under which deciding is possible — framing, evidence, census, timeline, recommendation. The tell that this is done badly is a meeting opening with "so, what do people think." A well-driven meeting opens with a recommendation and the objections already answered.

Dissent must be recorded, not resolved

Competent teams try to convert every objection into agreement before closing, which is how six-week decisions become twelve-week ones. Experts record the dissent verbatim, attribute it, and proceed. This looks like ignoring people and is the opposite: an attributed dissent is the strongest form of being heard, and it makes the later review honest.

The revisit trigger is what makes reversal cheap

The obvious reading of a revisit trigger is calendar hygiene. Its real function is political: it pre-authorises someone to reopen the decision without appearing disloyal. The tell that a team lacks one is a decision everybody privately thinks wrong and nobody raises, because raising it would read as attacking whoever made it.

Records are written for the person who was not in the room

Competent records summarise what was said; expert records state what a reader who has never heard of the decision needs in order to act — more constraint, less narrative. The tell is a record full of names and short on the constraint that drove the answer. Aparajita's document named six people and never said Claim B added twenty weeks.

Options rejected are the load-bearing section

A record listing only the chosen option is a press release. Experts give each rejected option its specific reason, because the common future question is not "why did we do this" but "why didn't we do the obvious thing," and the answer is usually a constraint since expired. The tell is an options section where every alternative failed for the same vague reason.

Who writes the record is a signal worth reading

When the Driver writes it, the record describes the process; when the Approver writes it, it describes the reasoning. When someone on the Informed list writes it, authority has outsourced the artifact to an observer, and the record will be accurate about the meeting and wrong about the decision.

7. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, decisions are mostly reversible and the scarcity is speed, so the honest practice is few records, thin ones, and a bias to a single empowered approver. In B2B and enterprise software, contractual commitments and security review make several functions genuine Agree-holders and the record doubles as audit evidence; here the RAPID distinction earns its keep. In platforms and marketplaces the issue is Anantya's — decisions transfer value between constituencies, so the approver is set by where the P&Ls converge. In hardware, irreversibility is physical: tooling and certification mean the revisit trigger must name a date before which reversal is still cheap. In AI products the roles do not change; the trigger does.

Stage changes the failure mode more than the practice. Below about forty people k is usually one and the founder approves by default; the discipline reduces to writing anything down, and the loss is institutional memory rather than reopened decisions. Between forty and three hundred, k rises fastest and the practice matters most; this is where the eleven-week reopen lives. Above a thousand the failure inverts: process appetite is high, and the risk is ceremonial records with nine contributors. One claim often made and not real: that regulated industries need heavier records. They need more careful veto censuses, because their vetoes are statutory.

8. Three worked examples

CaseStructureNumbersOutcome
Aparajita Imaging Devices
regulated hardware + AI		Hidden Agree-holder (CMO) filed as Contributor11 weeks reopened; ₹55.8 lakh/month deferred; ≈₹1.53 croreNamed the veto; CEO as Decider
Anantya Freight Exchange

B2B energy software — the failure		Template mandated on every decision above ₹1 lakh214 records/quarter; median 9 contributors; approval 6→19 daysRaised the threshold, capped contributors at four

The third case is the one that fails. Ambar Grid Systems, a Bengaluru firm selling demand-forecasting software to state distribution utilities, adopted decision records after losing a tender it blamed on internal confusion, and mandated a DACI on every decision above ₹1 lakh. In the first full quarter it produced 214 records, median contributor count nine, and median time from opening to sign-off rose from six days to nineteen. The lists were defensive: omission read as exclusion, so managers lobbied to be added, each addition bringing someone whose non-response blocked closure. The records covered everything and signalled nothing.

The recovery inverted the instinct. Ambar did not improve the template; it raised the threshold to ₹25 lakh, capped contributors at four, and made the Driver name Agree-holders explicitly. Records fell to 31 a quarter and median sign-off to seven days, while reopens — the metric the exercise exists to move — fell from eleven to three. The discipline is in the selection, not the paperwork.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
