Every early warning here is observable in the document itself, before any outcome is known: the artifact makes a governance defect legible when it is cheapest to fix. A reviewer comparing the Informed list with the execution plan catches the worst in two minutes.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is whether naming a single approver is always correct. The speed position, steelmanned: latency compounds, most decisions are more reversible than they feel, and every extra sign-off is a queue with a service time; a firm that names one approver and is wrong 15% of the time still outruns one right 95% of the time at three times the cycle. Its evidence is Ambar's six days to nineteen. The RAPID position: vetoes are not created by acknowledging them, and where they are statutory — CDSCO, RBI, SEBI, the DPDP Act's consent rules — calling a compliance officer a Contributor only guarantees the reopen arrives after the sunk cost. For the speed position to be wrong, real vetoes must be common; for RAPID to be wrong, most claimed vetoes must be preferences dressed as constraints.

The second concerns immutability. The ADR school holds that records must never be edited, only superseded, because the historical belief state is the asset. The objection is operational: chains become unreadable at scale, and a living document with a change log serves readers better. The evidence for immutability is that post-mortems in firms with editable records are systematically kinder to past decisions than the contemporaneous documents warrant. The evidence against is that nobody reads chains.

The third, least settled, is whether records improve decisions or merely accountability for them. No credible evidence shows that naming an approver makes the chosen option better; the observable effects are on latency, reopen rate and post-hoc learning. One camp treats that as sufficient. The other holds that the practice's popularity rests on an unearned implication of better outcomes. The counterfactual is unobservable, so nobody has settled it.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this fills in a template and circulates it. Someone who has internalised it does four things differently. They spend most of their effort before any writing, asking who can actually block in the plain form — "can you stop this?" — rather than the polite one. They escalate early and without drama when the census returns two vetoes and no common owner, because that is structural, not a relationship problem. They write the rejected options with more care than the chosen one. And they treat the record as a prediction: filing the CMO under Informed is a bet she will not block, and when it loses they revise their model of the organisation rather than complain she overstepped.

12. What each protagonist decided

Ishaan did not restart the Claim A versus Claim B debate. He rewrote the record with a Decider — the CEO, the only person above both the CMO and the VP Regulatory — an explicit Agree line naming the CMO, a rule that the CEO would choose between the two drafted claims and not a third, and a revisit trigger at 0.88 field sensitivity. The CEO chose Claim A in nine days, the CMO's dissent recorded verbatim. The eleven weeks, Ishaan concluded, had been spent not on a substantive disagreement but on discovering a veto one afternoon of honest questions would have surfaced in November.

Nandita escalated. She wrote the record with the COO as Decider, both VPs on the Agree line rather than buried among Contributors, and the pilot numbers stated without softening — including the nine-point fall in small-operator share, the fact most likely to sink her proposal. The COO approved a staged rollout: reliability-ranked default on the 340 pilot lanes plus 600 more, a floor on owner-operators' share of surfaced loads, and an automatic reopen below 18% nationally. Presenting the adverse number herself was what made the Agree line signable.

Discussion questions

1. Aparajita's reopen cost ₹1.53 crore; the veto census that would have prevented it costs an afternoon. Why do experienced teams skip it, and what does that imply about whether a template can fix the problem at all?

2. Ambar Grid improved outcomes by producing fewer records. When would that backfire, and what would you measure to know which regime you are in?

3. Nandita escalated rather than seeking one approver, which the DACI school would call a failure of nerve. Make the strongest case that she should have decided herself, and state what would have to be true about Anantya for it to hold.

Chirag Retail Cloud: Annexure C

An ambiguous case on commitments nobody remembers making

1. Sunday night, Jaipur

At twenty to midnight on Sunday, 15 November 2026, the marigold strings from Diwali were still taped above the door of the Chirag Retail Cloud office on Tonk Road, brown at the edges. Meghna Iyer, Vice President of Product, had the building to herself and three windows open: a signed contract annexure, a sprint board, and a document titled, an hour earlier, Who decided?

By Monday evening she owed the founder a recommendation; by Friday, 20 November, the board would want it defended. The choice, as put to her on Thursday, was simple to state: finish the United Arab Emirates localisation Chirag had contractually promised its largest client by 31 December, or finish the hallmarking-compliance release 214 Indian jewellery retailers needed before the Bureau of Indian Standards' next phase took effect on 1 February. Capacity existed for one, not both.

What kept Meghna at her desk was not the arithmetic. She had spent the weekend trying to establish who had committed Chirag to the December date, and had found six documents that disagreed. One said the matter had been deferred. One said it had been signed. One had been quietly relabelled by a user whose identity the audit log no longer retained. She had joined in March 2026; everyone who could have told her had a different, sincere, incompatible memory.

2. Chirag Retail Cloud

Chirag Retail Cloud was founded in Jaipur in 2016 by Devang Mehta, son of a Johari Bazaar gold retailer, who had watched his father's shop run on a DOS billing package and a cloth-bound register of gold-scheme instalments. Its product was a retail operating system for jewellers: billing at live gold rates, making-charge rules, old-gold valuation, hallmarking records, scheme ledgers and GST filing. By FY26 it served 2,140 storefronts across 380 retailers and booked ₹74 crore in recurring revenue, mostly from chains of four to sixty stores — the segment beneath Tanishq and Kalyan Jewellers, who built or bought their own.

One earlier decision shaped everything available to Meghna. In 2021 Chirag carried eleven customer-specific code branches. A Coimbatore chain on one of them went eight days without correct hallmarking records during Akshaya Tritiya because a trunk fix was never merged into it. Chirag refunded ₹1.1 crore and lost two accounts to the story. In January 2022 Devang adopted what the company still called the Trunk Rule: one code base, multi-tenant, configuration over customisation, no branch outliving a sprint. When Yugantar Growth Capital led a ₹48 crore round later that year, the Trunk Rule went into the diligence pack as evidence of engineering maturity, and Yugantar's partner repeated it until it hardened into doctrine.

The Trunk Rule is why the UAE work is expensive. Arabic right-to-left rendering, a second tax regime and a foreign anti-money-laundering report cannot be bolted onto one tenant; they must be built as configurable capability for all 2,140 storefronts, tested against all of them, and carried forever. As a fork the same work would take a third of the effort and violate the one policy Devang had never relaxed.

3. The industry

Indian jewellery retail is, in software terms, a compliance business wearing a consumer business's clothes. Since 2021 the Bureau of Indian Standards has required hallmarking with a six-digit HUID on gold jewellery, expanding district by district and, in later phases, across additional caratages; each phase pulls another set of small-town retailers into a records regime their billing software must support. Income-tax section 269ST caps cash receipts at ₹2 lakh per transaction, so the point of sale must split, flag and refuse. GST on gold and on making charges must reconcile to the rupee. Gold savings schemes, the cash engine of the mid-market jeweller, sit near the boundary of deposit regulation, and the DPDP Act obliges retailers to account for customer identity documents collected for two decades in photocopies.

Competition came from three directions: Ginesys and Logic ERP in the organised retail stack, Zoho pressing upward from the small end, and a Hyderabad challenger, Chakshu Jewel Systems, which had raised money in 2025 and undercut Chirag by thirty percent while promising "one-click BIS phase readiness." Chirag's defence had always been that it shipped compliance before the deadline, not after. Its renewals fell between January and March, just after the festive season and just before the BIS phase dates — so a late compliance release landed inside the renewal conversation.

The Gulf was the growth story: Dubai's gold trade and UAE retailers' appetite for Indian-built software at Indian prices had convinced Yugantar that Chirag could sell abroad. The Series C term sheet of January 2026 — ₹165 crore — carried a covenant: international revenue to reach twenty percent of ARR by FY28. In November 2026 it stood at 15.4 percent, all of it one client.

4. The situation

Yaadgar Gold Trading LLC, a family group running 62 stores across the UAE, Oman and Qatar from an office in Deira, signed with Chirag in 2024 on a ₹11.4 crore annual contract — Chirag's largest deal, its only international reference, and the sole basis of the covenant story told to the board. Exhibit 1 sets out how the commitment attached to it came to exist.

Exhibit 1: Timeline of the Gulf commitment

Exhibit 1. Reconstructed over the weekend of 14–15 November 2026 from CRM exports, a PDF of the signed agreement, one surviving minutes file and the Jira change history. Gaps in the sequence are gaps in the record, not in the activity.

Three beliefs held through 2026 have proved wrong. The first was that Annexure C's December date was, in Jatin Kohli's phrase, "a commercial aspiration with a date attached." Meghna read the clause on Saturday: liquidated damages of ₹18 lakh per week of delay, capped at ₹2.16 crore, and a right of termination for convenience if delivery slips 120 days.

The second was that the UAE anti-money-laundering requirement was a connector, an export in someone else's format. In October, Ritu Bansal's team learned that goAML submission needs registration, a schema materially unlike India's FIU reporting, Arabic field handling, and a validation cycle no number of engineers can compress.

The third was that the domestic hallmarking release was sixty percent complete. That figure came from a 2025 branch built by two engineers who had since left. Under the Trunk Rule it could not be merged; Sushant Kale's team concluded in October that nine of the fourteen remaining engineer-weeks were rework of code already in the repository that Chirag's own policy forbade using.

5. The people

Meghna Iyer, VP Product, Jaipur, joined in March 2026 from a Bengaluru logistics firm. Her stated position is that Chirag cannot responsibly choose between the releases until it knows what it promised. Her incentive is a first year judged on the Gulf launch she inherited. What she is not saying is that she suspects nobody ever decided anything, and that saying so to the board will read as blaming the founder who hired her.

Devang Mehta, Founder and CEO, Jaipur, signed Annexure C. His stated position is that the December date is non-negotiable because Chirag's word to a client is the asset. What he is not saying is that he does not remember the March Council item, and has privately asked his EA whether he was in that meeting.

What he is not saying is that he read the damages clause as boilerplate nobody would invoke, and that Yaadgar's procurement asked for it, not him.

His incentive is an organisation that has missed two of its last three quarterly commitments. What he is not saying is that two of his four senior backend engineers have interviewed elsewhere and his estimate assumes neither leaves.

Ritu Bansal, Head of Compliance, Bengaluru, is the only person to have read both the BIS phase notification and the UAE reporting schema. Her stated position is that the domestic release is not optional: retailers who cannot produce hallmarking records face consequences Chirag will be blamed for. Her incentive is a function measured only when something goes wrong. What she is not saying is that her October assessment of goAML rested on a partner's summary, not the authority's documentation.

Annika Vogel, Principal Designer, Berlin, owns the Arabic interface. Her position is that right-to-left is not a mirror of the existing screens: the billing grid, the gold-rate ticker and the scheme ledger each need rework, and a rushed version will be visibly worse than what Yaadgar uses today. Her incentive is a design system she has spent a year consolidating. What she is not saying is that she has already shown Salma Sheikh a prototype, and Salma liked it.

Nikhil Varma, Staff Data Scientist, Toronto, built the model in Exhibit 3's right-hand column. His position is that Chirag over-estimates localisation because it prices fear rather than scope. His incentive is a model he wants made load-bearing. What he is not saying is that his training set holds four localisation projects, none regulatory.

Salma Sheikh, Group IT Director at Yaadgar Gold Trading LLC, Dubai, countersigned Annexure C. Her stated position, in writing, is that Yaadgar expects delivery as contracted. Her incentive is a board that chose Chirag over a Dubai incumbent on her recommendation. What she is not saying is that Yaadgar's own goAML registration is incomplete, so the December date may matter less to her than the Arabic interface her store managers use daily.

6. Voices

Devang Mehta, Exec Sync, 12 November 2026

"Twenty-six weeks is not pessimism. Twelve of them are a validation cycle with a foreign authority; you cannot put four engineers on a queue and make the queue shorter. And I would ask, respectfully, who approved that we carry this in the trunk forever."

Sushant Kale, same meeting

"The model says eleven. I am not claiming eleven is right. I am claiming twenty-six has never been tested against outcomes, and nor has any estimate this company has produced in three years, because we never record what we predicted."

Nikhil Varma, chat thread #eng-planning, 12 November, 00:41 Toronto time

"Tickets are up, but not the way the chart is being read. Half my queue since October is people who cannot find the discount field on the new billing screen. Give me a week and I will tell you what is actually compliance."

Wei-Ling Tan, Singapore, direct message, 13 November

"We have asked twice for a status against Annexure C and received two different dates. Our position is that the agreement stands. I would add, personally, that the Arabic screens your designer showed me are what my store managers ask about, not the reporting module."

Salma Sheikh, Yaadgar Gold Trading LLC, email to Jatin Kohli, 13 November

"Nobody will fine Chirag for a BIS phase. They will fine our customers, who will tell Chakshu's salesman about it in January. That is the number nobody has put in a table."

Ritu Bansal, note to Meghna, 14 November

7. The options, as Meghna sees them

Option A: Deliver Annexure C in full by 31 December.
Twenty-six engineer-weeks against eighteen available means either the model is right or the domestic release slips to March, past the phase date and into the renewal window. Honours the contract and the covenant narrative; leaves 214 retailers to manage a phase change on the previous version.
Option B: Ship the hallmarking release first, renegotiate Annexure C.
Fourteen weeks lands the domestic release by mid-January. Damages accrue from 1 January to a cap of ₹2.16 crore, and Yaadgar acquires a termination right after 120 days. Requires Devang to reopen a clause he signed personally.
Option C: Partial UAE delivery — Arabic and VAT by December, goAML in Q1.
Fourteen weeks of the twenty-six, which fits alongside nothing else. Annexure C defines delivery as all three items; a partial one may not stop the clock, and Chirag's counsel has not been asked.
Option D: Contract the UAE work to a Dubai implementation partner.
Jatin's proposal: roughly ₹2.4 crore for a tenant-specific layer. Breaks the Trunk Rule in front of the investor who was told it was structural, and re-creates the condition that cost Chirag ₹1.1 crore in 2021.

Each option is a way of spending eighteen engineer-weeks. None touches the fact that Chirag will face the same question in February, when the next large client asks for something in a renewal conversation and someone says yes. Nor has anyone tested the premises underneath: whether Yaadgar's December need is the reporting module or the Arabic screens, whether Sushant's twenty-six or Nikhil's eleven is nearer the truth, how many of Ritu's 214 retailers are genuinely at risk in January. Meghna had noticed on Saturday that all four options treat the December date as a fact about the world rather than a fact about a document, and that the one person who could say what the client needs had been asked for a status twice and for her requirement not once.

8. The deadline and the constraints

Eighteen engineer-weeks exist before 31 January; hiring cannot add capacity inside that window, and two senior backend engineers are, unknown to Meghna, considering offers. Annexure C's damages begin on 1 January and its termination right matures at the end of April. The BIS phase takes effect on 1 February; domestic renewals run January to March against ₹31 crore of contracts. The covenant does not test until FY28, but the Yugantar partner sits on Friday's board. The Trunk Rule is not a contract and can be changed by the man who wrote it, at a cost to a story the board has heard for four years. And since August 2025 Chirag has had no forum whose notes survive ninety days.

9. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibit 2, state what Chirag can and cannot establish about who committed the company to 31 December 2026. Which artifacts are evidence, and which are noise?
  2. Exhibits 3, 4 and 5 each contain a number a busy executive would quote to the board. For each, say what the footnote reveals about how it was produced, and what you would need before repeating it.
  3. Rows 2 and 3 of Exhibit 2 cannot both be right. Does it matter, practically, which one is? Construct the argument for "yes, urgently" and the argument for "no, not this week."
  4. Annika has shown a prototype to the client, Nikhil's model contradicts engineering, Wei-Ling doubts the chart everyone cites. In each case, what would have had to be true about how Chirag records and routes information for that fact to reach Meghna before Saturday?
  5. Suppose Meghna proposes that no client-facing commitment be signed without a named approver and a recorded rationale. Who at Chirag loses something, and what will they say? Does the rule survive contact with a ₹11.4 crore renewal?
  6. It is Monday, 16 November. What does Meghna do before lunch, what does she recommend by evening, and what does she say to the board on Friday — about the choice, and about how Chirag came to be making it this way?

10. Sunday, 11:52 p.m.

Meghna's phone showed a WhatsApp from Salma Sheikh, sent at 10:14 p.m. Gulf time: Are we still on for Tuesday? She had not answered. Tuesday was a call scheduled a fortnight ago to walk through the Arabic screens, back when she assumed the December date was a plan rather than a clause.

The empty document was still titled Who decided? Below it she had typed one line and deleted it three times. The version left on the screen read: The company did not decide. The company signed. She could not tell whether that was the finding she owed the board or the accusation that would end her first year. Outside on Tonk Road a delivery scooter went past, festival lights still strung along its handlebars, and Meghna closed the contract window without closing the other two.
exp20v2-comm.decision.records:
Decision Records and DACI/RACI

Who is driver, approver, contributor, informed — and did we write it down?

1. A meeting that ends with a nod, not a name

On the morning of 14 August, Meera Iyer, VP of Product at Waqt Commerce Cloud, a Bengaluru-based checkout and fulfilment platform used by roughly 1,900 direct-to-consumer brands, walked into a conference room to settle a question circling for six weeks: which buy-now-pay-later provider should Waqt embed at checkout, Simpl or LazyPay. The commercial terms barely mattered on their own — both wanted a similar revenue share on the roughly ₹40 lakh in monthly transaction volume running through Waqt's BNPL button — but the two options pulled Waqt's roadmap in different directions, and eight people in the room had opinions about which direction was right.

Forty minutes later the meeting ended the way most of Waqt's meetings ended that quarter: with general nodding toward the option Meera had been leaning on, no vote taken, and no note sent. Three weeks later, the head of engineering discovered that compliance had never actually signed off on the disclosure language the chosen partner required under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending guidelines, and the integration had to be partly rebuilt. Nobody had lied in that room; nobody had even disagreed. What had gone missing was smaller and more consequential: nobody had written down who was deciding, who had to approve before it was final, and who merely needed to be told. The decision had a room full of witnesses and no author.

This is the gap that decision records, and the DACI and RACI frameworks used to populate them, exist to close. Meera's failure was not a failure of judgement — her instinct about the vendor was, in the end, defensible — it was a failure of documentation, and it cost Waqt roughly three weeks of delay on a decision that had already taken six weeks to reach.

2. The idea, defined without the jargon

A decision record is a short, durable written statement of four things: what was decided, why, who made the call, and when it can be revisited. It is not a meeting transcript and not a project plan; it is the smallest artifact that lets someone six months later answer "why did we do this?" without reconstructing the meeting from memory. DACI and RACI are the two most common templates for the "who" half of that record. DACI — Driver, Approver, Contributors, Informed — was popularised inside Intuit in the 2000s to speed up decisions that kept stalling in consensus-seeking meetings; it is built for one-off decisions with a clear moment of closure. RACI — Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — grew out of programme-management practice in the 1950s and 1960s, originally to assign ownership across the many tasks inside a large engineering project, and it is built for recurring work with many small owners rather than one big decision.

The sentence this topic reduces to: somebody has to be named as the person who decides, somebody has to be named as the person who can veto it, and everybody else has to know which of those two people they are talking to.

A decision record turns a conversation into an artifact: who decided, why, and who is accountable if it turns out to be wrong.

3. How it actually works, step by step

The mechanics are simple enough to state in five steps, but the steps practitioners skip are almost always the third and the fifth. First, name the decision precisely — not "improve checkout" but "which BNPL provider does Waqt integrate for the Q3 launch." Second, assign exactly one Driver: the person who runs the process, gathers input, and pushes toward a date. Third — the step Meera's team skipped — assign exactly one Approver, whose sign-off alone makes the decision final; people avoid this step because naming one approver forces everyone to admit that consensus is not actually how the decision will be made. Fourth, list Contributors whose expertise must be sought before the decision is final — here, compliance, finance, and engineering — and separately list who is merely Informed once it is made. Fifth, write it down somewhere everyone can find later, with the date, the options considered, the reasoning, and a trigger for when it should be revisited.

4. Waqt's decision, worked through

Redone properly, Waqt's BNPL decision would look like the table below, filed the day the process opened rather than reconstructed after the rebuild.

RoleName / functionResponsibility in this decision
DriverMeera Iyer, VP ProductRuns vendor evaluation, sets 21-day timeline, drafts the record
ApproverArjun Rao, Chief Product OfficerSole sign-off; decision is final only with his written approval
ContributorsFinance (Priya Menon), Compliance/Legal, Engineering leadMust be consulted on revenue share, RBI disclosure language, and integration cost before sign-off
InformedCEO, Head of Sales, Head of SupportTold the outcome once approved; not consulted beforehand

Run the arithmetic on what the missing Contributor line actually cost. Waqt's compliance flag arrived in week four instead of week one, because compliance had been Informed rather than Consulted — nobody had asked them to check the RBI's digital lending guidelines against the vendor's disclosure flow before the room nodded toward a choice. Fixing the integration added twenty-one days to a rollout expected to carry ₹40 lakh a month in transaction volume: 21/30 of a month, so the delay cost Waqt roughly ₹40,00,000 × 0.70 ≈ ₹28,00,000 in volume that simply ran through the old checkout flow, earning nothing on the new revenue share. Now change one input: suppose compliance had been listed as a Contributor from day one, at a cost of perhaps three extra days of Meera's process to gather that input up front. Three days is 3/30 of a month, so the exposed delay shrinks to roughly ₹4,00,000 — an ₹24 lakh difference traceable to one row in a table, not to any disagreement about which vendor was better.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

DACI answers "who decides," RACI answers "who does the work"

The two frameworks are often used interchangeably, which is the most common source of confusion. DACI is built for a one-time decision with a clean moment of closure — pick the vendor, set the price, choose the launch date. RACI is built for an ongoing set of tasks with many owners — who is Accountable for the vendor relationship each quarter. Using RACI for a single decision usually produces a long list of "Accountable" people, which quietly recreates the consensus problem DACI was invented to solve.

Driver is not decision-maker

The most common misreading of DACI is assuming the Driver decides. The Driver runs the clock and writes the memo; the Approver is the person whose name is actually on the line if the decision is wrong. Conflating the two lets a Driver announce a decision that was never actually approved, which is close to what happened at Waqt.

One Approver, not a committee

The framework insists on exactly one Approver because an approving committee reproduces the exact ambiguity decision records exist to remove — if three people approve and the outcome is bad, nobody is accountable, since everybody can point to the other two.

Consulted is not the same as agreeing

Being a Contributor means your input must be sought, not that it must be followed. Teams often confuse "consulted" with "vetoed," which either paralyses the Driver into seeking unanimous agreement or causes Contributors to disengage once disagreement fails to stop the decision.

A decision record freezes a moment, not a commitment forever

Every good record carries a revisit trigger — a date or condition, such as "revisit if RBI issues new guidance" — because treating a record as permanent turns useful documentation into concrete that nobody can update without a fight.

It records authority; it does not grant it

Writing "Arjun Rao is the Approver" does not make him the right person to approve it — that authority has to exist already, by role or delegation. A record that names the wrong Approver simply documents the wrong outcome more clearly.

It cannot rescue a bad decision

Clear roles produce clear accountability, not necessarily correct answers. Waqt could have run a flawless DACI process and still picked the weaker BNPL partner; the framework guarantees someone owns the outcome, not that the outcome is right.

Overuse turns into theatre

Not every choice needs a formal record — the colour of a button does not. The discipline is wasted, and eventually resented, when applied to decisions too small to need it.

6. How the shape changes with context

In a consumer product, decisions often move fast and the Approver is frequently a single product lead with wide latitude, because the blast radius of a wrong call — a button colour, an onboarding flow — is small and reversible; records there tend to be brief but still worth keeping for pattern recognition across many small bets. In a B2B product like Waqt, decisions carry contractual and compliance weight, Contributors expand to include legal and finance by default, and the record becomes evidence that due diligence happened. In a marketplace product, decisions affect two sides at once — buyers and sellers, or brands and shoppers — so the Informed list grows to include whoever represents the side not directly consulted. Company stage matters just as much: in an early-stage company, the Approver is often the founder by default, and the discipline lies mainly in writing the record down at all; in a large organisation, the discipline shifts to the opposite problem, where too many people plausibly qualify and the hard part is picking one and making it stick.

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is naming a committee as Approver, which shows up as a decision that keeps getting "reopened" because no single person's word was ever final; the underlying error is mistaking consensus for accountability, and the cheapest diagnostic is asking, out loud, "if this goes wrong in six months, whose name is on it" — if two or more names come up, the record is broken. The second mistake is confusing Contributors with Informed, which shows up exactly as it did at Waqt: a function that should have been asked beforehand instead finds out afterward and objects; the fix is a five-minute pre-check where the Driver reads the Contributor list aloud and asks each function whether it needs to weigh in before, not after. The third mistake is writing the record after the decision is already made, purely as a formality; the symptom is an "options considered" section that suspiciously matches only the option chosen. The fourth mistake is skipping the revisit trigger entirely, which surfaces months later as a decision nobody remembers agreeing to and nobody feels empowered to change; the fix is a single line — "revisit if X" — added when the record is first written.

8. What good looks like

Picture the same decision handled well. On day one, Meera opens a one-page document titled "Decision: BNPL provider for Q3 launch," names herself Driver, names Arjun Rao Approver, lists Finance, Compliance, and Engineering as Contributors with a deadline for their input, and lists the CEO, Sales, and Support as Informed. She circulates it before any vendor discussion begins, not after. Compliance flags the RBI disclosure requirement in week one, while it is cheap to fix, not week four, while it is expensive. When the room meets on day 21, the discussion is not "what should we do" but "here is what the Contributors found — Arjun, does this still meet your bar." Arjun approves in writing, with a one-line reason, and the record is updated with a revisit trigger tied to the next RBI guidance update. Nobody needs to guess who decided, because it was written down before anyone needed to ask.

9. What Meera decided, and two questions to sit with

Meera's actual resolution, once the rebuild was underway, was less about which vendor to pick — she stayed with her original preference — and more about rebuilding the process itself: a one-page DACI template that every product decision above a stated cost threshold had to carry before a meeting was scheduled, not after. The lesson was not that her judgement had been wrong, but that judgement without an accountable name attached to it is indistinguishable, from the outside, from luck. The natural next topic is decision rights and escalation paths — what happens when the Approver and a Contributor genuinely disagree and someone has to decide who decides — and, close behind it, how well-designed product review forums use this same discipline to make many small decisions a week without each needing a bespoke table.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. In the last significant decision your own team made, could you name the single Approver within ten seconds — or would two or three names come to mind?

2. Is there a Contributor on your current biggest open decision who has been told about it rather than asked, and what would it cost to ask them this week instead of after the fact?
exp40v2-comm.meetings:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Running Effective Meetings

Does this meeting exist to produce a decision, or should it be cancelled — and what if the honest answer is neither?

1. Two calendars, two problems

On Thursday 20 August 2026, Kavya Ramanathan, Vice President of Product at Farmaan Underwriting Cloud in Chennai, printed five weeks of minutes from a meeting she had inherited. Farmaan sells an automated underwriting workbench to Indian life and health insurers — the software that decides, seconds after a proposal form is submitted, whether a policy is issued straight through, referred to a human underwriter, or declined. Its customers are regulated by the IRDAI, and its release notes are read by compliance officers before users. The meeting was the Release Council: eleven people, every Thursday, ninety minutes, running since the Series B.

The minutes showed forty-seven agenda items and nine decisions recorded with an owner and a date. Her second number alarmed her more. For each of the nine she traced the date the question was first raised in writing to the date it was recorded as settled: the median gap was nineteen days, and two items dated from June. Meanwhile the release carrying a mandated change to the medical-declaration flow had slipped three weeks, pushing a ₹1.8 crore annual contract with a mid-sized health insurer past its go-live window. The Council's cost was easy to compute — eleven people, a fully loaded ₹4,100 an hour, ninety minutes, fifty weeks: about ₹33.8 lakh a year. That number was nearly irrelevant, because it was visible. The slip, worth some ₹10 lakh of deferred revenue and an unquantified amount of customer trust, was invisible and larger.

Fourteen days later and 1,100 kilometres north, Devendra Shirke, Head of Product at Fasal Sensor Works in Pune, faced the mirror image. Fasal makes a soil-moisture sensor node — a ₹6,400 device sold to farmer producer organisations across western Maharashtra with an irrigation-advisory app. On 3 September Deven was looking at a tooling freeze on 30 September, after which the injection mould for the enclosure would be cut; a revision would cost roughly ₹14 lakh and seven weeks. His firmware lead in Pune, his vendor's engineer in Rajkot and his field-operations manager in Kolhapur had not been in one conversation for five weeks. Every instinct trained by the modern literature told him to cancel things. His situation required him to add a meeting.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the object precisely. A meeting is the synchronous allocation of several people's attention to a single question, and it is the most expensive coordination instrument an organisation owns, because it consumes attention in parallel and cannot be time-shifted. The doctrine taught in product organisations compresses to four words — purpose, pre-read, decision, owner — with the rule that a gathering missing any one should not be improved but cancelled.

That doctrine is a screening heuristic, and it encodes a theory. A decision sits unmade for one of three reasons: the information needed is scattered across several heads; it is assembled but the people who must execute are not committed; or both exist and nobody knows who may say yes. Each blocker has its instrument. Scattered information is best assembled in writing, which is searchable and asynchronous. Missing commitment requires synchronous presence, because commitment is social — extracted by letting people voice dissent and then be bound. Missing authority requires a decision-rights fix, which is why this topic builds on decision records and DACI/RACI. A meeting called against the wrong blocker fails however well it is facilitated.

The intellectual history splits into four schools that agree on the symptoms and disagree on the cure. The managerial-leverage school, from Andrew Grove's High Output Management (1983), holds that meetings are the medium in which managerial work is performed, and separates process-oriented meetings, run on a cadence to exchange knowledge, from mission-oriented ones that produce a decision. Grove would sign "a recurring meeting can be legitimate indefinitely"; not "every meeting must produce a decision."

The written-narrative school, associated with Amazon's six-page memo and silent reading period, holds that the binding constraint is the quality of thinking reaching the room, and that slides let authors smuggle in claims prose exposes. It signs "no memo, no meeting" and "the decider holds a draft position beforehand." It does not sign "the meeting is where the decision gets made" — the meeting is where a drafted decision is stress-tested.

The genre-separation school, from Patrick Lencioni's Death by Meeting (2004), argues that meetings fail because incompatible purposes are mixed: a daily check-in, a weekly tactical review, a monthly strategic session and a quarterly offsite need different lengths and conflict levels, and one ninety-minute block does all four badly. It signs "cancel the mixed-purpose meeting"; not "replace it with nothing."

The deliberation school, running from Doyle and Straus's How to Make Meetings Work (1976) to Sam Kaner's participatory decision-making, is the one product managers forget exists. A group's value lies in divergence — options nobody held alone — and early decision-framing collapses the option set to whatever the organiser already believed. Kaner's "groan zone" is on this account the productive part. It signs "some meetings should have no decision and no owner"; it does not sign the doctrine at all.

The four are not reconcilable by synthesis; they disagree about what a group of people is for. The defensible position is conditional: which school is right depends on whether the scarce resource in the room is information, commitment, or imagination.

3. Mechanics, worked through

Expert practice has a quantitative core the doctrine hides. What matters is not the cost of a meeting but the latency of a decision, and latency obeys Little's Law: if a team holds W open decisions and closes λ per week, the average wait is L = W / λ. Farmaan's reconstructed log held twenty-three open questions; the Council closed nine in five weeks, or 1.8 a week, so L = 23 / 1.8 ≈ 12.8 weeks. The nineteen-day median Kavya had measured was the fast tail; the typical item waited three months.

That changes the intervention. Cancelling the Council saves ₹33.8 lakh a year and does nothing to L unless it cuts W or raises λ; done carelessly it raises L, because those questions lose their only scheduled point of resolution. The real levers are reducing how many questions need group resolution at all — a decision-rights move — and raising throughput per synchronous hour.

Throughput per hour is where attendance arithmetic bites, through two effects at once. A group of n people contains n(n−1)/2 conversational pairs, so each addition opens n−1 channels: four to seven roughly triples them, seven to eleven triples them again. And in a sixty-minute meeting with a chair taking ten minutes, eleven attendees have 4.5 minutes each against 12.5 at four — the difference between stating a position, hearing an objection and revising, and merely reacting. That is why large meetings feel like performances.

AttendeesPairwise channelsAirtime eachObserved behaviour
4612.5 minGenuine argument; positions revised in the room
7217.1 minWorkable; chair must sequence explicitly
11554.5 minTwo or three speak; the rest attend as audience
14913.6 minBroadcast; no decision without a drafted position

Kavya used this with her CEO: the Release Council was not a meeting of eleven but a broadcast with three participants and eight witnesses, mislabelled since the Series B. The remedy was arithmetic, not politeness — find the four who held information bearing on the decision, and make the other seven recipients of a two-paragraph outcome note.

The second implicit mechanic is the economics of the pre-read: not a courtesy but a transfer of cost from parallel to serial time. The Council opened with eighteen slides at two and a half minutes each — forty-five of the ninety minutes, times eleven attendees, is 8.25 person-hours consumed in parallel. The same content as a 1,400-word memo reads in ten minutes: 1.8 person-hours, plus three of the author's serial time. Total falls from 10.25 person-hours to 4.8, and the room now begins at the objection rather than the introduction.

Third is the sign-off window, which makes cancellation safe. An item leaving the Council moved into a written recommendation with a named decider and a fixed reply-by time — forty-eight hours for reversible items, five working days for anything touching a regulatory artefact. Silence at the deadline counts as assent, which converts the process from a queue into a clock; without that rule, asynchronous decision-making is a meeting of unbounded duration. Fourth, rarely written down: the chair must separate facilitator, expert and decider, because a chair who is also the strongest advocate cannot tell whether the room stopped arguing from conviction or fatigue.

4. When the doctrine applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: it applies when the decision is reversible and the cost of delay is linear. If two weeks late costs twice what one week costs, aggressive cancellation and asynchronous routing is correct, as at Farmaan for most scope decisions. It fails at Fasal, where delay is a step function: any slip past 30 September costs ₹14 lakh and seven weeks, and no slip before it costs anything.

Claim two: it applies when participants share a working vocabulary. A memo assumes readers decode it identically. "We will default the medical declaration to the prior-policy value" means one thing to a Farmaan engineer and another to a compliance officer hearing audit exposure. Where vocabulary diverges, synchronous time does translation no pre-read can do. Deven has it sharper: his Rajkot vendor and his firmware lead use "tolerance" for different quantities.

Claim three: it applies when the decision is separable from the relationship. Some meetings maintain a working relationship needed for decisions not yet visible; judged on decisions per hour they look wasteful and are not.

The doctrine actively misleads early in an ambiguous problem, when the group's job is to produce options rather than choose among them; at seams where the meeting's real function is mutual hostage-taking, each side demonstrating commitment by showing up; and at irreversible gates like Deven's, where the correct move is to add synchronous time.

Deven did that arithmetic explicitly. A weekly sixty-minute pre-freeze review with nine people at ₹3,600 an hour costs ₹32,400 an occurrence, ₹1.30 lakh over four weeks. From two prior tooling cycles he put at 35% the chance that mechanical, firmware and field people in one room would surface an enclosure defect otherwise found after the mould was cut. Expected saving: 0.35 × ₹14 lakh = ₹4.90 lakh, before counting seven weeks of selling season in a business bound to the sugarcane calendar — 3.8 to 1 on cost alone. The meeting was obviously correct, and the doctrine applied mechanically would have talked him out of it, because its purpose was not to produce a decision but to discover whether one was needed.

5. Hard edge cases

Regulated products. Farmaan's customers must evidence to the IRDAI who approved a change to underwriting logic and on what basis. Minutes are therefore an external artefact with an audit audience, and some committees cannot be cancelled because their existence is itself a control. The expert move is to separate the functions: a short minuted forum that records a decision already made, the real deliberation having happened earlier, in writing, among four people. Mature regulated firms say they deliberate in committee; in fact they deliberate before it and ratify inside it, in twelve minutes.

Hardware plus software. Fasal's calendar is pinned to physical irreversibility: mould cutting, last-time-buy notices, certification submissions. Meeting density should legitimately spike around each gate and then collapse; a flat cadence through a hardware programme gets the worst of both, too many meetings in the soft months and too few in the four weeks that matter.

Two-sided marketplaces. A meeting settling a question that affects both sides usually fails the purpose test, because two decisions with two owners are wearing one agenda item. The honest structure splits them and names which owner goes first, since the second is conditional on the first.

AI-native products. Decisions have shorter shelf lives, because a model update can invalidate a scope decision made six weeks ago, which argues for explicit expiry dates. The evidence base shifts too: where a product meeting ran on opinion, an AI feature meeting can run on an eval suite, and the expert habit is to refuse to convene until the eval has run. The failure mode is the reverse — convening weekly to look at cherry-picked outputs and calling it review.

Organisational seams. The hardest case is functions with different natural cadences: engineering on a two-week sprint, sales on a quarterly close, compliance on fixed filing dates. One weekly meeting across the seam is wrong for all three. What mature companies actually do, as against what their process documents claim, is keep one low-frequency, high-authority forum plus an informal pair of individuals who talk constantly and resolve most things before they reach it. When those two leave, the seam breaks and the process is revealed never to have worked.

6. What separates the expert from the competent practitioner

Cancellation is a routing decision, not a deletion. The competent practitioner cancels and reports a saving; the expert asks where the open questions will now be resolved and installs that path first. Tell-tale sign: three weeks after a publicised meeting cull, senior people start receiving ambush escalations at 9 p.m. The obvious reading — people are ignoring the new process — is wrong. The decisions had nowhere to go.

Pre-reads move cost; they do not remove it. A memo that saves eleven people forty-five minutes costs its author three hours, and where writing is unrecognised, memo quality decays within two quarters into a bulleted agenda with a new name. Tell-tale sign: pre-read word counts falling while clarifying questions in the room rise.

Silence is usually rank, not agreement. The competent chair asks "any concerns?" and hears none. The expert reads the airtime distribution and notices the two most junior attendees and the one dialling in from another city spoke ninety seconds combined. The obvious reading is consensus; the likelier one is that dissent was too expensive to voice, and will resurface as slow execution.

The output of many decision meetings is commitment, not choice. The decider frequently knows her answer before she walks in. Calling this a sham misreads the mechanism: the meeting exists so dissent is expressible and then binding. Tell-tale sign: the decision matches the pre-read's recommendation, yet those who argued against it execute without friction — the mechanism working.

Standing slots have option value. The purist deletes every recurring meeting; the expert keeps a few deliberately under-used, because thirty minutes cancelled three weeks in four is cheap insurance against the fourth. Tell-tale sign of error: a team with no recurring meetings whose urgent decisions travel by direct message to whoever is most senior and available.

Meeting load is a lagging indicator of unclear decision rights. When the same six names appear in every room, the diagnosis is undelegated authority, not calendar hygiene. Tell-tale sign: a calendar-reduction exercise that works for a quarter and relapses. The obvious reading is discipline decay; the real cause is that nothing was delegated, so the meetings had to come back.

Minutes have two audiences, one of them in the future. The competent practitioner writes minutes for attendees; the expert writes for whoever inherits the system in eighteen months and needs to know what lost and why. Tell-tale sign of the shallow version: decision logs full of outcomes and empty of rejected options.

7. Across product types and stages

In consumer products, where loops are fast and most decisions are reversible through experimentation, the meeting's job is to decide what to test rather than what is true, and aggressive cancellation is safe. In enterprise software like Farmaan's, many decisions are externally committed — to a customer, in a contract, before a regulator — and so effectively irreversible, which makes the pre-read and the minuted record matter more and the room smaller and more senior. Platforms and marketplaces carry the two-decisions-one-agenda pathology; hardware bends calendars around physical gates; AI products need review dates.

By stage the difference is real but narrower than claimed. Under thirty people, informal meetings work because everyone sees everyone's context, and the failure is under-recording, surfacing later as founders relitigating settled questions. Between thirty and three hundred — Farmaan's condition — the failure is proliferation without decision rights. Above a thousand it inverts: forums become so formalised that deliberation migrates into pre-meetings, and the calendar stops describing where decisions are made. One thing does not change: a decision nobody wrote down was not made.

8. Three worked examples

Farmaan, the redesign that worked. Kavya split the Council. A Tuesday written cycle carried every item to a named decider with a 48-hour reply window; a Thursday thirty-minute forum of five carried only items that had produced explicit written disagreement. Over eight weeks recorded decisions rose from 1.8 to 4.1 a week and the open stock fell from 23 to 14, so L = 14 / 4.1 ≈ 3.4 weeks against 12.8 — a 73% cut in latency, while synchronous time fell from 16.5 person-hours a week to 2.5.

Fasal, the meeting deliberately added. Deven's four pre-freeze reviews cost ₹1.30 lakh. In the second, on 10 September, the Kolhapur field manager mentioned that farmers were mounting nodes on bamboo stakes rather than the supplied post, putting the cable gland at an angle the design had not anticipated. Rotating the gland and adding a drip lip cost ₹1.9 lakh, eleven days before the freeze; found after tooling it would have cost ₹14 lakh and seven weeks. The meeting returned roughly ninefold — and would have failed the four-word test the day he scheduled it.

The one that failed. In April, Kavya's predecessor cancelled the Council outright, citing exactly this doctrine, with no sign-off window and no decider named per item. Within five weeks decisions had migrated to a WhatsApp group of seven senior people, made fast and recorded nowhere; the medical-declaration defaults were changed twice in opposite directions three weeks apart, because neither change was written down; and the compliance lead, with nowhere left to object, began blocking releases at the final gate — moving her objection from the cheapest point in the cycle to the most expensive. The Council was reinstated in June, larger, because reinstating a cancelled forum invites everyone who felt excluded. Recovery was not facilitation: Kavya had to publish a decision-rights map naming one decider for each of nine recurring decision types, get it endorsed in writing by the CTO and the compliance head, and only then re-split the forum — seven weeks to undo a cancellation that took one email.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Latency laundering — cost removed, delay hiddenCalendar looks better; releases slipWhere did the open questions go, and what is their reply-by date?Decisions re-made in opposite directions; rework at the costly gate
Quorum creepAttendee list grows by one or two a quarterWhich attendees hold information bearing on this decision?Broadcast disguised as deliberation; junior voices go silent
Pre-read that is really a deckSlides arrive an hour before; 20 minutes of expositionDoes the document state a recommendation in its first paragraph?Meeting time spent on comprehension, not judgement
Decision amnesiaThe same item recurs across three agendasCan anyone produce the prior decision in 30 seconds?Relitigation; execution stalls awaiting stability
Chair-as-advocate collapseObjections stop once the chair states a viewWho in this room is paid to argue the other side?Confident bad decisions, detected only in the market
Cadence mismatch at a seamOne function consistently arrives unpreparedDoes this forum's frequency match the slowest participant's planning cycle?The seam runs on two individuals' goodwill

Across all six the early warning is a calendar artefact while the cost lands in the product — which is why meeting hygiene is chronically under-managed: symptom and damage sit in different ledgers, owned by different people.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Whether a meeting should ever make a decision. The written-narrative position at its strongest: real-time group decision-making is vulnerable to anchoring, seniority effects and the last-speaker advantage, so the decider should arrive with a written position and use the room for disconfirmation. Its evidence is that groups amplify rather than correct shared bias. It would be wrong if the information needed were genuinely emergent — producible only by several people thinking aloud — which is what happened in Deven's second review. The counter is that pre-drafted positions make emergence impossible.

Whether recurring meetings should exist. The async-first position holds that a standing meeting is a documentation failure made permanent, and that teams spread across Chennai, Pune, Rajkot and Kolhapur prove it by functioning without one. The Grove position holds that regular process meetings are how standards propagate, and that teams without them develop expensive, invisible divergence in how shared terms are read. Async-first would be wrong if much coordination cost is tacit and non-writable, and the seam evidence suggests it is.

Whether rooms should be small or open. The small-room argument is the arithmetic above. The open-room argument is apprenticeship: junior product managers acquire judgement mainly by watching senior people argue, and four-person rooms starve them for years, producing a cohort that can run a process but cannot referee a disagreement. The usual compromise — observers who may not speak — satisfies neither, preserving the attention cost while removing the accountability that makes watching instructive.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this audits calendars, deletes meetings and reports a saving. Someone who has internalised it starts from the decision inventory rather than the calendar, and treats the meeting as one of three instruments, not the default. They add meetings as readily as they cut them, and name which blocker each addresses. They instrument latency rather than cost, because latency is what customers experience. They write the decision record before closing the room, including the rejected option. And when a meeting cannot be named, scoped or owned, they neither improve it nor delete it: they find out whether the blocker is scattered information, missing commitment or absent authority, and fix that.

12. The two decisions, and questions for discussion

Kavya did not cancel the Release Council. Having seen April, she judged the forum load-bearing for compliance evidence and for the seam between product and underwriting operations, and the defect to be decision rights, not the calendar. She published a decider per decision type, cut the standing forum to thirty minutes and five attendees, moved everything else to a written cycle on a 48-hour clock, and kept the minutes as the regulatory artefact they had always quietly been. Deven added his meeting, ran it four weeks and let it expire at the tooling freeze — a meeting with a scheduled death, which is the form most recurring meetings should take at birth.

Three questions worth an hour of argument. First: if a meeting's real output is commitment rather than choice, what evidence would distinguish a forum that genuinely binds people from one performing consensus, and could either protagonist produce it? Second: Kavya's predecessor applied the doctrine correctly as written and made things worse — was the doctrine wrong, incompletely specified, or correctly specified and wrongly sequenced? Third: Deven's most valuable meeting would have failed the four-question test the day he called it. What is the smallest amendment to the test that admits his meeting without also admitting the ninety-minute status update it was designed to kill?

13. Going deeper

Decision records and DACI/RACI — the substrate everything here rests on; without a named decider per decision type, every calendar fix relapses. Running a spec review — the next forum where synchronous time is most often wasted. Stakeholder mapping — consulted versus merely informed, the input to every attendance decision. Communicating with leadership — whether a cancelled meeting reads as discipline or evasion. Telling the customer story — what makes a pre-read persuasive. Demo and pitch craft — the genre where broadcast is correct. Writing as a PM superpower — without it, cancellation only creates latency. Status updates and stakeholder rhythms — where displaced information goes.

Hetu Credit Systems: The Calendar Reset

People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Wednesday, 7 October 2026, Revati Deshmukh was still at her dining table in Kondapur, Hyderabad, with two laptops open. On the left was the board pre-read she was to present at eleven the next morning, titled, optimistically, Operating Cadence: What We Learned. On the right was DD-0417, the decision record for a change to the collections contact-cadence engine, shipped on 22 July. It carried fourteen comments, three of them worried, and no approver. Nobody had convened a meeting about it, because under the new operating model there was no meeting to convene it into. Eleven weeks later that change had put Hetu Credit Systems' largest client in front of its regulator, and Revati was expected to tell the board whether the company should put its meetings back.

1. The company

Hetu Credit Systems was founded in Hyderabad in 2019 by Vikram Sahni, a former core-banking architect, and Farida Qureshi, who had spent nine years in risk and compliance at a mid-sized non-banking financial company in Mumbai. Their premise was narrow and correct: the institutions doing the lending — NBFCs, NBFC-MFIs, small finance banks — could not build origination, servicing and collections software at the pace the regulator changed the rules.

The Reserve Bank of India's Digital Lending Guidelines of September 2022 turned that premise into a business: every lender needed auditable consent trails, cooling-off periods and a defensible record of who had been contacted, how and when. By March 2026 Hetu had ₹168 crore of annual recurring revenue, 74 clients and 620 employees, with platform engineering in Hyderabad, a second centre in Bengaluru, data science in Kochi, compliance in Mumbai, customer operations in Chennai and a commercial office in Gurugram.

One earlier decision shaped everything after it. In March 2024 Hetu acquired Jugalbandi Data Labs, a twenty-nine-person Pune outfit whose queueing models were better than anything Hetu had built. The price was ₹46 crore, but the binding part was not the money. To retain the founding engineers, Hetu conceded a three-year autonomy covenant: Pune would keep its own release train, its own on-call rotation and — the clause that mattered in October 2026 — the right to set its own working practices until 31 March 2027. Legal waved it through as a cultural nicety. It meant any company-wide change to how decisions were made could be declined, politely and contractually, by the team that owned the retry queue.

2. The industry

The market was crowded with capable Indian firms. Perfios and Signzy held strong positions in onboarding and verification; Lentra and Yubi had built lending infrastructure; Setu and Juspay sat closer to the payment rails. Hetu competed on the least glamorous part of the loan lifecycle — servicing and collections — on the argument that this was where regulatory risk lived.

The argument was sound. Collections in India is governed not only by contract but by the Fair Practices Code, by RBI guidance on outsourcing and on the conduct of recovery agents, and, since the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, by consent obligations clients passed straight through to their vendors. Borrowers may be contacted only within permitted hours; every attempt must be logged. A lender that cannot produce that log to a supervisory team has a problem, and so does its software vendor. The macro backdrop pressed the other way: unsecured retail and microfinance credit had been through a stress cycle, and lenders were leaning on collections efficiency to protect margin. The festive quarter brought the year's disbursement and contact-volume peaks together, and Hetu's two largest clients were 19% of revenue between them.

3. The reset

By late 2025 Hetu had the meeting problem a company doubling headcount usually acquires: a Monday Platform Sync, a Tuesday Client Council, a Wednesday Risk Review, a Thursday Portfolio Council running two hours with twenty-six invitees, a Friday release readiness and a fortnightly architecture forum that was now a status parade. Parth Bhandari, who joined as Chief Operating Officer from a Gurugram consumer-internet company in mid-2025, pulled the calendar exports. At the December offsite he presented one slide: 8.6 hours per employee per week, ₹7.2 crore a year of loaded time, and a throughput curve flat for three quarters.

Hiranya Growth Partners, the Singapore-based investor that led the Series C, benchmarked Hetu against eleven portfolio companies and placed it in the worst quartile. The Calendar Reset launched on 12 January 2026 with rules that were simple and, on their face, sensible: every recurring meeting had to be re-justified or deleted; status became a dashboard; decisions became written documents with a recommendation, a comment window and a default; silence for 48 hours meant assent. Forty per cent of recurring meetings went in the first fortnight, including the Wednesday Risk Review and, in March, the Thursday Portfolio Council.

For two quarters it looked like an unambiguous success, and Exhibit 1 is the scorecard Parth circulated monthly to say so. In April Vikram used the numbers in a fundraising conversation; in June, Hiranya's operating partner asked whether Hetu could reach 3.5.

What the scorecard missed is in Exhibit 2, which Revati assembled only in late September, after the incident, by exporting and classifying the decision corpus. Uncontested decisions closed fast: a median of four days, 96% with an explicit approval. Decisions that attracted real disagreement did not. Sixty-three documents, 29% of the corpus, shipped on the 48-hour default with no approval comment at all. Exhibit 6 plots the two series: as meeting hours fell, the median cycle time for contested decisions rose from 9 days to 34. Exhibit 3 shows what happened operationally, and is the one the board is most likely to read wrongly. P1 incidents rose from 4 to 11 a quarter and client compliance observations from 2 to 9 — but loan volume rose 2.1 times, the Bengaluru migration landed in May, and three large clients went live in June. Whether the reset caused the incidents or merely shared a quarter with them, the data as collected cannot settle.

4. DD-0417

The chain is set out in Exhibit 4. In June, Jeevika Finance Network — an NBFC-MFI headquartered in Kolkata with 1,900 branches across eleven states, Hetu's largest client at ₹8.4 crore of annual contract value — asked for higher contact throughput ahead of the festive peak. Deepa Rao's team in Kochi proposed a revised retry policy: failed attempts would no longer be discarded at the end of a permitted-hours window but held in a queue and retried by priority. DD-0417 was published on 16 July with a recommendation, a comment window, and an appendix on queue-flush behaviour under backlog.

Eleven people commented. Aniruddh Kelkar's Pune engineers raised two implementation concerns and had them answered. Farida Qureshi wrote that permitted-hours enforcement had historically lived in the dispatcher rather than the queue, and that someone should confirm where it now lived. Nobody answered her. The window closed; the change shipped on 22 July inside the Pune release train, no approver named anywhere in the record. In the old world it would have gone to the Wednesday Risk Review, deleted five months earlier.

On 3 September, Jeevika's internal audit found that across four states, on eleven nights between 2 and 26 August, a backlog flush had produced contact attempts outside permitted hours — roughly 2,900 borrowers, most receiving a single automated attempt. Jeevika self-reported. Hetu patched the dispatcher in nine hours and could show that logging had captured every attempt, which was, as Farida put it drily, both the problem and the defence. The contract carries a 31 October notice date, and Manav Srinivasan in Chennai had spent three weeks trying to learn what Jeevika's board intended.

5. The people

Revati Deshmukh — VP Product, HyderabadOwns the recommendation; believes the reset removed the wrong forums, not too many. Has not said that she herself approved deleting the Wednesday Risk Review, because its agenda was 80% status — which it was.
Parth Bhandari — Chief Operating Officer, GurugramSays this was an engineering defect no meeting would have caught, and that reversing the reset costs Hetu its one operating-leverage story. Has not told the others that Hiranya's draft Series D terms make a further cut in meeting load a covenant.
Sneha Iyer — Head of Engineering, BengaluruWants the Portfolio Council reinstated in full with her as chair, framed as risk governance. Has not mentioned that her roadmap is a quarter behind, and that a standing forum is where dates get renegotiated without it counting as a slip.
Aniruddh Kelkar — Director of Engineering, PuneSays Pune never stopped meeting: a daily huddle and a Friday review, neither in any calendar export. Will invoke the covenant if a cadence is imposed. Has not said that four of six senior engineers hold offers.
Farida Qureshi — Co-founder & Head of Compliance and Risk, MumbaiWants a pre-ship compliance gate with a named approver and authority to block a release. Has not said in writing that she let the dispatcher question drop, having been told twice that the comment thread was the escalation path.
Manav Srinivasan — Chief Customer Officer, ChennaiWants a joint war room with Jeevika before 31 October. Has not shared that Jeevika's chief technology officer took a call with a competitor on 18 September.
Deepa Rao — Data Science Lead, KochiMaintains the model behaved as specified and the defect lay in the dispatcher, not in a policy choice. Has not emphasised that queue-flush behaviour sat in an appendix three people opened.
Vikram Sahni — Co-founder & CEO, HyderabadWants a decisive answer and dislikes reversing a flagship initiative two quarters in. Has not told anyone he restored a Monday founders' sync in May, five people, on no dashboard.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

"If the finding is that we shipped a regulated change with no approver, say that. If the finding is that we deleted a meeting, we will spend a crore a year buying back a feeling."

Parth Bhandari, call with Revati Deshmukh, 30 September

"The model did what the specification said: hold and retry. Somebody had to decide whether holding across a window boundary was acceptable. That is not a modelling question, and it was never asked of me."

Deepa Rao, incident review, 8 September

"Pune has not had a decision go missing this year. We talk every morning for twenty minutes. What the company cannot have is a two-hour Thursday call in which twenty-six people watch six argue."

Aniruddh Kelkar, email to Sneha Iyer and Revati Deshmukh, 2 October

"I asked the question on the document. I have the timestamp. I did not chase it, because I had been told twice that chasing things in private was the behaviour we were designing out. I would like us to be honest that the system told me not to."

Farida Qureshi, submission to the board pre-read, 5 October

"Their CTO's exact words were, and I am quoting, 'we do not know who at Hetu we would call.' That is not a product complaint. Please do not answer it with a roadmap."

Manav Srinivasan, message to Revati Deshmukh, 21 September

"Reinstate the Council. I will chair it. We can be honest about dates in a room in a way we cannot in a document thirty people can read forever."

Sneha Iyer, comment on the draft board pre-read, 6 October

8. The options as Revati sees them

A. Restore the Thursday Portfolio Council

Bring back the weekly forum, agenda limited to decisions, with a named chair. Exhibit 5 puts it at roughly ₹1.01 crore a year. It is visible, fast, and gives Sneha the room she wants. It also reverses the company's only proven operating-leverage story two quarters after the board endorsed it, and restores a forum whose agendas show it was 80% status the last time it ran.

B. Keep the reset and harden the document contract

No new recurring meetings. Instead, no document may open a comment window without a named approver, a decision date and an explicit default, and three or more dissenting comments escalate it automatically to a 30-minute live slot within 48 hours. Roughly ₹9 lakh a year, and it satisfies Hiranya. It assumes the escalation fires — and Exhibit 2 shows that under the current rules contested items did not escalate; they aged.

C. A compliance gate rather than a product forum

Give Farida a twice-weekly, 25-minute pre-ship gate with authority to block any release touching contact, consent or data handling. Cheap, narrow, aimed at what went wrong. It puts a bottleneck on one calendar while she has two roles unfilled since June, does nothing for the pricing, roadmap and staffing decisions Exhibit 2 shows aging just as badly, and requires Aniruddh to accept a company-wide gate over the Pune release train before March 2027.

Revati had written all three into the pre-read and had begun to suspect the list was the wrong list. Every option treats the calendar as the variable. None changes who is accountable for a decision, the one field DD-0417 left blank. None touches the possibility that Exhibit 3 tells a different story — that a company carrying 2.1 times the load with the same people would have had a bad quarter whatever its calendar looked like. And there is a version of the night's problem in which the meeting question is not the question at all: Jeevika's chief technology officer never said the product was wrong. He said he did not know whom to call.

9. Constraints

The board review is at eleven on Thursday. Jeevika's notice date is 31 October: ₹8.4 crore of annual contract value and, Manav believes, a reference two prospects are waiting on. Hiranya's draft Series D terms sit with the founders. The Pune covenant runs to 31 March 2027. Hetu is under a hiring freeze outside compliance, where Farida has not filled two roles since June, and DPDP consent-manager work must land by January 2027 for eleven clients. And the company's own numbers cannot be used both ways: if Exhibit 1's savings are real, Exhibit 5's costs are not comparable to them; if Exhibit 2's cycle times are the true measure of the reset, the baseline they are measured against was never collected.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, failed between 16 June and 22 July? State it in one sentence a board member would accept, and name the exhibit that supports it.
  2. Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 tell three stories about the same eight months. Which would you present first, and what does that ordering do to the conclusion?
  3. Exhibit 1 excludes Pune's huddles, the founders' Monday sync and every war room. If those were counted, what becomes of the reset's headline number, and would it have been approved in December 2025?
  4. Farida raised the right question and let it go. Was that the failure of a person, a forum, or a rule? What would have had to exist on 18 July for her comment to stop the release?
  5. Aniruddh can decline any company-wide cadence until March 2027; his unit has the best decision hygiene in the company and also shipped the change. How should Revati treat that?
  6. It is Monday, 12 October. Whatever the board said, Revati must act. What does she do first, what does she stop doing, and what does she promise to show the board in ninety days — knowing that if she is wrong about the cause, those ninety days are gone?

The night before

A little after one, Revati changed the title of the pre-read to Operating Cadence: What We Do Not Yet Know, looked at it for a minute, and changed it back. Parth would read the new title as a retreat and Sneha as an admission. She opened DD-0417 once more. Thirty-one people had viewed it; three had opened the appendix. The approver field was still blank, a small grey rectangle with nothing in it, and she could not work out whether the honest thing to tell the board was that the company had deleted the wrong meeting in March, or that it had never, in seven years, agreed who was allowed to say yes.

Product Management Knowledge Graph · Case Study

Daksh Systems: The Weekly Product Sync

Communication & Stakeholder Management · Running effective meetings

On the morning of Thursday, 24 September 2026, Ananya Raut sat in a glass-walled meeting room at Daksh Systems' Kalyani Nagar office in Pune, staring at a calendar invite titled "Weekly Product Sync — Recurring." The next occurrence was four days away, on Monday the 28th. Ananya, Group Product Manager for the Scheduling & Rostering line, had to decide, before that invite went out again, whether the meeting should run as usual, run differently, or not run at all. The decision could not wait: Daksh's largest Gulf account, Layali Hospitality Group, would take a renewal decision to its board on 9 October, and a scheduling-conflict bug that had been "discussed" at the Sync for four straight weeks still had no owner and no resolution.

Company background

Daksh Systems, founded in Pune in 2016, builds workforce and operations software for asset-heavy service businesses — hotel chains, hospital groups, multi-location retail — that need to roster staff, track shift compliance, and manage floor operations across dozens of sites. Its closest domestic comparisons are the operations modules inside Zoho and Freshworks, though Daksh sells a deeper, vertical-specific product built for Indian and Gulf Cooperation Council labour law from day one — which is what won it early customers that larger, more generic platforms could not serve well. By September 2026 Daksh had grown to roughly ₹95 crore in annual recurring revenue and 340 employees, with engineering split across Pune and Bengaluru, design anchored by a small studio in Berlin, data science in Toronto (acquired with a scheduling-optimisation startup in 2023), customer success in Singapore, and sales headquartered in New Jersey. The company was eighteen months from a planned IPO, and its board had been explicit that GCC hospitality — anchored by Layali — was the proof point investors wanted first.

The situation

The Weekly Product Sync had begun in early 2025 as a thirty-minute stand-up for six people. Eighteen months later it ran ninety minutes with fourteen attendees spanning five cities, its agenda a rolling mix of status updates, half-finished debates, and decisions raised, discussed, and carried forward without anyone formally deciding or being told to decide. Exhibit 3 traces that growth. The scheduling-conflict rule Layali's operations team had flagged — their thirty-one hotels sometimes assigned the same housekeeping supervisor to overlapping shifts when a manager used the app offline — had been on the agenda for four consecutive Mondays, consuming roughly twenty minutes each time, with engineers proposing different fixes and no one stating who would decide between them.

Seen from each city, the meeting looked different. From Bengaluru, Farhan watched four senior engineers sit through an hour of discussion that did not concern their sprint, waiting for the fifteen minutes that did. From Berlin, Lena had watched the Sync eat into the two-hour block she protected each Monday for design critique, now compressed to forty minutes. From Toronto, data science treated the meeting as optional and sent a written note instead. From Singapore, Meenal had stopped believing the Sync would resolve scheduling conflicts at all, and had begun drafting a memo warning that Layali's renewal was now genuinely at risk.

The people

Farhan Sheikh — Engineering Lead, BengaluruWants the Sync shortened or cancelled. His team sits through a meeting that rarely produces an instruction they can act on; two engineers have asked to stop attending.
Lena Fischer — Lead Product Designer, BerlinWants her design-critique time protected. Not opposed to the Sync itself, but wants clarity on when design input is actually needed rather than a standing obligation to attend just in case.
Meenal Kapoor — Customer Success Lead, SingaporeWants the scheduling-conflict decision made this week, in whatever format achieves that. She carries the Layali relationship and owns renewal risk on it.
Alan Fernandes — VP Sales (Americas & EMEA), New JerseyWants the recurring meeting kept. It is his one reliable window into product timelines, and he worries that killing it removes visibility he relies on with GCC and US prospects.
