Reuben notes that the lengthening intervals coincide with the 2024 retirement of the weekly qualitative note, but offers the observation without claiming causation.

7. Voices

Tanvi Menon to Sharmistha Rane, Slack, 29 October, 07:12 IST "I can give you a number or I can give you the truth, and right now they are different objects. If you put a split in front of Faisal — sixty per cent us, forty per cent them — he will hold you to it, and I cannot defend either figure."
Annika Voss, design lead, review call, 5 November, Berlin "Everyone in this call is arguing about which percentage to publish. Nobody has asked what fourteen hundred people in Riyadh saw. They saw nothing. A grey screen. We built a player that would rather show a viewer nothing than show them a programme without an advertisement, and we have been calling that a reliability metric for two months."
Faisal Al Suwaidi, shared WhatsApp group, 3 November, 16:22 GST "We have had four green months and my complaints have tripled. I am not accusing anybody. I am saying that if green and tripled can both be true then one of these two things is not measuring my business."

8. The options as Sharmistha sees them

A. Restate and disclose. Issue the October report as red, reopen September, pay roughly ₹85.6 lakh of credits, and tell the board on Friday that the company has done so. Sharmistha's note to herself reads: clean, expensive, and it makes the reference call on the 24th a conversation about how we behaved rather than about what broke. It also hands Lavanya Growth Capital a restatement during confirmatory diligence and hands Faisal a document he will show his own board.
B. Issue October as amber, reserve September. Accept that the exclusion can no longer be relied on for the current month while declining to reopen a closed quarter until cause is established. About ₹28.5 lakh of credits, a defensible technical position, and a smaller shock. It also requires Sharmistha to explain why a September that is now doubtful was green, and it puts the reopening decision inside the renewal window in March.
C. Issue as drafted; speak to Faisal separately. Keep the contractual artefact arithmetically correct and, before the reference calls, hold a scheduled conversation in which Lehja describes the timeout finding, the uncertainty, and the Ramadan hardening plan. Reuben's preference. It separates the legal document from the honest conversation — which is either a sophisticated reading of two different instruments, or exactly the behaviour Exhibit 4 is a record of.

9. The deadline and the constraints

Engineering capacity was the binding physical constraint. Yusuf had eleven engineers on the Gulf platform. The Ramadan hardening programme — concurrency headroom to 500,000 sessions, a revised fallback path, and load testing against the February profile — required all eleven from 1 December to the end of January, and Lisaan's Ramadan window opened in the second week of February with no possibility of movement. A forensic reconstruction of September, costed by finance at ₹68 lakh, would take three of those eleven for three weeks. Separately, Tanvi's reconciliation of Lehja's telemetry against the Laghav panel required viewer-level joins not permitted under the current data-processing agreement; amending it under the DPDP Act's consent and purpose-limitation requirements would take Lisaan's legal team, on Reuben's estimate, four to six weeks. And Chitrakathi Networks in Chennai, running the same release into an IPL-season peak, had no monthly report, no contractual colour, and no idea any of this was happening.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibits 1, 2 and 3 describe the same service over the same months and disagree. Which of them, if any, is measuring Lisaan's business, and what does each one's footnote tell you about why it says what it says?
  2. Exhibit 4 shows the interval between internal knowledge and client disclosure lengthening through 2026. Is that a reporting problem, an incentive problem, or an artefact of the 2024 decision to retire the weekly note — and how would you tell the difference?
  3. Read with the sequence in Exhibit 5: Lehja's 2023 commitment to a formula-driven status was sold as a promise of transparency. Trace how it became an instrument that made disclosure more expensive. Would you have signed it?
  4. Exhibit 6 shows the formal cadence attended by three of nine and an unlogged WhatsApp group carrying the real relationship. What has each channel taught Faisal about how much to trust Lehja, and can a cadence be repaired without first being named as broken?
  5. Sharmistha writes both the board slide and the customer report. Evaluate the argument that these should never be the same person's documents, against the argument that separating them is how a company ends up telling two stories.
  6. It is Monday morning, 16 November. What does Sharmistha send to Dubai, what did she say to the board on Friday, and what would she have to be willing to lose for each of those two sentences to be the same sentence?

At twenty to one, Sharmistha closed the board pack without changing slide nineteen and opened the October draft again. She typed a sentence beginning "During September and October our own platform may have contributed to", read it, and did not know whether the word may was honesty or cowardice. Outside, the last of the Diwali lights on the building opposite were still up, three weeks late, blinking on a timer nobody had bothered to reset. Her phone showed a message from Faisal, sent at 11.04 Dubai time, which she had not yet opened. She made a fresh cup of tea and sat down in front of both screens again.

Manthan Commerce Cloud: The Real-Time Sync Request

A short decision case on listening and questioning before advocacy

1. The scene

On Monday, 14 September, Arjun Mehta stood at the whiteboard on the fourth floor of Manthan Commerce Cloud's office in Bellandur, Bengaluru, looking at a slide he had already drafted twice. Arjun was Senior Product Manager for the Inventory and Order Routing line, and in five days he was due to present the Q3 roadmap to the founders and the board. One line item sat at the top of every draft: whether to commit scarce backend engineering capacity to a bespoke real-time inventory sync API demanded by Tarazu Retail FZE, a Dubai-based retailer and Manthan's largest Gulf account, or to a platform-wide reliability programme engineering had requested for two quarters. He had already drafted an email recommending the Tarazu build, and had not yet spoken properly to anyone who disagreed with him.

2. Company background

Manthan Commerce Cloud sold unified-commerce software: a single system that let retailers manage inventory, orders and fulfilment across stores, marketplaces and warehouses from one dashboard. Founded in 2018 by two former Flipkart supply-chain engineers, it had grown to roughly 210 employees and ₹96 crore in annual recurring revenue by mid-2026, serving about 340 retail and D2C brands across India and the Gulf. Its direct competitors were Unicommerce, Increff and Vinculum; Zoho Inventory served smaller retailers, while giants such as Reliance Retail built such systems in-house. Manthan's pitch was speed of setup and strong support, and it had used that reputation to win clients in Dubai and Abu Dhabi who wanted an Indian vendor comfortable with chaotic multi-channel retail across Indian and Gulf time zones.

Engineering split across two Indian cities — a 34-person core-platform team in Bengaluru and a 19-person integrations team in Pune. Design sat in a two-person studio in Berlin. A six-person data science function, led out of Toronto, mined order and inventory data for product decisions. Customer success ran out of Singapore, and enterprise sales for the Gulf ran from New Jersey.

3. The situation

Tarazu Retail FZE ran 46 stores across the UAE and Saudi Arabia plus a fast-growing online storefront, and had been a Manthan customer since 2023. Its contract was worth ₹3.2 crore in annual recurring revenue, Manthan's single largest account, up for renewal in 45 days. Over six weeks Tarazu had escalated three times: during two August flash sales, its storefront had shown items as available that were already sold out in-store, leading to cancelled orders and, Tarazu's team said, visibly annoyed customers on Instagram. Faisal Al-Rashid, Tarazu's VP of Operations, had told Manthan's sales head plainly that unless Manthan built "a real-time inventory sync API" before the next big sale — Diwali-adjacent promotions Gulf retailers increasingly ran to catch the NRI shopping calendar — Tarazu would start evaluating Unicommerce.

Neil Kapoor, Manthan's New Jersey-based Gulf sales head, passed this to Arjun with the subject line "non-negotiable — need on roadmap." Arjun's first instinct was to agree: losing the largest account before a board update would be a bad quarter to explain. But Priya Raghavan, the Bengaluru engineering lead, pointed out that "real-time sync" was Tarazu's phrase, not a specification Manthan had validated, and that granting it could commit engineer-weeks earmarked for reliability work across roughly forty other accounts. Arjun realised he had been treating a stated request as the requirement, without asking Tarazu's team what "real-time" needed to mean, or asking his own data scientists whether the failure pattern matched the assumed cause.

4. The people

Priya Raghavan — Engineering Lead, Pune. Priya had warned for two quarters that Manthan's sync architecture was failing under load roughly 40 times a month, disproportionately during flash sales. She wanted the quarter committed to reliability, and worried a bespoke Tarazu build would set a precedent while doing nothing for 39 other accounts with similar, less publicised problems.
Neil Kapoor — Sales Head, New Jersey. Neil owned the Gulf relationship and the renewal number. He wanted a fast, visible commitment ahead of the Diwali sale window, and admitted he had promised the account team he would "get this on the roadmap" before fully checking feasibility.
Kavya Iyer — Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Kavya managed the Tarazu relationship and had sat in on the escalation calls. She was less certain than Neil that Tarazu's engineers had a precise picture of the failure — one call revealed, almost in passing, that Tarazu's in-store point-of-sale system pushed stock updates only every fifteen minutes, which she suspected was closer to the real problem.
Daniel Cho — Data Scientist, Toronto. Daniel held the platform-wide sync logs but was not asked for an opinion until Wednesday, when he offered that he could pull the actual oversell incidents in under a day, if anyone wanted to know what was happening before committing engineering time.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows the pattern Priya had been citing: oversell and stock-mismatch incidents by segment, before anyone disaggregated Tarazu's pattern from the rest of the base.

Exhibit 1 — Sync failure incidents by account segment, Q2 FY26 (platform-wide)

Source: sync-error logs compiled by Daniel Cho's team, September 2026. "ARR at risk" flags accounts with an open escalation in the quarter.

Exhibit 2 lays out the revenue exposure and timing that made this a five-day decision.

Exhibit 2 — Top account exposure and renewal timing

Tarazu Retail FZE3.245 days3

Source: Manthan revenue operations, 14 September 2026.

By Wednesday, Arjun had asked Daniel to plot the week itself — a record of who he had spoken to and in what order, because he suspected his own sequence of conversations was part of the problem. Exhibit 3 is that timeline.

Exhibit 3 — The week's conversations, in order. The green marker on Wednesday is when Arjun first asked a question of his own data, rather than relaying someone else's framing.

6. The options

Option A — Commit the quarter to Tarazu's stated request

Build the sync API as Faisal described it, using eight to ten engineer-weeks from Pune. Upside: a fast, visible answer ahead of renewal. Cost: the reliability programme slips a quarter, the other 40 affected accounts (₹18 crore ARR) get no relief, and Manthan may build infrastructure that does not fix the oversells if the true bottleneck is the 15-minute POS push.

Option B — Hold the line on the reliability programme

Decline the bespoke build, explain the platform-wide roadmap to Tarazu, and offer a firm date. Upside: protects the broader client base and keeps engineering focused on wide leverage. Cost: real risk of losing Tarazu at renewal and a damaged Gulf pipeline.

Option C — Scope a narrower fix around the actual failure

Before committing capacity, use Daniel's data and Kavya's conversation with Tarazu's warehouse team to test whether the real need is oversell prevention during high-volume windows, not "real-time sync" generally. If the POS push is the dominant cause, build a smaller "flash-sale oversell guard" folded into the reliability programme. Upside: likely solves the actual pain at a fraction of the cost. Cost: requires convincing Neil and Faisal on a tight timeline, and depends on the diagnosis holding up.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. What did Arjun actually know on Monday, and how much of his draft recommendation rested on Neil's framing rather than on Tarazu's own operational reality?
  2. Re-read Priya's, Neil's, Kavya's and Daniel's positions in Section 4. Which view does Arjun most need to steelman — state as strongly and fairly as its holder would — before comparing Options A, B and C honestly?
  3. What questions, asked earlier in the week and of whom, would have let Arjun reach Wednesday's insight (the 15-minute POS push) by Monday afternoon instead?
  4. Given Exhibits 1–3, which option would you recommend to the board on Friday, and what would you tell Faisal Al-Rashid to make it credible to him?

8. A note for the learner

This case turns on a common failure: a product manager receives a stakeholder's stated request and treats it as the requirement, advocating for it before asking a clarifying question of the people closer to the problem. Neil's email was not dishonest — it accurately relayed what Faisal Al-Rashid said. But "real-time inventory sync API" is Tarazu's proposed solution, not their underlying need, and Arjun's first draft adopted it without testing it. The discipline this topic asks for is narrow and practical: ask before advocating, and be able to state the other side's position — Priya's, Neil's, Kavya's — as well as they would state it themselves.

A well-reasoned answer does two things a rushed one does not. It separates the stated request from the evidence about what is actually failing, using data already in the case rather than assuming "the client is always right" or "the client doesn't understand their own system." And it treats Priya's reliability concern and Neil's revenue concern as both legitimate: neither is wrong, each represents a real constraint from their own vantage point.

On that basis, Option C is the defensible path, provided Arjun completes the diligence Daniel's data made possible: confirm with Tarazu's warehouse team, not just Kavya's secondhand account, that the POS push is the dominant cause, and size the "oversell guard" against the reliability programme's existing plan rather than as new work. If that diagnosis holds, Option C converts a costly rebuild into a targeted fix that serves Tarazu, the other 39 escalated accounts, and the reliability roadmap at once — visible only once someone has asked the question rather than advocated for an answer. If it does not hold, Arjun has lost a few days, and Options A and B remain available. The cost of asking first is small; the cost of advocating first, as this case shows, is a quarter of engineering capacity on the wrong problem.

Manthan Commerce Cloud, Tarazu Retail FZE and all named individuals are fictional, created for classroom discussion. Real brands and institutions named are used solely as market context.

Nalika Metering Systems: What Sudhir Kamat Asked For

An open case on asking before advocating, and on steelmanning the view you have already decided against

1. Sunday night, Aundh

The monsoon had gone out of Pune on 11 October 2026, leaving the kind of warm, still evening in which Aditi Ranade normally slept well. She did not expect to. On the dining table of her flat in Aundh lay two printed documents. The first was a forty-one page bid response to Nakhlah Utility Services LLC, a Dubai operator running district water networks under a municipal concession; the tender closed at 17:00 Gulf Standard Time on Monday, 12 October. The second was a two-page note from Sudhir Kamat, Chief Operating Officer of Nirbadh Water Operations, the private concessionaire that ran water supply and billing for a cluster of Maharashtra municipalities and was Nalika's largest customer. Kamat's note asked, in one sentence, for hourly consumption telemetry from every meter in the Nashik and Nagpur districts by 1 January 2027.

Aditi was Director of Product at Nalika Metering Systems. She had spent eleven days assembling a case for saying yes to Kamat and putting the same capability at the centre of the Nakhlah bid. The deck was done. What she had not done, and what had sat under her ribs since Thursday, was ask Kamat why he wanted hourly data. She had asked many other people what they thought of hourly data. That, she suspected, was not the same thing.

2. The company, and a decision made in 2023

Nalika Metering Systems was founded in Pune in 2017 by Dr Vasudha Naik, formerly of a Nagpur engineering institute's hydraulics group, and Harish Bhatnagar, a telecom systems engineer. It sold what the sector called an AMI stack: ultrasonic smart water meters, the network carrying their readings, and the software turning readings into bills, leak alerts and regulatory reports. By FY26 it employed 410 people and reported ₹184 crore of revenue, ₹41 crore of it software ARR, with 11.4 lakh meters across nine Indian cities and one Gulf pilot.

The decision that shaped everything Aditi could now do was taken in 2023. Bidding for municipal contracts under AMRUT 2.0, Nalika quoted one bundled price per connection per month — meter, connectivity, software, maintenance — rather than selling hardware and software separately. It won on that structure, and locked itself into two things. The hardware margin was thin and fixed for eight years, so every rupee of unplanned device cost came out of Nalika's pocket, not the utility's. And to meet an eight-year battery warranty on meters from Rachit Meter Works of Vadodara, the firmware woke once a day, pushed a compressed batch of twenty-four readings over NB-IoT, and slept. Daily batch was never revisited; it was the physics of the commercial promise.

3. The industry

India's urban water sector in 2026 was being rebuilt with public money and measured, for the first time, at household granularity. The Jal Jeevan Mission had put metered connections into rural households; AMRUT 2.0 and the Smart Cities Mission pushed urban local bodies towards volumetric billing and non-revenue water targets. Established manufacturers such as Genus Power, HPL Electric and Secure Meters were moving from electricity into water; Siemens, Schneider and Honeywell competed at the systems-integration layer, often with L&T, TCS or Infosys as prime contractors on smart-city packages. Connectivity came from Jio and Airtel NB-IoT bands whose indoor coverage in dense, low-rise neighbourhoods was uneven and poorly documented.

Two regulatory facts bore on Aditi's Monday. Water meters required Legal Metrology approval against Bureau of Indian Standards specifications, and any firmware change altering measurement behaviour risked reopening a certification Nalika's hardware head had taken fourteen months to obtain. And the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, brought household consumption squarely into scope: a daily total said how much a family used; an hourly series said when they woke, when they left, and when the flat was empty. Nalika's contracts named the utility as data fiduciary and Nalika as processor — an allocation nobody had tested against a request to publish granular data.

Abroad, the opportunity was larger and the tolerance smaller. Nakhlah's tender covered 2.6 lakh connections over five years at roughly ₹96 crore, and had been shaped by Rafiq Sheikh, Nalika's International Business Director in Dubai, around the claim that Nalika could deliver hourly telemetry at city scale.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The sequence mattered, and Aditi had reconstructed it twice.

In April 2026, Nirbadh's contract was amended to add a non-revenue water target: from 38 per cent at handover to 22 per cent by 2030, with a checkpoint of 28 per cent in March 2027. Nalika's leak-alert module was the principal instrument for hitting it, and through Q1 FY27 its reported precision was 91 per cent — a figure that appeared in three sales decks and in the Nakhlah bid.

In June, Jyoti Marandi, Head of Field Operations in Indore, said in a weekly call that Nirbadh's crews were "not going out on most of the alerts". It was minuted as a training issue. In July, read success in Nagpur dipped and analytics reported it as 96.4 per cent, above the 95 per cent floor carrying a ₹40 lakh quarterly penalty. In August, Samar Qureshi's hardware group in Coimbatore closed a ticket on antenna gain variance in a batch of about 18,000 meters shipped in late 2025: "within tolerance, monitor".

On 28 September, Kamat sent his note. Rafiq read it in Dubai the same evening and wrote to Aditi and Vasudha that this confirmed a global pattern and that the Nakhlah bid should lead with hourly telemetry. Aditi began building the case. On 6 October, modelling batteries for the bid, she found that hourly reporting on the installed Rachit units cut expected life from eight years to roughly three and a quarter, implying a replacement liability of about ₹46 crore on the Nirbadh base alone against a cash position of ₹62 crore.

On 8 October two things came loose. Neha Ravindran, Head of Analytics in Hyderabad, confirmed under questioning that the 91 per cent figure covered only alerts crews had been dispatched to — roughly a quarter of those raised — and that the rest had no recorded outcome. And Jyoti, asked directly for the first time, said that since May her Indore desk had suppressed a class of low-confidence night-flow alerts before they reached Nirbadh's crews, because the crews had begun ignoring the queue wholesale. Analytics was never told; the suppressed alerts were not in the denominator either.

Aditi had by then spoken to Rafiq four times, Vasudha three, Harish twice, Neha twice, Jyoti once, and Sudhir Kamat not at all.

5. The people

Aditi Ranade — Director of Product, Pune. Eight years at Nalika, promoted eighteen months ago. Believes the company wins by understanding water, not by shipping fastest. Has circulated a draft recommendation supporting hourly telemetry, and knows reversing it publicly on Monday costs her something with Rafiq and the founders.
Dr Vasudha Naik — Co-founder and CEO, Pune. Wants the Nakhlah win as proof of an export story, and says Nalika should "never lose a deal on a capability question". She has not circulated the covenant in the Nistara Capital Partners term sheet: a Series C tranche contingent on ₹55 crore of ARR by 31 March 2027, against ₹41 crore today.
Harish Bhatnagar — Co-founder and VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Argues the quarter belongs to connectivity and read reliability; his 22 engineer-weeks cannot fund both. He has not said the over-the-air update pipeline his team owns failed twice this year on large fleets, which is much of why he resists pushing firmware to 3.9 lakh meters.
Samar Qureshi — Head of Hardware and Firmware, Coimbatore. Maintains the meters perform within specification and that read failures are a network problem, not a device one. He shepherded the Legal Metrology approval personally and treats any firmware change touching the measurement path as existential. He has not escalated the antenna variance beyond the closed ticket.
Jyoti Marandi — Head of Field Operations, Indore. Closest to the crews, furthest from the roadmap. Believes the alert product failed on workflow, not data frequency, and that hourly data makes the queue worse. Her team is measured on dispatch-to-resolution time, which improved sharply once she began suppressing alerts she told no one about.
Neha Ravindran — Head of Analytics, Hyderabad. Built the dashboards everyone quotes. Technically careful, organisationally quiet: she documented the precision definition in a footnote nobody read, and did not raise it when the number appeared in the bid. Her incentive is a clean quarterly report to the board.
Rafiq Sheikh — International Business Director, Dubai. Carries a Gulf number worth ₹96 crore over five years and a commission tied to it. Insists hourly telemetry decides the evaluation. He has not shared the full scoring rubric with Pune, and calls the technical annexure "standard".
Pieter van Dael — Hydraulic modelling consultant, Rotterdam. Retained forty days a year. Holds that Indian networks lose water at district level, and that without bounded district metering areas and pressure management, household telemetry of any frequency is noise. He is also bidding for a larger modelling engagement.
Sudhir Kamat — Chief Operating Officer, Nirbadh Water Operations, Nashik. Runs a concession under political scrutiny, with municipal elections due in 2027 and a complaint volume he answers for. He asked for hourly telemetry in eleven words. Nobody at Nalika has asked what he means to do with it.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets the commercial frame: where the meters are, what they earn, and how much rests on one counterparty.

7. Voices

"Every serious utility in the Gulf is moving to hourly. If we bid daily batch, we are the Indian vendor with the cheap meter. I need the roadmap line, not a research project."

Rafiq Sheikh, video call, 2 October

"I have no objection to hourly. I object to hourly on this fleet, pushed by an OTA pipeline that dropped 11,000 devices in March. Give me the quarter for reads and you will get telemetry that survives."

Harish Bhatnagar, engineering review, 5 October

"The crews are not lazy. They stopped opening the queue because in April they walked eleven sites and found nothing. Send them twenty-four times the data and they will stop opening it faster."

Jyoti Marandi, chat thread, 7 October

"I want to be precise. Ninety-one per cent is precision on dispatched alerts, not the model's accuracy. I wrote that in the footnote in March."

Neha Ravindran, call with Aditi, 8 October

"You are arguing about the sampling rate of a signal you have not bounded. Close the district metering areas first, or you are measuring a hundred thousand taps to find one broken main."

Pieter van Dael, email, 8 October

"We are not losing Nakhlah on principle. Find the way to yes, and tell me what it costs."

Vasudha Naik, corridor, 9 October

"Don't overthink the note. Get me the January date and I will handle my board."

Sudhir Kamat, WhatsApp reply to Aditi's request for a call, 10 October

8. The options as Aditi sees them

Option A — Commit to hourly telemetry on the Nirbadh base by January, and lead the Nakhlah bid with it. Her draft recommends this. It gives Kamat the eleven words he wrote and Rafiq the claim he wants. It consumes most of the 22 engineer-weeks, needs a firmware push Samar will contest and Harish distrusts, creates a battery exposure of about ₹46 crore against ₹62 crore of cash, and requires a DPDP position Nalika does not have.

Option B — Decline hourly, and spend the quarter on read reliability and the antenna batch. This protects the SLA, addresses Exhibit 2's lower rows, and is what Harish and, differently, Samar want. It tells Nalika's largest customer no, in writing, eleven weeks before a checkpoint, and forces Rafiq to bid without a capability he has already implied Nalika has.

Option C — Offer a bounded pilot: hourly on 25,000 meters in one Nashik district, batteries replaced at Nalika's cost, evidence in ninety days. Roughly ₹3 crore of hardware and eight engineer-weeks. It buys time and produces evidence, but defers the SLA problem, gives Rafiq something ambiguous to bid with, and may postpone the same argument to February with a smaller balance sheet.

All three share an assumption Aditi has begun to distrust: that the question is how often a meter should report. Exhibit 4 suggests what Kamat answers for in a municipal review is not leaks but 1.08 lakh disputed estimated bills, produced by meters that did not report — a completeness problem hourly telemetry would worsen on the meters already failing. Pieter implies neither frequency nor completeness is binding, and that Nalika has sold a household-level product into a district-level problem. Jyoti's suppression implies the alert product's real conversion is nearer 4,310 repairs from 41,200 alerts, failing in a workflow nobody owns. And Exhibit 6, if representative, makes the capability Rafiq built the bid around worth eight points of a hundred, while thirty sit on the read reliability Harish has been asking for.

She could not be sure of any of it. Exhibit 4 was unauthorised and its categories overlapped. Exhibit 6 was a partial page from a man with a commission. Pieter had a contract to sell. Jyoti had concealed something material for five months. Every source pointing away from Option A had a reason to.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The Nakhlah tender closed at 17:00 GST on Monday, 12 October; Dubai ran ninety minutes behind Pune, leaving Aditi until roughly 18:30 IST to change the bid's technical narrative, and Rafiq had said a late structural change needed re-approval he could not obtain. Kamat expected a written response by Monday evening. The board met on Thursday, with Aparna Seth of Nistara Capital Partners attending; the ₹55 crore ARR covenant would be discussed whether or not Aditi raised it.

The constraints were unforgiving and entangled. Twenty-two engineer-weeks existed in the quarter and could not be bought quickly at Bengaluru salary bands. Cash stood at ₹62 crore, about fourteen months of runway. The SLA carried a ₹40 lakh quarterly penalty below 95 per cent successful reads on a definition neither party had pinned down, and Exhibit 2 put Nalika above the line on one reading and below it on another. Any firmware change touching the measurement path put a fourteen-month Legal Metrology approval back in play. The DPDP Act made hourly household series a question of purpose and consent Nalika, as processor, could not answer alone. And the 2023 bundled price meant every replaced battery was Nalika's cost.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. List everything Aditi believes about Kamat's request; for each belief, name the evidence and the person it came from. How much of the case for Option A rests on a chain in which Kamat never appears?
  2. Exhibits 2 and 3 are internally consistent and externally misleading. What question, asked of Neha in March, would have kept the 91 per cent figure out of a tender document?
  3. Steelman Rafiq's position at its strongest, assuming he is honest, well informed, and Exhibit 6 unrepresentative. Do the same for Jyoti, assuming her suppression was sound operational judgement. What would have to be true for Aditi to act on each?
  4. Jyoti's suppression and Samar's closed ticket were each rational within that person's incentives. What would Nalika have to change for either to surface in May rather than October, and what does it cost to make such information cheap to say?
  5. Suppose Aditi reaches Kamat on Monday and has twenty minutes. Write the four questions she should ask, in order, and say what she would do differently on each possible answer. What would make him answer rather than repeat the request?
  6. It is 08:00 on Monday, 12 October, with a tender closing in Dubai, a commitment due in Nashik and a board on Thursday. What does Aditi do first, what does she decline to do, and what does she tell the board about how this decision was reached — including about her own eleven days?

11. Sunday, late

At a quarter past eleven Aditi put the bid face down and read Kamat's two pages again. Eleven words of request, and below them a paragraph about the municipal review set for the second week of January, which she had skimmed the first four times. She opened a blank document, typed "What is the January meeting for?", looked at it, and did not send it. Dubai would wake at half past nine. Kamat was on a site visit in Nagpur until noon. Somewhere in Maharashtra eighteen thousand meters were reporting, or not reporting, into a database nobody would query before Thursday.

Nalika Metering Systems, Nirbadh Water Operations, Nakhlah Utility Services LLC, Rachit Meter Works, Nistara Capital Partners and all named individuals are fictional, created for classroom discussion. Real companies, brands, missions and regulators appear solely as market context.
exp20v2-comm.listening:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Listening and Questioning

Am I asking before advocating, and can I steelman the other view?

1. Two calls, one Thursday

On the morning of 17 September 2026, Ananya Rawat, a senior product manager at Lokvani Commerce Cloud in Bengaluru, had two calls forty minutes apart, and each one arrived carrying a different verdict on what she should build next quarter. Lokvani sold a storefront-and-checkout platform to roughly 2,400 direct-to-consumer sellers across India, and had crossed ₹86 crore in annual recurring revenue that year. The first call was with Karan Mehta, the sales VP in Gurugram, who wanted a "smart repricer" that would let sellers auto-adjust prices against competitors, because it sat at the centre of a ₹4.2 crore enterprise pipeline he was chasing with a Jaipur skincare label expanding into forty new SKUs. The second call was with Fatima Sheikh, who ran support operations out of Kochi and had just pulled a number that alarmed her: 34% of new sellers were abandoning the onboarding flow before their first sale, and 310 existing sellers, worth a meaningful slice of renewal revenue, had logged tickets calling the seller dashboard confusing.

Both Karan and Fatima were experienced, well-liked colleagues, and both were certain. Ananya had one engineering pod for the next quarter, enough for one of these bets, not both. Her instinct, and the instinct of most competent product managers under this kind of pressure, was to pick a side quickly and start building the case for it. The topic this page is about is why that instinct, however natural, is usually the wrong first move — and what to do instead before a single line of the roadmap gets written.

Table 1 — the two asks, as first stated
Karan Mehta (Sales, Gurugram)Fatima Sheikh (Support, Kochi)
AskBuild a smart repricing featureSimplify the onboarding dashboard
Number cited₹4.2 crore pipeline34% setup drop-off; 310 sellers at risk
Time frameDeal closes in six weeksRenewals due this quarter

2. The idea

Listening and questioning, in the sense this page uses the phrase, is not general politeness or patience. It is a specific discipline: asking enough real questions to understand a position accurately, and to state it back so well that the person holding it would nod at your version of it, before you offer your own position at all. The second half of that discipline has a name — steelmanning, the deliberate construction of the strongest possible version of an argument you may end up disagreeing with, the opposite of a straw man built to be knocked down easily.

The intellectual roots run through two places. Chris Argyris, an organisational-behaviour researcher at Harvard, spent the 1970s and 1980s studying why smart, well-intentioned managers kept talking past each other, and named the pattern the ladder of inference: people climb from raw observation to belief in seconds, without noticing the climb, and then argue from the top of the ladder as though it were the bottom. Around the same time, Roger Fisher and William Ury, negotiators at Harvard Law School, published Getting to Yes (1981), which argued that most negotiators fail not because their position is weak but because they defend a position before anyone has established the underlying interest it serves. Product management absorbed both threads later, through the discipline now called continuous discovery — the habit of treating every stakeholder conversation, customer or internal, as a chance to update your model of the problem before you touch the solution.

The sentence Ananya could say in either meeting without sounding glib: "Before I argue for a fix, let me check I can argue your side of this as well as you can."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in a fixed order, and the order is the entire discipline — reverse it and you get advocacy wearing the costume of a question. The sequence starts with suspending your own conclusion long enough to state your intent: "I have a view, but I want to understand yours first" costs five seconds and changes how the next ten minutes go. From there, practitioners open with genuinely open questions — "what would happen if we didn't build this" rather than "don't you think support tickets matter more" — because a closed question smuggles the answer inside it.

Figure 1 — Karan and Fatima each climbed their own ladder in seconds. Questioning means walking a colleague back down their ladder to the data at the bottom, not arguing with them at the top.

The step practitioners most often skip is the paraphrase-and-confirm: saying back what you heard in your own words and asking "did I get that right," which forces both the accuracy of your listening and the visibility of any gap to the surface. Only after that confirmation does steelmanning proper begin — stating the other person's case in its strongest form, out loud, including the parts of it you privately doubt. Ananya's version, said to Karan, was roughly: "If we don't ship repricing, you lose a logo that would prove Lokvani can serve category leaders, not just small sellers — that's a positioning problem, not just one deal." Only once that lands as fair does advocacy begin, and even then it is framed as building on what was heard rather than replacing it.

4. A worked example

Ananya used a standard prioritisation formula, RICE — Reach times Impact times Confidence, divided by Effort — to make the comparison concrete, and the first pass used the numbers exactly as advocated, unexamined. Karan's reach estimate covered all 1,200 sellers active on paid plans, since any of them might theoretically want repricing; impact was rated 3 out of 3, "massive," because it was tied to a marquee deal; confidence sat at 80%, because Karan was confident; and effort was estimated at four person-months of engineering.

Table 2 — RICE score, before and after one clarifying question
PassReachImpactConfidenceEffortScore
1 — advocacy, as stated1,20030.84(1,200×3×0.8)/4 = 720
2 — one question asked18030.84(180×3×0.8)/4 = 108

The single question that produced the second row was simple: "of the sellers in your pipeline, how many have named repricing by name, unprompted, as a reason to buy?" The honest answer was six, all in one sub-category — sellers running more than 500 SKUs with volatile input costs, of whom Lokvani had 180 on the platform, not 1,200. Reach alone, corrected by one question, cut the score by 85%, before Fatima's side of the case had even been discussed. The lesson is not that Karan was dishonest; his instinct about the deal was probably right. It is that an unquestioned number, stated with confidence, travels through a roadmap discussion doing far more work than it has earned.

5. What a learner must notice

Listening is not agreeing

Steelmanning Fatima's case did not commit Ananya to building her fix; it committed her to being able to argue it as well as Fatima could, so that whatever she chose next was chosen against the strongest version of both options, not the weakest one.

It is not the absence of a position

A product manager who only asks questions and never advocates is not being humble, and after enough meetings the room reads it correctly as indecision. The discipline has two halves in a fixed order; skipping the second half is as much a failure as skipping the first.

It is easily confused with therapeutic active listening

Reflecting feelings back to make someone feel heard is a different skill, aimed at a different outcome. Here the goal of a paraphrase is to correct your model of the problem, not to soothe the speaker, and a paraphrase that changes nothing about what you do next has not done its job.

It struggles under real time pressure

When a payment gateway is down and merchants are losing sales by the minute, a directive call beats a round of steelmanning; the discipline earns its keep on decisions with a week or more of runway, not on incidents measured in minutes.

It cannot settle who is right

Understanding Karan's case fully, and Fatima's case fully, tells Ananya what each of them believes and why, with more accuracy than she had an hour earlier. It does not, by itself, tell her which bet the company should make; that judgment still has to be made, on evidence, afterward.

It depends on psychological safety that is not always present

A junior product manager asking a powerful VP genuinely open questions can be read as insubordination in some rooms, and questioning without any safety to disagree afterward becomes theatre — the appearance of inquiry with the outcome already fixed.

6. Where it looks different

In a consumer product, the person Ananya would be steelmanning is often absent from the room entirely — a user she has never met, whose "position" has to be reconstructed from support tickets, session recordings, and a handful of interviews, which makes the paraphrase step harder to check for accuracy. In enterprise B2B, exactly Ananya's situation, the stakeholder sits across the table and can correct her paraphrase on the spot, but carries organisational incentives — a sales quota, a support SLA — that colour which facts get mentioned first. In a marketplace, the discipline has to run twice in parallel, once for each side of the transaction, because a change that steelmans the seller's case can quietly damage the buyer's, and vice versa.

Table 3 — stage changes who gets steelmanned first
StageTypical first moveRisk if skipped
Early-stage (pre-PMF)Steelman the customer over the internal advocateBuilding the founder's pet feature instead of the market's need
Scaled company (Lokvani's stage)Steelman both internal functions before either customer segmentA functional turf war disguised as a product debate

7. Common mistakes

The first mistake is the rehearsed question — one asked purely to create an opening for your own point, recognisable because the asker stops listening the instant the other person starts answering. The cheapest catch is to notice whether you can repeat the answer back accurately five minutes later. The second is treating a single loud stakeholder's account as the reach number, exactly as the first RICE pass did; the diagnostic is to ask for one unprompted piece of evidence, as Ananya did, before the number goes into any model. The third is confusing volume of questions with quality of listening — ten questions that never touch the other person's actual interest are noise; the fix is to ask, after each answer, "so the real constraint for you is X — is that fair," and watch whether the answer is yes.

Table 4 — mistakes and their cheapest test
MistakeSymptomCheapest diagnostic
Rehearsed questionInterrupts the answerCan you repeat their answer accurately?
Unquestioned reachOne person's number becomes the plan's numberAsk for one unprompted data point
Question volume over qualityMany questions, no revised modelName the interest back and check it lands

8. What good looks like

By the following Tuesday, Ananya had run both conversations to their proper end. She could state Karan's case — a strategic logo, proof Lokvani served category leaders — better than Karan had first stated it himself, because she had pushed him to admit the pipeline rested on one seller, not twelve. She could state Fatima's case with the same precision: 310 sellers were not confused about repricing, they were failing at the first ten minutes of using the product at all, a problem that compounded every week it went unfixed. Neither VP left the conversation feeling dismissed, because each had watched her argue their own position back to them with more rigour than they had brought to it, before she said a word about what she planned to do.

9. What Ananya decided, and what comes next

She funded the onboarding fix for the quarter and told Karan, honestly, that repricing would ship after, once the sub-segment that actually wanted it was large enough to justify the effort — a decision Karan could accept because he had heard his own case treated seriously rather than overruled by fiat. The reasoning that made this defensible was not that support's number was bigger; it was that one clarifying question had already cut sales' number by 85%, while support's number had survived the same scrutiny intact.

From here, the discipline this page describes points toward its harder cousin: doing all of this across a language, a time zone, and a set of unstated cultural rules about how directly disagreement may be voiced at all — the subject of communicating across cultures, which this same module takes up next, because Lokvani's engineering pod sat in Pune and its next enterprise prospect, after the skincare deal, was based in Dubai.

Two questions worth sitting with: Whose case, right now, could you argue only in its weakest form — and what does that tell you about how much you have actually listened? And when did you last change a number in a plan because one honest question, not a new dataset, made you doubt it?
exp40v2-comm.listening:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Listening and Questioning

Near-expert depth: asking before advocating, and the arithmetic of a steelman.

1. Two rooms, one fortnight

On 4 March 2026, Rukmini Iyer, director of product at Bageshri Diagnostics Devices in Pune, sat with a field-service dashboard on the screen and two senior colleagues who had already made up their minds. Bageshri built the Sparsh 3, a point-of-care haematology analyser sold to hospital chains and pathology labs: an instrument licensed under CDSCO, used in NABL-accredited labs, and monetised through single-use reagent cartridges, which supplied 44% of the company's ₹212 crore in FY26 revenue. Of 1,180 installed devices, 21% were running fewer than 40 tests a week against a cartridge break-even of 55. Underused machines attract renegotiation at renewal and eventual removal.

Meera Salunkhe, the VP of field operations in Nagpur, had a diagnosis ready: the daily calibration routine was too fiddly for a junior technician, and the answer was a hardware revision with auto-calibration — ₹6.4 crore of tooling and two quarters of regulatory re-submission. Imran Qureshi, who ran the software pod in Hyderabad, had the opposite diagnosis: technicians were fine with calibration and lost instead in the result-review screen, an ₹1.1 crore fix shippable in seven weeks. Both were credible; both cited the same dashboard. Rukmini had no independent way to tell which opinion the evidence supported, with roughly ₹9 crore of committed spend and forgone time riding on it.

A week later and 840 kilometres south, Tanmay Bhatkal, group product manager at Bhramar Voice Cloud in Bengaluru, faced another version of the problem. Bhramar sold an AI voice agent making servicing and collections calls for NBFCs and small finance banks — 38 enterprise customers, ₹58 crore of ARR, and a compliance surface shaped by the RBI's digital-lending guidelines, TRAI's rules on commercial communication and the DPDP Act. On 11 March its largest customer, a Chennai gold-loan NBFC worth ₹7.5 crore of the renewal book, demanded "full script control": every model utterance drawn from a fixed, customer-authored library. Tanmay's ML lead, Jaya Menon in Toronto, called it product-destroying, since the system's measured advantage came from generating context-appropriate phrasing. Tanmay's instinct, like Rukmini's, was to marshal evidence and push back. This page is about why, in both rooms, the right first act was to ask.

2. The idea, and the camps that disagree about it

Define the practice precisely. Listening and questioning, as a product discipline, is the deliberate sequencing of inquiry ahead of advocacy, terminating in a test: you can state the other party's position in a form they endorse as at least as strong as their own, including the parts you expect to defeat. That test is the steelman, and it separates the discipline from politeness. Politeness lets someone finish their sentence; a steelman repairs their argument for them.

The intellectual history has three tributaries. The first is clinical: Carl Rogers's 1950s work on reflective listening, carried into management by Edgar Schein, whose Humble Inquiry (2013) argued that senior people substitute telling for asking and destroy the information flow they depend on. The second is negotiation theory: Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes (1981) separated stated positions from underlying interests, the move that makes "full script control" legible as a demand about something other than scripts. The third is epistemics: Anatol Rapoport's rules for disagreement, popularised by Daniel Dennett, which require re-expressing the opponent's position so well they say "I wish I'd put it that way" before you object. Chris Argyris supplies the connective tissue with the ladder of inference — people ascend from data to conclusion in seconds, then argue at the top, where no evidence lives.

Four schools disagree about how much of this to do, and the disagreement is real rather than semantic. The inquiry-first school (Schein, Torres-style continuous discovery) holds that the binding constraint on product quality is the accuracy of the team's model of the problem. It would sign: "every material decision should be preceded by one conversation whose purpose is to change your mind." It would not sign: "listening replaces judgement." The structured-dissent school — red teams, Rapoport's rules, Intel's constructive confrontation, Amazon's disagree-and-commit — holds that unstructured listening is captured by seniority. It would sign: "the steelman must be a named responsibility, not an attitude." It would not sign: "rapport produces truth." The behavioural school, canonically Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test, holds stated preference worthless beside behaviour and money. It would sign: "ask what they did last Tuesday and what they paid." It would not sign: "more conversations improve decisions." The decision-velocity school, clearest in Bezos's reversible-versus-irreversible distinction, prices inquiry's latency cost. It would sign: "for reversible decisions, shipping is cheaper than asking." It would not sign: "asking is free."

The four camps agree on one operational claim and no more: the cost of inquiry scales with calendar time, while the cost of being wrong scales with reversibility. Everything else they contest.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic

Experts run this in a sequence, and the sequence matters more than any technique in it. First, declared intent — this conversation is for understanding, not deciding — which sounds ceremonial and is not: it removes the listener's incentive to argue defensively. Second, retrospective rather than hypothetical questioning: "walk me through the last time this cost you something." Third, laddering: one "why does that matter" per answer until the answer stops changing, which walks a position (script control) down to an interest (audit defensibility). Fourth, numeric grounding: every qualitative claim converted into a count or a rupee figure. Fifth, paraphrase-and-confirm. Sixth — only sixth — advocacy.

Two steps are usually left implicit. One is the silence after the paraphrase: a practitioner who asks "did I get that right" and keeps talking has turned a test into a formality, and the useful sentence typically arrives four to seven seconds later. The other is the invitation to correct in the direction of strength — "what's the strongest part of your case I underweighted" — which surfaces the argument the person considers decisive, rarely the one they opened with.

The quantitative treatment is Bayesian, and worth working rather than naming. Rukmini began with a prior: on field-service tickets, Meera's hardware diagnosis seemed right with probability 0.55. She and two colleagues then ran fourteen hours of retrospective interviews with 18 lab technicians across 9 sites. The discriminator, fixed in advance: if calibration were the binding problem, roughly 60% of technicians should raise it unprompted when walked through their last difficult shift; if not, the rate should look like background noise, around 15%. Four of eighteen — 22% — raised it. The likelihood ratio is about 0.15/0.62 ≈ 0.24; prior odds of 1.22 multiply to posterior odds of 0.29, a probability of 0.23.

Figure 1 — The update. Likelihood ratio 0.24; prior odds 1.22; posterior odds 0.29. The interviews did not prove Imran right; they made Meera's expensive option the less likely of the two.

The second-order effect is the commercially decisive one: expected value of information. If choosing wrongly costs roughly ₹9.2 crore — tooling plus two quarters of delayed revenue recovery — then cutting the probability of a wrong call from 0.45 to 0.21 is worth about ₹2.2 crore. The interviews cost fourteen person-hours and ₹1.8 lakh in travel: a return near 120 to 1, and the number that wins the argument with a CFO who treats discovery as a soft cost.

Question form also has measurable yield. Bhramar's research team, which logged 40 enterprise conversations in FY26, tagged each question by type and recorded whether the answer changed a documented belief within a week.

Figure 2 — Not all questions are inquiry. Hypothetical and leading questions consumed 41% of Bhramar's conversation minutes and produced 4% of its belief revisions.

The obvious inference is wrong. The chart does not say hypothetical questions are useless; it says they are useless for learning. They remain useful for negotiating and for testing whether someone will commit publicly. The expert's move is to know which job a question is doing.

4. When the discipline applies, and when it misleads

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. First, reversibility: inquiry earns its cost when reversing the decision costs more than the inquiry. Rukmini's hardware revision, with CDSCO re-submission attached, is about as irreversible as a mid-size company's decisions get. Tanmay's is subtler — a scripted mode could be built and later deprecated, but withdrawing a compliance-linked feature at a regulated customer is far harder, so the test passes for him too, for a different reason.

Second, information asymmetry: inquiry pays when the other party holds evidence you cannot otherwise obtain. Meera's field engineers saw lab conditions Rukmini never would, and the Chennai NBFC's compliance head knew which audit finding triggered the script demand — an asymmetry that turned out to be the whole case.

Third, safety to disagree afterwards: questioning with a foreordained outcome is theatre, and is read as such within two rounds. Fourth, a clock that permits it. Where any of these fail, the discipline misleads. In a live incident — a cartridge lot recall, a voice agent breaching TRAI call-time windows — directive command beats inquiry, and a listening round during an outage is abdication rather than humility. Inquiry also misleads when the respondent has no relevant experience: a technician predicting adoption of an instrument she has never operated gives confident answers with no information content. And it misleads where incentive is strong and observation weak — a salesperson forecasting willingness to pay reports hope, not evidence.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product companies the failure is arithmetic: the same need is heard by two teams and counted twice in two business cases. Bageshri's instrument team and its lab-information-system team both interviewed one hospital chain and both booked the resulting ₹3 crore of retention value. In two-sided settings the discipline must run twice with opposing hypotheses, since the strongest version of the seller's case is often the weakest version of the buyer's.

Regulated environments invert a normal assumption. Ordinarily the stated position proxies an interest you must excavate; under regulation it is sometimes the interest itself, because a compliance officer's requirement is that a specific clause be demonstrably satisfied. The tell is whether the respondent can cite the instrument — a circular, a guideline, an audit finding — by name. If they can, treat the position as a constraint; if not, as a hypothesis about a constraint, which is a different object.

Hardware-plus-software adds an asymmetry of irreversibility inside one product: Bageshri's software pod runs five discovery cycles while the instrument team runs one, so the same evidence justifies a software change long before it justifies a mould change. AI-native products introduce a new object — the model is itself a stakeholder whose behaviour must be interviewed. Bhramar runs what Jaya Menon calls transcript archaeology: sampling 200 real calls a week and asking, of each failure, what the model appeared to believe the caller wanted. That is listening against a system that cannot be asked directly, closer to ethnography than to evaluation.

Figure 3 — The seam problem. Each handoff is a paraphrase nobody verified with the original speaker, and each one converts an observation into a solution.

What mature companies actually do, as against what their process documents claim, is keep a short circuit around the seams: a standing right for the product manager to reach the original speaker without the intermediating function's permission, used sparingly enough that field operations does not experience it as a raid.

6. The nuances that separate expert from competent

The steelman must be endorsed, not merely constructed. Competent practitioners write down the other side's case; experts read it back and wait for the counterparty to call it fair. The tell is the phrase "actually, the stronger version is…" — if you never hear it, your steelman is a straw man with better manners, since a genuinely strong restatement prompts refinement rather than assent.

Confidence and evidence are separate variables. The obvious reading is that a confident stakeholder is likely right. Inside a company, confidence tracks how often someone has told the story, not the evidence behind it. The tell is identical phrasing repeated across meetings: a polished account has lost exactly the caveats you need.

The first answer is a position; the third is usually the interest. Experts expect three passes and never treat the first coherent answer as arrival. The tell is tense: positions are stated in the abstract present ("we need control"), interests arrive in the past tense with a date ("in November the auditor flagged two calls").

A paraphrase that changes nothing downstream is decoration. The obvious reading of good listening is that the speaker feels heard. The expert's test is harsher: did any number, date or scope statement in the plan move? Bhramar keeps a one-line "what changed" field on every conversation record, and a month of zero entries counts as a research failure.

Asking is not free. Every discovery round spends stakeholder goodwill as well as calendar. Experts budget it — Rukmini asks no stakeholder for deep time more than once a quarter — because a function that feels endlessly interviewed and never acted upon stops answering honestly.

Steelmanning a position you will reject is a commitment device, not a courtesy. Once you state someone's case at full strength before witnesses, you cannot later defeat a weaker version without the room noticing. The tell is a practitioner who writes the opposing case before the recommendation.

Unprompted mention is the cheapest evidential discriminator available. Whether a concern surfaces before you name it carries most of the information in a discovery conversation, which is why Rukmini fixed her threshold in advance rather than deciding afterwards what counted as support. The tell of amateur analysis is a quotation count with no denominator.

The discipline is strongest where it feels most redundant. Confidence that you already understand a stakeholder — the colleague of three years, the customer visited monthly — marks the model most stale. The tell is "I know what they'll say," which is a prediction and therefore testable; experts test it on familiar counterparties about twice a year.

7. How it changes by product type and stage

Some differences are real and others overstated. In consumer products the counterparty is absent, so the steelman is reconstructed from behavioural traces and the confirm step is impossible — you cannot ask a churned user whether your account of her reasoning is fair. Consumer teams substitute experimentation for confirmation, a different method rather than a degraded one. In B2B and enterprise the counterparty is present, articulate and incentivised, which makes confirmation cheap and separating position from interest the dominant difficulty. Platform work adds the parallel steelman; hardware changes the economics of being wrong, not the technique. AI products add the model-as-respondent problem and one more: the counterparty's mental model of the system is usually wrong in both directions at once, so stated requirements encode misconceptions that must be surfaced before they are met.

Table 1 — What actually changes, and what does not
ContextWhat genuinely differsWhat does not differ
ConsumerNo confirm step; experiments substituteUnprompted mention still discriminates
B2B / enterprisePosition-versus-interest is the hard partLaddering depth, three passes
Platform / marketplaceTwo steelmans, deliberately opposedEndorsement test on each side
Hardware + softwareEvidence bar scales with irreversibilityThe questions themselves
AI-nativeModel behaviour must be interviewedConfidence tracks repetition

Stage matters more than most practitioners admit. Pre-product-market-fit, the scarcest input is contact with reality and the internal steelman is near worthless, because no internal party holds evidence. At Bageshri's and Bhramar's stage it becomes essential precisely because functions now hold genuinely different evidence. At large scale the failure inverts: internal advocacy is so abundant that the practice degrades into hearing everyone, and the job shifts to deciding which three of eleven positions deserve a real steelman.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

The first is Bageshri's cartridge pricing, October 2025. Three hospital chains demanded a 12% discount, which on ₹93 crore of cartridge revenue would have cost ₹11.2 crore a year. Laddering found the interest was not price but budget predictability: procurement heads were penalised for variance, not level. Bageshri offered a fixed annual commitment at a 3% discount with a locked rate, costing ₹2.8 crore, and all three signed. The steelman — "your procurement head is not cheap, she is measured on forecast accuracy" — was the whole insight.

The second is Bhramar's script-control demand. Tanmay flew to Chennai with no recommendation in his pocket and reached the interest on the third ladder: an internal audit had flagged eleven collection calls the NBFC could not reconstruct afterwards. The requirement was reconstructability, not authorship. Bhramar shipped a per-call decision log with immutable transcripts and supervisor override in five weeks for ₹42 lakh. The ₹7.5 crore renewal signed, the generative capability survived, and two other lenders bought the log.

The third went wrong. In 2024 Bageshri ran a listening tour on a battery-backup module for the Sparsh 2, aimed at labs in districts with unreliable supply. Thirty-four customers were asked whether reliable operation through outages would be valuable; thirty-one said yes, several emphatically. The module was tooled and priced at ₹18,000. Over the next year 2 of 190 eligible sites bought it, and ₹3.1 crore was written off.

Table 2 — The 2024 battery module: what was asked versus what was observed
Evidence typeSignalWhat it actually measured

Unprompted mention in visit notes3 of 34 (9%)Salience in daily work
Existing spend on generators/UPS27 of 34 had backupProblem solved elsewhere in the building

The failure was not insufficient listening; it was 34 conversations of the wrong kind. Every question was hypothetical, every respondent agreeable, and the decisive fact — that most labs sat in hospitals with building-level backup — lay unqueried in the team's own visit notes, because nobody asked what customers had already done. The recovery, led by Rukmini in 2025, was procedural: no capital-intensive item enters the plan without evidence of prior behaviour or spend, plus a ₹50,000 refundable-deposit pre-order test, which two later proposals faced and one failed, at a cost of ₹4 lakh rather than ₹3.1 crore.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

The failure modes are stable across companies, and each shows a warning sign well before the cost lands. The expensive ones are quiet: inquiry gone ceremonial, evidence gone anecdotal, a team no longer noticing the difference.

Table 3 — Failure modes, warning signs, and the cost of catching them late
Failure modeEarly warning signDiagnostic questionCost if caught late

Listening as delayThird round, same question"What changes that the last two did not?"Lost quarter; the team reads it as indecision

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disagreements survive contact with evidence. The first is whether internal stakeholder listening is worth much at all. The behavioural school argues, at its strongest, that internal stakeholders are biased by function and incentive, that their reports are two paraphrases removed from observation as Figure 3 shows, and that scarce hours belong with customers and instrumentation. The evidence is real: Bageshri's field-service tickets put 0.55 on a hypothesis that direct contact reduced to 0.23. For the position to be wrong, internal parties would have to hold evidence customers cannot supply — which at Bageshri they did, since only field engineers knew which sites had building-level backup.

The second is whether steelmanning should be assigned or cultivated. The structured-dissent camp holds that voluntary steelmanning fails under hierarchy and time pressure, and that the only robust mechanism is a named devil's advocate with a written brief; its evidence is how reliably unassigned dissent evaporates as seniority rises in the room. The cultivation camp answers that assigned dissent becomes ritual within four cycles, since everyone knows the objection is someone's job. For the assignment camp to be wrong, ritualisation would have to outrun hierarchical suppression; both decay curves exist and nobody has measured which is steeper.

The third is the price of latency. The decision-velocity camp holds that most decisions are reversible and that the inquiry tax — a week here, a fortnight there — compounds into lost years, pointing to firms that out-executed better-informed rivals. Its opponents point at the ₹9.2 crore Bageshri nearly spent on the wrong hypothesis, and note that reversibility is overestimated by those who will not carry the reversal. What would settle it is a reliable ex-ante classifier for reversibility; no one has one.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this asks better questions. Someone who has internalised it has different artefacts and a different reputation. Their memos carry the opposing case, written first and at full strength, with a named person who endorsed the wording. Their research notes carry a stated prior expectation, so the finding can surprise them. They can be observed changing a number in public — the clearest behavioural marker — and refusing to run a discovery round when the decision is cheap and reversible. Colleagues who lose arguments to them describe being understood rather than defeated, and bring them difficult information early.

12. What each of them decided

Rukmini funded Imran's ₹1.1 crore software change without closing the hardware question: she shipped the result-review fix to 120 low-utilisation sites as a controlled cohort, with a threshold fixed in advance of a 15% rise in weekly tests within ten weeks, and told Meera that if the cohort missed it the auto-calibration case would be funded next. Meera accepted, less because the posterior was 0.23 than because she had heard her own argument stated in a form she agreed was fair, and had been given a falsifiable route back.

Tanmay shipped the decision log rather than the script library, and declined to tell the Chennai compliance head she had asked for the wrong thing. He wrote her position — eleven unreconstructable calls, an audit finding with a date, a personal exposure — into the requirements document above his own recommendation, and sent it to her first for correction. She made two changes to his wording, both of which made her case stronger than he had made it.

Discussion questions. (1) Rukmini's posterior of 0.23 rests on a threshold set before the interviews. What would have happened to her decision, and to her credibility with Meera, had she set it afterwards? (2) When would Tanmay's reframing of a compliance demand as an interest be an evasion of a genuine regulatory constraint rather than a discovery of one? (3) Bageshri's ₹3.1 crore failure involved thirty-four customer conversations. If volume is not the safeguard, what should a board ask to see before approving a capital-intensive product decision?

13. Going deeper

Stakeholder mapping and management comes first: listening tells you what a stakeholder needs, mapping tells you whose needs bind the decision — how you pick the three cases worth a real steelman out of eleven. Communicating across cultures is the next constraint: paraphrase-and-confirm assumes a counterparty willing to correct you, which fails where public disagreement is costly. Communicating with leadership inverts the ladder, since executives arrive at the top of their own inference and your job is to compress evidence without losing its caveats. Telling the customer story is what good listening becomes once it must cross the seams in Figure 3. Demo and pitch craft is the advocacy half, where a steelman pays, since the strongest pitch answers the objection before it is raised. Writing as a PM superpower is the forcing function: a memo containing the opposing case cannot quietly weaken it later. Decision records and DACI/RACI convert what you heard into who decides. Running effective meetings supplies the mechanics — agenda, silence, seniority speaking last — that decide whether any of this survives a twelve-person room.

Managing Up and Across: the Orphan Share

Near-expert treatment. What your boss and peers are measured on, what their measures cannot price, and the three things an expert does about the difference.

1. Two decisions, two weeks apart

On Monday 16 November 2026 Yashvita Gaonkar had a day to spend an engineering quarter. She was group product manager for adjudication at Melghat Intelligence, a Bengaluru company whose software reads discharge summaries and pre-decides health-insurance claims for fifteen insurers. Melghat charged ₹18 a claim across 15,00,000 claims a month, an annualised run-rate of ₹32.40 crore; confident claims were auto-decided, the rest reviewed in-house.

Two items faced the planning lock. Option 1 lowered the confidence cut-off, raising straight-through processing from 62.0 to 71.0 per cent. Option 2 built the claim-level reason-code and audit-trail layer four insurers' compliance officers wanted, two before a February 2027 inspection by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. Option 1 moved two senior numbers; Option 2 moved none inside the year ending Wednesday 31 March 2027, the year of Melghat's Series C data room.

On Tuesday 1 December 2026 Yash Goregaonkar faced the mirror image at Murud Reefer Logistics in Navi Mumbai, matching refrigerated trucks to shippers: 4,180 trucks registered, 2,460 carrying a leased Murud logger, 312 shippers. Three pharmaceutical shippers would not tender without excursion alerts inside thirty minutes of a breach; today's loggers upload once a trip. Continuous uploading would win pharma demand, shorten every battery and let shippers dock owners' pay mid-trip. His boss's measures said yes; his peers' said no.

2. The idea, and what translation leaves behind

Managing up and across is learning what your boss and peers are measured on and shaping each request to connect to those measures. Gabarro and Kotter's 1980 argument that a subordinate co-owns the relationship, and Kaplan and Norton's 1992 scorecard, are its sources. This page is about what they omit.

A scorecard is a projection: it compresses the firm's prospects onto a few measures chosen for being cheap to observe and hard to dispute, and projection loses information. V. F. Ridgway catalogued the distortions in 1956 and Steven Kerr's 1975 "On the Folly of Rewarding A While Hoping for B" made them a commonplace; Holmström and Milgrom gave the point a formal spine in 1991, proving that where one task is measurable and another is not, effort moves to the measurable one.

Hence two terms. A proposal's priced share is the fraction of its value landing on some stakeholder's measure, in that stakeholder's period. Its orphan share is the remainder: value that is real and nobody is paid to notice. Translation serves the priced share alone, so whoever knows only translation under-proposes the work hardest to measure.

Four positions disagree. The translation school signs "an ask outside the decider's measure is an ask not yet made" and refuses "value no measure prices is not real". The multitask school, after Kerr, Holmström and Milgrom, signs "a persistent orphan share is a defect in the measurement system" and refuses "optimise inside a system you believe miscalibrated". The dependence school, from Kotter's 1977 study of lateral power, signs "peers respond to reciprocity rather than to their measures" and refuses "mapping measures is the main work". The issue-selling school, after Dutton and Ashford in 1993, signs "timing and bundling move more decisions than content".

3. Mechanics: the ledger, the clock and the discount

Expert practice has three stages the folk account runs together. The first is the alignment ledger: for each stakeholder, the measure, its shape, its period, and how far the proposal moves it, in the measure's own units. An empty cell is a finding.
