4. When the model holds, and when it misleads

Four conditions, all testable first. One: the measure must move on the ask, in its own units. Option 1 moves two, +9.0 points of STP and +10.7 of margin; Option 2 reads "nil" on every owned measure. Two: the period must contain the effect, or the measure must be a level. Option 1 passes on the level limb, since the exit-month readings take its whole step; so it clears both, while Option 2 fails both, its value landing after 31 March 2027. Three: a peer must agree without their own measure worsening. Here Option 1 fails: Gulavani cannot accept 59.5 against a cap of 45, nor Gitte uploads breaking the 90-day promise. Both need a side payment or a changed measure. Four: the system must be stable across the ask's horizon. Melghat's Series C will install investor-chosen metrics, so a February 2027 translation may be worthless by June.

Three cases mislead. A founder with no scorecard, hunting conviction rather than arithmetic, reads a measure-shaped ask as evasion. Where the proxy–intent gap is itself the subject of the ask — Murud's weekly active trucks — translating into the proxy accelerates the harm. Where two measures conflict, translation avoids an escalation that is owed.

5. Hard edges: seams, two sides, hardware, regulation, models

Seams concentrate orphan shares: a seam is where no single measure spans. Yash sits on three, and the hardware one yields to arithmetic. Murud's loggers carry 7,200 mAh; firmware draws 3.1 mA logging to flash, and each narrowband upload costs 1.4 mAh. With no uploads a battery lasts 96.8 days, comfortably clearing the 90-day swap cycle the contract promises. At a fifteen-minute cadence it lasts 34.5 days, forcing three swap visits a cycle rather than one: two extra visits at ₹310 across 2,460 leased loggers is ₹15,25,200 a cycle, ₹61.01 lakh over four 90-day cycles.

Figure 2. Both axes linear: 0–100 days vertically, gridlines every 25; 10–60 minutes horizontally, ticks every 10. The curve is 7,200 mAh ÷ (3.1 mA + 1.4 mAh × 60 ÷ cadence), in days. The shaded band is where both constraints hold.

The band is narrower than either constraint alone. The tender asks for an alert within thirty minutes of breach and Murud's pipeline adds four, so the worst-case cadence is twenty-six minutes, not fifteen — fifteen was Yash's paraphrase, never a requirement. The relevant battery threshold is not 90 days but 45, since two swaps a cycle cost one extra visit rather than two, and 45 days means a cadence of 23.6 minutes. At twenty-five minutes the logger lasts 46.4 days for ₹30.50 lakh a year. That one-minute margin sits inside the pipeline's own variance, so the number to renegotiate is the 90-day promise, which Gitte is scored against but did not set.

The two-sided seam does not yield that way, because the cost falls on a population that can leave. Multi-product firms meet it as a shared-component team measured on reliability, which prices an API change as risk and never as revenue three lines book. Under regulation the orphan share is a liability, so nobody competes to own it. In AI-native products quality is measured where measurement is cheap, in aggregate accuracy, while the value sits in the tail — where Melghat's audit trail lives. Mature companies rarely fix this with better scorecards; they use a standing forum with budget and no metric, then call it strategy.

6. Eight nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Shape decides the clock's bite, not importance. The tell is an expert asking "level at a date, or flow over a period?" before asking what it is. Late value is not automatically discounted: a level records its step whole, so identical work is worth its full annual effect on one scorecard and a sixth on another.

Capacity scarcity is usually scorecard scarcity. The tell is two items called competing that need different skills. Melghat's 24 engineers held 312 engineer-weeks a quarter, 68 per cent committed, so about 100 were free and Option 1 needed 33. The real constraint was the five-engineer adjudication-core squad: 65 engineer-weeks, 40 per cent committed, leaving 39, and the only one that could touch the decision path.

A peer's measure gives their constraint, not their price. The tell is a peer who agrees immediately: either they mispriced the ask, or they are buying something you had not noticed selling. Gulavani's cap of 45 was itself negotiated earlier, so it was moveable.

The orphan share is where the variance lives. The tell is that the softest probabilities attach to the item nobody owns. A stakeholder with a measure has a forecasting process and a reputation at risk; an unowned outcome has neither.

Credibility is a coefficient on every number you present. The tell is a boss restating your figure with a round-down — "so call it two points" — a calibration judgement delivered as arithmetic. The competent practitioner argues the figure; the expert asks which forecast produced the discount.

Asking a peer for an estimate changes the estimate. The tell is a number arriving faster than the work it describes could have been done. Gulavani first read Option 1 as breaching his cap; after seeing rework fall from ₹140 to ₹95 a case, he read it as the cap mattering less than cost per case.

Translating into a measure you think wrong is a commitment, not a tactic. The tell is finding yourself unable to argue against the measure next quarter without repudiating your own memo. Hence experts sometimes decline a winnable translation and spend the quarter on the measure.

The measure in force when the ask pays off is often not today's. The tell is a financing event, reorganisation or new finance partner inside the ask's horizon. An ask paying off in FY28 belongs in the FY28 scorecard, which means guessing it.

7. Product type and company stage

The real differences are in who owns the orphan. In consumer products it is long-horizon retention, orphaned because growth measures are weekly; the fix is a guardrail metric owned by someone senior enough to lose an argument. In enterprise software it is conformance work — audit trails, residency, questionnaires — priced only at renewal, hence the trust function. In marketplaces it is the weaker side's welfare, because liquidity aggregates an asymmetric population. In hardware it is service cost after the sale, Murud's 90-day promise.

By stage the difference is smaller than claimed. Early-stage founders are not measureless; their system is informal, so it changes in a conversation rather than a planning cycle, which makes re-specifying cheap. At scale the reverse holds and routing becomes the main skill. The clock, the shape distinction and the coefficient do not change by stage.

8. Three worked outcomes

Routing, at Melghat. Yashvita shipped Option 1 and carved a fourteen-engineer-week slice from Option 2: reason codes on the decision path only, enough for the two insurers inspected in February 2027, shipping Friday 22 January. Nine were interface work the platform squad could take, leaving five on the adjudication core: 33 plus 5 against 39. The slice went onto a line the chief revenue officer already reports, accounts at inspection risk.

Reading the contract, at Murud. Yash treated his fifteen-minute assumption as a hypothesis. Three pharma shippers with a combined annual freight spend of ₹96 crore were gated on the alert promise; at an 18 per cent win share that is ₹17.28 crore of booking value, and at an 8.5 per cent take rate ₹146.88 lakh a year of net revenue. Twenty-five minutes captured it for ₹30.50 lakh of service cost rather than ₹61.01 lakh.

The failure, and the recovery. On Monday 2 February 2026 Yash shipped a supply-side trip-quality score, translated into the supply growth lead's weekly active trucks. That measure rose 4.1 per cent over four weeks. Then shippers began quoting the score in rate negotiations, and over the next eight weeks it fell 6.8 per cent — a net 3.0 per cent below the start. He had translated into a proxy for owner prosperity, and it moved before the behaviour it stood for, so the early reading was a lag, not evidence. Recovery cost ₹18 lakh of guaranteed minimum loads across 240 owners, ₹7,500 each, to 30 June 2026.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

Fast-decaying value translated into a slow measure. Early sign: your benefit is annualised while the opportunity has a date. Diagnostic: "what is this worth starting in April, not January?" Caught late, the cost is the opportunity.

A peer's yes bought with a promise your measure cannot fund. Early sign: the exchange was verbal and nobody wrote down who pays. Diagnostic: "which line does this come out of, and whose?" Caught late, the cost is the relationship that prices later asks.

Over-indexing on the boss, missing the veto holder. Early sign: an approval meeting with nobody from the function that will run the thing. Diagnostic: "who can stop this after approval?" Caught late, work ships and is quietly unshipped.

A measurement system treated as fixed while being revised. Early sign: finance declines to confirm next year's definitions. Diagnostic: "will this measure exist, so defined, when the benefit lands?" Caught late, a translation argues for an unmeasured thing.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Translate, or re-specify? The translation school's strongest form: measurement systems are slow and above a product manager's authority, so contesting a measure costs a quarter of shipping, and most reform campaigns by middle managers fail. The multitask school's strongest form is Holmström and Milgrom's result itself: if the orphan share is structural, no skill in translation reaches it, so translation compounds mis-allocation; conformance work is reliably funded only after an incident. Settling it needs a base rate nobody has: how often a middle manager gets a line onto a senior scorecard.

Are measures the right primitive for peers? The dependence school argues that Gulavani's second reading came from being asked twice by someone he owed a favour, and that peers accept measure-worsening asks from colleagues they trust and refuse measure-improving ones from others. The ledger school replies that trust decides whether you get a hearing and the measure decides what survives it. Falsifying it needs peers' decisions to be uncorrelated with their measures once relationship strength is held constant.

Disclose the orphan share, or not? One camp holds that naming the value no measure prices is a costly signal, since an advocate does not volunteer the weakness of their own case. The other holds that it reads as advocacy and that Yashvita's 24.5 per cent haircut is what disclosure buys. The evidence is confounded: practitioners who disclose are also the better calibrated.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with the boss's metric in the first sentence. Someone who has internalised it has already asked three questions elsewhere: what shape is the measure, who owns the part no measure prices, and what is my discount here. They write "nil" without flinching and spend capital, rarely, on changing a measure.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Yashvita took Option 1 into the planning lock with Gulavani's cap breach in her own memo rather than discovered in the room, and asked Garje for one addition to the quarterly review: accounts carrying an open compliance block at quarter end. She tabled the full layer to FY28's first quarter with a named owner: the orphan needed a measure more than a champion.

Yash took the twenty-five-minute cadence, scoped visibility to pharma loads rather than trucks, and asked Gitte for a written amendment to the 90-day promise before the 18 December firmware freeze. His pilot said the supply cost was real, across the 54 days from Monday 7 September to Friday 30 October 2026.

Figure 3. Linear vertical scale, gridlines every 5 points from zero; the control bar reaches −2.6 and the pilot bar −14.5, so the bracketed gap is 11.9 points. The whisker is ±1 standard error of the pilot bar's own change, 2.58 points; the difference's is 2.61. The lane was not chosen at random.

Fill rate there fell from 94.1 to 89.6 per cent, so most loads re-matched: of 11,400 loads posted before and 11,620 during, 673 and 1,208 went unfilled. That 535 difference is a raw count; against the before rate the counterfactual is 686, so the rate-adjusted excess is 522 and the loss ₹1.23 crore rather than ₹1.26. On the raw count, 535 loads at ₹41,000 is ₹2.19 crore over 54 days, ₹14.83 crore annualised, ₹126.02 lakh a year of net revenue at the same take rate.

The netting is conditional, and the condition carries the sign. Against pharma's ₹146.88 lakh a year sit that loss and ₹30.50 lakh of service cost. If one lane's absolute loss were the whole network's — it is not, since the move touches all 2,460 leased loggers while the lane holds 186 active trucks of 4,180 registered — then 146.88 − 126.02 − 30.50 = −₹9.6 lakh a year. If the lane's 31 per cent pharma share is then read as the network's, the loss becomes ₹39.07 lakh and 146.88 − 39.07 − 30.50 = +₹77.3 lakh. The assumptions cannot both hold: the first understates a network loss, the second comes from a lane chosen for pharma volume. The flip is the conditional's consequence, not a finding, and Yash had no defensible network base to scale on.

  1. Option 2 moves no measure anyone owns, and the two options are complements rather than alternatives. Which fact should have changed Yashvita's decision, and which only her memo?
  2. Yash found the twenty-five-minute cadence in a tender rather than in a negotiation. When is that the better first move, and what does a practitioner lose by making it a habit?
  3. Would you disclose your own calibration, and what changes about the asks you make once you know a discount is applied either way?

13. Going deeper

Communicating with leadership
The single-encounter version, and a ledger ask's compression.
Organisational politics for PMs
Where this topic ends: with no translation available, power decides.
Stakeholder mapping and management
Supplies the ledger's roster, veto holders included.
Telling the customer story
The orphan share's instrument: absent a measure, a named account is the currency.
Demo and pitch craft
Turns a priced ask into a decision, where ledgers still fail.
Writing as a PM superpower
A ledger is written; its memo is what your coefficient is estimated from.
Decision records and DACI/RACI
Makes a peer exchange's side payments durable — the section 9 failure above.
Running effective meetings
Decides whether the veto holder is present before approval.
exp20v2-comm.up.down:
Managing Up and Across

1. Two engineers, six weeks

On Tuesday 3 November 2026, Vijeta Ethape, senior product manager for billing at Lintel Software in Pune, had two days before Thursday's planning review. Lintel sells invoicing software to mid-sized manufacturers: 400 accounts, ₹48 crore in annual recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly value of live subscriptions), averaging ₹12 lakh per account. Twenty-two accounts, worth ₹2.64 crore, had told their account managers the same thing: without a direct export to Tally, the accounting package most of them use, they would not renew.

Vijeta wanted two engineers for six weeks. A week earlier she had written to her director, Vaman Ewalkar: "Twenty-two customers are asking for this." He had replied: "Noted. Let's revisit in Q1." She read indifference. More likely there was arithmetic she could not see. Asked again on Thursday in the same terms, he would answer the same way, and the twenty-two accounts would drift toward their renewal dates with nothing built. Table 1 shows what the people in that room were measured on.

Table 1. What each person is measured on
PersonRoleMeasured on
Vaman EwalkarDirector of Product, her bossNet revenue retention for the year to 31 March 2027; eight committed roadmap items delivered on time
Vrushank EsalkarEngineering manager, peerSprint commitments kept; production incidents
Customer success leadPeerRenewals closed on time

Her difficulty was not persuasion. She did not yet know whose problem she was describing. If she asked for the wrong thing in the wrong terms, Lintel would put renewals worth 5.5 per cent of its ARR (the worst case) at risk, and she would spend her next year as the product manager who had cried wolf. If she asked in the right terms, the same two engineers might be released within the week.

2. The idea

Managing up and across is the practice of learning what your boss and your peers are measured on, and shaping each request so that it connects to those measures. John Gabarro and John Kotter gave the first half its name in "Managing Your Boss", a 1980 Harvard Business Review article arguing that a subordinate shares responsibility for the relationship, since the boss is fallible and dependent on others. The measurement half owes much to Robert Kaplan and David Norton, whose 1992 balanced scorecard formalised what organisations always did informally: reduce a manager's job to a few numbers and reward movement in them.

The problem it solves is common. A sound idea is stated in the proposer's units (customers asking) when the decider will be judged in other units. Net revenue retention (NRR), the measure that matters most to Vaman, is the share of last year's recurring revenue still present this year after churn, downgrades and expansion. Vijeta could repeat one sentence in the meeting without sounding glib: "Before I ask you for anything, let me show you which number on your scorecard it moves, and which one it puts at risk."

Figure 1 draws the idea. Every arrow passes through a box, and every box but hers carries a scorecard. The customer success lead is a different kind of peer: she supplies evidence rather than resources, and Vijeta's ask also helps her own measure, renewals closed. That alignment is worth noticing early, because it gives Vijeta an ally whose motive she does not have to guess.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics run in six steps, and the last three are the ones practitioners leave unsaid.

First, find the scorecard. Vijeta read Vaman's goals in the annual plan, asked the finance partner how product bonuses are computed, and then asked Vaman directly what March needed to look like for him. Direct asking works more often than people expect; the discomfort belongs to the manager asking, not to the one answering. Most directors answer in detail, because few subordinates ever ask.

Second, find the clock. A measure has a period. Vaman's year ends on 31 March 2027, so revenue saved after that date helps someone else's scorecard.

Third, find what is being protected. Every scorecard implies a fear. A director judged on on-time delivery fears surprises more than he wants speed, and a request that arrives late in a planning cycle looks like exactly the surprise he dreads.

Fourth, translate the ask into the decider's unit, with arithmetic. Fifth, price the cost in the same currency. Two engineers come from somewhere, and an ask naming only its benefit reads as naive; Vaman will price the cost himself and assume the worst. Sixth, offer a way to say yes that survives a mistake: a smaller version, a checkpoint, a named swap. A director approving under uncertainty needs an exit as much as a reason.

Across, the mechanics differ in one respect. A peer cannot be instructed, so the exchange must leave both scorecards no worse than before.

4. A worked example

Vijeta began with the revenue at risk. Table 2 sets out each line so that Vaman can challenge any one of them.

Table 2. Retention value of the Tally export, full-year view (₹ lakh)
LineFigureBasis
Starting ARR4,800400 accounts × 12
At-risk ARR26422 accounts × 12
Loss chance without / with export50% / 10%Customer success judgement
Expected ARR saved105.6264 × (0.50 − 0.10)
NRR gain2.2 points105.6 ÷ 4,800

The at-risk accounts are assumed to average the same ₹12 lakh as the base. Expansion revenue is ignored.

The two loss chances are judgements, not measurements, and Vijeta labelled them so. On those judgements the export is worth 2.2 points of NRR. The method does not depend on the particular numbers: if the customer success lead had said 40 per cent without and 20 per cent with, the same table would give 264 × 0.20 = ₹52.8 lakh, or 1.1 points. Vaman could replace any judgement and watch the result move.

Now change one input. The export would ship in the first week of January, and only renewals after that date can be saved within Vaman's year. Nine of the twenty-two accounts renew between 11 January and 31 March 2027. They hold 9 × 12 = ₹108 lakh; the expected saving is 108 × 0.40 = ₹43.2 lakh, and 43.2 ÷ 4,800 is 0.9 points. The other thirteen accounts renew after 31 March 2027, so the ask lost more than half its value to Vaman without losing a rupee of its value to Lintel. Figure 2 sets the two views side by side.

The cost side came next. Vaman has eight committed items. Vrushank's first estimate was that losing two of his ten engineers would delay one of them, so on-time delivery on the published plan would fall from 8 of 8 to 7 of 8, or 87.5 per cent. Whether 0.9 points of retention justifies 12.5 points of delivery is Vaman's exchange rate to state, not Vijeta's.

5. Nuances

A metric is not a motive. The scorecard says what Vaman is paid for, not why he cares. Roger Fisher and William Ury's 1981 distinction between positions and interests applies: the scorecard is strong evidence of the interest, never proof.

Written and lived scorecards differ. The plan says one thing; the questions asked in reviews reveal another. Note which numbers a director quotes unprompted, and which items he moves to the top of an agenda when he is tired. A stated priority that never appears in his questions is probably not on the scorecard that pays him.

The clock decides the value. The second pass in Section 4 is the general case. A benefit landing after the measurement period is invisible to the person deciding. This is not selfishness; it is the system working as designed. A sensible manager still values the long-run benefit, but discounts it against the number he must report.

Peers are traded with, not told. Vrushank owes Vijeta nothing. Currency flows both ways: early notice of requirements, incident data, credit in front of Vaman, a promise to take the blame if the swap goes badly. Going over a peer's head spends trust that cannot easily be recovered.

It is not flattery, and not yet politics. Impression management shapes how you appear. This shapes what you ask. It also differs from executive communication, which is one message to a senior audience; managing up is that discipline sustained over a relationship. Organisational politics, the next topic, begins where translation fails.

What it cannot tell you. It tells you how to be heard, not whether you are right. A feature worth 2.2 points is not thereby worth building, and a badly designed metric will reward badly designed asks.

Questions before relying on it. A newcomer should ask four. How recent is my knowledge, given that reorganisations reset scorecards? Was I told, or did I infer? Whose estimates sit inside my arithmetic? Would I show the translation to the person it concerns?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; small and large

Table 3. Typical scorecards by product type
SettingBoss is often measured onPeer who collides
ConsumerRetention; experiment speedMarketing, on acquisition cost
B2BNRR; renewals; delivery datesSales, on quota; engineering, on commitments
MarketplaceLiquidity on both sides; trust and safetySupply operations; risk

In a five-person start-up the boss is the founder, the scorecard is mostly runway, and a request is answered in minutes; the scorecard is personal and changes monthly. In a large company the scorecard is written, annual and cascading, so the boss's boss matters nearly as much, and the finance partner knows the rules. Vijeta's B2B setting sits between: a formal year-end, but a director who still reads accounts personally. The same skill applies in all three settings; only the list of measures, and the identity of the colliding peer, changes.

7. Common mistakes

Table 4. Three mistakes, with the cheapest check
Symptom seen from outsideUnderlying misunderstandingCheapest diagnostic
Asks answered "noted" or "later"; escalation repeats the same askBelieves customer demand is itself a reason to the deciderWrite the ask as one sentence naming the boss's metric. If you cannot, you have not found it.
A peer agrees in the meeting and delivers nothingTreats agreement as commitment, ignoring the cost to the peer's scorecardBefore the meeting, ask "What does this cost you this quarter?"
The boss challenges the numbers and the decision reverses next weekPresents judgements as factsMark every input measured or judged; delete any you cannot source.

8. What good looks like

Take the same Thursday. Vijeta arrives having spoken to each person. Vrushank tells her that item six, the audit-log redesign, is already forecast two weeks late in his own data, though the published plan shows 8 of 8; she asks whether the engineers could come from that item. The customer success lead agrees the probabilities and names the nine renewals. Her one page shows both views of retention, 2.2 and 0.9 points, and a plain cost line: delivery was heading to 7 of 8 whether or not the engineers move. She asks for a decision with a checkpoint on Friday 11 December, at which point the build can be stopped if the export proves larger than estimated. Vaman can say yes without being exposed, and Vrushank has been asked rather than told. The page is brief, and it opens with Vaman's number rather than Vijeta's.

9. Closing

Vijeta chose to lead with 0.9 points, not 2.2. The larger figure was defensible, but Vaman's year ends in March, and a number he could shrink in the room would have cost her the credibility to be believed on the rest. She presented 2.2 as upside beyond his period, to be credited to Lintel rather than to him. On Thursday 5 November he approved the swap, with the engineers starting Monday 16 November and finishing by Friday 25 December.

Learn next: organisational politics for PMs. When two scorecards conflict and no translation reconciles them, the question is no longer one of language but of power, and that is where the topic leads. Revisit communicating with leadership too, since this topic is that skill over time.

Two questions to sit with. Which two or three measures of your own boss can you name today, and for each, was it told to you, read, or guessed? And if a boss's scorecard rewarded something you believed harmful to customers, at what point would translating your ask into it stop being managing up and become complicity?
exp40v2-comm.cross.cultural:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Communicating across cultures: whose code becomes the standard

Treat the problem as translation and it stays personal and endless. Treat it as the design of a shared written code and it becomes measurable — and then it becomes a question about who pays.

1. Two decisions, three days apart

On Thursday 22 October 2026 in Bengaluru, Lavangika Thergaonkar, Senior Vice-President for Product at Dhruvtara Systems, read the last of the eight release scorecards covering its Plain Writing Standard. Dhruvtara sells field-service software to utilities and runs 460 product and engineering staff across seven locations. The standard, drafted in Amsterdam by Lohitashwa Tupe and in force from release 3 on Friday 7 August 2026, required every status note to state a date risk in one unhedged sentence. Its record was equivocal: the share of defects first discovered in the final week before go-live rose sharply, then fell back once Tupe replaced the standard's central requirement.

She had to decide by Friday 30 October whether to renew the standard for 2027, re-anchor it, or withdraw it, with a 4,100-technician utility rollout due live on Monday 11 January 2027.

Three days earlier, on Monday 19 October, Lekhya Torne, head of product at Doordrishti Labs in Hyderabad, faced the same problem in another form. Doordrishti's product drafts customer-support replies that human agents send, edit or rewrite. Over the four weeks from Monday 21 September to Sunday 18 October it produced 23,000 drafts across four markets, of which 15,618 went out untouched — a pooled 67.9 per cent. Japan, at 48.0 per cent, was the lowest of the four. Her engineering lead wanted per-market register models; her board met on Friday 4 December. She spoke that morning to Lochanika Thube in Tokyo, three and a half hours ahead of Hyderabad all year, and then to Amsterdam, three and a half hours behind on 19 October and four and a half from 25 October.

Both decisions turn on the same question, and neither is settled by asking people to be more culturally aware.

2. The idea, and the three schools that split over it

Define a code as the mapping a writer uses from what they mean onto what they put on the page: which word marks which level of alarm, who may contradict whom in which channel, whether silence means assent. Competence here is the management of mismatch between the sender's encoding map and the receiver's decoding map, and the quantity of interest is the decode error — inferred severity minus intended severity on a shared scale.

The intellectual history begins with a practical failure. Edward T. Hall, training American diplomats at the Foreign Service Institute, published The Silent Language in 1959 and Beyond Culture in 1976, introducing high- and low-context communication. Geert Hofstede derived power distance from IBM employee surveys in Culture's Consequences (1980), and Fons Trompenaars offered a partly incompatible set in 1997. The GLOBE programme (House and colleagues, 62 societies, 2004) contributed most by separating practices from values — what people do from what they say should happen — which on hierarchy often pointed opposite ways. Erin Meyer's The Culture Map (2014) made positions explicitly relative; Michele Gelfand's tight-loose work (2018) moved attention from the content of norms to their strength.

Three schools disagree. Each signs a proposition the others will not.

The dimensional school
Signs: country positions are informative priors that beat no prior. Will not sign: a position suffices to act on in a single pair of people.
The situated school
Brendan McSweeney's 2002 critique of Hofstede's inference from survey means is its charter. Signs: most variance that looks national is occupational and individual. Will not sign: dimension scores carry no information.
The channel-engineering school
Signs: a written format with stated numeric thresholds removes most decode error without changing anybody's disposition. Will not sign: a format changes who feels permitted to raise a problem — Amy Edmondson's psychological-safety territory, a different mechanism.

3. Mechanics: measure the ladder, then choose the anchor

Expert practice has four steps and the fourth is almost never stated. First, map the ladder: the vocabulary actually in use, per channel, not the handbook's. Second, estimate the decode error for a named sender-receiver pair. Third, decide whether to move the map (train people) or replace the ladder (numbers for words). Fourth, choose the anchor — the position everybody else must move toward.

Tupe did the first two properly, though not until October, after the scorecards turned. He pulled every written date warning sent from Bengaluru to Amsterdam in the quarter to 30 June 2026 — the last full quarter before the standard, so the sample sits in one regime — 150 notes, each scored for true severity, 0 to 10, by two-reviewer post-mortem consensus. Separately, on 8 October, twelve Amsterdam reviewers placed the three recurring phrases on the same scale with no context; the figures below are their medians.

Table 1. Decode error on one ordered pair: Bengaluru writes, Amsterdam reads. All 150 notes fall in the quarter to 30 June 2026, before the standard.
Phrase as written in BengaluruNotesMean true severityAmsterdam's decoded severityDecode error
"a concern"725.13.0+2.1
"a risk to the date"547.86.0+1.8
"will not make the date"249.18.5+0.6
Total / note-weighted mean1506.714.96+1.75

Footnote. The bottom row is weighted by note count, not a mean of the three row means; those unweighted means are 7.33, 5.83 and +1.50, so the pooled error is 0.25 points larger. "True severity" is a post-hoc consensus about consequences, not a measurement of intent; within-row spread is unreported, so nothing here describes a single note.

Dhruvtara's policy requires a call within one working day at 5.0 or above. Apply the pooled error of +1.75: a note of true severity s decodes at s − 1.75, which clears 5.0 only when s reaches 6.75. Every warning whose true severity falls between 5.0 and 6.75 therefore decodes below the trigger — a dead band 1.75 points wide, 17.5 per cent of the scale. The error is not constant across rungs: at the bottom rung it is +2.1, so there the band runs to 7.1. The "a concern" row, mean 5.1, sits inside it either way. This is a property of the ladder the standard inherited, measured before the standard existed: it predicts what abolishing the middle rung would do rather than measuring what it did. Section 8's scorecards are the test; Table 1 holds no evidence from their period.

Why pairwise calibration stops scaling at about five offices

The obvious remedy is to calibrate each pair. With n locations that is n(n − 1)/2 relationships: 10 at five offices, 21 at Dhruvtara's seven. Anchoring on one written code requires n calibrations — seven — since each office need only be mapped to the standard. The marginal arithmetic is starker: an eighth office adds seven pairs but one spoke.

The step nobody states: where to put the anchor

Dhruvtara ran a survey in which each location placed itself on a written-criticism directness index, 0 for the most direct in writing and 10 for the most indirect. These are the teams' own relative judgements, not measurements. Define the adaptation burden of an anchor as the sum over offices of staff times the distance that office must travel, in person-index-points.

Table 2. Dhruvtara's seven locations, and the adaptation burden of three candidate anchors. Burden = staff × |index − anchor|.
LocationStaffIndexBurden at 1.5Burden at 4.5Burden at 6.5
Amsterdam401.50120200
Warsaw322.53264128
Boston563.511256168
São Paulo244.572048
Bengaluru1806.59003600
Chennai967.557628896
Tokyo329.024014480
Total46035.01,9321,032720

Footnote. The index column's total is a sum, so the unweighted mean of the seven positions is 35.0 / 7 = 5.00 and the midpoint of the range is (1.5 + 9.0) / 2 = 5.25. Burdens at those two anchors follow from the staff and index columns: 954 and 915. India holds 276 of 460 staff, 60.0 per cent.

Half of 460 is 230. Ordering the offices by index, cumulative staff reaches 152 at São Paulo and 332 at Bengaluru, so the headcount-weighted median is 6.5. That anchor minimises total burden over the whole scale, not just among five candidates: 6.4 gives 735.6, 6.6 gives 740.4. The unweighted median, 4.5, minimises the sum of office distances — one office, one vote — at 1,032. The range midpoint, 5.25, minimises the worst single move, holding every office to 3.75 points, at 915. Amsterdam's 1.5, the anchor Dhruvtara chose, costs 1,932 — 2.68 times the minimum — because that is where the board sits.

4. When the analysis applies, and when it inverts

The decode error must be stable. The same phrase from the same office should predict the same true severity across two periods at least. Neither has tested this: Dhruvtara has Table 1's one quarter and Doordrishti one four-week window, so both act on a snapshot.

The receiver's action threshold must be written down. Dhruvtara's is 5.0 on a stated scale. Doordrishti's is whatever makes a reviewer reach for the edit key, written nowhere — so the measurement is of the reviewer, not the market.

The adapters must be identifiable people in countable numbers. Here the analysis inverts. Dhruvtara's burden lands on 460 named humans, so the weighted median bites. Doordrishti's encoder is a model, holding seven codes as cheaply as one, so the constraint becomes the consistency of what the company promises; the median argument applied there is applied where its premise fails.

The failure must be about intensity, not permission. If juniors are silent because contradicting a manager in a shared channel is not done, re-anchoring a vocabulary changes nothing. The diagnostic is whether the silence is channel-specific — nothing in the release channel, three paragraphs in a direct message.

5. Hard edges and organisational seams

A multi-product company can need opposite anchors. Dhruvtara's tooling team can run plain and blunt; its regulated submissions cannot, because in a European Union Medical Device Regulation file hedging carries legal meaning: "may" is not a weaker "will" but a different claim.

Two-sided businesses face a harder version, since the neutral code between a Mumbai wholesaler and a Berlin buyer is not the midpoint of their norms but the register in which an obligation is enforceable, which may sit outside both. Hardware adds lead time: a supplier's "no problem" is a commercial posture, not a capability statement, so a decode error becomes a tooling order on a wrong assumption. AI-native products put the code inside the product, where preference data inherits its annotators' norms and a locale-softened reply reads downstream — to a reviewer or a court — as a weaker commitment than the blunt version.

What mature companies say they do at these seams is cultural-awareness training. What they do is narrower: they force a few artefacts — a numeric risk field, a decision record naming who decided, a rule that an undocumented decision did not happen — and post one bilingual senior person at each seam, off the org chart.

6. Eight things an expert notices that a competent practitioner does not

The anchor is a distributive choice that defaults to decision rights. The tell is a standard written in the language of universal clarity whose every worked example comes from one office's prose. The obvious reading — we picked the clearest norm — is wrong, because clarity is measured in the reader's code and the authors were their own readers.

Burden is an L1 quantity, so the median governs, not the mean. The tell is a standard parked at an average that is no office's position. Splitting the difference minimises squared distance, which nothing here cares about: Dhruvtara's mean anchor costs 954 against the median's 720, a 32.5 per cent premium.

Compressing the vocabulary relocates the failure. The tell is an escalation distribution that loses its middle — quiet stretches punctuated by red flags. Cutting hedged middles looks like cutting ambiguity, but a three-rung ladder reduced to two leaves a writer choosing between understatement and alarm, and most problems are mid-rung.

An edit rate measures the editor. The tell is that the worst-fitting market also has the thinnest local review coverage. Before treating Doordrishti's Japanese 48.0 per cent as a fact about Japanese customers, an expert asks what share of those drafts a resident reviewed.

Silence is channel-specific, and that asymmetry is the instrument. The tell is a person whose public-channel output is near zero and whose private-thread output is high. Read as disengagement it is wrong: the channel's audience sets the threshold, and the private volume supplies a control condition free.

Latency encodes intensity in some codes and deference in others. The tell is a four-minute reply at 23:00 local time to a note from two levels up. Read as responsiveness it flatters everyone; in a high-hierarchy code it is a status signal, so latency measures urgency only once you have checked it does not track seniority.

"Should be" and "as is" point opposite ways. The tell is a survey in which an office asks for franker written criticism beside a channel log containing none. GLOBE's separation of practices from values found this inversion on hierarchy. A survey is an aspiration measure; planning a rollout on it is planning on a wish.

Translators are load-bearing and invisible. The tell is that decode errors spike in the week one particular person goes on leave. Read as a strong individual it earns them a bonus; read correctly it is a single point of failure, and the remedy is to write down what they do.

7. Where product type and stage actually change the answer

In consumer products the counterparty is the user, register is a product surface, and the instrument is complaint and uninstall, not internal escalation. In enterprise sales a buyer's silence after a demo is usually a statement about decision rights, and a commitment's register eventually has contractual consequences. Platforms carry the neutrality problem above; hardware converts decode error into inventory; AI products move the encoder inside the product, the one genuinely new case.

Where the difference is not real it should be said plainly: the internal problem — a release note crossing an office boundary and losing a severity point and three quarters — is identical in all five. Claims that a product category needs its own communication culture are marketing.

Stage changes the remedy, not the mechanism. At three locations there are three pairs and the founders hold them all in their heads, so a written standard is overhead. At five it is ten pairs against five spokes and the arithmetic has turned. At seven it is 21 against 7, and only the anchor question is left.

8. Three worked cases

Case one: a mismatch rate that was measuring its own reviewers

Table 3. Doordrishti Labs, drafted replies by market, four weeks to Sunday 18 October 2026.

Footnote. The three disposition columns are mutually exclusive and sum to drafts. The bottom-right figure is pooled over all 23,000 drafts, 15,618 / 23,000 = 67.9 per cent, not a mean of the four market rates.

Lekhya split the Japanese row by where the reviewer sat. Reviewers resident in Japan handled 1,890 of the 2,700 drafts and sent 756 unedited, 40.0 per cent; a Bengaluru night team on the Japanese overnight queue handled the remaining 810 and sent 540 unedited, 66.7 per cent. The parts reconcile: 1,890 + 810 = 2,700 and 756 + 540 = 1,296. The 26.7-point difference carries a standard error of 2.00 points, so it is 13.3 standard errors — not noise. On the only 1,890 drafts that bear on Japanese customers the mismatch is 60.0 per cent rather than 52.0. Correcting the denominator made the problem larger and disqualified 810 drafts.

Case two: pricing an anchor before signing it

Table 2's force is in the per-person figure rather than the totals. At Amsterdam's anchor each of Bengaluru's 180 staff must move 5.0 index points — more than the whole spread between Amsterdam and São Paulo, 3.0 points. The 1,212-point gap between 1,932 and 720 is the price of putting a standard where the board reads rather than where the organisation writes.

Case three: the standard that failed, and a recovery that only half worked

Eight fortnightly releases ran on alternate Fridays from 10 July to 16 October 2026. The standard took effect at release 3, on 7 August, so releases 1 and 2 are the pre-standard baseline. After release 6 on 18 September, Tupe replaced the unhedged-sentence rule with a numeric field: days of float remaining, an integer, any value of five or below routed automatically to a twenty-minute call.

Releases 1 and 2 put 57 of 150 defects in the final week, 38.0 per cent. Releases 5 and 6 put 91 of 175, 52.0 per cent — a 14.0-point rise against a standard error of 5.47, or 2.6 standard errors. The mechanism was the dead band: the standard abolished the hedged middle rung without moving the anchor, so writers with mid-severity problems had no permitted way to say so and waited. Releases 7 and 8, under the float field, put 52 of 160 in the final week, 32.5 per cent — 19.5 points better than the worst of the two releases shown under the standard, 3.7 standard errors. Releases 3 and 4 were not scored this way, so the standard's worst pair may have been worse. But against the pre-standard 38.0 per cent, 32.5 is a 5.5-point gain with a standard error of 5.42: one standard error. Dhruvtara had repaired its damage and could not yet show it had beaten doing nothing.

9. Failure modes and their early warning signs

Anchoring by default. Early sign: every worked example in the draft standard comes from one office. Diagnostic: which location is the headcount-weighted median on the scale this standard governs, and what is the burden at our anchor against that median's? Cost late: 1,932 against 720 person-index-points, plus the two releases of worse timing in Figure 3.

Measuring the reviewer and reporting the market. Early sign: the market with the worst fit also has the thinnest local coverage. Diagnostic: what share of these drafts was handled by a resident of the market? Cost late: Doordrishti came within a board meeting of funding four register models against a figure that was 40.0 per cent, not 48.0, on the drafts that counted.

Mistaking a dead band for compliance. Early sign: written warnings thin out in the middle of the severity range while the extremes hold. Diagnostic: what is the widest true-severity band decoding below our action threshold, and what share of the notes in the measured window fell inside it? Cost late: mid-severity problems surface in the final week, where remediation is dearest.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Person or channel? The channel-engineering position rests on Table 1 and Figure 3: swapping a word for an integer moved the final-week share 19.5 points without retraining anybody. The person-centred position rests on the comparison the page cannot win — one standard error against the pre-standard baseline — and holds that formats relocate a problem rooted in who may contradict whom. It is wrong if a format's gain survives a change of personnel; the channel position is wrong if that gain decays as writers learn to pad their float.

Anchor at the weighted median, or where decision rights sit? The median position has 720 against 1,932. The steelmanned opposite is not laziness: the register a company commits in externally is the one its board, counsel and largest customers read, and an organisation writing amber-and-float internally while writing "we may experience some delay" outside keeps two codes and pays the translation twice. The 1,212-point gap is then the honest price of a single register. It would be wrong if the external register could be produced mechanically from the internal one.

Should an AI encoder localise register at all? For: the edit rates, and a marginal human adaptation cost near zero. Against: register carries implied commitment strength, so a locale-softened promise and a locale-blunt one are different promises, and nobody has shown the commitment can be held constant while the register varies. Unresolved; the measurement that would settle it does not exist.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this names the ordered pair and the channel before interpreting a message, and asks a mismatch rate's denominator before discussing its size. They price an anchor before signing a standard and say out loud which office must move. They prefer an integer to an adjective in any field crossing a code boundary, and treat their own fluency in two codes as a liability to document rather than a talent. And they will say in a meeting that they do not know whose code a sentence was written in.

12. What each of them decided

On Friday 30 October Lavangika kept the float field, re-anchored the written standard at 6.5, and accepted a two-register design: the internal code at the headcount-weighted median, the external one at Amsterdam's position, with one named person per seam to move between them. Her reasoning was that the 1,212-point charge was defensible only if somebody owned it, and nobody had. Lekhya held one global voice for anything constituting a commitment, localised only non-commitment text, re-routed the Japanese overnight queue to resident reviewers, and will re-measure over the four weeks from Monday 2 to Sunday 29 November.

  1. Dhruvtara's board sits in Amsterdam and reads in Amsterdam's register. On what evidence could Lavangika have argued for the 6.5 anchor before the eight releases produced Figure 3 — and would that argument have been honest?
  2. The float field beat the standard by 3.7 standard errors and the pre-standard baseline by 1.0. Which comparison should govern the 2027 renewal, and what would you measure to break the tie?
  3. If Doordrishti's encoder holds seven codes at no marginal cost, the adaptation-burden argument does not apply. What replaces it as the constraint, and how would you put a number on it?

13. Going deeper

  • Working in diverse and global teams — who sits where, which sets the index distribution this page prices.
  • Listening and questioning — the receiving half of the decode error, and the question "yes" cannot answer.
  • Stakeholder mapping and management — locates decision rights, where an anchor drifts by default.
  • Communicating with leadership — the external register: the one direction you cannot re-anchor.
  • Telling the customer story — unlocks the consumer case, where register is a product surface.
  • Demo and pitch craft — live, unlogged channels, where calibration happens in the room.
  • Writing as a PM superpower — a badly written standard anchors nothing.
  • Decision records and DACI/RACI — turns "we agreed" into something another code can read.
exp20v2-comm.cross.cultural:
Communicating across cultures

Why did that message land badly in the other office?

1. A status update that said "on track"

On Tuesday 6 October 2026, Kalpak Shringarpure, Director of Product at Curlew Works, a Pune company that sells scheduling software to freight operators, opened the release channel and read a single line from Hamburg. Kunjika Sambhus, who led the fourteen-person engineering office there, had written: "I have some concerns about the rate-card migration." On the previous Friday Pune's weekly update had called the same migration "on track".

The migration mattered. A national third-party logistics customer had signed a contract worth ₹4.8 crore a year, with go-live fixed for 30 November 2026 and a penalty of 2 per cent of annual value for every week of delay, which is ₹9.6 lakh a week. Kalpak had to decide that week whether to add Pune engineers, renegotiate the date, or do nothing.

The difficulty was not the schedule. It was the two sentences. In Pune the word "concerns" in a written note to a senior colleague was a mild courtesy. In Hamburg, by Kunjika's own later account, it was the strongest word she was willing to put in writing before escalating. Pune read a footnote; Hamburg had sounded an alarm. Each office believed it had been perfectly clear, and each was reading the other's message in its own code.

2. The idea

Cross-cultural communication, as management use it, is the discipline of separating what a message says from what its sender's norms make it mean. Three families of norm do most of the work. Context is how much of the meaning sits in the words themselves (low-context) versus in shared background, tone and what is left unsaid (high-context). Directness of negative feedback is how plainly criticism is stated. Hierarchy, which Hofstede called power distance, is how far people expect authority to be unequal and who may disagree with whom.

The ideas came from people who had watched messages fail. Edward T. Hall, an American anthropologist who trained diplomats for the US Foreign Service in the 1950s, described high- and low-context communication in Beyond Culture (1976). Geert Hofstede, a Dutch researcher, drew power distance from employee surveys at IBM across dozens of countries and published it in Culture's Consequences in 1980. Erin Meyer, a professor at INSEAD, combined and relabelled such dimensions as eight scales in The Culture Map (2014), and stressed that each scale is relative: a position only means something against another party.

Kalpak could say the following in a meeting without sounding glib: "Before we judge the message, let us translate it." The sentence is deliberately modest. It claims nothing about whose norm is better.

3. How it works

The method has four steps, and the third is the one practitioners skip. First, locate the sender on the relevant scale, relative to the receiver. Second, read the message as written in the sender's code: what would an ordinary, unremarkable message look like from this person, and how far does this one depart from it? Third, find the baseline: every writer has a default level of hedging, and information lies only in the departure from it. Fourth, re-encode the message into the receiver's code before acting on it.

Applied to Kunjika's note, the steps run as follows. Figure 1 places Hamburg at 1 on the criticism scale, so a Hamburg writer's baseline is plain speech; a departure toward softness, such as "concerns", is a large move for her. Pune sits at 6, so a Pune reader's baseline is already hedged, and the same word registers as a small one. Re-encoding means telling Kalpak that Kunjika's sentence carries the weight of a Pune sentence like "this will not make the date unless something changes".

The reverse direction works the same way, and it is where Pune's "on track" went wrong. The step that is usually left implicit is the third: nobody checks the sender's baseline against data. Culture-map positions are priors, and a prior should be tested against the record of what a phrase has actually predicted. That is what the next section does.

4. A worked example

Kalpak's analyst pulled forty Pune status updates from the previous year and recorded, for each phrase, whether the work shipped by its committed date. Hamburg readers, taking the words literally, had been assuming a rate for each phrase: 90 per cent for "on track", 70 per cent for "on track, minor risks" and 40 per cent for "some challenges".

Pune phraseUpdatesShipped on timeActual rateReader's assumed rateReader expected on time
On track201260%90%18.0
On track, minor risks12975%70%8.4
Some challenges8337.5%40%3.2
Total / pooled402460%74%29.6

The arithmetic: 12 + 9 + 3 = 24 shipped from 40 updates, a pooled rate of 60 per cent. The reader expected 20 × 0.90 = 18.0, 12 × 0.70 = 8.4 and 8 × 0.40 = 3.2, a total of 29.6, or 74 per cent of 40. The overestimate is therefore 29.6 − 24 = 5.6 updates, or 14 percentage points. More than all of it sits in the first row, where 18.0 were expected against 12 delivered, a shortfall of 6.

Notice what the table suggests. Bare "on track" shipped on time less often (60 per cent) than "on track, minor risks" (75 per cent). One possible reading is that bare "on track" was a courtesy default and a qualifier signalled real content, but with 20 and 12 updates the 15-point gap is under one standard error of the difference, so this sample cannot distinguish that reading from noise.

Second pass. Change one input: replace the reader's assumed rate for bare "on track" with the observed 60 per cent and leave the other two alone. Expected on time becomes 20 × 0.60 + 8.4 + 3.2 = 12.0 + 11.6 = 23.6, or 59 per cent of 40, against 24 actual. The error falls from 5.6 updates to 0.4. One recalibrated phrase removes about 93 per cent of the gap (5.2 of 5.6).

One caution before celebrating. Twenty updates is a thin base: the standard error on 12 of 20 is about 11 points, so the 30-point gap on "on track" is about 2.7 standard errors (using the observed 60 per cent to compute the error, the conservative choice), convincing but not final, and the 9-of-12 and 3-of-8 rates are too small to say that they differ from the assumptions at all.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

Scales are relative, not absolute.

Placement depends on who is across the table. A team that seems blunt to Pune may seem evasive to a team in Amsterdam. Always state the pair.

A tendency is not a person.

Kunjika Sambhus was born in Nashik and had worked in Germany for eleven years; her baseline had moved. Averages describe distributions that overlap heavily, and a pair of individuals can sit opposite to what their offices suggest.

Context and directness are different scales.

A message can be explicit and still hierarchical, or implicit and still blunt. Treating them as one "direct versus polite" axis is the commonest blur and it produces wrong re-encodings.

"Yes" has several meanings.

It can mean "I agree", "I heard you" or "I will not contradict you here". The diagnostic is not a better translation of the word but a question that cannot be answered with it: "What would have to be true for this to slip?"

Hierarchy decides who may say no.

Where authority distance is large, a junior writer will not contradict a manager in a shared channel, and silence there is data about the channel, not agreement.

Second-language writing is not a culture.

Hedges, blunt imperatives and missing pleasantries are often a limited vocabulary. Separate proficiency from norm before attributing intent.

The method cannot tell you why this person wrote this.

It generates hypotheses about a baseline, not facts about a mind. Before relying on it, ask three questions: relative to whom, based on how many messages, and what does the sender's own record show?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and large

In consumer products the culture in question is usually the user's. Tone in notifications, refund messages and app-store replies is read against a local baseline, and a literal translation of a warm English message can read as either cold or intrusive. In B2B the issue is mostly between buyer, seller and delivery teams: an enterprise buyer's "we will revert" or silence after a demo carries a hierarchy signal, because the person speaking may not own the decision. Curlew's case is not of this type, since its exchange was internal between Pune and Hamburg, but the customer contract supplied the stakes.

Marketplaces add a third problem, since two sides with different norms must trust one platform. Seller support scripts that suit a Mumbai wholesaler may offend a Berlin buyer, and the platform's own written rules have to be neutral enough for both.

Size changes the remedy. In an early-stage company with three or four cross-office pairs, personal calibration is enough: the founders know each other's baselines. In a large company the pairs multiply beyond what anyone can learn, so the baseline has to be written down in conventions such as status codes with stated thresholds and templates for escalation.

7. Common mistakes

Judging the message in your own code. The symptom is a sentence like "Hamburg is abrasive" or "Pune hides problems". The misunderstanding is that one's own baseline is neutral. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the sender to restate the message in different words and compare their intensity with your reading.

Assigning norms by passport. The symptom is staffing or tone decided by nationality. The misunderstanding is mistaking a tendency for a trait. The diagnostic is to read the person's last five messages before assuming anything.

Asking only one side to change. After a workshop, Hamburg is told to soften and Pune to speak up, and surprises continue. The misunderstanding is that awareness equals calibration. The diagnostic is counting, per release, the number of issues that first surfaced late; if the count does not fall, the conventions have not changed.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Kalpak's Tuesday would have been uneventful. He would have recognised "concerns" from Hamburg as a high-intensity signal and called Kunjika within the hour with a specific question: what would have to be true for the date to hold? The Friday update would have used codes whose thresholds both offices had signed, and Hamburg's reading of the codes would have matched Pune's from the first week, because the table in section 4 had existed a year earlier. Kunjika would not have needed to choose between silence and an alarm, since a mid-intensity word would already have had an agreed meaning. Neither office would need to become the other; each would simply be legible to the other.

9. What Kalpak decided

On Friday 9 October, Kalpak did three things. He phoned Kunjika, who named the real risk: a rate-card import that took eleven hours on test data. He added two Pune engineers to it. And he replaced "on track" with three codes: green, meaning the team can absorb a one-week slip; amber, meaning it cannot; red, meaning a date is already lost. A two-week miss would have cost ₹19.2 lakh in penalties, so the codes paid for themselves quickly. He chose to change the vocabulary rather than lecture either office, because a definition can be checked against outcomes and a lecture cannot.

To learn next, study working in diverse global teams for the structural side, and listening and questioning for the receiving side, since what a listener hears depends on the same baselines.

Two questions to sit with. (1) Think of the last message that surprised you. What was the sender's baseline, and how far from it was that message? (2) If you had to build your own table like the one in section 4, which phrase in your organisation would you test first, and what would count as evidence that you were wrong?
exp20v2-comm.board:
Board and Investor Communication

What a board actually wants from a product update.

1. The thirty-one slides

On Monday 2 November 2026, Ilhan Pansare, chief product officer of Aquila Ledger, reopened last quarter's board deck and counted thirty-one slides. Aquila, a Pune company, sells software that matches mid-sized manufacturers' purchase invoices against the tax data their suppliers file under India's goods and services tax (GST). It held ₹14.4 crore in cash and spent ₹80 lakh a month, which is eighteen months of runway, meaning the time before cash runs out at the current spending rate.

The board would meet on Thursday 12 November; pre-reads, the documents directors read beforehand, were due Monday 9 November. Ilhan's reconciliation module, planned for 15 September, had shipped on 27 October, forty-two days late. At the previous meeting he had walked directors through releases, and Irfana Pimputkar, the partner representing the lead investor, had asked, "So are we all right?" He could not answer in a sentence. Ishrar Palav, an independent director and former finance chief at a manufacturer, said only that he would welcome fewer screenshots.

Now Ilhan needed ₹75 lakh for contract engineers who could win back the lost six weeks of customer onboarding. Wrapped in another feature tour, the request would probably be refused or, worse, approved without scrutiny, and either way the board would trust his next update a little less. He also knew the cost of caution: if the six weeks were not recovered, customers who had waited for the module would sign with a competitor's tool before the year closed, and the next round of funding would be negotiated on a thinner story. Indivara Palande, the chief executive, gave him one instruction: the board does not want an update, it wants to know what it is being asked to do.

2. The idea

A board is the group of directors, elected by shareholders, who carry a legal duty of care (a fiduciary duty) over the company. A board update is a short, decision-oriented account that lets people who see the company a handful of times a year, with little product context, judge whether management is steering well and whether to approve, advise or intervene.

The board has three levers, and an update is useful only if it is aimed at one of them. It can approve things management may not do alone, such as large spending; it can advise, lending directors' experience and contacts; and it can intervene, which in the extreme means replacing the executive team. Everything else in a good update serves to show which lever, if any, should move.

The practice grew out of a problem. Early management reports were activity logs, and directors, who meet quarterly and hold day jobs elsewhere, could not tell a healthy company from a busy one. Venture investors tightened the norm from roughly the 2000s, asking for a plan, a variance and an ask; Amazon's habit of replacing slides with written narrative memos, from about 2004, pushed the same discipline into prose.

The sentence Ilhan could repeat without sounding glib: tell the board what you need decided, what it costs in cash and months, and what would change your mind.

3. How it actually works

Six steps, two of them usually left unsaid. First, name the decision or say that there is none; an update with no ask is still valid, but then it must say what the board should conclude. Second, translate the product facts into the board's currency: cash, runway, recurring revenue, risk. Third, report against the plan the board approved, because directors remember the plan, not your internal roadmap. Fourth, price at least two alternatives, including doing nothing.

The unsaid steps come around the meeting. Fifth is pre-wiring: calling each director beforehand so that nothing in the room is news to them. Sixth is closing the loop: at the next meeting, the first page reports what happened to every earlier ask. Figure 1 shows the reading order, and the table shows the variance block Ilhan began with.

ItemPlanActual
Reconciliation module launch15 Sep27 Oct
Days late042
Pilot accounts live at launch2014

Notice what the six steps have in common: each reduces what the director must infer. A director who must work out the cost of the ask, or guess whether a delay is serious, will either guess generously or guess harshly, and management loses control of the conversation either way. The block is deliberately boring. Its job is to let Irfana see in ten seconds that the slip is six weeks and the pilot is thirty per cent short (14 against 20), so that the conversation can move to what to do rather than to what happened.

4. A worked example

Aquila's customers buy ahead of a fixed window each year, and an account that misses it waits twelve months. Onboarding is planned at twelve accounts a month, so the six weeks (1.5 months) lost to the slip are 18 accounts that fall out of the window. Each pays ₹3.6 lakh a year, the annual contract value, and gross margin, the share of revenue left after delivery costs, is 80 per cent. The contractors would build the bulk-import tools that remove the onboarding bottleneck, so they buy back onboarding capacity rather than new features. Every figure below recomputes from these inputs.

Ishrar's test, which Ilhan adopted, is first-year gross profit protected per rupee spent; he wants more than one. Pass one gives 18 × ₹3.6 lakh = ₹64.8 lakh of annual revenue at risk, ₹51.84 lakh of gross profit, and ₹51.84 ÷ ₹75 = 0.69. Fail. The cost to runway is also stated: cash would fall to ₹1,365 lakh, and 1,365 ÷ 80 = 17.1 months, a loss of 0.94 months.

₹ lakh unless statedPass 1Pass 2
Onboarding rate, accounts per month1220
Accounts lost to the slip (× 1.5 months)1830
Annual revenue at risk (× 3.6)64.8108.0
Gross profit at 80%51.8486.40
Cost of contractors75.075.0
Gross profit per ₹1 spent0.691.15

Pass two changes one input. The sales head holds 40 signed letters of intent expected to onboard over two months, which is 20 a month. Now 30 accounts fall out, ₹108 lakh of revenue is at risk, gross profit is ₹86.40 lakh, and 86.4 ÷ 75 = 1.15. Pass. The sales head's number is an upper case, not a forecast, since letters of intent convert unevenly. Break-even sits between the passes: ₹75 lakh ÷ ₹2.88 lakh of gross profit per account (0.8 × 3.6) is 26.04 accounts, and ÷ 1.5 months is about 17.4 accounts a month. One input flipped the verdict, which is what the board needs to see: the decision turns on the onboarding rate, not on the engineering.

Simplification: the year-one view ignores renewals in year two, which would favour the spend, and assumes the contractors recover all six weeks.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

The board is several audiences

Irfana wants a growth story that supports the next funding round; Ishrar wants controls and cash discipline. One update can serve both only if the ask is priced in cash and in recurring revenue. Neither wants the other's concern hidden from them, and a seat-by-seat view of the room helps the writer decide which paragraph to lead with.

Variance beats absolute

"We shipped to 14 pilot accounts" means nothing until set against 20. Directors judge management by the gap between promise and delivery, because that gap predicts the next promise. A small, honestly explained miss builds more credit than a large target met without explanation.

Translate, and name the denominator

A product metric reaches the board only through a stated link to cash or revenue. "Activation is up" must say activation of what: 14 accounts is a different base from 40 letters of intent.

Bad news travels early and flat

The slip should reach Irfana by phone a week ahead, in one plain sentence with the cause and the remedy. Pre-wiring also lets her raise objections privately, where changing her mind costs her nothing. Directors forgive delay; they do not forgive learning of it in the meeting.

It is not a roadmap review

Management owns the roadmap. The board tests whether resources and risks fit the plan, so a demo is a supporting exhibit, never the argument. If a director starts redesigning the product, the update has probably failed to show which lever it wants pulled.

What it cannot tell you

A clean update cannot show that the strategy is right; Aquila could report perfect variance on the wrong market. Nor can it forecast the future; it records evidence to date and states assumptions. Before relying on any update, ask who in the room approved the plan, what hurdle they use, and what you would do if they said no.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace; early and late

In consumer products, directors want retention by cohort (users grouped by sign-up month) and the cost of acquiring each user; metrics move daily, so the update must separate signal from noise. In B2B, as at Aquila, they want pipeline, contract value, onboarding time and concentration, meaning how much revenue sits with a few customers. In marketplaces they want liquidity, the share of listings that transact, on both sides.

At seed stage, a board of three may sit with the founder over tea, and product is the company, so the update is a conversation. At scale, committees and formal papers appear, directors see only the few largest bets, and a product leader must compress a portfolio into three or four decisions.

7. Common mistakes

The feature tour

Symptom: directors ask about screens, then fall quiet. Misunderstanding: the board audits outcomes, not output. Diagnostic: cover each slide title and write "so we ask you to…"; if it stays blank, cut the slide.

The buried slip

Symptom: a director learns of a delay from someone outside the room. Misunderstanding: boards prize predictability over good news. Diagnostic: call two directors beforehand; any surprise means rewrite. A second sign is a deck whose worst news sits on slide twenty-six.

The unpriced ask

Symptom: "let's take this offline." Misunderstanding: an ask must be priced in the board's currency, and a director cannot weigh what has no price. Diagnostic: complete the sentence "₹X buys Y, and costs Z months of runway."

8. What good looks like

Ilhan's memo is two pages. Page one opens with the ask and its price, then the variance table, then both passes, then the single input that decides. Irfana and Ishrar have each had a call. At the meeting, nobody asks what the module does; they argue over whether 20 accounts a month is believable, which is exactly the argument the company needs. The memo also states what would change Ilhan's mind: if onboarding stays at the plan rate of twelve a month through December, he will withdraw the second tranche himself. The last page lists every earlier ask and its outcome, so Ishrar can see that promises get followed up.

9. What Ilhan decides

He does not ask for all ₹75 lakh. Pass one and pass two straddle the 1.00 hurdle, and the deciding input, the onboarding rate, will be known within weeks. He requests ₹37.5 lakh now, costing 0.47 months of runway, and the second ₹37.5 lakh released automatically once accounts onboard at 20 in a month, comfortably above the 17.4 break-even. The board can say yes without betting on a forecast, and Ilhan has bound himself to evidence he can be held to. Several of the ideas above show up in this choice: variance to plan, a named denominator, and an early call to each director.

To go further, read about how plans and targets are set, since variance only means something against a plan the board believes, and then about fundraising expectations, which shape what investors want to hear.

Questions to sit with. First, which line of your last update would a director have to take on trust, and what would remove the need? Second, if your ask failed Ishrar's hurdle on the plan rate but passed on a hopeful one, how would you present it honestly?
exp40v2-comm.board:
People, Leadership & Organisation · Communication & Stakeholder Management

Board and investor communication

What a board actually wants from a product update — and why the answer is a scored track record rather than a deck.

1. Two rooms, thirteen days apart

On Thursday 22 October 2026, Jaitri Ruikar, chief product officer of Bhingri Studio in Bengaluru, had eleven days. Its subscription app dubs and captions short-form video into eight Indian languages. On 30 September 2026 it held ₹52.0 crore against a burn of ₹2.60 crore a month — twenty months of runway — and billed 1,75,000 paying subscribers at ₹240 a month, or ₹4.20 crore of monthly revenue. The board would meet on Friday 6 November, papers due Monday 2 November; Jaitri wanted ₹4.80 crore to move rendering onto the device.

The pre-read Jogita Rajmane had asked for unsettled her. Jogita, the partner at Bhingri's lead investor, wanted not the plan but the last four quarters of Jaitri's forecasts, with the outcome beside each one. Jaymala Renapurkar, the independent director and a former chief financial officer, was blunter: she would not vote for an ask priced off a forecast whose record she could not inspect. Jeenal Rukhande, the chief executive, feared the score would resurface in the Series C.

On Friday 23 October, in Nashik, Jyotiraditya Rawade faced the mirror image. Bakhar Instruments, which he co-founded, makes a point-of-care anaemia screener, a Class B medical device. Bakhar held ₹41.0 crore against a burn of ₹1.64 crore a month. On Thursday 19 November its board would be asked for ₹6.40 crore — 3.90 months of runway — to tool a second line before the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation rules on a licence variation filed on 7 September 2026, a decision expected by Wednesday 31 March 2027. Jashmeet Rairkar, the investor director, wanted a probability on that licence; Jyotiraditya offered 0.75, the consultant 0.60. Two of the last three meetings had gone on the gap.

Both boards wanted the same thing in different currencies: a reason to believe the next number they would be given.

2. The idea, and who disputes it

A board update is how a board maintains two estimates at once: the state of the business, and management's reliability as a reporter of it. The first is cheap and decays slowly. The second is expensive, decays with every unexplained miss, and is what prices an ask. A director who trusts the reporter can approve a number she cannot verify; one who does not must verify all.

The problem is structural. Fama and Jensen's 1983 separation of decision management from decision control described a body that must monitor choices it did not make, and the Cadbury committee of December 1992 located the failure in the quality of information reaching directors. India's Companies Act, 2013 fixes four board meetings a year and the SEBI listing regulations of 2015 a minimum information pack: both fix frequency and content, neither credibility. The scoring apparatus came from elsewhere — Glenn Brier's 1950 score for weather forecasts, Allan Murphy's 1973 decomposition, and Philip Tetlock's forecasting tournaments from 2005, which established that calibration is measurable and trainable.

Five positions divide on signable propositions. The governance minimalists sign “the board sees reserved matters and nothing else”; they refuse “product leaders should present to the board.” The narrative-memo school, from Amazon's six-pager of around 2004, signs “prose read in silence beats any deck”; it refuses “an update's value is the record it accumulates.” The instrumentation school signs “the same twelve numbers every quarter”; it refuses “management chooses which metrics matter.” The decision-procurement school signs “an update with no ask should be one page”; it refuses “the board hears everything material when nothing is asked.” The calibration school, Jogita's, signs “publish a score on management's probabilities”; it refuses “one aggregate score is enough.”

3. Mechanics: the forecast ledger, worked through

The practice is narrow. Each quarter management states a few claims, each with a probability and a resolution criterion — a date, a measure and a source — agreed before the quarter starts. Each resolves to one or zero, and nothing is re-argued. Exhibit 1 is Jaitri's ledger for the four quarters to 30 September 2026.

Exhibit 1. Bhingri Studio: forecast ledger, four quarters ended 30 September 2026.

Realised: autodub 24 Mar, Hindi model 11 Jun, pilot 14 Sep 2026; conversion 3.4%, render cost ₹1.40 a minute, retention 35%, rating 4.4, gross margin 59.0%, churn 7.1%. Conversion is measured on installs in the quarter, retention on the weekly-active share of each sign-up cohort, churn on the paying base at 1 September. The stated-p column sums to the hits predicted, 6.400, against 6 realised.

The Brier score is the mean squared error of the stated probabilities: 2.060 over ten claims, or 0.206. 6 of the 10 resolved as forecast, 60 per cent, against a mean stated probability of 0.640: in aggregate Jaitri was overconfident by four points. Murphy's decomposition says more. Grouped by the probability stated, the score splits into reliability, how far each group's realised rate sat from its stated probability; resolution, how far the groups separated from the base rate; and uncertainty, which belongs to the world.

Exhibit 2. Murphy decomposition of Exhibit 1, grouped by stated probability; base rate ō = 0.600.
