The arithmetic: 34 per cent of 11,000 is 3,740; the observed 412 is 11.0 per cent of 3,740; 412 × ₹1,850 is ₹7,62,200. For availability, October has 31 × 1,440 = 44,640 minutes; 330 ÷ 44,640 is 0.74 per cent downtime, so availability is 99.26 per cent. The contract promises 99.9 per cent, and a shortfall between 99.0 and 99.9 earns a credit of 10 per cent of the monthly fee, ₹480 lakh ÷ 12 = ₹40 lakh, so ₹4 lakh.

Pass 2 changes one input: the same 330 minutes at 02:00, when Vanmala takes 200 orders an hour (1,100 in all). Availability and credit are identical, because the contract counts minutes, yet the harm falls to roughly a tenth. In the real case the credit (₹4.00 lakh) covered about half the revenue lost (₹7.62 lakh), and neither figure touched the question Anturkar was asking. The availability figure is a projection, valid only if October has no further outage; one more bad hour would lower it to 99.13 per cent (390 minutes ÷ 44,640 is 0.87 per cent), still inside the same credit tier. The tier changes only below 99.0 per cent, which is more than 446 minutes of downtime in the month.

5. Nuances

Response time is not resolution time

Executives judge the first hour. A call returned in twenty minutes with a plan to fix by Friday beats a perfect root-cause report a week later.

Apology is not admission

"We failed you on Tuesday and I am sorry" accepts responsibility for an experience. Statements about legal fault or fixed compensation belong to the contract and, if needed, to counsel. Newcomers often avoid apologising for fear of the second and so deliver neither. The test is simple: the apology should name what happened to the customer, not what the supplier's systems did.

Escalation, complaint and incident are different things

An incident is a technical event; a complaint is an expression of dissatisfaction; an escalation is a change of audience. An executive escalation can follow a perfectly ordinary incident, as here, and the incident team may have finished while the escalation has only begun. Treating the closure of the ticket as the end of the matter is how suppliers are surprised by calls like this one.

Contractual remedy is not harm

Pass 2 above shows the gap. Quote the credit as the contract's answer, never as the answer to his anger. A chief executive judges harm by what he must explain to his own board, not by the clause in the schedule.

Recovery can build loyalty, but only once

The "service recovery paradox", the finding that some customers become more loyal after a well-handled failure than after none, is conditional on severity and appears to vanish when failures repeat. Do not plan on it.

The demand is a proposed remedy, not the need

Anturkar asked for a feature, but what he needed was assurance that festive-season stock would not go stale. Asking "what would you have to see to feel safe on 8 November?" often yields something Hirval can lawfully and cheaply give.

The method has edges

It cannot tell you whether the account is worth a concession. It does not cover a personal-data breach, which brings duties under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; legal counsel comes first there. A newcomer should ask: who else has been told something different, and what have we already put in writing?

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

In consumer products an "executive" escalation is usually public: a post tagging the founder, answered within the hour, with no contract to cite. In B2B, as here, the executive is named, the contract is the reference, and the renewal date supplies the leverage. In a marketplace the supplier serves two sides, so a promise to a seller's chief executive (a fee cut, a ranking change) may harm buyers or other sellers and must be tested against both. The same test applies to B2B accounts that share a platform: a custom fix for one retailer can slow every other retailer's release.

Scale changes who takes the call. In an early-stage company the founder usually does, with no written escalation matrix, and the risk is that the founder promises features outright. In a large company, account teams, legal and a formal ladder exist, and the risk reverses: the customer's executive speaks to a middle manager who cannot decide anything. The remedy in both cases is the same, a named person with pre-agreed authority who is neither too junior to act nor so senior that every promise becomes the company's.

7. Common mistakes

Promising the roadmap to end the call

Symptom: engineering discovers dates in a sales email. Misunderstanding: that a promise costs nothing. Diagnostic: read the last three outgoing emails and ask whether anyone else's priorities would have to move to keep them.

Explaining before owning

Symptom: the customer repeats the same question twice. Misunderstanding: that anger is a request for information. Diagnostic: count how many sentences pass before someone says "we".

Many voices

Symptom: the customer quotes three different dates. Misunderstanding: that more senior contact shows more concern. Diagnostic: keep a single log of every outbound statement and check it for contradictions.

Credit as apology

Symptom: a discount offered in the first minute, and the tone worsens. Misunderstanding: treating anger as a price problem. Diagnostic: ask whether the offer was a response to something the customer said.

8. What good looks like

Ahire opened by saying that Vanmala's customers had waited on orders for hours and Hirval was responsible. She gave the timeline: confirmed cause, a configuration change to the queue at 14:08; unknown, why the alert fired only at 16:20. She named Ardhapurkar as owner, with herself accountable, and set three dated actions: a fix review by Monday, a safeguard test by 16 October, and daily stock-sync reports through Diwali. Asked about the feature, she said she would not sign a date she could not defend, and would bring him an engineering estimate by 22 October. She did not argue with his figure for the loss; she asked for Vanmala's own numbers and offered to reconcile them with the logs. By the end, Anturkar had said what mattered to him: not the date, but that nobody at Hirval should learn about a stock failure after his shoppers did.

9. Closing

Ahire rejected Avsare's draft. She sent the written summary at 15:30 the same day and the estimate on 22 October, with an interim safeguard of five-minute stock checks for Diwali week. Her reasoning was that a missed roadmap date would convert one incident into two broken promises, while a dated plan of smaller things could be kept.

To go further, study key account management, for deciding which customers merit a concession, and customer-facing communication, because an escalation is that discipline under pressure.

Questions to sit with. First, if Anturkar had asked for the date again at the end of the call, what would you have been prepared to say, and what would it have cost? Second, which of your own accounts holds a promise you would not want read aloud to your engineers?
exp20v2-comm.bad.news:
Delivering Bad News About the Product

A case-style explainer on reporting slips, misses and failures early, with causes and options.

1. The audit on the Thursday evening

On Thursday 11 June 2026, Dhruvan Kudalkar, a product manager at Sarovar Fleet, a Pune company selling vehicle-tracking software to logistics operators, finished reading an audit he had commissioned himself. The product was Sarovar Reroute, a feature that proposes new routes to dispatchers when a truck falls behind. Twelve customers had piloted it since Monday 4 May. General availability was promised for Monday 13 July, and nine customers had signed contracts naming that date, with ₹3.6 crore a year of revenue attached.

The audit sampled 400 suggestions that dispatchers had accepted. In 60 of them, 15 per cent, the truck arrived more than ten minutes later than the original plan would have delivered it. Taking the pilot to generate about 7,000 suggestions a week across the twelve customers (an assumption used throughout), dispatchers accepted only 40 per cent, against a target of 60. Dhairav Kharat, the head of engineering, suspected the live traffic feed, which refreshed every fifteen minutes where the design assumed two. A test of a faster feed in three cities would report on Friday 26 June.

The chief executive, Dilnavaz Karnik, would tell the board on Thursday 25 June that Reroute was on track. Dhruvan had to decide whether to speak now, with a suspicion in place of a cause and no recovery date at all, or to wait a day past that meeting for a result. Waiting felt prudent. This page argues that it was the dangerous course.

2. The idea

Delivering bad news about a product means giving the people who depend on your work an accurate picture of its state, as soon as you hold information that would change one of their decisions, together with what you know of the cause and what they can do about it. Three phrases carry the weight. Accurate, because softening and exaggerating both distort. As soon as, because news loses value with every decision taken without it. Their decisions, because a report is tested by what the recipient can now do, not by how she felt reading it.

No single person invented the practice. Its formal vocabulary comes from project management and from safety-critical industries, where reporting norms hardened after failures that were known to people inside an organisation and not to the people above them. Nothing here is a rule of law. The sentence Dhruvan could repeat in a meeting: “I would rather give you a smaller truth today than a complete one after your decision is made.” Three different claims hide inside the word “bad”.

Kind of newsWhat is trueReroute example
SlipIt will do what was promised, laterDate moves; the 40 per cent acceptance was merely early
MissIt ships, but below the promised resultAcceptance settles near 40 per cent, not 60
Will not workThe mechanism fails or does harmSuggestions that make trucks later
Dhruvan did not yet know which row he was in; the honest message says so.

3. How it actually works

The first step is to sort what you hold into three piles. For Dhruvan, known: 60 of 400 audited suggestions were worse than the plan, and acceptance was 40 per cent. Suspected: feed latency. Unknown: whether a faster feed fixes it, and how long a rollout takes in the other cities. Each pile is reported under its own label, because the recipient will otherwise treat a suspicion as a finding or a finding as a rumour.

The second step, usually left implicit, is to find the recipient’s clock, not yours. Dilnavaz’s clock ran to the board on 25 June, and the customers’ to 13 July. Dhruvan’s own clock, the test on 26 June, mattered to neither. The third step is to classify the news as slip, miss or failure. The fourth is to write in this order: the conclusion, the evidence, the cause with its status, the options, what you need from her, and when you will next report. The fifth, also usually omitted, is to state what you got wrong.

The figure shows why the fifth step matters less than the second. Path B is not a worse message; it is the same message arriving after Dilnavaz has spoken to the board.

4. A worked example, three ways

Here is the same news written three times. The first is evasive.

Evasive. Pilot feedback has been mixed and the team is working through integration items with a few customers. We continue to target mid-July, subject to final validation.

Nothing in it is false, and a reader can learn nothing from it. The second is brutal.

Brutal. Reroute is broken. Fifteen per cent of its suggestions make trucks later. Engineering underestimated the traffic feed. We will miss July and I do not know when it will work.

It asserts a cause nobody has confirmed, assigns blame, offers no options, and spares its author nothing while sparing the recipient no work. The third is straight.

Straight. Reroute is not ready to ship on 13 July as promised, and I cannot yet give you a new date. Known: in an audit of 400 accepted suggestions, 60 (15 per cent) arrived more than ten minutes later than the original plan; dispatchers accept 40 per cent against a target of 60. Suspected, not confirmed: the traffic feed refreshes every 15 minutes where we designed for two. Unknown: whether a faster feed fixes it; a test reports on Friday 26 June. If it works I estimate four to eight weeks to ship, 24 July to 21 August; if not, I have no date. I recommend we switch the pilot to display-only today, call the nine customers by Wednesday, and tell the board on 25 June that the date is unconfirmed until the 26th. Acceptance had sat below target for three weeks and I read it as slow adoption; I did not audit quality until 11 June.

Central estimateTell Fri 12 JuneWait for Fri 26 June
Days from audit to pause115
Late trips at 60 a day60900
Days left before the board13none; already held
Days left before 13 July3117
Suggestions: 7,000 a week; 40 per cent accepted is 2,800; 15 per cent of those is 420 a week, or 60 a day, counting seven days a week.

The money is a separate exposure. Nine contracts at ₹40 lakh a year make ₹360 lakh, which is the ₹3.6 crore. A go-live credit of ₹1.5 lakh each, payable if general availability falls later than 27 July, makes ₹13.5 lakh, 3.75 per cent of the ₹360 lakh, with a 14-day grace after 13 July. Only the early end of Dhruvan’s range, 24 July, escapes it, and he could not know that on 12 June, which is precisely why the customers needed the range.

Second pass. Change one input: the audit finds 12 worse of 400, which is 3 per cent. The harm falls to 84 a week, 12 a day; waiting costs 180 trips, not 900. The news now looks like a miss, perhaps survivable in display-only mode on the original date. Telling early still wins by 168 trips, and by the board clock, which did not depend on the rate at all.

5. The nuances

Certainty is the wrong threshold.

The incentive to wait until you are sure is the same incentive to wait too long, because certainty usually arrives after the decisions it would have informed. The better test is whether what you know could change something the recipient will do before you would otherwise tell her.

Slip, miss and failure are different claims.

Calling a miss a slip promises a recovery the product may never deliver; calling a slip a failure triggers panic and cancelled work. If you cannot tell which, say that, and say what would settle it.

Not knowing the date is reportable.

Give the date you will know the date, the range under a stated assumption, and what would void the range. Dhruvan’s four to eight weeks only holds if the feed test works. A range without its assumption is a promise in disguise.

Evidence has a size.

A rate from 400 audited trips carries an interval, which for 15 per cent runs from about 11.5 to 18.5. Had Dhruvan audited 40 trips and found 6, the same 15 per cent would span about 7 to 29 on the Wilson method; a plain normal interval, 4 to 26, is unreliable with only 6 events and sits too low at both ends. Say how many you looked at and how they were drawn: these intervals assume a random sample, and trips clustered in a few customers would make them too narrow.

Label the cause by its status.

An explanation says what is known about why; an excuse says why it was not your fault. Give the first, with its status, and include your own part. The straight message above lets Dilnavaz see the misreading of acceptance herself; she will find it anyway, and her trust in the rest depends on who told her.

Framing is allowed; omission is not.

Order, tone and a recommendation are legitimate. The test is whether the recipient, shown everything you knew when you wrote, would feel misled. Softening that changes what she would do fails it.

Some news travels beyond the room.

Companies can owe prompt disclosure to lenders, investors, regulators or contracted customers, and the terms differ by contract and jurisdiction; this page states none as settled. Whether Reroute triggered any such duty at Sarovar Fleet is a question for counsel. Dhruvan’s job was to put the facts in front of Dilnavaz early enough that someone could ask.

6. Consumer, B2B and marketplace

SettingWho hears firstWhat goes wrong
ConsumerUsers, via reviews and social postsThe public finds out before leadership
B2BNamed accounts, by contractA clause fires on a date nobody reread
MarketplaceOne side; the other reactsNews to drivers or sellers moves demand

Reroute is B2B, which is why Dhruvan needed the nine names and the credit clause on the page. In a consumer product the audience is not a list, so the discipline is a pre-agreed trigger: a metric drop of a stated size is escalated within a stated day. In a marketplace, remember the news changes the other side’s behaviour, so sequence matters.

Size changes the failure. In a ten-person company the chief executive hears everything and the risk is that nothing is written. In a large one the message passes through layers, each of which softens it a little; the remedy is to send the straight version to the decision-maker directly and copy the layers.

7. Common mistakes

Reporting the symptom without the decision. From outside: updates dense with metrics and no request. Misunderstanding: that informing is reporting. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what the reader would do differently after reading it. If nothing, the message is a diary entry.

Waiting for the root cause. From outside: leadership learns sideways, from a customer or an engineer. Misunderstanding: that a report must be complete to be credible. Diagnostic: write down the date you first suspected a problem and the date you told anyone; the gap is the cost.

Over-correcting into the brutal version. From outside: the reply addresses your tone, not the plan. Misunderstanding: that severity is honesty. Diagnostic: label each sentence as fact, labelled inference, request or option; cut the rest.

8. What good looks like

On Friday 12 June, Dhruvan sent the straight message to Dilnavaz and Dhairav together and asked for thirty minutes. She asked three questions: how sure was the 15 per cent, what did display-only cost the pilot, and who at the customers should hear first. By noon the pilot was display-only. Before any dispatcher noticed a pattern, Dhruvan phoned Dattaram Kothekar, who ran operations at a Nashik pilot customer, and told him in two sentences what he knew and when he would know more. He then sent a one-line update every Friday, including one that said nothing had changed.

9. What Dhruvan decides, and what to read next

Dhruvan sent the message on the Friday morning, not after the test. His reasoning: Dilnavaz could use thirteen days and could do nothing with a result that arrived after the board. He accepted that he might look foolish if the feed fix worked on 26 June; being early and partly wrong costs a conversation, and being late and right costs the recipient’s options. Dilnavaz told the board on the 25th that the date was unconfirmed, and why.

Read next the page on difficult conversations, which extends this to news that lands on people, and the page on status updates and stakeholder rhythms, which covers the cadence that makes Friday’s update ordinary.

Two questions to sit with. Think of the last time you held back something because it was not yet certain: whose decision fell due before the certainty arrived? And which of the three messages would you write under pressure, and what in your situation makes it the likely one?
exp40v2-comm.bad.news:
Delivering Bad News About the Product

Why the incentive to delay is a structure rather than a character flaw, what is owed to whom, and how an organisation’s answer to the last report sets the timing of the next.

1. Two managers, two Mondays

On Monday 1 June 2026 a laboratory report reached Ekaraj Laghate, product manager for the swap network at Toranmal Energy Networks, which runs 150 battery-swap stations for electric three-wheelers across Maharashtra. Each station holds 35 packs, so the network carries 5,250 at ₹16,000 each to replace. On Monday 4 May firmware release 4.2 had gone to 64 stations, covering 2,240 packs. On Friday 29 May the laboratory pulled 175 packs with about four weeks on 4.2 and found 21, or 12.0 per cent (standard error 2.46 points), past the 8 per cent capacity-loss threshold against a design expectation of 2 per cent. Nothing had failed; the packs were ageing six times faster than they should. The remaining 86 stations were due to receive 4.2 over the weekend of Sunday 28 June, the chief executive Ela Lahane would take pack economics to the board on Thursday 2 July, and a cell teardown saying why was due on Monday 20 July. Eight months earlier Edhas Lavekar had lost the Nagpur launch for escalating a charging fault that proved to be a bad rig.

On Tuesday 3 March 2026 in Bengaluru, Esanya Ligade opened the subgroup breakdown of a four-week shadow run. Tansa Intake, her product at Tansa Intelligence, reads motor-claim documents for insurers and routes them for adjudication. From Monday 2 February to Sunday 1 March it ran beside the human team at Tirora General Insurance on 48,000 documents, under a three-year contract worth ₹4.20 crore, of which ₹1.20 crore falls in year one. Field-level accuracy on Tirora’s live mix was 87.0 per cent against a contracted service level of 92.0, measured quarterly, with a credit of 2 per cent of the annual fee for each full point below, capped at 10 per cent. Go-live was Monday 6 April; the steering committee met on Thursday 12 March; a fine-tuned model for scanned documents would report on Friday 20 March. The benchmark on which 92.2 per cent had been promised was one Esanya built herself in September 2024.

Neither was deciding how to phrase anything. Each was deciding when to speak. The timing is governed by an incentive structure that is locally rational and collectively ruinous, and the structure can be written down.

2. The idea, and the four positions on it

Delivering bad news about a product is the transfer, to each person holding a decision that depends on the product, of an accurate account of its state at the earliest moment at which that account would change what they do, with the status of the cause and the options still open. It is indexed to decisions rather than events, because one fact is news to one person and noise to another, and the deadline is set by the recipient’s calendar, not the reporter’s confidence.

The practice has no single author. Its vocabulary arrived from three traditions that were not talking to each other. Project controls contributed the idea that a date is a forecast with a distribution, so a slip is a revised estimate and not a confession. Organisational psychology contributed the finding, filed under the reluctance to transmit unpleasant messages, that people delay and soften bad news even when no penalty attaches to telling it. Accident research in high-reliability settings contributed the observation that serious failures are usually preceded by an interval in which somebody inside already knew. All three circle one problem: information cheap to move while it is useful becomes expensive to move once it is certain.

Four positions on who decides that the moment has come are worth separating; capable practitioners hold all four and argue past one another.

PositionWould signWould not sign
Disclosure (high-reliability)Any anomaly goes on a fixed channel the day it is seenThat a manager should filter for materiality first
Ownership (operator)An escalation with no options attached is an abdicationThat a naked suspicion belongs in a leadership forum
Fiduciary (compliance)The clock starts at awareness, not confirmationThat notice may be traded against certainty
Calibration (forecasting)Point-estimate dates manufacture bad newsThat there is a right moment to escalate at all
All four answer the same question — when does the duty bite — and goodwill does not reconcile them.

3. The mechanics: pricing one more week

Treat Ekaraj’s problem as a weekly decision governed by four quantities. h is the harm from one more week of not knowing: taken as linear and held beyond the four weeks observed, 12.0 per cent over about four weeks is 3.0 per cent a week, which on 2,240 exposed packs is 67 packs, or ₹10.72 lakh. α is the share of that harm the reporter carries personally, through standing and bonus; put it at 0.25, generously. F is his private cost of a report that proves a false alarm, and w his own estimate that the coming week will show the anomaly benign, so no report is ever needed.

Waiting a week is privately attractive when w × F exceeds α × h, here ₹2.68 lakh. With a week-one w of 0.30, waiting pays whenever avoiding a false alarm is worth over ₹8.93 lakh — a year’s variable pay and some standing, an ordinary valuation. The table takes two values of F: ₹9 lakh, what Ekaraj would have said before the Nagpur affair, and ₹27 lakh, what he says after it.

WeekwGain at F = ₹9 lakhGain at F = ₹27 lakhαh as pricedαh in fact
10.302.708.102.682.68
20.221.985.942.682.68
30.161.444.322.682.68
40.121.083.242.682.68
50.110.992.972.686.32
60.050.451.352.686.32
Week 1 begins Monday 1 June; money in ₹ lakh per week. Every w is Ekaraj’s own estimate, and w5 is decisive: below 0.099 its gain falls under ₹2.68 lakh and he reports on 29 June. The last column rises because the 28 June push takes exposure from 2,240 packs to all 5,250: 158 packs a week at ₹25.28 lakh, of which 0.25 is ₹6.32 lakh.

At F = ₹9 lakh waiting wins in week one by ₹2,000 and loses thereafter, so Ekaraj reports on 8 June having burnt ₹10.72 lakh. At ₹27 lakh, pricing delay at a flat ₹2.68 lakh because nobody put the 28 June push on his page, he would wait five times and report on 6 July with ₹68.16 lakh gone. Each decision was defensible; nobody lied, nobody froze, and the loss is more than six times as large.

That step is the mechanism. A manager asked six times whether one more week is worth it answers yes five times and no on the sixth; asked once, on 1 June, whether to wait until 6 July, he answers no — 0.25 × 68.16 is ₹17.04 lakh against a best single-week gain of 0.30 × 27, or ₹8.10 lakh. This is not weakness of will: a sequential problem with a step in its cost function has a different solution from the committed one, and the fix is to convert the first into the second by fixing, in week one, the date the answer is due.

The second piece of mechanics is usually left implicit: what is owed to whom. Experts list recipients, each with the decision that starts their clock, working backwards from the earliest.

Who is owedWhat starts their clockWhat they can still do
Anyone who will repeat it in publicA statement being drafted that your information changesNot say it
Anyone who must change a planA dated decision of theirs resting on the productStop, defer or re-sequence
A counterparty with a dated promiseThe date or metric in doubt, not yet missedRe-plan their own rollout
Anyone exposed to harmThe exposure, not its confirmationStop using the thing
Finance, legal and complianceThe possibility that an obligation existsTake advice in time
Row five is deliberately weak. Duties of disclosure to lenders, insurers, regulators or contracted customers can exist and differ by instrument and jurisdiction; whether either situation here triggers one is for counsel.

4. When the argument holds, and when it misleads

The case for early reporting is conditional; stating it as a virtue is how organisations acquire escalation channels nobody reads. Four conditions make it bind.

ConditionToranmalTansa
A recipient’s decision falls due before your certainty dateYes: 28 June and 2 July precede the 20 July teardownYes: 12 March precedes 20 March
The news changes what they do, not only what they knowYes: the push can be heldYes: go-live can be staged by type
Harm accrues while you waitYes: 67 packs a week, rising to 158No: the shadow run harms nobody
You are the earliest holder of the informationYes: the laboratory reports only to engineeringNo: Tirora has the logs
Two of four for Tansa. Esanya’s urgency rests on the recipient’s clock alone, which is enough.

The argument misleads on routine variance inside a declared band. A metric moving within the range you told people to expect is not news, and reporting it trains the organisation to discount you, raising everyone’s threshold on the day something real happens. It misleads again when the recipient has no decision: a report to someone who can only worry is anxiety dressed as candour. Ask what the recipient can do; if nothing, find who can.

5. Edge cases and organisational seams

Hardware plus software is hardest, because a software defect acquires a physical consequence that cannot be rolled back. Toranmal can revert firmware 4.2 in an afternoon; it cannot un-age the 269 packs that 12.0 per cent of 2,240 already represented. Where the remedy has a lead time — procurement, a service visit, a recall — that belongs in the first message, because it is what the recipient must start now.

AI-native products break a shared assumption: there is often no defect to find. Tansa’s subgroup rates were identical in both runs, so 87.0 against 92.2 per cent is pure composition, and managers raised on “what broke on Tuesday” hunt a regression that does not exist. Two-sided products add a wrinkle: the news is itself an intervention, since telling one side moves the other before any fix lands, so sequence is part of the message.

The seam is where most late reports are made, and it is structural, not personal. Toranmal’s battery laboratory reports to Erina Lamgaonkar in engineering; it saw 12.0 per cent on 29 May and had no reason to know a push was set for 28 June, because the deployment calendar lives with the network team. Nobody withheld anything: the information and the clock sat in different reporting lines, which is ordinary at this size. Mature organisations say they run a blameless escalation process. What they run is two channels: a slow written one for the record, and a fast call to whoever’s plan is about to be wrong, which carries the news first. Experts use the second to set the clock and the first to make it durable.

6. Eight things that separate an expert

The marginal question is the wrong question.

A competent manager asks whether one more week is worth it and gets a defensible yes. The expert sees it returning next week on the same terms and converts it into a commitment: a report-by date fixed in week one, whatever is known then. The tell is a problem whose “we will know by” date has moved twice while its escalation date has not.

The person estimating w benefits from w being high.

Ekaraj’s 0.30 is a judgement by the one man who would rather not write the memo. The tell is a self-resolution estimate that never revises downward, or is quoted without the evidence that moved it. The correction is arithmetic, not humility: let someone with no stake set it, or use a frequency — how often has this anomaly been nothing here?

Sunk harm is not an argument in either direction.

The 269 packs already past threshold on 1 June are irrelevant to the choice; the live variable is 67 a week, then 158. Experts open with the forward rate. The tell is a memo leading with cumulative damage, which reads as accountability, works as sympathy-seeking, and invites argument about the past instead of a decision.

Slip, miss and will-not-work carry different duties, not different tones.

A slip is a scheduling fact, owed to whoever holds the calendar; a miss is a contractual fact, owed to whoever signed; a will-not-work is a strategy fact, owed to whoever allocated the money. Esanya’s 87.0 per cent is a miss on the contract and arguably a will-not-work for small-workshop documents, and those claims go to different people. The tell is a new date for something with no mechanism.

The report that incriminates the reporter carries the most information.

Esanya built the 92.2 per cent benchmark, drawing 9,120 of its 12,000 documents from four large garages that submit typed PDFs. The composition error is hers. Omitting it is less honest and less useful, since the reader cannot then judge whether the mix will drift again. The tell: an expert’s memo already contains the sentence a hostile reviewer would write.

The reply to the last report prices the next one.

F is set by precedent, not policy. Toranmal’s handling of Edhas Lavekar in October 2025 moved Ekaraj’s private cost of being wrong from about ₹9 lakh to about ₹27 lakh, and the table above would turn that one change into a report four weeks later and a loss more than six times as large. The diagnostic is not the written policy but how the last false alarm was treated, by name.

Composition can move a headline with nothing getting worse.

Tansa’s subgroup rates, 95.7 per cent typed and 81.2 scanned, were unchanged between benchmark and shadow run; only the mix moved, from 24 per cent scanned to 60. The expert asks for subgroup rates before asking what broke. The tell is a team hunting a regression in a model nobody retrained.

Precision is rarely the uncertainty that matters.

Sampling error on the 28,800 scanned documents is about 0.23 of a point at their 81.2, and 0.18 at the 90 the fine-tune promises — nothing beside a mix that has already moved 36 points. A memo reporting a confidence interval and no sensitivity has measured the cheap uncertainty. The tell is a decimal carried past the assumption under it.

7. How the practice changes across product types and stages

The duty map above does not change; which clock binds first does. The common error is a B2B instinct brought to a consumer problem, or the reverse.

SettingWhat the news is usually aboutBinding clock
ConsumerA metric moving, cause unknownPublic discovery through reviews and posts
B2B and enterpriseA dated promise or a contracted metricThe customer’s own rollout plan, days ahead
Platform and marketplaceSupply, trust or payout behaviourThe other side reacting before the fix lands
Hardware and physical goodsUnits already in the fieldThe remedy’s lead time, not the date of the fault
AI productsA distribution that moved, not a defectThe first live decision on a degraded output
Tansa sits in rows two and five at once, which is why its binding clock is 12 March and not 6 April.

Stage changes the failure mode rather than the duty. In a thirty-person company everything is known and nothing written, so the failure is a decision nobody can reconstruct. Past two hundred people the information and the clock separate, as at Toranmal, and the failure becomes a seam. At scale the message crosses layers that each soften it; the remedy is routing — send the unsoftened version to the decision-holder and copy the layers.

8. Three worked examples

Toranmal, on the numbers. Reporting on 2 June adds almost nothing to the 269 packs already lost and preserves two options: holding the 28 June push, which protects 3,010 packs on 86 stations, and giving Ela Lahane a month to settle what the board hears on 2 July. Reporting on 6 July adds ₹68.16 lakh and preserves neither.

Tansa, where the arithmetic is the message. Esanya’s memo is largely a decomposition: 60 per cent of Tirora’s live mix is scanned at 81.2 per cent and 40 per cent typed at 95.7, giving 87.0; the benchmark’s 76 per cent typed gave 92.2; and to reach the contracted 92.0 on the live mix the scanned rate must reach 89.5 per cent. The fine-tune is expected to deliver 90.0, which would give 92.3. At 87.0 the quarterly credit is five full points, so 10 per cent of ₹1.20 crore, or ₹12.00 lakh — the cap meaning the credit stops growing here and will not measure anything worse.

Tapola Commerce, where early reporting failed. In 2025 Enisha Lasurkar escalated a checkout-completion fall from 71.4 to 62.1 per cent on its second day, and the rollout was halted for six days. The cause was a telemetry change that dropped the success event on one Android build carrying 13 per cent of sessions: 0.87 times 71.4 is 62.1, and nothing was wrong. She was right on what she held. The recovery that mattered was a change of instrument — a rule that a move beyond four points triggers a twenty-four-hour instrumentation check before any halt, plus a public statement from her director that the escalation had been correct. Eleven weeks later a genuine 4.1-point fall still took nine days to surface, which is what an unrepaired F looks like.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

Four recur often enough to name, each with the question that catches it early.

Failure modeEarly warningDiagnostic questionCost of catching it late
Serial deferralA “we will know by” date that has moved twiceHow often has this date moved, and what changed each time?₹68.16 lakh in place of ₹10.72 lakh
Escalating up before acrossEngineering hears it from the chief executiveWho can start the fix, and have they been told?The repair begins after the meeting
The pre-cooked messageThe memo arrives with the mitigation already chosenWhich option did I remove from the recipient?The best option is gone before anyone sees it
The quiet downgradeA target edited with no memo attachedWho was told the number moved, and when?Discovery by a customer or auditor
The third is the one competent managers commit, because it looks like ownership.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first open question is the materiality filter. The disclosure school holds that a manager filtering anomalies before escalation substitutes their judgement for the organisation’s, citing accident histories in which the filtered item mattered. The ownership school replies that an unfiltered channel has its own latency: a team receiving forty anomalies a week reads none by week three, so filtering does not disappear but moves to the recipient, who has less context. Both are right about their own failure mode. Settling it needs a measurement nobody takes — latency on events that mattered, before and after a filter is removed.

The second is whether blameless reporting works. The evidence usually cited, from aviation and clinical incident reporting, shows volume rising sharply when penalties are removed. The sceptical reading is that volume is not signal, and that the cases here are those where the reporter is implicated, which no policy makes costless. To refute the sceptics you would show latency on implicating reports falling, not counts rising. Esanya is that test case, and Tansa has no data.

The third is ownership of the message. One camp holds that the function which found the problem should report it unmediated, because translation is where softening happens. The other holds that the product manager owns the promise and therefore its retraction, and that an engineering escalation without a commercial frame produces panic. The compromise — both, in one message — is held by few.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this writes better memos; someone who has internalised it changes the inputs. They measure their own latency, in days between first suspicion and first report, and quote it unasked. They write the recipient’s clock down before they finish gathering evidence, because the clock, not the evidence, sets the deadline. They send the uncomfortable version first and the complete one second, since a recipient who can act in week one beats one impressed in week three. They never write “we are monitoring” without a date. And when somebody else raises a false alarm, they say so publicly and in that person’s favour, knowing that this act, repeated, is the only lever that moves F for everyone around them.

12. What each manager did

Ekaraj Laghate reported on Tuesday 2 June, the day after the laboratory report, overriding his own weekly calculus: the committed and sequential questions had different answers, and he trusted the committed one. The 28 June push was held, 86 stations stayed on the old firmware, and Ela Lahane told the board on 2 July that pack economics were under revision, and why. Esanya Ligade sent the decomposition to Ekamjeet Ladgaonkar on 4 March and to Ekvira Lohote at Tirora on 6 March, six days before the steering committee, proposing a staged go-live on typed documents while the scanned model was tested against 89.5 per cent. She led with the benchmark’s composition and named it hers.

Three questions. First: Toranmal’s numbers make waiting privately rational in week one at any false-alarm cost above ₹8.93 lakh. Which of α, w and F is cheapest to move, and who moves it? Second: Esanya’s expected fix clears the service level by 0.3 of a point, seventeen days after she first knew. Is “we will miss unless a pending result lands as expected” more useful to Tirora than a report that waits, and what does your answer assume about Tirora? Third: Edhas Lavekar’s escalation was wrong and was punished. What should Toranmal have done the day the rig was found faulty, and what would it have cost?

13. Going deeper

Difficult conversations — the same news landing on a person, not a plan; it unlocks what routing cannot. Status updates and stakeholder rhythms — cadence makes an early report ordinary, the cheapest way to lower F. Stakeholder mapping and management — the duty map above, with clocks attached. Communicating with leadership — how a message survives the layers it crosses. Telling the customer story — what Tirora’s board hears, in whose words. Demo and pitch craft — where over-promising is made, two quarters before retraction. Writing as a PM superpower — the decomposition above is the whole skill. Decision records and DACI/RACI — naming the decision-maker early keeps a report off the wrong clock.
exp40v2-comm.exec.narrative.deck:
The Executive Narrative Memo at Depth

Three objectives that cannot all be maximised, and the arithmetic that decides where the pages go

1. Two memos, seven months apart

On Thursday 10 September 2026 Triveni Dhotre, vice-president of product at Kshamata Instruments in Pune, sent six pages to five people. Kshamata builds the A2, a point-of-care blood analyser; 2,800 sit in clinics and NABL-accredited laboratories, each running about 300 single-use cartridges a month. The cartridge sells for ₹58 and carries ₹31 of contribution. The instrument goes out near cost: Kshamata clears ₹48,000 on each of the 62 machines it ships a month and lives on what they consume.

Triveni wanted to end that. Her memo asked the executive committee to publish the cartridge interface so laboratories could run third-party reagents, on the argument that reagent freedom was why purchases went elsewhere and that volume would rise from 62 machines a month to 95. The committee — chief executive Tarunika Diwadkar, Takshak Dombale in finance, Tanvish Dhadphale in service — met on Monday 14 September and read in silence for twenty minutes.

Seven months earlier, on Friday 30 January 2026, Tapomoy Deuskar had sent six pages to nine people at Kaniyam Systems in Bengaluru. Kaniyam reads and prices motor own-damage claim documents for six general insurers; 186,000 pass through monthly. He wanted to settle the small ones, under ₹25,000, with no human reviewer. Tejovati Deglurkar, his head of risk and compliance, had four objections, and he had answered all four in print before she could raise them. The committee sat seventy minutes on Tuesday 3 February. Tejovati said nothing.

Both memos were good. Both were wrong in ways the format cannot detect, and one in a way the format caused.

2. The idea, and the three things people want from it

An executive narrative memo is a document of roughly six pages, written in connected sentences rather than slides, that argues for one decision, exposes the evidence, answers the strongest objections and ends by asking for a specific response, read in silence by those who will decide. Its lineage runs through the one-page memo long reported at Procter & Gamble, the military staff study, Barbara Minto's pyramid principle from McKinsey in the 1960s, and the narrative that displaced slides at Amazon from around 2004.

What it does not settle is what the document is for. Three schools answer differently; each signs propositions the others reject.

The falsification school holds that the memo exists to expose the claim whose failure would reverse the decision. It signs: make the memo easier to refute than to agree with, and an objection you cannot state in its owner's words you have not understood. It will not sign that a memo must close on one recommendation; two live options are a legitimate ending when the evidence does not separate them.

The commitment school holds that the memo exists to produce a decision that holds once the room empties. It signs: a memo that wins the vote and loses the owner of the risk has failed, and the ask must be one option, because a room invited to choose defers. It will not sign answering objections in print beforehand: saying it aloud and being answered before peers is what makes consent.

The record school holds that the memo exists to be re-read in eighteen months by someone who must explain the decision to a regulator. It signs: every figure carries its basis and date in the same sentence, and the memo states what would have changed the decision. It will not sign the six-page limit; a record omitting its evidence is no record, so it appends.

Detect error, produce commitment, preserve accountability: not simultaneously maximisable. The rest of this page concerns the two places they collide — allocating pages to claims, and handling objections.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic of where the pages go

Competent practitioners write the decision sentence first. Experts then do what textbooks leave implicit: before drafting, they compute how much of the decision each claim carries and allocate pages in that proportion, not by the evidence to hand. Kshamata shows the method and its limit.

Her metric was the change in monthly contribution at the installed base of 10 September 2026 — a snapshot, not a valuation, and labelled so. The defection share s is the fraction of installed cartridge volume moving to third-party reagents; the uplift u is extra machines sold monthly. Installed volume is 2,800 × 300 = 840,000 cartridges a month. A defecting cartridge loses ₹31 and returns a ₹4 certification fee, so costs ₹27: 840,000 × ₹27 = ₹226.80 lakh of exposure per unit of s. An extra machine adds ₹0.48 lakh.

Now the allocation: for each claim, take the swing in the metric across its plausible range, times the probability a reader will not grant it. Along u = +33, moving s from 10% to 50% moves the answer ₹90.72 lakh; down s = 30%, u across its range moves it ₹21.60 lakh. The fee, if ₹4 proved unenforceable, is worth 840,000 × 0.30 × ₹4 = ₹10.08 lakh.

Space follows available evidence, not decision weight: the ordinary error. But the method has a limit it cannot see. Exhibit 2 lists three claims; there was a fourth, invisible because Triveni had assumed it. An A2 bought because it takes third-party reagents will, by construction, run them, so a new machine's contribution over a 48-month life becomes ₹48,000 plus 48 × 300 × ₹4 = ₹1,05,600, against ₹48,000 plus 14,400 × ₹31 = ₹4,94,400 today: 21.4 per cent of its present worth. Volume must therefore rise 4.68-fold, 62 machines a month to 290. The survey promised 1.53-fold.

Stated so, the memo collapses. But she had set the new-buyer defection share to one without writing it down. At one half, a new machine's cartridges blend to ₹17.50, lifetime value is ₹3,00,000, the required multiple falls to 1.65-fold, and 1.53 is within touching distance. The recommendation turns on an assumption absent from a memo whose allocation was, by its own method, excellent — absent partly because its swing is lifetime value per machine while Exhibit 2's column is monthly contribution. It had no home in the table, so the table never asked.

The second mechanic is the attention budget: six pages is a proxy for the minutes the room will give. Triveni timed three colleagues reading her page four at 142, 150 and 158 words a minute, and used 150. Her first draft ran 4,050 words with three exhibits at about forty-five seconds each: 29.25 minutes against a twenty-minute read, 46 per cent over. What she sent ran 2,550 words and two exhibits, 18.5 minutes, the last ninety seconds held for re-reading page one.

4. When the form applies, stated as tests

Is reversal dear? Price it as a share of the decision. Publishing a cartridge interface and withdrawing it from laboratories that bought on the promise is near unreversable. Kaniyam's threshold is a configuration value, which looks cheap — but a month settles 44,640 claims that cannot be unsettled, so a reversible switch sits on an irreversible stock.

Do the readers disagree with each other? Name two who would answer oppositely: Dombale and Dhadphale, on whether service capacity is a cost or a moat; at Kaniyam, risk and sales. If the only disagreement is writer against room, a conversation is cheaper.

Is the load-bearing claim measurable first, and at what price? Kshamata's was: 420 of the 2,800 machines, 15 per cent, sit in Maharashtra, and HbA1c is 38 per cent of cartridge volume, so a single-assay single-state trial exposes 47,880 cartridges a month, and 30 per cent of those defecting costs ₹3.88 lakh a month net of the ₹4 fee — about ₹17.9 lakh over twenty weeks, taking 52/12 weeks to the month, or ₹20.5 lakh gross of the fee. Kaniyam's was already measured on 4,000 audited claims. Where measurement beats argument on speed and price, the memo is the wrong instrument.

Where it actively misleads. When the obstacle is a conflict of interest rather than a gap in reasoning, a memo makes it legible without resolving it, and legibility hardens positions. A memo written to obtain a decision already taken converts a political act into an auditable one, which serves nobody.

5. Hard edges, and what the seams do

In a multi-product company the decision metric belongs to a portfolio the author does not own, so the swing that matters sits two levels above the writer. Kshamata's grid is contribution, but Diwadkar's binding constraint was a licence: opening the interface on a licensed in-vitro diagnostic device needs an amendment from the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation, and Kshamata's four amendments took 9, 12, 16 and 26 weeks, a median of 14. That gate is nowhere in Exhibit 1, and a memo that footnotes it has mis-weighted its own argument.

In regulated and hardware settings the record school wins the appendix argument by force, because the auditor is real. Kaniyam's position with the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India is that an automated settlement remains the insurer's decision, so the insurer's committee must be able to reconstruct the basis: Tapomoy's memo had to serve two rooms with different memories.

At the organisational seam, mature companies do something they rarely describe: the memo is pre-read privately by the person most likely to block it, days early, then rewritten to answer the objection they actually raise rather than the one imagined. Companies say they circulate to everyone equally. The useful version is asymmetric and uncomfortable, and it is how commitment gets served without abandoning the written form.

6. Eight distinctions that separate the expert

The ask names its own reversal condition

An ask without an "unless" gets re-litigated, because the room cannot stop the thing later except by refusing it now. The tell is a page one carrying a number but no tripwire. The obvious reading, that naming a failure condition weakens the request, is backwards: Diwadkar approved a smaller ask because it carried one.

Pre-emption is a dial, not a virtue

Answering an objection in print saves the room minutes and costs its owner a stage. The tell is a silent meeting followed three weeks later by a written objection from the person whose risk it is. Competent practitioners maximise pre-emption; experts choose a level, and choose whose objection to leave unanswered.

Every rate is a population at a date

The expert's first question about a defection share is not how large but whose: installed base and new buyer defect for different reasons and at different rates, and Kshamata's memo used one symbol for both. The tell is a rate with no denominator in the same sentence, and that is how the conclusion inverted.

One-at-a-time sensitivity hides the worst corner

Varying inputs singly from a base case produces a cross, not a grid, and a cross never visits the corners. Exhibit 1's worst cell is −106.20: high defection with almost no uplift, laboratories switching reagents on machines they own. That is both the most plausible near-term path and the one a cross cannot reach.

Avoidable cash is not fully-loaded cost

A saving is a saving only if a budget line falls. The tell is a memo that cannot name the cost centre whose number drops next quarter. Fully-loaded rates are built for pricing, where they are right, then borrowed for savings, where they are wrong by the salary component.

Six pages is a time budget wearing a page count

The limit's real content is the room's twenty minutes, which is why the expert has timed the read while the competent practitioner counted pages. The tell is dense exhibits beside an author who cannot say how long it takes. Two tables cost ninety seconds, seven and a half per cent of the budget.

A memo exposes a conflict; it cannot adjudicate one

The tell is an objection that changes shape each time it is answered: first the number, then the timing, then the precedent. Three shapes in three rounds says the stated objection is not the real one, and more evidence will not close it. The obvious reading, that the writer was unclear, wastes a month.

An appendix is either cited or decorative

The test is whether the body points at a specific page for a specific claim. The tell is an appendix with no inbound references, meaning the writer used it to avoid choosing. The record school is right that evidence must survive the meeting; unreferenced evidence has survived nothing.

7. What changes by product type and by stage

In consumer products the load-bearing claim is almost always a behaviour rate, measurable faster than six pages can be written, so the memo shifts from argument to resource allocation. In B2B and enterprise it is frequently one named customer's intent, which cannot be measured, only asked; the objection section then carries the weight evidence carries elsewhere. In platforms and marketplaces the only real difference is two demand curves, so two swings. In hardware the reversal condition must be dated to a tooling or licence commitment rather than a metric, because after that date the metric cannot act.

AI products differ in kind: the load-bearing claim is a distribution, not a point, so the memo must carry an error profile, and that profile has a shelf life. Kaniyam's audit ran on model version 4.2 of December 2025; version 4.4 shipped on 11 March 2026 with a different mix of over- and under-payment. Evidence can expire between circulation and rollout.

By stage, the arithmetic is the memo's own cost. Triveni spent nine working days; at a loaded ₹18,000 a day that is ₹1.62 lakh against a grid spanning ₹112.32 lakh a month, or 1.4 per cent. Nine days is about a seventh of one person's 63-working-day quarter: affordable where product is a department, conspicuous where it is two people, which is why early-stage memos run three pages to readers who share the context. The cost does not fall with scale; what it buys does.

8. Two more worked cases

Kaniyam, February 2026. Of 186,000 motor own-damage claims a month, 61 per cent are under ₹25,000, or 113,460. On a stratified audit of 4,000 such claims the model matched the adjuster within ₹500 on 3,704 of the 4,000, 92.6 per cent; of the 296 mismatches, 82 of the 4,000, 2.05 per cent, were over-payments averaging ₹2,300 and 214 of the 4,000, 5.35 per cent, under-payments. Review costs ₹41 a claim, one under-paid claimant in six complains, and a grievance costs ₹1,850; the top-up is not incremental, since it was always owed.

₹ lakh a monthClaims under ₹25,000Claims under ₹8,000
Human review avoided46.5218.30
Over-payment cost−53.50−4.86
Grievance handling−18.72−5.35
Total, net monthly effect−25.70+8.09

Exhibit 3. The narrow band covers 24 per cent of claims, 44,640 a month; 1,574 of the 4,000 audited claims fell in it, 39.3 per cent, with 19 of the 1,574 over-paid, 1.21 per cent, averaging ₹900, and 61 of the 1,574 under-paid, 3.88 per cent. Applied to 44,640 that is 540 over-payments and 1,732 under-payments, of which 289 complain; the wide band gives 2,326, 6,070 and 1,012. The one-in-six and ₹41 figures apply to both columns.

The memo asked for ₹25,000 and the arithmetic inside it argued for ₹8,000 — the useful kind, in which the room sees the better answer because the writer printed inputs, not conclusions. The committee approved the narrow band, worth ₹97.08 lakh a year.

Kshamata, March 2025 — the failure. Tanvish Dhadphale's memo asked for ₹1.9 crore to build remote recalibration, on the ground that it would remove 68 per cent of 1,120 field visits a quarter, 762 visits, at ₹7,400 each: ₹56.39 lakh a quarter, a payback of 3.4 quarters. It was approved on the strength of a well-written page four. But the ₹7,400 was fully loaded, including engineer salary, and only two of fourteen engineers left; avoidable cash per visit was ₹2,150 of travel and consumables, so the saving was ₹16.38 lakh a quarter and the payback 11.6 quarters. Eleven months passed before anyone recomputed it, because the memo named no condition for checking. Kshamata now requires every rupee figure to state in the same sentence whether it is avoidable cash or fully loaded; and the twelve engineers who stayed moved onto installations, which is where the capacity to ship 95 machines a month — the uplift at the centre of Triveni's memo eighteen months later — came from.

9. Failure modes and their early signs

The fully-loaded saving

Early sign: no budget line falls after approval. Diagnostic: which cost centre's number drops, and by how much, next quarter? Cost of catching it late: ₹1.9 crore committed against a payback more than three times the one approved, undetected for eleven months.

The fully-ramped benefit

Early sign: a year-one figure that is exactly twelve times a steady-state month. Diagnostic: what is the mean months of life for units added this year? Machines added at each month-end average 5.5 of 12 months, 45.8 per cent, so a full-year claim overstates year one 2.18 times; added at month-start the mean is 6.5 months and the multiple 1.85.

The silent room

Early sign: the person who owns the risk does not speak, and their objections were the ones answered in print. Diagnostic: who has not spoken, and which of their objections did I pre-empt? Cost of catching it late: five weeks of the narrow band's ₹8.09 lakh a month, about ₹9.3 lakh on the same 52/12 convention.

The cross mistaken for a grid

Early sign: the sensitivity analysis varies one input at a time from a base case. Diagnostic: which combination is causally likely and absent from my table? Cost: the unpriced corner, at Kshamata a loss of ₹106.20 lakh a month, twice the base case.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

One option or two. The commitment position is that a room asked to choose will defer, and deferral is the dearest outcome available. The falsification position is that closing on one option conceals the comparison doing the work: a reader who cannot see the rejected option cannot audit the reasoning. Each is wrong if the other's failure mode is rare, and nobody has measured which is.

Answer objections in print, or leave them for the room. Kaniyam supplies evidence for both sides at once, which is why the argument survives. Of 17 objections raised in its meeting, 11, or 64.7 per cent, were already answered in the memo; those 11 took 22 minutes, a mean of 2.0, while the 6 that had not took 42 minutes, a mean of 7.0 — 3.5 times dearer. At that rate all 17 would have needed 125 minutes in a 70-minute slot. Against it, 2 of the 17, 11.8 per cent, came back in writing on 24 February from the reader who had stayed silent, and the rollout due on Monday 2 March went live on Monday 6 April.

Appendices. The record school's case is that a decision an auditor cannot reconstruct is a decision nobody made, which in regulated settings is near unanswerable. The limit's case is that an appendix is where unranked evidence goes to avoid ranking. What would settle it is a measurement of whether appendices are read, by whom and when, and the field has none — nor a counterfactual for the deeper claim, that prose produces better thinking than slides, since no one has run it with the author held constant.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied the form writes six good pages. Someone who has internalised it computes the swing before writing a sentence, states on page one the number that would reverse their own recommendation, knows which reader they are not pre-empting, has timed the read, writes the basis beside the figure as a reflex, and treats a failed memo as a measurement failure, not a persuasion failure. The tell is small: asked a question in the meeting, they answer with the denominator first.

12. What the two protagonists decided

Diwadkar did not approve the open interface. She approved a single-assay trial in Maharashtra for twenty weeks, with installed-base defection as the measured quantity and a stated stopping rule, at about ₹17.9 lakh; it is due to report in the week of 15 February 2027. Triveni had recommended the full opening and was overruled by her own Exhibit 1 — a success to the falsification school, and to the commitment school a dear way to learn what a trial begun six months earlier would have told her.

Tapomoy got the narrow band he had not asked for. For his next memo he added a convention of his own: page one names the one reader whose objection he has deliberately left for the room.

Three questions for discussion.

1. Exhibit 2 allocates pages by swing times scepticism and still omitted the assumption that decided the case. What property must a claim have to appear in such a table, and what does that exclude?

2. Kaniyam's meeting supports both sides of the pre-emption argument. Which measurement, available before 30 January, would have told Tapomoy where to set the dial?

3. Diwadkar converted a decision into a measurement. Under what conditions is that a failure of the memo rather than a success of it?

13. Going deeper

Communicating with leadership — which decisions deserve this form at all.

Writing clearly — sentence craft makes a connective visible enough to attack.

Stakeholder mapping and management — whose objection you are choosing not to pre-empt.

Telling the customer story — the evidence page two needs and arithmetic cannot carry.

Demo and pitch craft — when a demonstration beats a paragraph.

Writing as a PM superpower — the habit behind it; why drafting is the analysis.

Decision records and DACI/RACI — what the record school wants once the meeting ends.

Running effective meetings — the silent read works only in a meeting designed for it.
exp20v2-comm.exec.narrative.deck:
The Executive Narrative Memo

How to make a strategic case in six pages that survives a room of executives

1. Six pages before a Monday

On Thursday 12 November 2026, Sukanya Chitrao, head of product at Jetavan Logistics in Pune, had four days to write the most expensive request of her year. Jetavan runs a marketplace on which 12,000 truck operators a month find loads from shippers. It pays those operators 21 days after delivery. Sukanya wanted to pay them within a day, using Jetavan's own money, and she needed ₹2.4 crore of build budget and the chief executive's blessing to do it.

The executive committee met on Monday 16 November. Its practice, set by chief executive Samiksha Chavare, was that nobody presented slides. Each member read a printed memo in silence for twenty minutes, wrote questions in the margin, and only then spoke. Saisha Chaphalkar, the finance head, had already told Sukanya in the corridor that a payments product "is a lending business wearing a logistics costume."

Sukanya's first draft was a twelve-slide deck she had used with her own team. She could talk to it for forty minutes. But a deck would not hold her reasoning when she was not in the room, and Saisha would read the room's silence as consent to the lending objection. What was at stake was concrete: a no would leave operators waiting three weeks while a rival could win the 3,000 operators she expected to value speed, in the quarter Jetavan hesitated. A careless yes, on the other hand, could put ₹30 crore of Jetavan's cash into other people's invoices.

This page follows what Sukanya learned about the form she was about to use: the executive narrative memo.

2. The idea

An executive narrative memo is a document of about six pages, written in complete sentences and paragraphs rather than slides or bullet points, that argues for one decision, shows the evidence, answers the strongest objections, and ends by asking for a specific response. Executives read it together, in silence, at the start of the meeting that will decide.

It was invented to fix a particular failure. Slides let a presenter skip the logic between two assertions, because the speaker supplies it aloud and the audience cannot see that it is missing. Amazon, reportedly from around 2004 under Jeff Bezos, replaced slide presentations in senior meetings with such memos, on the view that a paragraph cannot be written without stating how one claim leads to the next. The format has since spread to many technology companies and to business-school assessment, where it is a standard way to test whether a student can reason.

The reasoning behind it is simple. Writing in sentences forces the writer to commit to connectives such as "because", "therefore" and "unless". A reader can then attack the connective, which is where weak arguments actually break. The sentence Sukanya could repeat without sounding glib was this: "Read silently, argue second, so the disagreement is about the reasoning rather than about who presents best."

3. How it works

The memo has a job at each page, and the order follows the questions an executive asks, in the order they ask them. Figure 1 shows the allocation Sukanya settled on.

The first step is the one practitioners leave implicit: decide the decision before writing. Sukanya's note to herself read: "Approve ₹2.4 crore and a ₹30 crore working-capital line to pay operators within one day, as a six-month pilot." Everything else is selected for its power to support or threaten that sentence.

The second implicit step is choosing the strongest objection and writing it first, in its owner's voice. Page five is not a defensive appendix. Sukanya wrote Saisha's lending objection as Saisha would, then answered it with a number. The third is cutting: roughly two-thirds of what the writer knows will not fit, and the cutting is the analysis. Finally, the memo is read cold by someone who was not in the room, because the test is whether the argument stands without the author.

A practical test for the draft is to read only the first sentence of every paragraph. If those sentences, strung together, do not tell the story of the argument, the paragraphs are carrying claims they do not announce, and a skimming executive will miss them. Sukanya rewrote eleven of her openings this way. She also timed the read: at a steady pace, six pages took her a little under fifteen minutes, which left the committee room to think inside its twenty.

4. A worked example

Page four carries the arithmetic, and Sukanya showed every line. Her inputs: 12,000 active operators; 25 per cent expected to take instant payout (3,000 operators); each settles ₹1.5 lakh of freight a month; Jetavan charges 1.2 per cent of the amount paid early; money is advanced 20 days sooner on average (21 days reduced to 1); Jetavan's cost of capital is 11 per cent a year; and defaults, meaning freight later disputed or reversed after payment, are 0.4 per cent of volume.

The steps: monthly volume is 3,000 × ₹1.5 lakh = ₹4,500 lakh, or ₹45 crore. Fees are 1.2 per cent of that, ₹54 lakh. Because each rupee is advanced 20 of 30 days, cash outstanding at any time is ₹4,500 lakh × 20/30 = ₹3,000 lakh, or ₹30 crore. Financing it costs ₹3,000 lakh × 11 per cent ÷ 12 = ₹27.5 lakh a month. Defaults cost ₹4,500 lakh × 0.4 per cent = ₹18 lakh.

₹ lakh per monthBase case (0.4% defaults)Second pass (1.0% defaults)
Fee income54.054.0
Financing cost27.527.5
Default loss18.045.0
Net contribution8.5-18.5
